en: The Abhidharma-dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra, Volume One.
Composed by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
I prostrate to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, the truly pure and priceless jewels;
now I collect these aggregates of all dharmas and bestow them universally upon all living beings.
The Abhidharma is like the great ocean, the great mountains, the great earth, and the vast void.
Fully encompassing the boundless wealth of the noble Dharma, I shall now diligently and concisely reveal it.
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
The factors of enlightenment, pure fruits, practices, and noble lineages; the right efforts, bases of power, mindfulness, truths, and meditative absorptions.
The immeasurable formless absorptions, the factors of enlightenment, the faculties, bases, aggregates, elements, and dependent origination.
At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:

"Those who have not pacified the five fears, transgressions, and enmities will, in this present life, be collectively censured and loathed by the noble ones. They are called those who violate the precepts and bring harm upon themselves; they possess guilt and are subject to reproach, generating much demerit. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the perilous evil realms and are reborn in hell."
What are the five? They are as follows:
first, one who takes life, due to the condition of taking life, gives rise to fear, guilt, and resentment;
not abandoning the taking of life—this is called the first.
Regarding taking what is not given: due to the conditions of robbery and theft, one gives rise to fear, guilt, and enmity.
Not being free from robbery and theft is called the second [unwholesome path].
Regarding sexual misconduct: due to the conditions of improper conduct, one gives rise to fear, guilt, and enmity.
Not abstaining from sexual misconduct is called the third [unwholesome path].
Regarding false speech: because of the conditions of falsehood, one gives rise to fear, guilt, and resentment.
Not abstaining from falsehood is called the fourth.

Regarding "those who indulge in the taste of various liquors, which are bases for negligence": because of the condition of indulging in the taste of various liquors, which are bases for negligence, one gives rise to fear of transgression and enmity.
Not to abandon such drinking and other bases for negligence is called the fifth [basis].

Those who remain unpacified regarding these five fearsome sins and enmities are, in this present life, censured and loathed by all noble ones; they are called transgressors of the precepts who bring harm upon themselves. Possessing guilt and subject to reproach, they generate much demerit, and at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the perilous evil destinies and are reborn in hell.

“Those who are able to pacify the five fears, transgressions, and enmities will, in this present life, be praised and admired by the noble ones; they are called those who maintain the precepts and guard themselves. Being without fault or reproach, they generate abundant and superior merit; at the dissolution of the body after death, they ascend to a peaceful and auspicious realm and are reborn among the devas.”
What are the five? They are as follows:
one who abstains from taking life, by virtue of abstaining from the conditions for killing, extinguishes fear, guilt, and enmity.
To be able to abstain from taking life is called the first.
One who abstains from taking what is not given, by virtue of abandoning the conditions for robbery and theft, extinguishes fear, guilt, and enmity.
To be able to abstain from robbery and theft is called the second [precept].
One who abstains from sexual misconduct, by virtue of abandoning the conditions for misconduct, extinguishes fear, guilt, and enmity.
To be able to abstain from sexual misconduct is called the third [precept].
To abstain from false speech means that, by abandoning the conditions for falsehood, one extinguishes fear, guilt, and enmity.
To be able to abstain from falsehood is called the fourth [precept].

Regarding "abstaining from the consumption of intoxicants, the basis of heedlessness": because one abstains from the consumption of intoxicants, which is the condition for heedlessness, one extinguishes fear, transgression, and enmity.
To be able to abstain from drinking alcohol and all such bases of heedlessness is called the fifth [precept].

Those who are able to pacify these five fearsome enemies of transgression will, in this present life, be held in common esteem by all the noble ones; they are called those who maintain the precepts and guard themselves. Being without fault or reproach, they generate abundant and superior merit, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, they ascend to a peaceful and auspicious realm, being reborn among the devas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to summarize the preceding meaning, spoke these verses:
"Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, Lying, and indulgence in intoxicants— These five fearsome transgressions lead to enmity and bondage;
They are reviled and loathed by the noble sages."
One is called a violator of precepts who harms oneself;
having committed offenses, one invites misfortune and, upon death, falls into perilous and evil realms, being born within the various hells.
One should abandon killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, as well as lying and addiction to intoxicants.
Freed from the five fears and the enmity of transgressions, Admired and praised by the noble and the wise,
One is said to maintain the precepts and guard oneself; Being free from fault, one brings forth supreme merit, And upon death,
ascends to a peaceful and auspicious realm, To be born within the celestial worlds.
"To what extent is one called an *upāsaka*?

It refers to any layman clad in white who possesses male faculties, has taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, has given rise to a profound and pure mind, and utters words of truth, declaring: 'I am an *upāsaka*; may the Venerable One remember me and protect me with compassion.'"
One who is thus [endowed] is called an *upāsaka*.
What is meant by "being able to train in one part"?

It refers to the aforementioned *upāsaka* who, having taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha and made a sincere declaration, is only able to abstain from killing but does not abstain from the other four [unwholesome actions]; such a person is said to be "able to train in one part."
Furthermore, what is meant by "able to train in a small portion"?

It refers to a lay follower (*upāsaka*), as previously described, who, having taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha and made a sincere declaration, is able to abstain from killing and stealing, yet does not abstain from the remaining three [unwholesome actions]. This is called being able to train in a small portion.
Furthermore, what is meant by "able to train in many parts"?

It refers to the aforementioned upāsaka who, having taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha and made a sincere declaration, abstains from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, yet does not abstain from the remaining two [precepts]. This is called being able to train in many parts.
Furthermore, what is meant by being "able to train in the full measure"?

It refers to the aforementioned upāsaka who, having taken refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha and made a sincere declaration, is fully able to abstain from the five [precepts]; such a person is said to be "able to train in the full measure."
A lay follower (*upāsaka*) who accomplishes five qualities is able to benefit only himself and not others.
What are these five? They are as follows:

the aforementioned lay follower personally abstains from killing and so forth, up to abstaining from intoxicants and all occasions of negligence, yet he is unable to exhort others to abstain from killing and so forth, up to abstaining from intoxicants and all occasions of negligence. This is called a lay follower who accomplishes five qualities and is able to benefit only himself and not others.
A lay follower (*upāsaka*) who accomplishes ten qualities is able to benefit himself and others, yet cannot benefit them extensively.
What are these ten? They are as follows:

the aforementioned lay follower personally abstains from killing living beings up to and including intoxicants and all occasions of negligence, and is also able to exhort others to abstain from killing living beings up to and including intoxicants and all occasions of negligence; however, he is unable to feel joy, celebrate, or offer consolation upon seeing others who have likewise abstained from killing and the rest. Such a person is called a lay follower who accomplishes ten qualities and is able to benefit himself and others, yet cannot benefit them extensively.
A lay follower (*upāsaka*) who accomplishes fifteen qualities is able to benefit both himself and others, and can bring extensive benefit.
What are these fifteen? They are as follows:

the aforementioned lay follower personally abstains from killing living beings up to and including intoxicants and all states of negligence; furthermore, he encourages others to abstain from killing living beings up to and including intoxicants and all states of negligence; and he rejoices in and congratulates others who abstain from killing and so forth. This is called a lay follower who accomplishes fifteen qualities, capable of benefiting both self and others, and capable of bringing extensive benefit.
A lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has accomplished eight qualities is able to benefit only himself but not others.
What are these eight? They are as follows:
the aforementioned lay follower possesses pure faith himself, yet he is unable to exhort others to possess pure faith; [and so forth].
One may personally possess pure ethical discipline, yet be unable to encourage others to possess pure ethical discipline;
one may personally possess generosity and renunciation, yet be unable to encourage others to possess generosity and renunciation;

and while one may personally exert effort to frequently go to the monastery to pay respects to the assembly of virtuous bhikṣus, one may be unable to encourage others to likewise exert effort and frequently go to the monastery to pay respects to the assembly of virtuous bhikṣus.
One is able to listen to the true Dharma with utmost sincerity oneself, but cannot encourage others to listen to the true Dharma with utmost sincerity;
having heard the Dharma oneself, one is able to retain it without forgetting, but cannot encourage others to retain it without forgetting;
having retained the Dharma oneself, one is able to contemplate and discern its meaning, but cannot encourage others to contemplate and discern its meaning.

Having reflected for oneself and become one who is able to correctly and diligently practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipanna) and conduct themselves with harmony and respect (sāmīcīpratipanna) as a follower of the Dharma, they are unable to exhort others to correctly and diligently practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma and to conduct themselves with harmony and respect as followers of the Dharma.
Thus, a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has accomplished these eight qualities is able to benefit only himself and not others.
A lay follower who has accomplished sixteen qualities is able to benefit both himself and others, yet cannot benefit them extensively.
What are these sixteen?

They refer to the aforementioned upāsaka who, being himself endowed with pure faith, is also able to encourage others to be so; and so on, as previously explained, up to one who, having personally investigated for himself, is able to correctly and diligently practice the dharma in accordance with the dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipanna*) and achieve conduct of harmony and respect (*sāmīcīpratipanna*) in accordance with the dharma, and is also able to encourage others to correctly and diligently practice the dharma in accordance with the dharma and achieve conduct of harmony and respect in accordance with the dharma; yet, he is unable to see others who are endowed with pure faith and so forth, and thus cannot rejoice or offer them congratulations. Such a person is called an upāsaka who has accomplished sixteen dharmas and is able to benefit himself and others, but is not able to bring extensive benefit.
An upāsaka who accomplishes twenty-four qualities is able to benefit himself and others, and is also able to bring extensive benefit. What are these twenty-four qualities? They are as follows:

the aforementioned upāsaka himself possesses pure faith and is also able to encourage others to possess pure faith; and so on, in detail, until: having personally investigated for himself the meaning of the Dharma as a witness, he is able to correctly and diligently practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipanna), achieving conduct in harmony and respect (sāmīcīpratipanna) and conduct in accordance with the Dharma; and he is also able to encourage others to correctly and diligently practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, achieving conduct in harmony and respect and conduct in accordance with the Dharma; furthermore, he is able to see others who possess pure faith and the like, and to rejoice, celebrate, and comfort them. Such a person is called an upāsaka who accomplishes twenty-four qualities, able to benefit himself and others, and able to bring extensive benefit.
If one accomplishes ten dharmas, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one falls into a perilous and evil destination and is born in hell.
What are these ten?
First, taking life;
2. Taking what is not given;
3. Sexual misconduct; 4. False speech;
5. Divisive speech; 6. Harsh speech;
7. Frivolous speech;
8. covetousness; 9. ill will; 10. wrong view.
If one accomplishes these ten dharmas, at the dissolution of the body after death, one will fall into a perilous and evil destination and be born in hell.
If one accomplishes [the following] ten dharmas, at the dissolution of the body after death, one will ascend to a peaceful and auspicious destination and be born among the devas.
What are the ten?
First, abstaining from taking life;
second, abstaining from taking what is not given; [and so forth].
3. Abstinence from sexual misconduct;
4. Abstinence from false speech;
5. Abstinence from divisive speech;
Sixth, abstaining from harsh speech;
seventh, abstaining from frivolous chatter;
eighth, non-covetousness.
Ninth, freedom from ill-will;
tenth, right view.
If one accomplishes these ten qualities, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one will ascend to a happy destination and be reborn among the devas.
If one accomplishes twenty dharmas, at the dissolution of the body after death, one will fall into the perilous and evil destinies and be born in hell.
What are these twenty? They are:
killing living beings oneself and also exhorting others to kill; [and so on, as extensively explained] up to: giving rise to wrong views oneself and also exhorting others to give rise to wrong views.
If one accomplishes these twenty qualities, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one falls into the evil destinies and is born in the hells.
By accomplishing twenty qualities, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one ascends to the happy destinies and is born among the devas.
What are these twenty? They are:

personally abstaining from killing and also being able to exhort others to abstain from killing; and so on, as explained at length, up to personally giving rise to right view and also being able to exhort others to give rise to right view.
If one accomplishes these twenty dharmas, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one will ascend to a peaceful and happy destination and be born among the devas.
If one accomplishes thirty dharmas, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one will fall into a perilous and evil destination and be born in hell.
What are these thirty? They are:

not abstaining from killing oneself, encouraging others to kill, and seeing others not abstain from killing, one expresses joy and offers words of comfort; and so on, in detail, up to: giving rise to wrong views oneself, encouraging others to give rise to wrong views, and seeing others give rise to wrong views, one expresses joy and offers words of comfort.
If one accomplishes these thirty qualities, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one falls into a perilous and evil destination and is born in hell.
By accomplishing these thirty qualities, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one ascends to a peaceful and auspicious destination and is born among the devas.
What are these thirty? They are:

personally abstaining from taking life, encouraging others to abstain from taking life, and feeling joy and offering consolation upon seeing others abstain from taking life; and so on, in detail, up to personally giving rise to right view, likewise encouraging others to give rise to right view, and feeling joy and offering consolation upon seeing them give rise to right view.
If one accomplishes these thirty dharmas, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one ascends to a peaceful and happy realm and is born among the devas.
If one accomplishes these forty dharmas, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one falls into a perilous and evil realm and is born in hell.

What are these forty? They are: personally not abstaining from killing; encouraging others to kill; seeing those who do not abstain from killing, expressing joy and offering words of comfort; praising and extolling the deeds of those who kill. This is explained in detail up to: personally giving rise to wrong views and likewise encouraging others to give rise to wrong views; seeing those who give rise to wrong views, expressing joy and offering words of comfort; and praising and extolling the deeds of those who hold wrong views.
If one accomplishes these forty qualities, at the breaking up of the body after death, one falls into a perilous and evil destination and is born in hell.
By accomplishing these forty qualities, at the breaking up of the body after death, one ascends to a peaceful and auspicious destination and is born among the devas.

What are these forty? They are: personally abstaining from taking life; encouraging others to abstain from taking life; rejoicing in and consoling others seen abstaining from taking life; and praising and extolling the deeds of those who abstain from taking life. This is explained in detail up to: personally giving rise to right view and likewise encouraging others to give rise to right view; rejoicing in and consoling others seen giving rise to right view; and praising and extolling the deeds of those who possess right view.
If one accomplishes these forty dharmas, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one will ascend to a peaceful and happy destination and be born among the devas.
There are five precepts for a lay follower (upāsaka).
What are the five?
To abstain from taking life until the end of one's life is called the first.
To abstain from taking what is not given until the end of one's life is called the second.
Until the end of life, one abstains from sexual misconduct; this is called the third.
Until the end of life, one abstains from false speech; this is called the fourth.
Until the end of life, one abstains from drinking various intoxicants and all bases for negligence; this is called the fifth.
Regarding the first [point], what is meant by one who is capable of killing?
As the Blessed One said:

"There is one who kills, who is violent and evil, whose hands are stained with blood, who is addicted to slaughter, and who, toward all sentient beings and the noble classes of living beings, is without shame and without compassion; even down to the *kuṇapa* and *piśācas*, he does not refrain from killing. Such a person is called one who is capable of killing."
What is meant by one who possesses the taking of life?

It refers to one who does not feel deep revulsion toward killing, who does not distance themselves from it or abandon it, and who dwells established in its accomplishment; such a person is called one who possesses the taking of life.
What is meant by "violent and evil"?
It refers to the gathering of various instruments of slaughter, such as bows, swords, and staves; this is called "violent and evil.
What is meant by "blood-stained hands"?

This refers to those who slaughter sheep, chickens, or pigs; those who catch birds or fish; hunters and robbers; executioners; those who bind dragons; jailers; those who cook dogs; and those who set snares and traps—these are called "blood-stained hands."
Why are these called "blood-handed"?

It is because, although they frequently bathe, apply fragrant unguents, wear fresh and clean garments, crown their heads with flower garlands, and adorn their bodies with ornaments, they are nonetheless named "blood-handed."

Why is this so? Because they do not feel deep revulsion toward evil deeds, nor do they distance themselves from or abandon them; they cause the blood of sentient beings to arise, to arise repeatedly, to be born, to be born repeatedly, to accumulate, and to flow forth. For this reason, they are called "blood-handed."
What is meant by "addiction to harming"?
It refers to cases regarding sentient beings where there is harm without killing, or both harm and killing.

Regarding "harm without killing": it means using various instruments of killing and violence, such as bows, swords, and staves, to oppress and afflict sentient beings without completely severing their life-force; this is called "harm without killing."

"To harm and also kill" means to afflict sentient beings with various instruments of killing and injury, such as bows, swords, and staves, and furthermore to completely sever their lives; this is what is called "harming and also killing."
To take delight in and be attached to acts of killing—this is called being addicted to killing.
What is meant by being shameless and lacking compassion toward the superior classes of sentient beings?
Furthermore, let us distinguish between ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and superior types (*viśeṣa*):
those who are worldlings are called "ordinary beings," while the disciples of the Blessed One are called "superior types.
Moreover, those sentient beings who possess greed, hatred, and delusion are called "ordinary beings."
If sentient beings are free from greed, hatred, and delusion, they are called superior beings (*viśiṣṭa*).
Furthermore, if sentient beings possess craving and grasping, they are called ordinary beings (*sattva*);
if sentient beings are free from craving and free from grasping, they are called superior beings.
Furthermore, those sentient beings who are compliant and non-oppositional are called "ordinary beings" (*sattva*);
those sentient beings who are non-compliant and oppositional are called "superior types.
Moreover, those sentient beings who lack intelligence and possess ignorance are called "ordinary beings."
If sentient beings are wise and possessed of clear insight, they are called "superior types.
Furthermore, those sentient beings who have not yet abandoned desire and greed are called "ordinary beings" (*sattva*);
if sentient beings have already abandoned desire and greed, they are called "superior types."
Furthermore, those sentient beings who have already become free from the greed of desire but are not disciples of the Buddha are called "ordinary beings" (sattva);
if those sentient beings have already become free from the greed of desire and are disciples of the Buddha, they are called "superior types" (viśeṣa-jana).
In this context, those who are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*), while the disciples of the Blessed One are called "superior types" (*viśeṣa*). Why is this?
"Superior" refers to *nirvāṇa*;
because they are able to attain, accomplish, and realize it, they are therefore called "superior types."
As it is said in a verse:
"Universally conforming to the world, I have traveled throughout every land and city;
Seeking one who excels me, I find no one realized, nor any to rely upon."
Therefore, in this context, those who are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*), while the disciples of the Blessed One are called "superior types" (*viśeṣa*).

Regarding these sentient beings and superior types, one ought to feel shame and compassion; yet, to be without shame or modesty, without remorse or disgrace, and without pity or compassion toward them—this is what is meant by being "without shame and without compassion" toward sentient beings and superior types.
What is meant by saying that even down to the kuntha and pipīlika insects, none are free from killing?
"Kuntha" refers to small insects such as mosquitoes and the like.

From the *piplaka*—which refers to various ants—down to these minute and fragmented sentient beings, they all give rise to malicious intent and desire to commit killing; for this reason, they are called "those capable of taking life."

In this context, what is meant by "killing," what is meant by "taking life," and what is meant by "abstaining from taking life," such that it is called the first training rule for a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who abstains from taking life even unto the end of his life?

What is called "birth" refers to when sentient beings have the notion of "sentient being," or when living beings have the notion of "living being," or when those who live have the notion of "one who lives," or when those who are nourished have the notion of "one who is nourished," or when persons have the notion of "person"—this is what is called birth.

Regarding the taking of life: it refers to conceiving the notion of a "sentient being" toward a sentient being, the notion of a "living creature" toward a living creature, the notion of a "life-sustainer" toward a life-sustainer, the notion of a "nourisher" toward a nourisher, and the notion of a "person" (pudgala) toward a person; furthermore, when an evil mind, an unwholesome mind, a destructive mind, a harmful mind, or a murderous mind has arisen and is present, one intentionally deprives a sentient being of its life through such an act, such application, such deliberation, such exertion, and such vigor.
By means of such karma, such application, such reflection, such exertion, and such valor in killing sentient beings, one intentionally takes life; this is called taking life.

Regarding the lay follower (*upāsaka*) previously mentioned, who is able to skillfully discern, feel revulsion for, distance himself from, cease, guard against, refrain from committing, not perform, not transgress, abandon, block, not resist, not oppose, and not overstep this taking of life—this is called "abstaining from taking life. Therefore, it is said that "abstaining from taking life until the end of life" constitutes the first training rule (*śikṣāpada*) of the lay follower.
Regarding the second [unwholesome path], what is meant by one who takes what is not given?
As the Blessed One said:

"There is one who takes what is not given; whether in a town or in a forest, taking things that have not been given with a mind of theft, and not relinquishing the act of theft—such a person is called one who takes what is not given."
What is meant by one who possesses the taking of what is not given?

It refers to one who does not deeply feel revulsion toward taking what is not given, who does not distance themselves from it nor abandon it, and who dwells established in its accomplishment; such a person is called one who possesses the taking of what is not given.
What is meant by "in a town or city"?
It refers to a place surrounded on all sides by city walls.
What is meant by "in a forest hermitage" (araṇya)?
This means there are no city walls surrounding it on all sides.
What is meant by "not giving"?
It refers to that which is held by another, which is neither relinquished nor discarded, and is neither bestowed nor given as a gift.
What is called "property"?
It refers to the various articles of livelihood, animate or inanimate, that are possessed by others; these are precisely what are termed the category of "ungiven property.
What is meant by taking with a mind of theft such that it does not depart from the nature of theft?

This refers to taking what has not been given—that which is not included in one's own possessions—with a thieving mind, without any sense of aversion toward or desire for renunciation; such is called "taking with a thieving mind what is not included in one's possessions, without abandoning the thieving mind."

Therefore, it is called "one who takes what is not given. In this context, what is meant by "not given," what is meant by "taking what is not given," and what is meant by "abstaining from taking what is not given," such that one is called a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has abstained from taking what is not given until the end of life? This is the second training rule.

"Non-giving" refers to not relinquishing, not discarding, and not bestowing or granting to others those various requisites for life—whether animate or inanimate—that have been taken possession of by another; this is called non-giving.

Taking what is not given means: regarding the various articles of livelihood possessed by another, one forms the perception that they are possessed by another and that they have not been given; furthermore, one brings before oneself a malicious mind, an unwholesome mind, a mind of plunder, a mind of theft, a mind of seizure, a mind of attachment, and a mind of appropriation. Based on such karma, such preparatory effort, such reflection, such exertion, such vigor, such means, and such path, with deliberate intent, through seizing and taking what is possessed by another, one lifts [the object] from its original place.

Through such karma, such application, such reflection, such exertion, such vigor, such means, and such path, one takes possession of the various requisites of life belonging to others; by means of an intentional thought characterized by attachment and grasping, one lifts them from their original place—this is called taking what is not given.

Regarding the lay follower (*upāsaka*) previously mentioned, who is able to properly discern, feel revulsion toward, distance himself from, cease, guard against, refrain from, not perform, not commit, not practice, and not transgress taking what is not given; who abandons it, blocks it, does not resist it, does not oppose it, does not contradict it, and does not overstep it—this is called being free from taking what is not given. Therefore, it is said that "until the end of life, he is free from taking what is not given," which is the second training rule (*śikṣāpada*) of the lay follower.
Regarding the third [unwholesome action], what is meant by one who engages in sexual misconduct?
As the Blessed One said:

"There is one who engages in sexual misconduct with the wives of others who are protected by others—namely, those protected by their parents, brothers, sisters, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, or kinsmen; those who are subject to punishment, those who are subject to obstacles, or those subject to both punishment and obstacles—even down to those who have been given as a pledge through the throwing of a flower garland."

In such circumstances, giving rise to the affliction of desire, they entice, coerce, and engage in sexual misconduct together; failing to abstain from such misconduct, they are thus called those who practice sexual misconduct.
What is meant by one who engages in sexual misconduct?

It refers to one who does not feel deep revulsion toward sexual misconduct, who does not distance themselves from it or abandon it, and who dwells established in its practice; such a person is called one who engages in sexual misconduct.
"His wife" refers to the seven kinds of wives.
What are the seven?
First, the wife given by pouring water; [and so forth].
2. A wife acquired through wealth;
3. A wife captured by force;
4. A wife through mutual affection.
Fifth, the wife provided with food and clothing;
sixth, the cohabiting wife;
seventh, the momentary wife.
A "water-giving wife" refers to one whose parents give water to a man and bestow their daughter upon him as his wife; she becomes the mistress of his household and is thus called a water-giving wife.
A "wealth-purchased wife" refers to one whom various men acquire as their own wife by trading for her with a small or large amount of wealth; she is thus called a wealth-purchased wife.
Regarding "seizing women by force during military expeditions," this refers to men who, while attacking another country, plunder other women to take as their own wives.

Furthermore, there are kings who, having defeated an enemy nation, take whatever they desire and abandon the rest; likewise, there are men who, using their physical strength, seize other women to take as their own wives.
Those of such a kind are called "women captured by force.

As for a "woman chosen by affection" (*manorathabhāryā*): this refers to a woman who, out of her own conviction and affection, desires to dwell in a man's household as his wife; she is called a woman chosen by affection.
A "wife for food and clothing" refers to a woman who, for the sake of food and clothing, wishes to remain as a wife in a man's household; she is called a wife for food and clothing.
A "co-resident wife" refers to a woman who goes to a man's household and says to him:

"I offer this body of mine to be entrusted to you; may all that belongs to us be shared without distinction, supporting one another to the end of our years, hoping for offspring who shall perform the ancestral sacrifices after we have passed away."
A "co-wife" (*sahajīvinī*) refers to one who shares a husband.
A "momentary wife" (*kṣaṇikā bhāryā*) refers to a woman who takes pleasure in being a wife to a man for only a brief period; she is called a momentary wife.

Regarding those who are under guardianship, "protected by her mother" refers to a woman whose father is insane, mentally deranged, oppressed by grief and suffering, has renounced the world, has fled far away, or has passed away; her mother raises her alone and guards and protects her, privately instructing her:
"Whatever you do, you must first inform me before it may be done."
This is called protection by the mother.
Regarding protection by the father: it refers to a woman whose mother has become insane, or whose mind is deranged, and so forth, up to and including her death.
Her father raises her alone, guarding and protecting her, and privately instructing her as previously described; this is called "guardianship by the father.
Regarding "guardianship by brothers," it refers to a woman whose parents have become insane, or whose minds are deranged, and so forth, up to their passing away.
The brother raised her in solitude, guarding and protecting her, and privately exhorted her, saying:
"Whatever you intend to do, you must first inform me before it may be carried out."
This is called protection by brothers.
Regarding protection by sisters: it refers to a woman whose parents have become insane, or whose minds are deranged, and so forth, up to their having passed away.
"Sister-guarding" refers to a woman who is raised alone and is protected, guarded, and admonished as previously described; this is called sister-guarding.

"Guarding by parents-in-law" refers to a woman whose husband is either insane, mentally deranged, or—expanding upon the full description—has even passed away, and she thus resides under the care of her parents-in-law.
Her parents-in-law said to her, "Do not grieve;
you should find peace within yourself.
We shall provide you with all the necessities of food and clothing, and we will care for you with no difference from our own son."
Her parents-in-law, showing her kindness and compassion, guarded and protected her, privately instructing her:
"In whatever you do, you must first consult and inform us before you may proceed."
This is called protection by parents-in-law.
Regarding protection by kinsmen: it refers to a woman for whom, excluding her mother and husband, other relatives of a different surname are termed "kinsmen."
As for this woman, being guarded and protected by her relatives is called "guarding by relatives. Regarding "guarding by kinsmen":
it refers to a woman who, apart from her father, elder brothers, and so forth, has other members of the same clan as her kinsmen.
As for this woman, she is guarded and protected by her own kin; thus she is called "protected by kin.

Regarding those who are "subject to punishment," this refers to women who have no relatives of their own and are not prostitutes; if they are assaulted and the king becomes aware of it, they may be executed, bound, banished, or stripped of their wealth—this is what is meant by being subject to punishment.

Regarding "having obstacles" (*sāvaraṇā*): this refers to a woman who, though living in a lowly station, has no kinsmen yet possesses a master or an impediment; she is called "one with obstacles. Regarding "possessing both obstacles and punishment" (*sāvaraṇā-daṇḍā*):

this refers to a woman who has neither her own retinue nor is of lowly status, but who dwells in dependence upon another and is thus hindered by him; if she is assaulted or coerced, and the one upon whom she depends inflicts punishment, she is called "one possessing both obstacles and punishment."
Furthermore, as stated above, all women, according to the circumstances upon which they rely, encounter obstacles and punishments. Why is this so?
Because by their very nature, women are subject to constraints;

those who act contrary to propriety will suffer execution or imprisonment, have their property confiscated, or be expelled and disgraced. Therefore, all women are said to be possessed of obstacles and punishments.
What is meant by "the lowest form of pledge, such as the offering of a flower garland"?

It refers to a woman who has already accepted from a man either a flower, a garland, various necklaces, ointments, powdered incense, or any other token of commitment; this is what is called "the lowest form of pledge, such as the offering of a flower garland."
What are those referred to as "such persons"?
They are men, *paṇḍakas*, and those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
What is meant by "those who practice the holy life"?
This refers to bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsikās, and female followers of non-Buddhist paths, down to women living as householders who practice asceticism.
It refers to a man who, having abandoned his own wife and concubines, says to them:
"O virtuous ones!
Set yourselves free to practice the various holy conducts."
Having heard this, he accepted and upheld it, practicing asceticism without indolence.
What is meant by "giving rise to the affliction of desire," and so forth, up to "not abandoning sexual misconduct"?

It refers to the manifestation of lustful craving for the realm of desire; regarding those with whom one should not engage, to entice, coerce, or force them into committing sexual misconduct, and to feel no weariness toward nor seek to distance oneself from such acts—this is what is meant by "giving rise to the affliction of desire," and so forth, up to "not abandoning sexual misconduct."

Therefore, it is called "one who practices sexual misconduct. Within this context, what is meant by "desire," what is meant by "sexual misconduct," and what is meant by "abstaining from sexual misconduct," such that one is described as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who, even unto the end of life, abstains from sexual misconduct—this being the third training rule?
What is called "desire" refers to sexual greed or the objects of such greed.

Sexual misconduct refers to engaging in temporary union with those aforementioned improper objects; this includes, at the very least, improper and unseemly conduct even with one's own wife, as well as intercourse at inappropriate times or in inappropriate places—all of which are termed sexual misconduct.

Regarding the lay follower (*upāsaka*) previously mentioned, who is able to skillfully discern sexual misconduct, feels weary of it and distances himself from it, brings it to rest and guards against it, does not commit it, does not perform it, does not practice it, and does not transgress it; who abandons it, blocks it off, does not resist it, does not oppose it, does not contradict it, and does not overstep it—this is called being free from sexual misconduct. Therefore, it is said that "until the end of life, he is free from sexual misconduct," which constitutes the third training precept (*śikṣāpada*) of the lay follower.
Regarding the fourth [course of action], what is meant by one who speaks falsely?
As the Blessed One has said:

there is one who speaks falsely, whether before an impartial person, or before a great assembly, or before the royal court, or before those who uphold the principles of justice, or before their own kinsmen, when they are interrogated as follows:
"Alas, man! You should speak only what you know; do not speak what you do not know.
You should speak only what you have seen; do not speak what you have not seen."
Having been questioned thus, he speaks what he does not know as if he knows it, and what he does know as if he does not know it;
he speaks what he has not seen as if he has seen it, and what he has seen as if he has not seen it.

Whether for his own sake, for the sake of others, or for the sake of fame and profit, he deliberately speaks false speech with full awareness and does not refrain from such falsehood; this is what is called one who utters deceptive speech.
Who is said to be one who possesses false speech?

It refers to one who does not deeply loathe false speech, who does not distance themselves from it or abandon it, and who dwells established in its accomplishment; such a person is called one who possesses false speech.
What is meant by "either facing a level and upright [surface]"? There are three kinds of level and upright surfaces:
first, the level and upright surface of a village; [the second, the level and upright surface of a field; and the third, the level and upright surface of a road].
Second, the city is level and upright;
third, the kingdom is level and upright.
When these various forms of level uprightness are assembled and present before one for joint examination and interrogation, it is called "interrogation before the level and upright."
What is meant by "in the presence of a great assembly"?
There are four kinds of great assemblies:
first, the kṣatriya assembly; [and so forth].
2. the assembly of brahmins;
3. the assembly of householders;
4. the assembly of śramaṇas.
When this great assembly gathers before one and conducts a joint interrogation, it is called "in the presence of the great assembly.
What is meant by "in the presence of the royal family"?
It refers to kings, as well as other ministers and officials who manage public affairs; if they gather before one and conduct an interrogation, it is called "in the presence of the royal family."
What is meant by "confronting those who uphold the principles"?

It refers to when a group of those who are well-versed in the Vinaya and firm in their correct discernment have assembled and are present together to conduct an investigation and interrogation; this is called "confronting those who uphold the principles."
What is meant by "in the presence of kinsmen"?
It refers to when various kinsmen have gathered and are present together to conduct an inquiry; this is called "in the presence of kinsmen.
What is meant by "conducting an inquiry" and so forth?
That is to say, whether for the sake of verification or to thoroughly examine his person, the assembled multitude should collectively and appropriately interrogate him, saying:
"Ho! O man! Now, before this assembly, you ought to speak with sincerity and fully disclose the facts of the matter."
If one has seen, heard, sensed, or known a matter, it is appropriate to proclaim, designate, and point it out.
If one has no such seeing, hearing, or other cognitions regarding a matter, one should not proclaim, designate, or point it out.
This is what is meant by "interrogation through joint examination" and so forth.
What is meant by "claiming to know what one does not know"?
It refers to that which has been experienced and cognized by the auditory consciousness; this is called "having heard."

That person has no auditory consciousness that has ever experienced or cognized [the sound], yet they conceal such notions, tolerances, views, and pleasures, saying, "I have heard it. This is called claiming to know what one does not know.
What is meant by "knowing while claiming not to know"?
It refers to that which has been experienced and cognized by the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), which is termed "having heard.

When one possesses such experience and cognition through the ear-consciousness, yet conceals this perception, tolerance, view, and inclination, saying "I did not hear it," this is called "knowing while claiming not to know."
What is meant by "claiming to have seen what was not seen"?
It refers to that which has been experienced and cognized by the visual consciousness being called "already seen.

When one has not experienced or cognized anything through visual consciousness, yet conceals this fact while harboring such a notion, tolerance, view, and inclination, saying "I have already seen it"—this is called claiming to have seen what was not seen.
What is meant by "claiming not to have seen what was actually seen"?
It refers to that which has been experienced and cognized by the visual consciousness; this is termed "having already seen.

When one possesses such experience and cognition through visual consciousness, yet conceals this perception, acceptance, view, and inclination, saying "I did not see it," this is called "claiming not to have seen what was actually seen."
What is meant by "for another" or "for oneself"?
It refers to a certain class of people who commit acts of robbery; when kings or others arrest and interrogate them, they ask: "Are you a thief?"
Having asked this, he thought to himself in secret:
"If I answer truthfully, I will surely be killed, bound, banished, or stripped of my wealth by the king and his attendants."
"I should now conceal, hide, and cover up the truth from myself; therefore, with full awareness, I shall speak a falsehood.
Having reflected thus, he replied to the king and the others:
"I truly did not commit the act of taking what was not given."
This is called "for oneself. What is meant by "or for another"?
It refers to a certain class of kinsmen or friends who engage in robbery; when the king or others act as witnesses, they seize and interrogate them, saying:
"Do you know whether this man has committed robbery or theft?
Having been thus questioned, he thought to himself in secret:
"If I answer truthfully, my kinsmen and friends will surely be executed, imprisoned, exiled, or stripped of their wealth by the king and his officials."
"I ought now to conceal and hide that matter; therefore, with full awareness, I shall speak a falsehood.
Having reflected thus, he replied to the king and the others, saying, "I know that my friend certainly did not commit the act of taking what was not given."
This is called "for the sake of others.
What is meant by "for the sake of gain and fame"?
It refers to a certain class of persons who have many desires, many thoughts, and many aspirations, and who reflect as follows:
"I shall employ such and such deceptive means so that I will certainly obtain agreeable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
Having thus reflected, he pursues them through skillful means; therefore, with full awareness, he utters false speech. This is what is called [lying] for the sake of fame and profit.
What is meant by "deliberately speaking falsehood with full awareness"?

It refers to intentionally and clearly intending to conceal one's own perceptions, tolerance, views, and inclinations, and repeatedly proclaiming, establishing, and indicating matters that contradict those very perceptions and so forth; this is called deliberately speaking falsehood with full awareness.

In this context, what is called "falsehood," what is called "false speech," and what is called "abstaining from false speech" that is designated as the fourth training rule of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), namely: "to abstain from false speech until the end of life"?

To speak of "falsehood" (*mṛṣā*): it refers to that which is unreal in fact, such as false conceptions and the like; being unreal is termed "deception" (*vañcanā*), and thus it is called "falsehood. Regarding "false speech" (*mṛṣāvāda*):
when, through greed, hatred, or delusion, one speaks in contradiction to the perception of reality so as to cause another to understand it, this is termed "false speech."

Regarding the lay follower (*upāsaka*) previously mentioned, who is able to properly discern false speech, feels aversion toward it, and distances himself from it; who ceases, guards against, does not perform, does not do, does not practice, and does not transgress it; who abandons and blocks it, and neither resists nor opposes, neither contravenes nor oversteps it—such a person is said to be "free from false speech. Therefore, it is called the fourth training rule (*śikṣāpada*) of the lay follower: "to remain free from false speech until the end of life."

Regarding the fifth [precept], what is meant by "various intoxicants," what is meant by "drinking various intoxicants," what is meant by "the basis for negligence," and what is meant by "abstaining from drinking various intoxicants and the basis for negligence," such that it is called the fifth training rule of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) which consists of abstaining from drinking various intoxicants and the basis for negligence until the end of life?
Regarding "all types of liquor," this refers to *sura*, *maireya*, and *madhvika*. As for *sura*:

it refers to rice, barley, and so forth, which are steamed or boiled according to the prescribed method, mixed with the juice of malt and yeast, and infused with various medicinal herbs; when fermented, it acquires the color, aroma, and flavor of wine, and once drunk, causes stupor and intoxication—this is called *sura* liquor.

*Maireya* refers to the juice of various roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits that, without being mixed with malt or yeast, is fermented until it possesses the color, aroma, and flavor of wine; having been drunk, it causes stupor and intoxication, and is thus called *maireya* liquor.
Regarding the term *madhu*, it refers to grape wine, or alternatively to *sura* and *meraya* wines; because they cause intoxication once drunk, they are collectively termed *madhu*.
"Drinking various wines" means swallowing, sipping, or gulping down the aforementioned types of wine; this is called drinking various wines.

The basis of negligence refers to the aforementioned various intoxicating liquors; having drunk them, they cause the mind to give rise to arrogance, stupor, intoxication, and madness, such that one no longer recognizes the distinction between the honorable and the lowly. Grave delusions and evil karma all arise because of this; as it is the support for negligence, it is called the "basis of negligence."

Regarding the lay follower (*upāsaka*) previously mentioned, who is able to exercise wise discernment regarding the drinking of various liquors, who feels aversion for it and remains far removed from it, who brings it to rest and guards against it, who does not do it, does not perform it, does not practice it, and does not transgress it; who has abandoned and blocked it, and who neither resists nor opposes it, and neither violates nor oversteps it—such a person is said to be one who abstains from the drinking of various liquors and all grounds of negligence. Therefore, this is called the fifth training rule (*śikṣāpada*) of the lay follower: "abstaining from the drinking of various liquors and all grounds of negligence until the end of life."
Regarding these five types, why are they called "trainings" (*śikṣā*) and why are they called "bases" (*sthāna*), such that they are termed "bases of training" (*śikṣāpada*)?

That which is called "training" refers to the constant, diligent, firm, and correct cultivation of application (*prayoga*) in order to fulfill what is as yet unfulfilled within these five bases; therefore, it is called "training."
What is called a "basis" (*sthāna*) refers to the abstention from killing and so forth; because these are the foundations upon which training relies, they are termed "bases.
Furthermore, since the abstention from killing and so forth is itself called "training" (*śikṣā*) and also called a "basis," it is therefore termed a "basis of training" (*śikṣāpada*).
Do all upāsakas take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha?
With the exception of those worldly upāsakas, all others take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
There are those who take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha but are not upāsakas; namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsikās, and so forth.
Are all upāsakas disciples of the Blessed One? This should be treated according to four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).

There are upāsakas who are not disciples of the Blessed One; that is to say, those upāsakas who have not yet attained the vision of the truths (satyadarśana) and have not yet realized the future fruit through direct intuition (abhisamaya).

There are disciples of the Blessed One who are not *upāsakas*, namely: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and *upāsikās*. Having already attained the vision of the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*), they are capable of realizing the future fruit through direct intuition (*abhisamaya*).
There are also lay followers who are disciples of the Blessed One—namely, those lay followers who have already realized the truths and are capable of directly realizing the future fruit.

There are those who are neither upāsakas nor disciples of the Blessed One, namely: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and upāsikās who have not yet attained the vision of the truths and are unable to realize the future fruit;
as well as other ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) who have not seen the truths.
Is it the case that all those included within the Sangha Jewel necessarily attain concord and respect within the Sangha?
This should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There are those who are included within the Sangha Jewel but do not attain concord and respect within the Sangha; namely, the *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, *śrāmaṇerī*, *upāsaka*, and so forth, who have already attained the vision of the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*) and are capable of realizing the future fruits.

There are those who attain the harmony and respect of the Saṃgha but are not included within the Saṃgha Jewel; these refer to bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who have not yet attained the vision of the Truths and are unable to realize the future fruit through direct observation.

There are those who are included within the Sangha Jewel and also attain harmony and respect with the Sangha; namely, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who have already realized the truths and are capable of directly realizing future fruits.

There are those who, though included within the Sangha Jewel, do not attain the concord and respect of the Sangha; namely, the female trainees (śikṣamāṇā), male novices (śrāmaṇera), female novices (śrāmaṇerī), male lay followers (upāsaka), and female lay followers (upāsikā) who have not yet attained the vision of the truths and are unable to realize the future fruit through direct insight;
as well as other ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) who have not seen the truths.
*Abhidharma-dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
