Chapter Two: The Factors of Stream-entry (Srotāpatti-aṅga). At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
“There are four kinds of dharmas; if one practices them with right diligence, such a person is said to be one who accomplishes much.
What are these four?”
That is to say: associating with virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, attending to it with correct mental application, and practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
You, bhikṣus, should train yourselves thus: "I shall associate with and make offerings to virtuous persons;

I shall listen to the true Dharma with a respectful and single-minded heart; I shall correctly contemplate its profound and subtle meaning; and I shall diligently practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to summarize the preceding meaning, spoke these verses:
“Excellent is the sight of a virtuous person; It can sever doubt and increase wisdom.
It causes the ignorant to become wise; The wise should draw near to such a one.”
"One should associate with virtuous persons;
for when one associates with them, doubt is severed and wisdom increases, so that the ignorant may become wise.
Who, then, are these virtuous persons?
This refers to the Buddha and his disciples; furthermore,
it refers to all those individuals who are endowed with ethical discipline and virtue, free from all blemishes, perfected in the dharmas of self-mastery,
worthy of succeeding to the position of a teacher, and possessed of supreme qualities— those who possess a sense of shame, acknowledge their faults, and are skillful.
Guarding well his training, possessing knowledge and vision, delighting in reflection, loving deliberation, and rejoicing in the nature of investigation;
being intelligent and endowed with awakened wisdom, having stilled the pursuit of existence and belonging to the class of those possessed of wisdom;

he moves away from greed toward the cessation of greed, away from hatred toward the cessation of hatred, away from delusion toward the cessation of delusion; he is disciplined, moving toward discipline, and tranquil.

They incline toward tranquility and proceed to tranquility; they incline toward liberation and proceed to liberation; they incline toward transcendence and proceed to transcendence; they incline toward sublime awakening and proceed to sublime awakening;

they incline toward nirvāṇa and proceed to nirvāṇa. They delight in being disciplined and compliant with the truths, remain free from arrogance and negligence, and take pleasure in wisdom, patience, gentleness, and mildness.
They ascend the straight path as it is seen, being solely intent on self-subjugation and solely intent on self-peace.
Tranquil and focused upon Nirvana, he merely maintains his body while traveling through various kingdoms, cities, royal capitals, and villages to seek food, clothing, and other necessities;
he is endowed with integrity and discipline, fully possessing both integrity and discipline;
he is endowed with patience and gentleness, fully possessing both patience and gentleness; and he is endowed with the practice of making offerings.

Possessing reverence and being endowed with both worship and respect; possessing right conduct, possessing the guarding of the sense faculties, and being endowed with both right conduct and the guarding of the sense faculties;
possessing proper deportment and proper behavior, and being endowed with both proper deportment and proper behavior;
and possessing faith, ethical discipline, learning, renunciation, and wisdom—being personally endowed with pure faith, they are also able to encourage others [therein].
One who exerts themselves to establish sentient beings in the possession of pure faith, and likewise exerts themselves to establish sentient beings in the possession of ethical discipline (*śīla*),
learning, renunciation, and wisdom— such a person is called a "noble being" (*satpuruṣa*).
Why is he called a "virtuous person" (satpuruṣa)?

Because the one described as a virtuous person has abandoned unwholesome qualities and accomplished wholesome qualities; having fully perfected the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, he is therefore called a virtuous person.
If one can draw near to, serve, revere, and make offerings to these aforementioned virtuous persons, this is called "drawing near to virtuous persons.
What is meant by "listening to the true Dharma"?

This refers to approaching and making offerings to virtuous persons (satpuruṣa), who—regarding points that have not yet been clearly understood, they clarify them; regarding points that have not yet been awakened to, they cause one to awaken to them—expound, designate, establish, and reveal through the skillful means of penetrating the profound and subtle meanings of phrases with wisdom, correctly revealing them by way of immeasurable doors: that suffering is truly suffering, origination is truly origination, cessation is truly cessation, and the path is truly the path.
What is meant by "correctly revealing through immeasurable doors that suffering is truly suffering"?

It refers to correctly revealing the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and, in brief, the suffering of all five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
As a verse says:
"The arising of the aggregates is suffering; birth and emergence are also suffering.
Once born, there is the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, and the suffering of death."
The arising of afflictions is suffering; once arisen, their persistence is also suffering.
For the unwise, there is the suffering of regret; for the unsubdued, there is the suffering of death.
Sentient beings lacking wisdom suffer, increasing the agony of the *kaṭasi* (the cemetery).
"The suffering of birth and death for fools, the suffering of wandering through many eons"—
these are called the various ways of correctly demonstrating that suffering is indeed suffering.
What is meant by "correctly revealing through immeasurable doors that true origination is indeed origination"?

It refers to correctly revealing craving (*tṛṣṇā*), craving for renewed existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*), craving accompanied by delight (*nandī-sahagatā tṛṣṇā*), and the craving for this and that (*tatratatrābhinandinī tṛṣṇā*) as the cause, the root, the path, and the preliminary condition for the manifold sufferings of the past, future, and present; as that which can act as the condition for birth, arising, and co-arising; and as that which can give rise to and cause the suffering of the present life to arise, from which suffering after the breaking up of the body is produced.
As a verse says:
"Because of craving, one abandons the skilled physician; The root of the abscess is the *kaṇṭaka* weed and thirst.
Until all [afflictions] are subdued, One repeatedly experiences manifold sufferings."
Just as when the roots of a tree have not been pulled out, though it be cut again and again, it grows back;
so long as the latent tendency of craving has not been uprooted, one repeatedly experiences manifold sufferings.
Like a poisoned arrow lodged in the body, it destroys one’s physical form, strength, and so forth.
"Sentient beings possess craving within, which destroys all roots of goodness.
These and other such statements are called the correct exposition of the truth of origination through immeasurable doors, demonstrating that "origination is truly origination."
What is meant by "correctly revealing through immeasurable doors that true cessation is indeed cessation"?

It refers to the correct revelation that the aforementioned craving, craving for renewed existence, craving accompanied by delight, and craving for this and that, are—without remainder, forever abandoned, cast off, vomited out, exhausted, detached from passion, ceased, stilled, and utterly vanished—called the dwelling, called the island, called the protection, called the refuge, called the destination, called the sorrowless, called the disease-free, called the unshakable, called the non-submerging, called the non-blazing, called the non-feverish, called the secure, called the tranquil, called the auspicious, called the fortunate, and called *nirvāṇa*.
As a verse says:
“The ultimate fruit of the śramaṇa, Praised by those who are self-disciplined;
With the conceit of ‘I’ extinguished without remainder, One eternally realizes the path to the deathless.”
The destination, the dwelling, the refuge, the abode, The supreme palace praised by the Buddha— Tranquil, extinguished, and boundless, The further shore is eternally secure.
Relying upon this, suffering is exhausted and ceases; Liberated, without a cave, it is ultimate.
The ultimate goal, worthy of offerings, is that which the wise practice and the noble delight in.
It is entirely free from old age, sickness, and death; it is without sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or grief.
Subtle, difficult to perceive, and boundless, this Truth of Cessation has no counterpart.
These are called the various ways in which the true cessation is correctly revealed as "this is cessation.
What are called the various ways in which the true path is correctly revealed as "this is the path"?

That is to say, it correctly reveals that this path and this practice are able to sever, abandon, vomit out, exhaust, detach from defilement, extinguish, pacify, and bring about the permanent cessation and disappearance of all suffering in the past, future, and present.
What, then, is this? It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
As it is said in a verse:
“This single course of the majestic one, Is like the path of birds—pure and void.
The destination of the Sage’s meditative concentration, He has proclaimed for the sake of the multitude.”
Out of compassion, he taught the single path; seeing this path brings an end to the limits of birth.
This path can cross over the floods of the past, future, and present.
It is capable of ultimate taming and tranquility, and it can exhaust the stream of birth and death.
Able to penetrate many realms, able to open and clarify the path of the eye;
like the swift current of the Gaṅgā, quickly rushing toward the great ocean,
you reveal the path of vast wisdom and swiftly realize nirvāṇa.
"Out of compassion for all beings, you turn the Wheel of Dharma never heard before;
you instruct the devas and humans—homage to you who have crossed the ocean of existence.
These are called the various gateways through which the true path is correctly revealed as the true path.

If, regarding these aforementioned true teachings (*saddharma*), one delights in hearing, delights in listening, delights in receiving and upholding, delights in bringing to completion, delights in understanding, delights in examining, delights in investigating, delights in scrutinizing, delights in penetrating, delights in touching, delights in realizing, and delights in attaining realization; for the sake of hearing the Dharma, one traverses perilous paths, crosses over remote roads, and wanders upon level ground without hesitation or difficulty;

and for the sake of upholding it, one repeatedly applies the faculty of the ear to the sounds of the spoken Dharma, giving rise to the superior auditory consciousness—this is called "listening to the true Dharma."
What is called "proper mental attention"?
It means that after hearing the true Dharma from a virtuous person, one inwardly rejoices and exults, saying:
"How marvelous is the World-Honored One!"
They are able to expound such profound and sublime True Dharma:

that which the Buddha has taught as suffering is truly suffering; that which the Buddha has taught as its origin is truly its origin; that which the Buddha has taught as its cessation is truly its cessation; and that which the Buddha has taught as the path is truly the path.

By means of such internal self-congratulation, joy, and exultation, he draws his mind toward [the object], applying and thoroughly applying attention and generating the resolve; he carefully and correctly examines the profound and subtle meaning of the words. This is called "appropriate mental attention" (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
What is meant by "practice in accordance with the Dharma"?

It refers to having revolved around and thoroughly examined the profound and subtle meaning through correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), whereby there arise the five sublime wholesome dharmas born of renunciation and seclusion: namely, faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Regarding those five superior wholesome dharmas produced within himself through renunciation and seclusion, he practices them with firm stability, practicing them continuously and increasing his application; this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma."

By practicing with diligence the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*), one attains entry into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktvaniyāmāvakrānti*).
That one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth is due to the diligent cultivation of the practice in accordance with the Dharma.
One is able to practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma by means of contemplating the profound and subtle meaning according to reason.
One is able to contemplate the profound and subtle meaning by means of respectfully hearing the True Dharma.

Furthermore, one is able to hear the true Dharma by virtue of being able to attend upon and make offerings to virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*). If one can attend upon and make offerings to virtuous persons, one hears the true Dharma;

having heard the true Dharma, one is then able to contemplate its profound and subtle meaning according to principle (*yoniśas*); having contemplated the profound and subtle meaning according to principle, one is then able to advance in the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*); and once one has diligently practiced the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, one attains entry into the state of rightness and departure from the mundane (*samyaktvaniyāma*).

Just as when it rains heavily upon a mountain peak, first the mountain streams fill; once the mountain streams are full, the small channels fill; once the small channels are full, the large channels fill; once the large channels are full, the small rivers fill; once the small rivers are full, the large rivers fill; and once the large rivers are full, the great ocean fills—the great ocean being filled only through such gradual succession.

The great ocean of the Noble Path is likewise: one must first approach and make offerings to virtuous friends before hearing the True Dharma; having heard the True Dharma, one can then contemplate its profound and subtle meaning according to principle; having contemplated the profound and subtle meaning according to principle, one can then advance to practice the "Dharma-conforming Dharma-practice" (dharmānudharmapratipatti); and once the diligent cultivation of the Dharma-conforming Dharma-practice has reached perfection, one finally attains entry into the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).

Once one has entered into the state of rightness and transcendence of birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one is said to have already produced the Noble Eightfold Path, namely right view and so forth as previously explained.
These four types are called the factors of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-aṅga*).

Because by means of these four kinds [of factors], one is able to obtain and acquire, to reach and follow along with, to accomplish and fulfill, to touch and realize, and to manifest the stream of the Noble Path, they are called the "limbs of stream-entry" (srotāpattyaṅga).

Furthermore, regarding these four types, through repeated cultivation and intensive practice with respect to the objects sought, one is able to obtain and acquire them, reach and follow after them, accomplish and fulfill them, and touch and realize them.
Because they enable one to realize [the fruit], they are called the factors of stream-entry (*srotāpattyaṅga*).

Furthermore, because these four kinds [of factors] can conform to, increase, adorn, polish, and serve as the constant auxiliary provisions for the stream of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), they are called the factors of stream-entry.

Furthermore, these four are called the factors of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-aṅga*) because they serve as the factors for entering the stream by means of speech, designation, and the conventional expression of perceptions and conceptualizations.
Chapter Three: On Verified Clarity (*Avetyaprasāda-varga*), Part One. At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:

"If there are sentient beings who, with faith, listen to and accept your instructions and are able to practice them, you should, out of compassion, exhort and encourage them through skillful means, establishing them so that they abide within the four types of verified clarity."
What are the four? They are:
verified confidence in the Buddha, verified confidence in the Dharma, verified confidence in the Saṅgha, and the precepts cherished by the noble ones. Why is this so?
Whatever elements of earth, water, fire, and wind there may be—these four great elements may indeed be altered;
however, for those noble disciples who have attained these four forms of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*), there shall certainly be no alteration.
Because these learned noble disciples have accomplished these four kinds of verified clarity, it is impossible for them to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.

Therefore, if there are those who, with faith, listen to and accept your teachings and are able to practice them, you should compassionately encourage and exhort them through skillful means, establishing them so that they abide within the four kinds of verified clarity.
What is the verified confidence in the Buddha?
As the Blessed One said:

"This noble disciple recollects the Buddhas with such characteristics, namely: This Blessed One is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons, a trainer of people, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Bhagavān."
That which is called "this" refers to this desire realm, or this world, or this Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, that which is called "this" refers to this very body, which maintains its composure, possesses its physical frame, and has acquired its own individuality as an aggregate.
Furthermore, the phrase "those here" refers to the Buddhas and their disciples born in this place, as well as the various sages (ṛṣi), the Munis, the wise, the well-disciplined, and the well-tamed.
Furthermore, the term "this" refers to this very teaching and instruction, this well-spoken Dharma; therefore, it is called "this.

As for the term "noble disciple" (*ārya-śrāvaka*): "noble" refers to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; because one takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, one is called a noble disciple.

To recollect the Buddhas with such characteristics means that by means of these characteristics, this gateway, and this principle, one gives rise to mindfulness, continuous mindfulness, focused mindfulness, and recollection toward all Buddhas—being without forgetfulness or loss, without omission or leakage, not losing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and possessing the mental faculty of clear recollection; for this reason, it is called "recollecting the Buddhas with such characteristics."
What is called "that which is designated" (saṃjñā) refers to such characteristics, such marks, such kinds, and such categories; therefore, it is called "designation.
What is called "this" refers to such morality, such Dharma, such wisdom, such supernormal powers, such liberation, and such frequent abidings; therefore, it is called "this."
Regarding the term "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*), it shall be explained later.
Regarding the term "Tathāgata," as the World-Honored One has said:

from the night the Bodhisattva realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, until the night he entered the realm of *parinirvāṇa* without remainder, everything he spoke, proclaimed, and expounded during that interval was entirely suchness (*tathatā*). It was without falsehood, without change, true, in accordance with reality, and without inversion. Having perceived all this through such right wisdom of reality as it is, he spoke; therefore, he is named Tathāgata.
Regarding the Arhat, there are briefly two kinds of Arhat-nature:
first, the conditioned;
second, the unconditioned.
What is the conditioned nature of an arhat?

It refers to the attainment of that fruit and the attainment of that attainment; the faculties and powers of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the morality of one beyond training, the wholesome roots of one beyond training, the ten qualities of one beyond training, and all other such dharmas belonging to the category of those beyond training—this is called the conditioned nature of an arhat.
What is the unconditioned nature of an arhat? It refers to the permanent severance of all afflictions—greed, hatred, and delusion;

transcending all realms of existence and cutting off all paths; the eternal stilling of the three fires, the eternal cessation of parching thirst, the eternal departure from arrogance and negligence, and the eternal destruction of the cave-dwelling of the self; crossing over the four torrents; the unsurpassed ultimate, the unsurpassed tranquility, the unsurpassed exhaustion of craving, and the nirvana of detachment and extinction. This is called the unconditioned nature of an arhat.
The Tathāgata has fully and perfectly accomplished such a nature of an arhat, both conditioned and unconditioned, as described; therefore, he is called an arhat.

Furthermore, greed, hatred, delusion, and all other afflictions are to be abandoned; the Tathāgata has eternally severed and thoroughly known them, just as the root and crown of a tāla tree are utterly cut off so that nothing remains, and he has attained the state of dharmas that shall never arise again in the future; therefore, he is called an arhat.

Furthermore, the three types of misconduct—of body, speech, and mind—all ought to be abandoned forever; because the Tathāgata has eternally abandoned them and possesses thorough knowledge of them, and so forth as extensively explained, he is called an Arhat.

Furthermore, all past Buddhas have already distanced themselves from evil and unwholesome dharmas; they have attained the state wherein all defilements, the blazing of future existence (*punarbhava*), and the ripening fruits of suffering shall never arise again in the future.
The present Buddha is likewise so; therefore, he is named Arhat.

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has accomplished the most supreme and auspicious merits and virtues; he is worthy of receiving the highest and most exquisite offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites. For these reasons, he is called an Arhat.
As a verse says:
"Whatever things in the world are fit for enjoyment, Of various kinds and most excellent, The Tathāgata accepts them all; Therefore, he is named Arhat."
Regarding the term "Perfectly Awakened One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha), as the Blessed One has said:
"All phenomena that exist and all states of correctness—the Tathāgata knows, sees, understands, and perfectly awakens to them all; therefore, he is called the Perfectly Awakened One."

Furthermore, regarding the "equal dharmas," these refer to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. Because the Tathāgata has fully understood and perfectly awakened to all of these with complete knowledge and vision, he is called the "Perfectly Awakened One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha).

Furthermore, regarding all suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, he is able to realize the path; he is able to realize the path that leads to the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship; he is able to realize the paths that lead to the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of psychic powers, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the divine ear, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of others' minds, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of recollecting past lives, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of death and rebirth, and the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows; he is able to exhaust greed, hatred, delusion, pride, arrogance, and defilement. Because the Tathāgata has attained perfect enlightenment regarding all these through being perfectly enlightened by way of cause, way, principle, and characteristic, while abiding with sincerity, firmness, and earnest attention, he is called "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
Regarding "one perfected in knowledge and conduct," what is meant by "knowledge"?
It refers to the three types of higher knowledge (vidyā) of the Buddha that belong to those beyond training (aśaikṣa):
first, the realization through direct knowledge consisting of the recollection of past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyā).
Second is the realization through the knowledge of death and rebirth of one beyond training;
third is the realization through the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows of one beyond training—these are called "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*).
What are the "practices" (*caraṇa*)?
This refers to the Buddha’s unlearned (aśaikṣa) restraint of body, restraint of speech, and purity of livelihood; these are called his conduct (*caryā*).

Furthermore, all of the Buddha’s sublime and excellent deportments—whether walking, coming, looking back, looking ahead, bending, stretching, bowing, or rising, as well as wearing the saṃghāṭī robe and holding the robes and bowl—are entirely dignified and orderly; these are called his conduct.
This "conduct" (caryā) and "knowledge" (vidyā), taken together, are called "knowledge and conduct.

The Tathāgata has fully and perfectly accomplished such knowledge and conduct, which are entirely pure, entirely sublime, and entirely faultless; therefore, he is called "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (vidyā-caraṇa-sampanna).

Regarding the term "Sugata" (Well-Gone): it refers to the Buddha having accomplished the supreme bliss and tranquility of proceeding toward the sublime Dharma without hardship or difficulty; thus, he is named Sugata.

Furthermore, regarding the various difficult-to-traverse dharmas produced by greed, hatred, delusion, and other afflictions, the Tathāgata has eternally severed and fully known them—just as the trunk and crown of a *tāla* tree are severed so that nothing remains—and has attained the state of non-arising for all time in the future; therefore, he is named Sugata.

Furthermore, just as all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past, all mounted the path of reality free from falsehood to proceed toward supramundane, sublime merit, reaching once and for all the state of no further regression;
so too is the present Buddha, and for this reason he is called the Sugata.

Regarding the "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*): the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*) are called the world; because the Tathāgata knows, sees, understands, and has attained perfect enlightenment regarding them, he is named the Knower of the World.

Furthermore, it is said that the five destinies are called the world; the Tathāgata knows, sees, understands, and has attained perfect enlightenment regarding them, and is therefore called the Knower of the World (*lokavid*).

Furthermore, it is said that the six sense bases are called the world; the Tathāgata knows, sees, understands, and has attained perfect enlightenment regarding them, and is therefore called the Knower of the World.

Furthermore, it is said that all bases (*āyatana*) subsumed within the three realms are called the "world" (*loka*). Because [the Tathāgata] arises from them, originates from them, and emerges from them; because he is born because of them, arises because of them, and emerges because of them—the Tathāgata knows, sees, understands, and perfectly awakens to them. Therefore, he is named the "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*).
Regarding the "Unsurpassed Great Being" (*anuttara-puruṣa*):

as the Blessed One has said, among all sentient beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless; with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—the Tathāgata is declared therein to be the foremost, the most excellent, the most venerable, the highest, and the unsurpassed. For this reason, he is called the Unsurpassed Great Being.
The Tamer of Men refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who briefly employs three kinds of skillful taming methods to tame all sentient beings to be converted:
first, those who are consistently gentle;
second, those who are consistently harsh; [and third, those who are both].
Third, regarding those who are sometimes gentle and sometimes harsh:
how is it that the Tathāgata is consistently gentle toward a certain class of beings? It means that for their sake, he teaches:

"This is bodily wholesome conduct, and this is the karmic maturation resulting from such bodily wholesome conduct; this is verbal wholesome conduct, and this is the karmic maturation resulting from such verbal wholesome conduct; this is mental wholesome conduct, and this is the karmic maturation resulting from such mental wholesome conduct; these are the devas and humans, these are the happy realms, these are the worlds of bliss, and this is nirvāṇa. This is called the Tathāgata being consistently gentle toward that class of beings.
In what way is the Tathāgata consistently harsh toward a certain class of beings? It is when he teaches them:

"This is bodily misconduct and the karmic maturation resulting from this bodily misconduct; this is verbal misconduct and the karmic maturation resulting from this verbal misconduct; this is mental misconduct and the karmic maturation resulting from this mental misconduct; these are the hells, these are the animal realm, these are the realm of hungry ghosts, these are the perils, these are the evil destinies, and these are the states of downfall. This is called the Tathāgata being consistently harsh toward that class of beings.
How is it that the Tathāgata is gentle toward some and harsh toward others?
It means that at certain times he teaches them excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind;
or at other times he teaches them the karmic maturation resulting from such excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind.
At times he speaks to them of misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind;
at times he speaks to them of the karmic maturation resulting from misconduct of body, speech, and mind;
and at times he speaks to them of gods and humans, of the happy realms, of worlds of bliss, and of nirvana.
Or, at certain times, he speaks for them of the hells, the animal realm, and the world of hungry ghosts—the perils, the evil destinies, and the states of downfall.
This is called the Tathāgata’s [discernment of] those of a gentle or coarse nature among that class of beings.

In that regard, by means of these three kinds of skillful methods of training, the Tathāgata thus subdues, thus brings to rest, thus pacifies, and thus causes them to abandon forever and without remainder all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion; he thus causes them to exhaust forever and without remainder all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, making them eternally subdued, eternally stilled, and eternally tranquil. Having attained supreme training, having attained preeminent training, and having attained supreme coolness, he has forever eliminated crookedness and impurity, and has effectively extinguished pride, concealment, flattery, and turbidity. For this reason, the Tathāgata is named the "Trainer" (Vināyaka).
Regarding the "Teacher of Gods and Humans," it is as the World-Honored One told Ānanda:

"I am not merely the teacher of the fourfold assembly—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; rather, I am also the teacher, the supreme teacher, and the following teacher for all gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, as well as for the multitudes of gods and humans. I am their model, the supreme model, and the following model; I am their general and their guide. For this reason, the Tathāgata is named the Teacher of Gods and Humans."

That which is called "Buddha" refers to one who has already fully aroused and attained the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s post-learner knowledge, vision, clear discernment, awakening, wisdom, illumination, and realization; therefore, he is named Buddha.
Furthermore, for example, there was a great brahmin who came to the Buddha’s presence and, with an exquisite verse, praised and questioned the Buddha, saying:
“I bow my head to the World’s Teacher, The one named the Supreme Awakened One.
For what reason do his parents and others Address the Venerable One by the name ‘Buddha’?”
The World-Honored One, out of compassion for that brahmin, also addressed him in verse, saying:
“Brahmin, you should know: I am like the Buddhas of the past and future;
Having achieved the marks of an Awakened One, Therefore, I am named Buddha.”
Brahmin, you should know: I observe that the activities of the three periods of time all possess the nature of arising and ceasing; therefore, I am named Buddha.
Brahmin, you should know: regarding what ought to be known and what ought to be abandoned, I have [attained]...
Having accomplished the task of realization and cultivation, I am therefore named Buddha.
O Brahmin, you should know that regarding all objects, I possess omniscient knowledge and vision; therefore, I am named Buddha.
O Brahmin, you should know: throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have cultivated all pure practices;
having passed through countless births and deaths, now, in this final body, I am free from the dust, defilements, and poisonous arrows.
"Because I have realized unsurpassed enlightenment, I am named Buddha.
Regarding the term Bhagavat: one who possesses wholesome dharmas is called Bhagavat, because he has perfected all unsurpassed wholesome dharmas;
or, one who has cultivated wholesome dharmas is called Bhagavat, because he has already cultivated all unsurpassed wholesome dharmas.

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has perfectly cultivated the precepts, the body, the mind, and wisdom; he has accomplished great compassion that is boundless and immeasurable, and has realized infinite dharmas; thus he is named Bhagavān.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses great majestic power; he is able to go and arrive, to destroy and to establish, and to exercise sovereign mastery—thus he is named Bhagavān.

Moreover, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has forever destroyed all evil and unwholesome states such as greed, hatred, and delusion; he has forever destroyed the blazing fruits of suffering and karmic maturation belonging to future existence and its defilements; and he has forever destroyed future birth, aging, sickness, and death—thus he is named Bhagavān.
As it is said in a verse:
"Having forever destroyed greed, hatred, and delusion, along with evil and unwholesome dharmas,
and being endowed with the supreme untainted dharmas, he is therefore called the Bhagavat."

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was able to personally penetrate and realize the Dharma not yet heard by others, attaining supreme awakening; he achieved knowledge of the present life and unobstructed wisdom, and was well-versed in the fruits of practicing the holy life in the future. For the sake of his disciples, he analyzed and explained these matters, establishing great assemblies to universally bestow benefits upon all sentient beings; thus, he is named Bhagavān.
As it is said in a verse:
“The Tathāgata establishes a Dharma assembly, Universally compassionating those without refuge;
Thus the Teacher of Gods and Humans, I prostrate to him who ferries beings across the ocean of existence.”

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, teaches the Dharma to his disciples according to their needs, causing them all to rejoice, revere, believe, and accept it; they practice as instructed, and his fame is heard everywhere throughout all regions, with none who do not praise and pay homage to him—he is thus named Bhagavān.

If a noble disciple recollects the Buddhas with such characteristics—rooted in vision, associated with realized knowledge, characterized by faith, the nature of faith, manifest faith, conformity and approval, longing and the nature of longing, mental realization, and purity of mind—this is called "verified confidence in the Buddha."

If one can thus exhort and establish others, it should be known that this is called "skillful means of exhortation and establishment" for causing them to abide in verified clarity regarding the Buddha.
What is verified clarity regarding the Dharma?
As the Blessed One said:

"This noble disciple recollects the True Dharma through such characteristics, namely: the Buddha’s True Dharma is well-expounded, visible here and now, free from fever, timely, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise within."
That which is called "this" refers to this desire realm, or this world, or this Jambudvīpa.

Furthermore, that which is called "this" refers to this very body, which maintains its composure, possesses its physical form, and has acquired its own substantial entity through the aggregation [of the elements].

Furthermore, the term "here" refers to this place where Buddhas and their disciples, various sages and munis, those who are wise, those who are well-disciplined, and those who are well-subdued are born.
Furthermore, the term "this" refers to this very teaching and instruction of the well-spoken Dharma; therefore, it is called "this. Regarding the term "noble disciple" (*ārya-śrāvaka*):
"noble" (*ārya*) refers to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; one is called a noble disciple because of taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

To recollect the True Dharma by means of such characteristics refers to the mindfulness, recollection, focused attention, and mindful recollection that arise toward the True Dharma by way of these characteristics, these gateways, and these principles—being non-forgetful, non-losing, non-neglecting, non-leaking, not losing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and possessing the mental quality of clear recording; therefore, it is called "recollection of the True Dharma by means of such characteristics."

Regarding "well-spoken," this refers to what the Buddha has taught: that suffering is truly suffering, its origin is truly the origin, its cessation is truly cessation, and the path is truly the path; therefore, it is called well-spoken.

If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, were to speak of what is not suffering as suffering, what is not the origin as the origin, what is not cessation as cessation, and what is not the path as the path, it could not be called well-spoken;

because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speaks of suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path, the True Dharma of the Buddha is called "well-spoken."

Regarding the term "directly perceived" (*pratyakṣa*): it refers to when one correctly cultivates the path of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as taught by the Blessed One; because one enters the clear realization of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path within this very life, it is called "directly perceived."

If, when one is correctly practicing the path of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as taught by the Blessed One, one does not enter into the clear realization of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path within this very life, then the True Dharma of the Blessed One would not be "visible in this life" (*pratyakṣa*).

However, because one enters into the clear realization of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path within this very life while correctly practicing the path of clear realization regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as taught by the Blessed One, the True Dharma of the Buddha is called "visible in this life."

Furthermore, when one correctly cultivates the path taught by the Blessed One—which is capable of severing the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, and the vision of the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation—one severs all latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation within this very life; therefore, it is called "directly perceived" (sākṣātkṛta).

If, when one is correctly practicing the path taught by the Blessed One—which is capable of severing the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, and the vision of the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation—one does not immediately sever all latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation within this very life, then the True Dharma of the Blessed One would not be "visible in this life" (sandiṭṭhika).

However, because when one is correctly practicing the path taught by the Blessed One—which is capable of severing the latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, and the vision of the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation—one does immediately sever all latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation within this very life, the True Dharma of the Buddha is called "visible in this life."

Furthermore, when one correctly cultivates the path that leads to the cessation of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, and the vision of the path—as taught by the Blessed One—along with those to be abandoned through cultivation, one realizes in this very life the cessation of all those latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, the path, and cultivation; therefore, it is called "directly perceived" (sākṣātkṛta).

If, when one is correctly practicing the path taught by the Blessed One that leads to the realization of the cessation of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation, one does not realize the cessation of those latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation within the present life, then the True Dharma of the Blessed One would not be "visible in the present" (*pratyakṣa*).

However, because when one is correctly practicing the path taught by the Blessed One that leads to the realization of the cessation of the latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation, one immediately realizes the cessation of those latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation, the True Dharma of the Buddha is called "visible in the present."
Regarding the term "without fever" (*atapa*), it refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, which is called "without fever.
Why is this? "Fever" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Within the Noble Eightfold Path, all afflictions are neither attained nor proximately attained; they do not exist, nor do they exist equally. Therefore, the True Dharma of the Buddha is called "Free from Fever" (*anupatāpa*).
Regarding "timely" (*kāla-yukta*): it refers to the Noble Eightfold Path being called "timely.

Why is this? Because when one correctly cultivates the path of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as taught by the Blessed One, one immediately enters into the clear realization of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; therefore, it is called "timely."

If one were to enter the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path only after having correctly cultivated the path to the clear realization of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as taught by the Blessed One, then the True Dharma of the Blessed One would not be "timely" (*akālika*).

However, because one enters the clear realization of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path at the very moment of correctly cultivating the path to that clear realization as taught by the Blessed One, the True Dharma of the Buddha is called "timely."

Furthermore, when one correctly cultivates the path taught by the Blessed One—which is capable of severing the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, and the vision of the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation—one simultaneously severs all latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation; therefore, it is called "timely."

If one were to first cultivate the path taught by the Blessed One that can sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, and the vision of the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, and only afterwards sever all latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, then the True Dharma of the Blessed One would not be "timely.

However, because at the very moment one cultivates the path taught by the Blessed One that can sever the latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, one simultaneously severs all such latent tendencies, the True Dharma of the Buddha is therefore called "timely."

Furthermore, when one correctly cultivates the path for the cessation of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) taught by the Blessed One—those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, and the vision of the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation—at that very moment, one realizes the cessation of all those latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation; therefore, it is called "timely."

If one were to first cultivate the path taught by the Blessed One that leads to the realization of the cessation of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation, and only afterwards realize the cessation of those latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation, then the True Dharma of the Blessed One would not be "timely" (*kāla-anupraviṣṭa*).

However, because at the very moment one cultivates the path taught by the Blessed One that leads to the realization of the cessation of the latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation, one simultaneously realizes the cessation of those latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation, the True Dharma of the Buddha is called "timely."
Regarding the term "guidance," it refers to the Noble Eightfold Path as being called guidance.

Why is this? Because through the cultivation and repeated cultivation of the Noble Eightfold Path, one is able to lead toward, guide toward, follow, and pursue the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; therefore, the Buddha’s True Dharma is called guidance.
Regarding the term "near observation," it refers to the Noble Eightfold Path as being called near observation.

Why is this so? Because through the cultivation and repeated cultivation of the Noble Eightfold Path, one is able to know and see suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path to its cessation as they truly are; therefore, the Buddha’s True Dharma is called near observation.

Regarding "the wise realize it within": the Buddha and his disciples are called the wise. Concerning the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as taught by the World-Honored One, the wise personally know, see, understand, and perfectly awaken to them as suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; therefore, the True Dharma of the Buddha is called "realized within by the wise."

If a noble disciple, by means of such characteristics, recollects the True Dharma (saddharma) with vision as its root and in association with realized knowledge—possessing faith and the nature of faith, the nature of manifest faith, compliance and approval, longing and the nature of longing, mental realization and mental purity—this is called "verified confidence in the Dharma" (dharma-avetyaprasāda).

If one is able to encourage and establish others in this way, it should be known that this is called "skillful means of encouragement and establishment to cause them to abide in verified confidence in the Dharma.
What is verified confidence in the Saṃgha?
As the Blessed One said:

"This noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha with such characteristics, namely: the disciples of the Buddha who are endowed with excellent conduct, upright conduct, rational conduct, conduct in accordance with the Dharma, harmonious and respectful conduct, and conduct that follows the Dharma."

Within this Saṅgha, there are those entering the stream and those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry; those entering the stage of once-returning and those who have attained the fruit of once-returning; those entering the stage of non-returning and those who have attained the fruit of non-returning; and those entering the stage of arhatship and those who have attained the fruit of arhatship. Thus, there are in total these four pairs and eight classes of individuals (pudgala).

The community of the Buddha’s disciples is complete in virtue, complete in concentration, complete in wisdom, complete in liberation, and complete in the knowledge and vision of liberation; they are worthy of invitation, worthy of veneration, worthy of respect, the unsurpassed field of merit, and worthy of offerings from the world.
That which is called "this" refers to this desire realm, or this world, or this Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, that which is called "this" refers to this very body—possessing its own maintenance and concentration, having its own physical frame, and having acquired its own aggregate-body.

Furthermore, when it says "here," it refers to this place where Buddhas and their disciples, various sages and munis, those who are wise, those who are well-disciplined, and those who are well-tamed are born.
Furthermore, the term "this" refers to this very teaching and instruction of the well-spoken Dharma; therefore, it is called "this.

As for the term "noble disciple" (*ārya-śrāvaka*): "noble" (*ārya*) refers to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; because one has taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, one is thus called a noble disciple.

To recollect the Saṅgha by means of such characteristics refers to the arising of mindfulness, constant recollection, focused attention, and mindful remembrance toward the various members of the Saṅgha by way of these characteristics, these gateways, and this principle; it is that which is not forgotten, not lost, not omitted, and not leaked, which does not lose its dharmic nature, and possesses the mental quality of clear recording—therefore, it is called "recollecting the Saṅgha by means of such characteristics."
Regarding "sublime conduct," the World-Honored One has taught that there are four types of practice:

first, the practice of suffering with slow progress; second, the practice of suffering with swift progress; [third, the practice of pleasure with slow progress; and fourth, the practice of pleasure with swift progress].
Third, the practice with ease and slow progress;
fourth, the practice with ease and quick progress.
Because the community of the Buddha’s disciples practices within these, they are called "sublime practices" (*sucarita*).
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has spoken of four kinds of conduct:
first, unstable conduct; second, stable conduct; [third, conduct leading to suffering;
and fourth, conduct leading to happiness].
Third, the practice of subduing;
fourth, the practice of tranquility.
The community of the Buddha’s disciples practices only the latter three, and is therefore called the "Sublime Conduct" (Brahmacarya).
Regarding "straightforward conduct," this refers to the Noble Eightfold Path being called straightforward.
Why is this? Because the Noble Eightfold Path is not circuitous, not crooked, and not devious; it is straightforward, level, and leads directly to its destination.
When the community of the Buddha’s disciples practices within this, it is called "straightforward practice.
As for "practice in accordance with reality," the Noble Eightfold Path is what is meant by "in accordance with reality.
When the community of the Buddha’s disciples practices within this, it is called "practice in accordance with reality."

Furthermore, the Blessed One has taught that the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and right concentration—along with their requisites and equipment—are called "conformable to reality."
As the Blessed One said:

"This is the single path leading all sentient beings to complete purification, to transcend sorrow and lamentation, to extinguish grief and suffering, and to realize the Dharma according to reality; namely, noble right concentration together with its requisites and equipment—the seven factors of the noble path—which are called the requisites and equipment for noble right concentration."
What are the seven?
They are right view through to right mindfulness.
By means of noble right concentration?
Because it is cultivated and brought to fulfillment through the guidance of the seven factors of the path, it is called the "noble equipment for right concentration.
When the community of the Buddha’s disciples practices within this, it is termed "practice according to reality."
Regarding "practice in accordance with the Dharma": Nirvāṇa is called the Dharma, and the Noble Eightfold Path is called the practice in accordance with the Dharma.
When the community of the Buddha’s disciples practices within this, it is termed "practice in accordance with the Dharma."
Furthermore, the Prātimokṣa is called the Dharma, and the Prātimokṣa restraint is called the "conformity to the Dharma" (anudharma).
When the community of the Buddha’s disciples practices within this, it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (dharmānudharmapratipatti).
Furthermore, bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and purity of livelihood are called the Dharma; to receive and uphold this Dharma is called "conformity with the Dharma" (anudharma).
When the community of the Buddha’s disciples practices within this, it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (dharmānudharmapratipatti).

Those who practice harmony and respect are the community of the Buddha’s disciples; they share one precept, one training, one teaching, and one Prātimokṣa; they possess the same precepts, the same training, the same teaching, and the same Prātimokṣa.
The training rules that one who has been ordained for a hundred years should study, a newly ordained person also studies;
the training rules that a newly ordained person should study, one who has been ordained for a hundred years also studies.
Just as those who have received full ordination for a hundred years should train in the dharmas to be learned, so too should those who have newly received full ordination train;
and just as those who have newly received full ordination should train in the dharmas to be learned, so too should those who have received full ordination for a hundred years train.

When the community of the Buddha’s disciples is able, within this, to share a single nature of precept, a single nature of training, a single nature of exposition, and a single nature of the Prātimokṣa—possessing a commonality of precepts, a commonality of training, a commonality of exposition, and a commonality of the Prātimokṣa—it is called "harmonious and respectful conduct."

Furthermore, the community of the Buddha’s disciples mutually respect and defer to one another; toward those who are senior in years, they rise to greet them, join their palms in salutation, offer greetings and prostrations, and manifest signs of harmony and reverence.
When the community of the Buddha’s disciples practices in this manner, it is called "harmonious and respectful conduct" (*sāmagrī-vinaya*).
Regarding "practice in accordance with the Dharma": the Noble Eightfold Path is what is meant by "the Dharma.
When the community of the Buddha’s disciples follows and traverses within that path, it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharma-pratipatti*).

The remainder of Chapter Three, "The Factors of Clear Conviction" (*śraddhā-viśuddhi*). Regarding the phrase "among this Saṃgha": within the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, this indicates the collection (*rāśi*), the aggregate (*skandha*), the division (*nikāya*), and the summarized meaning (*saṃkṣepārtha*).

One who is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-pratipannaka) has already attained the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) capable of realizing the fruit of stream-entry; that is to say, immediately following this [path], one realizes the fruit of stream-entry.

Regarding the craving and malice of the desire realm, they have not yet abandoned most categories through the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*); having previously not yet attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths, they now cultivate such clear realization. This is termed being a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry.

The fruit of stream-entry refers to one who, within this present life, has already permanently abandoned and fully understood the three fetters—namely, the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Abiding in this state of abandonment, yet not yet having progressed to seek the realization of the fruit of once-returning, is called the fruit of stream-entry.

Regarding the candidate for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*): one who has already attained the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) capable of realizing the fruit of once-returning—that is, one who will realize the fruit of once-returning immediately thereafter—is so called.

This refers to one who, regarding the craving and aversion of the desire realm, has either previously abandoned most categories thereof by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), or is now cultivating the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four noble truths which they had not previously realized, or is one who, abiding in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), is able to advance toward the realization of the fruit of once-returning; such a person is named a candidate for once-returning.

The fruit of once-returning refers to one who, within this present life, has already attained the permanent abandonment and full knowledge of the three fetters, as well as the abandonment of a great portion of sensual desire and ill will.
Abiding in this state of abandonment, yet being unable to further progress toward the realization of the fruit of non-returning, is called the fruit of once-returning.

Regarding the candidate for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmipratipannaka*): one who has already attained the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) capable of realizing the fruit of non-returning—that is, one who will realize the fruit of non-returning immediately after this [path]—is called a candidate for non-returning.

This refers to one who, through the mundane path, has either previously and permanently abandoned the sensual desire and ill-will of the desire realm, and is now cultivating the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths which they had not previously realized; or one who, abiding in the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), is able to further seek and attain the realization of the fruit of non-returning. Such a person is named a candidate for non-returning.

The fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) refers to the permanent abandonment and full comprehension within the present life of the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni), namely: the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), adherence to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), sensual desire (kāmacchanda), and ill will (vyāpāda).
Abiding in this state of abandonment, yet not yet having advanced to seek the realization of the fruit of Arhatship, one is called a Non-returner (Anāgāmin).

As for the candidate for Arhatship (Arhattva-pratipannaka), they have already attained the path of non-interruption (ānantarya-mārga) capable of realizing the fruit of Arhatship; that is to say, through this uninterrupted path, they shall realize the supreme fruit of Arhatship.

Alternatively, having already abided in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), one who is able to further seek and realize the fruit of arhatship is called one "proceeding toward arhatship" (arhattvapratipannaka).

As for the fruit of arhatship: it refers to the state in which, within this very life (dṛṣṭadharme), all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion have been permanently severed; this is called the fruit of arhatship.

Regarding the "four pairs of individuals" (catvāri puruṣayugāni): the first pair consists of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry; the second pair consists of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the one who has attained the fruit of once-returning; the third pair consists of the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the one who has attained the fruit of non-returning; and the fourth pair consists of the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the one who has attained the fruit of arhatship.

The "eight types of individuals" (aṣṭau pudgalāḥ) refers to the distinct establishment of the eight categories of individuals, such as those entering the stream (srotāpatti-pratipannaka) and so forth.
The phrase "the assembly of the Buddha's disciples" indicates that the community of the Buddha’s disciples possesses supreme qualities.
Perfection of ethical discipline means that the Sangha of those in training and those beyond training is fully accomplished in the ethical discipline of those in training and those beyond training.

Perfection of meditative concentration means that the Sangha of those in training and those beyond training is fully accomplished in the meditative concentration of those in training and those beyond training.
Endowment with wisdom means that the Sangha of those in training and those beyond training is fully accomplished in the wisdom of those in training and those beyond training.
Endowment with liberation means that the Sangha of those in training and those beyond training is fully accomplished in the liberation of those in training and those beyond training.

"Endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation" refers to the community of learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*) who have fully accomplished and perfected the knowledge and vision of liberation of both learners and non-learners.
"Worthy of invitation" means they are worthy of gifts, worthy of offerings, and worthy of sacrificial oblations; therefore, they are said to be "worthy of invitation."

Regarding the term "should be bent" (*āvaṭa*): it refers to having already practiced giving, having practiced giving well; having already made offerings, having made offerings well; having already performed sacrifices, having performed sacrifices well; and having achieved great fruits and benefits with little exertion. Therefore, it is called "should be bent."
Regarding those who should be revered: whether one recognizes them or not, one should rise to meet them, bow the body, join the palms, prostrate at their feet, and greet them with praise, asking:
"Have you attained well-being through your right arrival and right conduct?"
It is called "worthy of veneration.
As for the term "unsurpassed," it is as the World-Honored One told the assembly of bhikṣus:

"Among all congregations of harmonious groups, the community of the Buddha’s disciples is the foremost, the most honored, the most excellent, the highest, and unsurpassed; therefore, it is called 'unsurpassed.'"
Regarding the term "field of merit," as the World-Honored One told Ānanda:

"Among the multitudes of gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, including both devas and humans, I see none who are as worthy of receiving gifts already bestowed, well-bestowed gifts; worthy of worship already performed, well-performed worship; or worthy of sacrifice already offered, well-offered sacrifice, as is my Saṃgha."

Ānanda, you should know that if one has already bestowed gifts upon my Saṅgha, bestowed them well; already made offerings, offered them well; already performed sacrifices, sacrificed well—then by performing even a small amount of labor, one obtains great fruit and benefit.
Furthermore, when Śakra, Lord of the Devas, arrived at Vulture Peak Mountain, he praised and questioned the Buddha with these exquisite verses:
"I prostrate to the one capable of eloquent exposition, Who has reached the further shore of all phenomena,
And transcended all terrors— The Great Honored One, Gautama."
There are immeasurable sentient beings who, delighting in merit, practice generosity;
they constantly give rise to sincere faith and cultivate the various merits that serve as a basis for existence.
We pray that the Buddha will look upon us with compassion and explain the truly supreme field of merit.
“May immeasurable sentient beings obtain great fruits from even small acts of giving.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, the World-Honored One addressed the Lord of Devas with these sublime verses:
“If immeasurable sentient beings, desiring merit, practice generosity...”
Those who constantly give rise to sincere faith and cultivate merit based on the Three Jewels—
now for your sake, I shall describe the truly supreme field of merit,
so that immeasurable sentient beings may obtain great fruit from even a small offering.
Those who practice the four noble paths and abide in the four noble fruits are the true Saṅgha worthy of offerings, endowed with supreme morality, concentration, and wisdom.
This is the truly excellent field of merit for the Saṅgha; its virtues are exceedingly vast and great.
Capable of providing immeasurable benefit and moisture, like the four great oceans;
the Subduer’s supreme disciples have already emitted the light of the Dharma,
and are worthy of receiving supreme offerings as well as supreme sacrifices.
Giving alms to even a few monks is equivalent to giving to the entire Sangha;
one will surely obtain a great fruit, as praised by the Omniscient One.
Among all fields of merit, the field of the Sangha is the most supreme.
Praised by all Buddhas, giving yields the most supreme merit.
By bestowing even a small gift upon the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, one obtains a great fruit;
therefore, those who are wise and discerning should make offerings to the Sangha.
The noble assembly upholds the sublime Dharma and is endowed with clear conduct and meditative concentration;
therefore, among the Three Jewels, giving to the Saṅgha is supreme.
With a mind purified in three ways, one gives robes, food, and drink to the Saṅgha.
One will surely obtain a most excellent retribution, becoming a virtuous person among gods and humans.
Certainly, throughout successive births, one shall be free from the poisonous arrows of defilement,
transcend all evil realms, and enjoy the supreme bliss of gods and humans.
Having personally gathered precious wealth, one gives it with one's own hands for the benefit of both oneself and others;
thus, one will surely obtain a great fruit.
All those who are wise and practice giving with pure faith—
"One shall be born in the realm of peace and bliss, And experience sublime joy and intelligence.
Because it is said thus, they are called "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Those who are worthy of offerings by the world are the noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*), for they are able to purify the world and serve as vessels worthy of offerings.
Because they have practiced the path of purity worthy of offerings;
because they have accomplished the state of being worthy of offerings through the three types of pure karma, they are called "worldly ones worthy of offerings.

If a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha with such characteristics—seeing it as the root, associated with realized knowledge, characterized by faith and the nature of faith, manifest faith, conformity and approval, longing and the nature of longing, mental realization, and mental purity—this is called "verified confidence in the Saṅgha."
If one can thus exhort and establish others, it should be known that this is called "skillful means of exhortation and establishment to cause them to abide in verified clarity regarding the Saṃgha.
What is the "precept cherished by the noble ones"?
It refers to the untainted restraint of body, restraint of speech, and purity of livelihood; this is called the precepts beloved by the noble ones.
For what reason are they called the precepts beloved by the noble ones?

The Buddhas and their disciples are called "noble ones" (*ārya*). Because they cherish, delight in, tolerate, comply with, and do not oppose these precepts, they are called the "precepts cherished by the noble ones" (*āryakānta-śīla*).

If one is able to exhort and establish others in this way, it should be known that this is called "exhorting and establishing through skillful means so that they abide in the precepts beloved by the noble ones.
4. The Fruits of the Śramaṇa Life. Chapter Four. At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
“There are four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
What are the four? They are as follows:”
They are the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.
What is the fruit of stream-entry?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of the fruit of stream-entry:
First is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding what is called the conditioned fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*): it refers to the attainment of that fruit and the attainment of that attainment; the faculties and powers of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the morality of one in training, the wholesome roots of one in training, the eight factors of one in training, and all other dharmas of one in training belonging to that category—these are called the conditioned fruit of stream-entry.

That which is called the unconditioned fruit of stream-entry refers to the permanent abandonment of the three fetters within this state, as well as the permanent abandonment of those types of fettering dharmas; that is to say, the permanent abandonment of the eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the permanent abandonment of those types of fettering dharmas—this is termed the unconditioned fruit of stream-entry.
What is the fruit of once-returning?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of the fruit of once-returning:
first, the conditioned; [second, the unconditioned].
The second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding what is called the conditioned fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*): it refers to the attainment of that fruit and the attainment of that attainment; the faculties and powers of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of one in training, the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of one in training, the eight factors of one in training, and all other dharmas of one in training belonging to that category—these are called the conditioned fruit of once-returning.

What is called the unconditioned fruit of once-returning refers to the permanent abandonment of the three fetters within this state, as well as the permanent abandonment of those types of fettering dharmas; that is to say, the permanent abandonment of the eighty-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and the permanent abandonment of those types of fettering dharmas, along with the extensive abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion, and the extensive abandonment of those types of fettering dharmas. This is termed the unconditioned fruit of once-returning.
What is the fruit of non-returning?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of the fruit of non-returning:
first, the conditioned; [second, the unconditioned].
The second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding what is called the conditioned fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*): it refers to the attainment of that fruit and the attainment of that attainment; the faculties and powers of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the morality of one in training, the wholesome roots of one in training, the eight factors of one in training, and all other dharmas of one in training belonging to that category—these are called the conditioned fruit of non-returning.

That which is called the unconditioned fruit of non-return (*anāgāmiphala*) refers to the permanent abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*) within this state, as well as the permanent abandonment of those types of fettering phenomena; that is to say, it is the permanent abandonment of the ninety-two latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the permanent abandonment of those types of fettering phenomena. This is termed the unconditioned fruit of non-return.
What is the fruit of arhatship?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of the fruit of arhatship:
first, the conditioned; [second, the unconditioned].
The second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

As for what is called the conditioned fruit of arhatship (*saṃskṛtam arhattvaphalam*), it refers to the attainment of that fruit and the attainment of that attainment, as well as the faculties and powers of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the morality of one beyond training, the wholesome roots of one beyond training, the ten qualities of one beyond training, and all other such dharmas of one beyond training belonging to that category; these are termed the conditioned fruit of arhatship.

What is called the unconditioned fruit of arhatship refers to that state in which all afflictions, such as greed, hatred, and delusion, have been eternally severed; wherein one has transcended all realms of existence and cut off all paths of rebirth; wherein the three fires are forever stilled, the four torrents have been crossed, arrogance and negligence are eternally abandoned, parching thirst is forever extinguished, and the cave-dwelling of the self is forever demolished; it is the unsurpassed ultimate, the unsurpassed tranquility, the unsurpassed exhaustion of craving, and the cessation through detachment—this is termed the unconditioned fruit of arhatship.
Chapter Five: The Pathways of Practice. At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
“There are four pathways of practice.”
"What are the four? They are:
the practice with difficulty and slow progress, the practice with difficulty and quick progress, the practice with ease and slow progress, and the practice with ease and quick progress.
What is meant by "the practice with difficulty and slow progress"?
As the Blessed One has said: "Any bhikṣu who is oppressed, humiliated, and injured by the five aggregates of clinging—

because he is thus constrained and seized by these five kinds of aggregates of clinging, which follow him constantly until the end of life like the bearing of a heavy burden— he will develop a profound sense of revulsion toward these five aggregates of clinging, and will censure, disparage, and reject them."
The arising of revulsion, disparagement, and repudiation toward these very five aggregates of clinging is here termed "suffering.
From this, there subsequently arise the five faculties—faith and the others—which are dull, obtuse, feeble, and inferior.
Because these five faculties are dull, blunt, feeble, and inferior, they can only slowly realize the unsurpassed exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
This term "slowly" means not urgent, not rapid, not swift, not easy, and not a quick realization.
Regarding the term "unsurpassed," as the World-Honored One has said:
"Among all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, I declare that freedom from passion is the foremost, the most venerable, the most excellent, the highest, and the unsurpassed."
