Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity (*upekṣā*) he possesses, these are called superior practice (*viśeṣa-carita*).

This sublime practice, together with the previously mentioned concentration of desire, is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice through concentration of desire.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to unwholesome desires accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion; he reflects thus:
"I should not now give rise to unwholesome desires accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion."

"However, it is right for me to abandon unwholesome desires associated with greed, hatred, and delusion, and to cultivate and accumulate wholesome desires associated with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
Through the predominant power of this desire, he attains samādhi; this is called the samādhi of desire.

Having accomplished the concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*), he generates desire for the purpose of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen; and so on, as explained at length, up to the purpose of establishing wholesome states that have already arisen and even maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity (*upekṣā*) he possesses, these are called the superior practices (*adhicaryā*).

This sublime practice and the previously mentioned concentration of desire are collectively termed the "basis for psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice of the concentration of desire.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to unwholesome desires that are not free from greed, hatred, and delusion; he reflects thus:
"I should not now give rise to unwholesome desires that are not free from greed, hatred, and delusion."

"However, it is right for me to abandon unwholesome desires that are not free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and to cultivate and accumulate wholesome desires that are free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Through the predominant power of this desire, one attains *samādhi*; this is called "desire-*samādhi*" (*chanda-samādhi*).

Having accomplished the concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*), he arouses desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states; this is explained at length up to: for the sake of establishing arisen wholesome states and so forth, even unto the stabilization of the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity (*upekṣā*) he possesses, these are called "superior practice" (*viśeṣa-caryā*).

This very sublime practice, together with the previously mentioned concentration of desire, is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice through the concentration of desire.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who dwells in a state of joyful aspiration toward all wholesome dharmas, and he reflects:
"It is most appropriate that I dwell in a state of joyful aspiration toward wholesome dharmas."
Through the predominant power of that desire, he attains samādhi; this is called "desire-samādhi" (*chanda-samādhi*).

Having accomplished desire-samādhi, he arouses desire in order to abandon arisen unwholesome states, and so on, as extensively described, up to in order to maintain and sustain arisen wholesome states. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity he possesses therein is called "superior practice" (*adhicitta-pratipatti*).

This very superior practice, together with the previously mentioned concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*), is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice through the concentration of desire" (*chanda-samādhi-pāṭibhāna-iddhipāda*).
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to wholesome desire and reflects thus:
"That I now give rise to such wholesome desire is most appropriate."
Because he attains samādhi through the predominant power of that desire, it is called "desire-samādhi.

Having accomplished desire-samādhi, he arouses desire in order to abandon arisen unwholesome states; this is explained in detail up to: in order to cause arisen wholesome states to remain firm, and so on, up to maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity he possesses, these are called the "superior practice" (adhipateyya).

These aforementioned superior practices and the previously described desire for concentration (*chanda-samādhi*) together are termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of superior practice through the desire for concentration" (*chanda-samādhi-padhāna-saṃskāra-iddhipāda*).
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to a virtuous desire accompanied by non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, and he reflects:
"It is most appropriate that I have now given rise to this virtuous desire accompanied by non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion."
Because he attains *samādhi* through the predominant power of that desire, it is called "desire-*samādhi*" (*chanda-samādhi*).

Having accomplished desire-*samādhi*, he arouses desire for the sake of abandoning arisen unwholesome states; this is explained at length up to: for the sake of stabilizing arisen wholesome states and so forth, up to maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, effort, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity he possesses therein, these are called the "superior practices" (*adhicariya*).

These aforementioned superior practices and the previously described desire-concentration (*chanda-samādhi*) together are termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of superior practice through desire-concentration" (*chanda-samādhi-prahāṇa-saṃskāra-ṛddhipāda*).
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to a virtuous desire free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and he reflects:
"It is most appropriate that I have now given rise to a virtuous desire free from greed, hatred, and delusion."
"Because he attains *samādhi* through the predominant power of that desire, it is called 'desire-*samādhi*.

Having accomplished desire-*samādhi*, he arouses desire in order to abandon arisen evil and unwholesome states; [this is] explained at length until: in order to cause arisen wholesome states to remain firm, and so on, up to maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so on, up to equanimity he possesses, this is called 'excellent practice' (*adhicitta*)."

These very superior practices (*adhiprajñā*) and the previously mentioned concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*), taken together, are termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of superior practice through the concentration of desire" (*chanda-samādhi-adhiprajñā-siddhi-ṛddhipāda*).

All concentrations of desire arise from desire, are accumulated by desire, are of the same category as desire, and are produced by desire; therefore, they are called the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of superior practice through the concentration of desire."

Regarding the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the basis of concentration through diligence" (*vīrya-samādhi-prahāṇa-saṃskāra-ṛddhipāda*): what is diligence, what is concentration, what is excellence, and what is the basis of practice, such that it is called the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the basis of concentration through diligence"?

In this context, "diligence" refers to the exertion, vigor, fortitude, intensity, and fervor that arise based on the wholesome dharmas born of renunciation and seclusion; it is an unrestrainable, resolute application of the mind that is unceasing—this is called diligence.

Samādhi refers to the mental abiding, equal abiding, close abiding, and settled abiding that arise through the predominant influence of diligence; it is non-distraction, non-disorder, withdrawal, and concentration, characterized by one-pointedness of mind—this is called samādhi.
"Victorious" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path arising from the predominance of diligence; this is called "victory.
"Victorious practice" refers to a bhikṣu who, relying on past diligence, attains samādhi; this is called "diligence-samādhi."

Having accomplished the samādhi of diligence, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states that have already arisen; this is explained at length up to: for the sake of establishing wholesome states that have already arisen and so forth, up to maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called superior practice.

This very superior practice, together with the previously mentioned diligence regarding *samādhi*, is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of superior practice through diligence.

As it is based on past diligence, so it is for future and present [diligence]; for wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; for that bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; for that of the learner (*śaikṣa*), the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and neither-learner-nor-non-learner; and for diligence to be abandoned by seeing, by cultivation, or not to be abandoned—the detailed explanation is likewise for all these.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who dwells with an inferior, feeble, weak, and extremely weak application of effort toward all wholesome dharmas. He reflects thus:
"I should not now dwell with an inferior, feeble, weak, and extremely weak application of effort toward all wholesome dharmas."
"However, it is right for me to abide in all wholesome qualities with diligence that is not low, not feeble, not inferior, not weak, and not extremely weak.
Through the predominant power of this diligence, he attains samādhi; this is called "diligence-samādhi."

Having achieved the samādhi of diligence, he generates desire for the purpose of abandoning unwholesome states that have already arisen; this is explained at length up to: for the purpose of stabilizing wholesome states that have already arisen, even unto maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called superior practice.

These very sublime practices, together with the previously mentioned diligence in *samādhi*, are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice of diligence in *samādhi*.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to unwholesome diligence, and he reflects:
"I should not now give rise to unwholesome diligence."
"However, it is right for me to abandon unwholesome diligence and cultivate wholesome diligence.
Through the predominant power of this diligence, he attains samādhi; this is called the samādhi of diligence.

Having accomplished the samādhi of diligence, he arouses desire for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen; this is explained at length up to: for the sake of stabilizing wholesome states that have already arisen, even unto maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity he possesses, these are called superior practice.

This sublime practice, together with the previously mentioned diligence and concentration, is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting of the accomplishment of the sublime practice of diligence.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to unwholesome diligence accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion; he reflects thus:
"I should not now give rise to unwholesome diligence accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion."

"However, it is right for me to abandon the unwholesome effort associated with greed, hatred, and delusion, and to cultivate the wholesome effort associated with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
Through the predominant power of this effort, he attains samādhi; this is called "the samādhi of effort."

Having accomplished the samādhi of diligence, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states that have already arisen; this is explained at length up to: for the sake of stabilizing wholesome states that have already arisen, even unto maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity he possesses, these are called superior practice.

This sublime practice, together with the previously mentioned diligence in *samādhi*, is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting of the accomplishment of the sublime practice of diligence in *samādhi*.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to a diligence that is not free from greed, hatred, and delusion; he reflects thus:
"I should not now give rise to a diligence that is not free from greed, hatred, and delusion."
"However, it is right for me to abandon unwholesome diligence that is not free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and to cultivate wholesome diligence that is free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Through the predominant power of this diligence, he attains samādhi; this is called diligence-samādhi (vīrya-samādhi).

Having accomplished the samādhi of diligence, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states that have already arisen; [as explained at length] up to: for the sake of establishing wholesome states that have already arisen and even for the sake of maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called superior practice.

This very superior practice, together with the previously mentioned diligence and concentration, is collectively termed the "basis for psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of diligence.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who dwells in various wholesome dharmas with a diligence that is neither slack nor even extremely weak; he reflects thus:
"It is most appropriate that I dwell in wholesome dharmas with a diligence that is neither slack nor even extremely weak."
Through the predominant power of that diligence, he attains samādhi; this is called "diligence-samādhi.

Having accomplished diligence-samādhi, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, and so on, as extensively described, up to the stabilization of arisen wholesome states and even the sustaining of the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called "excellent practice" (adhipateyya).

This very superior practice, together with the previously mentioned diligence and concentration, is collectively termed the "basis for spiritual power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of diligence through concentration.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to wholesome diligence and thinks to himself:
"It is most appropriate that I have now given rise to such wholesome diligence."
Through the predominant power of that diligence, he attains samādhi; this is called "diligence-samādhi.

Having accomplished diligence-samādhi, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, and so forth, as extensively described, up to the stabilization of arisen wholesome states and even the maintenance of the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called "superior practice" (adhipateyya).

This very superior practice, together with the previously mentioned diligence and concentration, is collectively termed the "basis for psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of diligence through concentration.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to wholesome diligence accompanied by non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, and he reflects:
"It is most appropriate that I have now given rise to wholesome diligence accompanied by non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion."
Through the predominant power of that diligence, he attains samādhi; this is called "diligence-samādhi.

Having accomplished diligence-samādhi, he arouses desire for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states that have already arisen, and so on, as explained at length, up to the sake of maintaining and stabilizing wholesome states that have already arisen, even unto the stabilization of the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called "superior practice" (adhicitta).

This very superior practice, together with the previously mentioned diligence and concentration, is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting of the accomplishment of superior practice through diligence.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to wholesome diligence that is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and he reflects:
"It is most appropriate that I have now given rise to wholesome diligence free from greed, hatred, and delusion."
Through the predominant power of that diligence, he attains samādhi; this is called "diligence-samādhi.

Having accomplished diligence-samādhi, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, and so on, as extensively described, up to the stabilization of arisen wholesome states and even the sustaining of the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity he possesses, these are called "superior practice."

This very sublime practice (*pradhāna-caryā*) together with the previously mentioned diligence and concentration (*samādhi*) are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice through diligence" (*vīrya-samādhi-pradhāna-saṃskāra-iddhipāda*).

All concentrations of diligence arise from diligence, are accumulated by diligence, belong to the category of diligence, and are produced by diligence; therefore, they are called the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice through diligence."

Composed by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The Third Dharma Master Xuanzang, by Imperial Decree, translated:

The remainder of Chapter Eight, on the Bases of Psychic Power (*ṛddhipāda*). Regarding the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of concentration of mind" (*cittasamādhipradhānābhinirhāra-ṛddhipāda*): what is "mind," what is "concentration," what is "superiority," and what is "superior practice," such that it is named the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of concentration of mind"?
Regarding this, "mind" refers to the mind, mentation, and consciousness that arise based on the wholesome dharmas produced by renunciation through leaving the household life; this is called "mind.

"Samādhi" refers to the mental abiding, thorough abiding, close abiding, and stable abiding, as well as non-distraction, non-confusion, withdrawal, concentration, and one-pointedness of mind, which arise through the predominance of the mind; this is called "samādhi."
"Victorious" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path arising through the predominance of the mind; this is called "victorious.
Regarding "victorious practice": it refers to a bhikṣu who, relying on a past mind, attains samādhi; this is called "mind-samādhi."

Having accomplished the concentration of mind (*citta-samādhi*), he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states; this is explained in detail up to: for the sake of establishing arisen wholesome states and even for the sake of maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, vigor, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity (*upekṣā*) he possesses, these are called the superior practices (*viśeṣa-carita*).

This very superior practice, together with the previously mentioned mental samādhi, is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of superior practice through mental samādhi.

Just as it is based on the past mind, so too is it extensively explained in relation to the future and present minds; to wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate minds; to minds bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; to minds that are in training (*śaikṣa*), beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and neither in training nor beyond training; and to minds to be abandoned by seeing, by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned. Thus it is for all such cases.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who dwells with a mind that is low, feeble, inferior, weak, and extremely weak regarding all wholesome dharmas; he reflects thus:
"I should not now dwell with a mind that is low, feeble, inferior, weak, and extremely weak regarding all wholesome dharmas."
"However, it is right for me to abide in all wholesome dharmas with a mind that is not depressed, not weak, not inferior, not feeble, and not utterly feeble.
By the predominant power of this mind, he attains samādhi; this is called "mind-samādhi."

Having accomplished the concentration of mind, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states; this is explained at length up to: for the sake of establishing arisen wholesome states and so forth, even unto maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, effort, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called "superior practice."

This sublime practice, together with the previously mentioned mental concentration (*citta-samādhi*), is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice of mental concentration.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to an unwholesome thought and reflects:
"I should not give rise to an unwholesome thought now."
"However, I ought by principle to eliminate unwholesome states of mind and cultivate wholesome states of mind.
Through the predominant power of this thought, he attains samādhi; this is called "samādhi of mind."

Having accomplished the concentration of mind (*citta-samādhi*), he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states; this is explained in detail up to: for the sake of establishing arisen wholesome states and so forth, even unto maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, vigor, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity (*upekṣā*) he possesses, these are called the superior practices (*viśeṣa-carita*).

This sublime practice, together with the previously mentioned mental concentration (*citta-samādhi*), is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice of mental concentration" (*citta-samādhi-pradhāna-saṃskāra-ṛddhipāda*).
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to an unwholesome mind accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion; he then reflects:
"I should not now give rise to an unwholesome mind accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion."
"However, it is right for me to abandon the unwholesome mind associated with greed, hatred, and delusion, and to cultivate the wholesome mind associated with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
By means of the predominant power of this mind, he attains samādhi; this is called "mental samādhi."

Having accomplished the concentration of mind, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states; this is explained at length until: for the sake of stabilizing arisen wholesome states and so forth, up to maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, vigor, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity he possesses, these are called superior practice.

These aforementioned superior practices and the previously described mental samādhi are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of superior practice through the mind.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to an unwholesome mind that is not free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and he reflects:
"I should not now give rise to an unwholesome mind that is not free from greed, hatred, and delusion."

"However, it is right for me to eliminate unwholesome states of mind that are not free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and to cultivate wholesome states of mind that are free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
By the predominant power of this thought, he attains samādhi; this is called "samādhi of the mind."

Having accomplished the concentration of mind, he generates desire for the purpose of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states; this is explained at length up to: for the purpose of stabilizing arisen wholesome states and so forth, even unto maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, vigor, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called superior practice.

This sublime practice, together with the previously mentioned mental concentration (*citta-samādhi*), is collectively termed the "basis for psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice of mental concentration.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who dwells in all wholesome dharmas with a mind that is neither depressed nor even extremely weak; he reflects thus:
"It is most appropriate that I dwell in wholesome dharmas with a mind that is neither depressed nor even extremely weak."
By the predominant power of this mind, he attains samādhi; this is called "mind-samādhi.

Having accomplished mind-samādhi, he arouses desire for the purpose of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, and so forth, up to the purpose of stabilizing arisen wholesome states and even maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called "superior practice" (*adhicitta*).

These aforementioned sublime practices and the previously described mental samādhi are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice of mental samādhi.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to a wholesome mind and reflects:
"It is most appropriate that I have now given rise to such a wholesome mind."
By the predominant power of that mind, he attains *samādhi*; this is called "mind-*samādhi*.

Having accomplished mind-*samādhi*, he generates desire (*chanda*) for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states; as it is explained at length, up to generating desire for the sake of stabilizing, maintaining, and upholding arisen wholesome states. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity (*upekṣā*), he possesses—this is called "excellent practice" (*adhicitta-pratipad*).

These aforementioned superior practices and the previously described mental samādhi are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of mental samādhi.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to a virtuous mind accompanied by non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, and he reflects:
"It is most appropriate that I have now given rise to this virtuous mind accompanied by non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion."
By the predominant power of that mind, he attains samādhi; this is called "mind-samādhi.

Having accomplished mind-samādhi, he arouses desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, and so on, up to: for the sake of establishing arisen wholesome states and even for the sake of sustaining the mind. Whatever desire, effort, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called "superior practice."

These aforementioned superior practices and the previously described mental samādhi are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of superior practice through mental samādhi.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to a virtuous mind free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and he reflects:
"It is most appropriate that I have now given rise to this virtuous mind free from greed, hatred, and delusion."
By the predominant power of that mind, he attains *samādhi*; this is called "mind-*samādhi*.

Having accomplished mind-*samādhi*, he arouses desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, and so on, up to: for the sake of stabilizing arisen wholesome states, even unto maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, vigor, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity (*upekṣā*) he possesses, these are called "superior practice" (*adhicitta*).

These very sublime practices and the previously mentioned mental samādhis are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of sublime practice through mental samādhi.

All mental samādhis arise from the mind, are accumulated by the mind, are of the same nature as the mind, and are produced by the mind; therefore, they are called the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of sublime practice through mental samādhi."

Regarding the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the excellence of concentration through contemplation" (*vīmaṃsā-samādhi-padhāna-saṃkhāra-iddhipāda*): what is contemplation, what is concentration, what is excellence, and what is the application of effort, such that it is called the basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the excellence of concentration through contemplation?

In this context, "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to the discernment, thorough discernment, and supreme discernment of phenomena; the understanding, equal understanding, and proximate understanding; the sagacity, penetration, investigation, intelligence, awakening, clarity, and wise activity arising from the wholesome states produced by renunciation and seclusion for one who has gone forth—this is called contemplation.

Samādhi refers to the mental abiding, thorough abiding, close abiding, and stable abiding that arise through the predominance of contemplation; it is non-distraction, non-disorder, withdrawal, cessation, concentration, and one-pointedness of mind—this is called samādhi.
"Victorious" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path arising from the predominance of contemplation; this is called "victorious.
"Victorious practice" refers to a bhikṣu who, relying on past contemplation, attains samādhi; this is called "contemplative samādhi."

Having accomplished the concentration of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-samādhi*), he generates desire for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen; [as explained at length] up to: for the sake of establishing wholesome states that have already arisen, even unto maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, vigor, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity (*upekṣā*) he possesses, these are called "superior practice" (*viśeṣa-carita*).

These very superior practices (*viśeṣacaryā*) and the previously mentioned meditative absorptions of observation (*vipaśyanā-samādhi*) are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of the meditative absorption of observation.

As it is with observation based on the past, so it is extensively explained for observation based on the future and the present; the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; the trainee (*śaikṣa*), the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and neither-trainee-nor-one-beyond-training; and those to be abandoned by seeing, those to be abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned. It is the same in detail for all these cases.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who dwells in non-examination regarding all wholesome dharmas; he reflects thus:
"I should not now dwell in non-examination regarding all wholesome dharmas."
"However, it is right for me to abide in and carefully examine all wholesome phenomena.
Through the predominant power of this examination, he attains samādhi; this is called the samādhi of examination (vipaśyanā-samādhi).

Having accomplished the samādhi of contemplation, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states that have already arisen; [this is] explained at length up to: for the sake of stabilizing wholesome states that have already arisen, even unto the maintenance of the mind. Whatever desire, vigor, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called superior practice.

These aforementioned superior practices and the previously described contemplative samādhi are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of superior practice through contemplative samādhi.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to unwholesome contemplation and thinks to himself:
"I should not give rise to unwholesome contemplation now."
"However, it is only right that I should eliminate unwholesome contemplation and cultivate wholesome contemplation.
Through the predominant power of this contemplation, he attains samādhi; this is called *vipaśyanā-samādhi*.

Having accomplished the samādhi of contemplation, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states; this is explained at length up to: for the sake of establishing arisen wholesome states and so forth, even unto maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, vigor, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called "superior practice."

This sublime practice (*adhiprajñā-caryā*) together with the previously mentioned meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of contemplation is collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice of the samādhi of contemplation.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to unwholesome contemplation accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion, and he reflects:
"I should not now give rise to unwholesome contemplation accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion."

"However, it is right for me to abandon unwholesome contemplation associated with greed, hatred, and delusion, and to cultivate wholesome contemplation associated with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
Through the predominant power of this contemplation, he attains samādhi; this is called "samādhi through contemplation."

Having accomplished the samādhi of contemplation, he arouses desire for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen; this is explained at length up to: for the sake of establishing wholesome states that have already arisen and even for the sake of maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, exertion, faith, or even equanimity he possesses is called "superior practice."

These aforementioned superior practices and the previously described meditative concentration of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-samādhi*) are collectively termed the "basis for psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of the meditative concentration of contemplation.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to an unwholesome contemplation that is not free from greed, hatred, and delusion; he then reflects:
"I should not now give rise to this unwholesome contemplation that is not free from greed, hatred, and delusion."

"However, it is right for me to abandon unwholesome contemplation that is not free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and to cultivate wholesome contemplation that is free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Through the predominant power of this contemplation, he attains samādhi; this is called *vipaśyanā-samādhi*.

Having accomplished the concentration of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-samādhi*), he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states; this is explained at length up to: for the sake of stabilizing arisen wholesome states and so forth, even unto maintaining the mind. Whatever desire, vigor, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity (*upekṣā*) he possesses, these are called superior practice (*viśeṣa-carita*).

These aforementioned superior practices and the previously described meditative concentration of observation are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of the meditative concentration of observation.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who dwells in the careful observation of all wholesome dharmas, and he thinks:
"It is most appropriate that I dwell in the careful observation of wholesome dharmas."
Through the predominant power of that contemplation, he attains samādhi; this is called "contemplation-samādhi" (*vipaśyanā-samādhi*).

Having accomplished contemplation-samādhi, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, and so forth, up to generating desire for the sake of establishing, stabilizing, and maintaining arisen wholesome states. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, he possesses—this is called "superior practice" (*adhicitta-pratipatti*).

These aforementioned superior practices and the previously described meditative concentration of observation are collectively termed the "basis for psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of the meditative concentration of observation.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to skillful observation and reflects thus:
"It is most appropriate that I have now given rise to such skillful observation."
Through the predominant power of this contemplation, he attains samādhi; this is called "contemplation-samādhi" (vipaśyanā-samādhi).

Having accomplished contemplation-samādhi, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, and so on, as extensively described, up to the stabilization of arisen wholesome states and even the sustaining of the mind. All his desire, diligence, faith, and so on, up to equanimity—these are called "superior practice" (adhicitta-pratipatti).

These aforementioned superior practices and the previously described meditative concentration of observation are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of the meditative concentration of observation.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to a virtuous observation accompanied by non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, and he reflects:
"It is most appropriate that I have now given rise to this virtuous observation accompanied by non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion."
Through the predominant power of this contemplation, he attains samādhi; this is called "samādhi through contemplation.

Having accomplished samādhi through contemplation, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen unwholesome states, and so on, as extensively described, up to the stabilization of arisen wholesome states and the maintenance of the mind. All his desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity, is called "superior practice."

This sublime practice and the previously described meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of observation are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the sublime practice of the meditative concentration of observation.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to a wholesome observation free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and he thinks:
"It is most appropriate that I have now given rise to this wholesome observation free from greed, hatred, and delusion."
By the dominant power of this contemplation, he attains samādhi; this is called "contemplation-samādhi" (*vipaśyanā-samādhi*).

Having accomplished contemplation-samādhi, he generates desire for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, and so on, up to generating desire for the sake of stabilizing, maintaining, and upholding arisen wholesome states. Whatever desire, diligence, faith, and so forth, up to equanimity he possesses, these are called "superior practice" (*adhicitta-pratipatti*).

This very superior practice (*adhiprajñā*) and the previously mentioned meditative concentration of observation (*vipaśyanā-samādhi*) are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of the meditative concentration of observation.

All meditative concentrations of observation arise from observation, are accumulated by observation, belong to the category of observation, and are produced by observation; therefore, they are called the "basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of the superior practice of the meditative concentration of observation."
Why are these four called *ṛddhipāda* (bases of psychic power)?

Herein, "psychic power" (*ṛddhi*) refers to all that possesses the nature of psychic power—whether it has possessed the nature of psychic power in the past, will possess the nature of psychic power in the future, or possesses the nature of psychic power in the present.

That dharma is precisely the transformation of one into many and the transformation of many into one; it may manifest or become hidden, being transformed by the vision of wisdom. Solid and thick obstructing objects such as walls and stones pass through the body without hindrance, as if treading upon empty space; one can emerge from or submerge into the earth with sovereign ease and without obstruction.
Just as one can draw water from flowing through solid obstructions or even through space while standing in water;

or just as one may sit cross-legged upon level ground and travel back and forth through the air without any hindrance, like a bird in flight; or just as one can reach out and touch the sun and moon disks—which possess great divine power and majesty—as easily as reaching for one’s own alms bowl; and even reaching up to the Brahma-world with sovereign mastery over transformations, such that their wondrous functions are difficult to fathom—therefore, they are called "divine" (*deva*).

In this context, "foot" refers to the diligent and uninterrupted cultivation of those dharmas until they reach the stage of accomplishment; because it can give rise to those dharmas and serve as their basis, it is called a "foot."

Furthermore, these four sublime concentrations are also called "powers" (*ṛddhi*) and also called "bases" (*pāda*); they are so named because their functioning is difficult to fathom and because they serve as the basis for superior qualities.

Furthermore, regarding the four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*): these are merely conventional designations, conceptual constructs, and verbal expressions termed "bases of supernormal power," because Buddhas and their disciples, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have all collectively established such names.

Furthermore, regarding the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): they consist of the accomplishment of the superior practices of the four types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—namely, those based on desire, effort, mind, and investigation—as previously described;

these collectively are termed the "bases of psychic power. Chapter Nine: The Foundations of Mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Part One. At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"I shall now briefly explain for you the method of practicing the four foundations of mindfulness.
That is to say, a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body in this internal body; endowed with right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, he removes worldly greed and sorrow."
Abiding in contemplation of the body with regard to that external body, if one possesses right effort, right mindfulness, and right awareness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
Abiding in contemplation of the body with regard to both internal and external bodies, if one possesses right effort, right mindfulness, and right awareness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
The detailed explanation for the three—feelings, mind, and phenomena—regarding both the internal and external is likewise the same.
This is the method for the present cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness;
it should be understood that the past and future bhikṣus who cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness do so in the same manner.
"How does one dwell in contemplation of the body with regard to this internal body, possessing right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, removing worldly greed and sorrow?
'Internal body' refers to one's own body that exists within the present continuum and has been attained without being lost."

Regarding "contemplating the body within this internal body," it refers to a bhikṣu who, from the feet to the crown of the head, observes and contemplates this internal body according to its various locations as being filled with manifold impurities and foulness—namely, that within this body there are only various kinds of hair, body hair, nails, teeth, filth, skin, flesh, sinews, veins, bones, marrow, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, fat, grease, brain, membranes, pus, blood, abdominal fat, tears, sweat, mucus, saliva, the two receptacles of raw and cooked food, and excrement and urine.

When one contemplates the sign of impurity in this way, the discernment, thorough discernment, and supreme discernment that arise regarding phenomena; the understanding, equal understanding, and proximate understanding; the mental agility, penetration, investigation, sagacity, clarity of awakening, and the practice of wisdom—this is *vipaśyanā*, which is the contemplation of the internal body and is also called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
When one achieves this contemplation—manifesting its practice, universal practice, pervasive practice, shifting movement, and analytical understanding—it is called "abiding.

That practitioner of contemplation is able to arouse diligent effort that is vigorous, resilient, fierce, blazing, difficult to restrain, and characterized by an unremittingly exhortative mind; furthermore, being able to act with such urgency and swiftness therein is called "possessing right effort."

That practitioner of contemplation is able to give rise to the discernment of phenomena up to vipaśyanā; furthermore, they are able to cause this arisen superior wisdom to progress to the stage of being superior, more superior, and most superior, reaching fulfillment and complete fulfillment—this is called being endowed with right knowledge.

That practitioner of contemplation, possessing mindfulness and recollection, focused attention and remembrance—being without forgetfulness or loss, without omission or leakage, not losing the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and having a mind characterized by clear recollection—is said to be "endowed with right mindfulness."

Regarding all objects of desire, whatever constitutes greed, intense greed, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, fondness, infatuation, relishing, pervasive relishing, internal bondage, longing, immersion, the accumulation of suffering, and that which is of the nature of greed or born of greed—this, in its entirety, is termed "greed."

The mental distress arising from contact associated with the feeling of sorrow—characterized by uneven reception and subsumed under the category of dejection—is collectively termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*).

When that practitioner cultivates this contemplation, he is able to sever, fully comprehend, distance himself from, thoroughly distance himself from, subdue, thoroughly subdue, obscure, and eliminate both greed and sorrow as they arise toward the world; therefore, it is said that he "removes worldly greed and sorrow."

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, with regard to this internal body, contemplates and reflects upon the distinctions between the various elements, thinking: "Within this body there are only various earth elements, water elements, fire elements, wind elements, space elements, and consciousness elements."

When one contemplates the characteristics of the various elements (*dhātu*) in this manner, the discernment of phenomena (*dharma-pravicaya*) that arises, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, constitutes the contemplation of the internal body;
it is also called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, all as previously described.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who observes and contemplates this internal body as being full of many defects and afflictions; that is to say, this body is like a disease, like an abscess, like a piercing arrow, a source of harm; it is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, subject to fluctuation; it is weary, exhausted, frail, and gravely ill—a phenomenon subject to ruin; it is swift and unceasing, decaying and non-eternal, unreliable, and a phenomenon subject to transformation.

When one contemplates the defects of the body in this manner, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of the internal body and is also called the application of mindfulness to the body.
Abiding with right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.
How does he dwell observing the body in the external body?
If one is endowed with right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one removes worldly greed and sorrow.

Regarding the "external body," this refers to one's own body that exists within the present continuum but has not yet been attained or has already been lost, as well as all bodily forms belonging to other sentient beings.

Regarding the contemplation of the body by following the body externally: this refers to a bhikṣu who, within the body of another, observes and contemplates from the feet to the crown of the head according to their respective locations, seeing it as filled with various kinds of impurities and foulness—namely, that within that body there are only various hairs of the head and body, nails, teeth, and so forth, up to and including feces and urine.

When one contemplates the signs of impurity in this manner, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, constitutes the contemplation of the external body and is also termed the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who contemplates and reflects upon the differentiation of the elements within another’s body, perceiving that within that body there are only various earth elements, water elements, fire elements, wind elements, space elements, and consciousness elements.

When one contemplates the characteristics of the various elements (*dhātu*) in this manner, the discernment of phenomena (*dharma-pravicaya*) that arises, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, constitutes the contemplation of the external body and is also called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who contemplates and reflects upon the many defects within another’s body, thinking: "That body is like a disease, like an abscess," and so on, as extensively explained, up to: "it is a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay."

When one contemplates the faults and afflictions of the body in this way, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, constitutes the contemplation of the external body and is also called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Abiding with right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.
How does one abide in the contemplation of the body with regard to the internal and external body?
If one is endowed with right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one removes worldly greed and sorrow.
Regarding "the internal body," this refers to one's own body, which exists within the present continuum and has been attained without being lost.

The "external body" refers to one's own body that is currently within the continuum but has not yet been attained or has already been lost, as well as the bodily characteristics of other sentient beings.
These two types taken together are called the internal and external body.

Regarding "contemplating the body by following the body internally and externally," this refers to a bhikṣu who combines his own body and the bodies of others into a single aggregate, and observes and contemplates them from the feet to the crown of the head according to their respective locations, seeing that they are filled with various kinds of impurities and foulness—namely, that these and those bodies consist only of various hairs, body hair, nails, and teeth, and so on, in detail, up to feces and urine.

When one contemplates the signs of impurity in this manner, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, constitutes the contemplation of the body internally and externally, and is also termed the application of mindfulness to the body.
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who combines his own body and the bodies of others into a single aggregate, observing and contemplating the distinctions between the various elements (dhātus), thinking: "In these and those bodies, there are only various earth elements, water elements, fire elements, wind elements, space elements, and consciousness elements."

When one contemplates the characteristics of the various elements (*dhātu*) in this manner, the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) that arises, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, constitutes the contemplation of the body internally and externally; it is also called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who unites his own body and the bodies of others into a single aggregate, contemplating and reflecting upon their many defects and afflictions; that is to say, these and those bodies are like diseases and like abscesses, and so on, as extensively explained, up to: they are phenomena subject to transformation and decay.

When one contemplates the defects of the body in this manner, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of the body internally and externally, and it is also called the application of mindfulness to the body.
Abiding with right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.
How does he abide observing feelings internally?
If one possesses right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
Internal feeling refers to one's own feeling, which exists within one's present continuum and has been attained without being lost.

Regarding the contemplation of internal feelings as feelings: it means that a bhikṣu, with respect to these internal feelings, observes and contemplates the various characteristics of internal feelings; when experiencing a pleasant feeling, he knows as it truly is, "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling"; when experiencing a painful feeling, he knows as it truly is, "I am experiencing a painful feeling"; and when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows as it truly is, "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."

When experiencing a pleasant bodily sensation, he knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a pleasant bodily sensation. When experiencing a painful bodily sensation, he knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a painful bodily sensation. When experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant bodily sensation, he knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant bodily sensation."

When experiencing a pleasant mental feeling, one knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a pleasant mental feeling. When experiencing a painful mental feeling, one knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a painful mental feeling. When experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant mental feeling, one knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant mental feeling."

When experiencing a pleasant feeling with attachment, he knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling with attachment. When experiencing a painful feeling with attachment, he knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a painful feeling with attachment. When experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling with attachment, he knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling with attachment. When experiencing a pleasant feeling without attachment, he knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling without attachment. When experiencing a painful feeling without attachment, he knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a painful feeling without attachment. When experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling without attachment, he knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling without attachment."

When experiencing a feeling of pleasure that is dependent on craving, he knows as it really is: "I am experiencing a feeling of pleasure that is dependent on craving. When experiencing a feeling of pain that is dependent on craving, he knows as it really is: "I am experiencing a feeling of pain that is dependent on craving. When experiencing a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure that is dependent on craving, he knows as it really is: "I am experiencing a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure that is dependent on craving."

When experiencing a feeling of pleasure that is dependent on renunciation, one knows as it truly is: "I experience a feeling of pleasure that is dependent on renunciation. When experiencing a feeling of pain that is dependent on renunciation, one knows as it truly is: "I experience a feeling of pain that is dependent on renunciation. When experiencing a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant that is dependent on renunciation, one knows as it truly is: "I experience a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant that is dependent on renunciation."

When one thus contemplates the characteristics of internal feelings, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, is the contemplation of internal feelings; it is also called the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
The accomplishment of this contemplation—ranging from its active manifestation and subsequent practice up to its stage of liberation—is called "abiding.
When that practitioner of contemplation is able to arouse diligent effort and even further acts with such urgency and swiftness, they are said to be "endowed with right exertion."
That practitioner of meditation who is able to initiate the discernment of phenomena and even bring it to fulfillment and complete fulfillment is said to be "endowed with right awareness.
That practitioner of meditation who possesses mindfulness, recollection, and even the quality of mental clarity and retention is said to be "endowed with right mindfulness."
Regarding all objects of desire, whatever constitutes greed, intense greed, and even that which belongs to the category of greed or arises from greed, is collectively termed "greed" (*rāga*).

Whatever mental unease and uneven sensation arise from contact conducive to painful feeling (*daurmanasya-vedanīya-sparśa*), and which is subsumed under dejected sensation, is collectively termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*).

When that practitioner cultivates this contemplation, they are able to sever, fully comprehend, and even cause the disappearance and extinction of the two states of greed and sorrow that arise regarding the world; therefore, it is said that they eliminate worldly greed and sorrow.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, regarding internal sensations, contemplates and reflects upon their many faults and afflictions, thinking: "These sensations are like a disease, like an abscess," and so on, as extensively explained, up to: "they are phenomena subject to transformation and decay."

When one contemplates the disadvantages of feeling in this manner, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of internal feelings and is also called the application of mindfulness to feelings.
Abiding with right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, all as previously described.
How does he abide in the contemplation of external feelings by following feelings?
If one is endowed with right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.

External feelings refer to one's own feelings that are present within one's current continuum but have not yet been attained or have already been lost, as well as all the feelings belonging to other sentient beings.

Regarding the contemplation of external feelings by following them: it means that a bhikṣu observes and contemplates the various characteristics of the feelings of others; when experiencing a pleasant feeling, he knows as it truly is that he experiences a pleasant feeling; when experiencing a painful feeling, he knows as it truly is that he experiences a painful feeling; and when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows as it truly is that he experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

To speak at length, up to: when experiencing a feeling of pleasure that is dependent on renunciation, one knows as it really is that feeling of pleasure dependent on renunciation; when experiencing a feeling of pain that is dependent on renunciation, one knows as it really is that feeling of pain dependent on renunciation; and when experiencing a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure that is dependent on renunciation, one knows as it really is that feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure dependent on renunciation.

When one contemplates the characteristics of external feelings in this way, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of external feelings; it is also called the foundation of mindfulness established upon feelings.
Possessing right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness,
he removes worldly greed and sorrow,
as previously described.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who contemplates and reflects upon external sensations as being full of many faults and afflictions,
thinking: "Those sensations are like a disease, like an abscess."
Explaining at length up to: "these are phenomena subject to transformation and decay.
When one thus contemplates the disadvantages of feeling, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, [is what is meant].
This is the contemplation of external feelings;
it is also called the foundation of mindfulness of feelings.
Abiding therein with right effort, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, one removes worldly greed and sorrow, as was explained previously.
How does one dwell observing feelings in internal and external feelings?
It is by possessing right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, thereby removing worldly greed and sorrow.
"Internal feeling" refers to one's own feelings that exist within one's present continuum and have been attained without being lost.

External feeling refers to one's own feelings that are either currently present within one’s own continuum but have not yet been attained or have already been lost, as well as all the feelings belonging to other sentient beings.
These two types, when taken together, are called internal and external feelings.

Regarding the contemplation of feelings in internal and external feelings: this refers to a bhikṣu who, having combined his own and others' feelings into a single aggregate, observes and contemplates the characteristics of these feelings. When experiencing a pleasant feeling, he knows as it truly is that he is experiencing a pleasant feeling; when experiencing a painful feeling, he knows as it truly is that he is experiencing a painful feeling; and when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows as it truly is that he is experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

To speak at length, up to: when experiencing a feeling of pleasure that is dependent on renunciation, one knows as it truly is that one is experiencing a feeling of pleasure dependent on renunciation; when experiencing a feeling of pain that is dependent on renunciation, one knows as it truly is that one is experiencing a feeling of pain dependent on renunciation; and when experiencing a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure that is dependent on renunciation, one knows as it truly is that one is experiencing a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure dependent on renunciation.

When one contemplates the characteristics of all feelings in this manner, whatever discernment of phenomena there is, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, constitutes the contemplation of internal and external feelings; it is also called the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who unifies his own and others' feelings into a single aggregate, contemplating and reflecting upon the defects and dangers of all feelings, thinking: "These and those feelings are like a disease, like an abscess," and so on, as extensively explained, up to: "they are phenomena subject to transformation and decay."

When one contemplates the disadvantages of feeling in this manner, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of internal and external feelings; it is also called the application of mindfulness to feelings.
Abiding with right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, one removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously explained.
How does one dwell observing the mind internally?
If one possesses right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
"Internal mind" refers to one's own mind, which exists within the present continuum and has been attained without being lost.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind within the internal mind: it refers to a bhikṣu who, observing and reflecting upon the various characteristics of the internal mind, knows as it truly is when there is a mind with greed that "there is a mind with greed within," and knows as it truly is when there is a mind free from greed that "there is a mind free from greed within."

When there is a mind of hatred within, he knows as it truly is that there is a mind of hatred within; when there is a mind free from hatred within, he knows as it truly is that there is a mind free from hatred within.

When there is a mind of delusion within, he knows as it truly is that there is a mind of delusion within; when there is a mind free from delusion within, he knows as it truly is that there is a mind free from delusion within.

When the mind is concentrated internally, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is concentrated internally. When the mind is distracted internally, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is distracted internally.
When the mind is sunken internally, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is sunken internally. When the mind is uplifted internally, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is uplifted internally."

When the mind is constricted internally, he knows it as it truly is: "The mind is constricted internally. When the mind is expansive internally, he knows it as it truly is: "The mind is expansive internally.

When the mind is agitated internally, he knows it as it truly is: "The mind is agitated internally. When the mind is not agitated internally, he knows it as it truly is: "The mind is not agitated internally."

When the mind is not internally settled, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is not internally settled. When the mind is internally settled, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is internally settled.

When the mind is not internally concentrated, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is not internally concentrated. When the mind is internally concentrated, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is internally concentrated."

When the mind is not cultivated internally, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is not cultivated internally. When the mind is cultivated internally, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is cultivated internally.

When the mind is not liberated internally, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is not liberated internally. When the mind is liberated internally, he knows it as it truly is: "the mind is liberated internally."

When one contemplates the internal characteristics of the mind in this manner, all discernment regarding phenomena up to vipaśyanā constitutes the contemplation of the internal mind, which is also called the mindfulness-establishment of the mind.
The accomplishment of this contemplation, including its active manifestation, its subsequent practice, and even its stage of analytical application (*adhimukti-caryā*), is called "abiding.
When that practitioner of contemplation is able to arouse diligent effort and even acts with such urgency and swiftness therein, they are said to be "endowed with right exertion" (*samyag-vyāyāma*).
That practitioner of contemplation who is able to give rise to the discernment of phenomena, up to and including its fulfillment and complete fulfillment, is said to be "endowed with right knowledge.
That practitioner of contemplation who possesses mindfulness, recollection, and even the quality of mental clarity and retention, is said to be "endowed with right mindfulness."
Whatever greed, intense greed, and even the various forms of greed that arise toward objects of desire is collectively termed "greed" (*rāga*).
Whatever mental sorrow, unbalanced feeling, and dejected feeling produced by contact conducive to the experience of sorrow is collectively termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*).

When that practitioner cultivates this contemplation, they are able to sever, fully comprehend, and even cause the disappearance and extinction of the two states—greed and sorrow—that arise regarding the world; therefore, it is said that they eliminate greed and sorrow for the world.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who observes and contemplates the various internal states of mind as being full of many faults and afflictions, thinking: "This mind is like a disease, like an abscess," and so on, up to: "it is a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay."

When one contemplates the faults of the mind in this way, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of internal states; it is also called the application of mindfulness to the mind.
Abiding with right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.
What is the dwelling in contemplation of the mind by following the mind with respect to that external mind?
If one is endowed with right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
"External mind" refers to one's own mind when it exists within the present continuum but has not yet been attained or has already been lost, as well as all minds belonging to other sentient beings.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind by following the mind externally: this refers to a bhikṣu who observes and reflects upon the various characteristics of the minds of others; he knows a mind that has greed externally as it truly is—a mind with greed externally—and so on, up to knowing a liberated mind externally as it truly is—a liberated mind externally.

When one contemplates the external characteristics of the mind in this manner, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of the mind externally, and it is also called the application of mindfulness to the mind.
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who observes and contemplates the various external states of mind, perceiving many faults and afflictions therein; that is to say, he regards that mind as being like a disease, like an abscess, and so forth, up to: it is a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay.

When one contemplates the faults and afflictions of the mind in this way, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, is the contemplation of the external mind, and it is also called the mindfulness-establishment of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Abiding with right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.
How does one dwell observing the mind in the internal and external mind?
If one possesses right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
"Internal mind" refers to one's own mind that exists within the present continuum and has been attained without being lost.

The "external mind" refers to one's own mind when it is not present within the current continuum—either because it has not yet been attained or has already been lost—as well as all minds belonging to other sentient beings.
These two types combined are termed the "internal and external mind."

Regarding the contemplation of the mind by following the mind internally and externally: this refers to a bhikṣu who, taking the minds of both himself and others as a single aggregate, observes and contemplates the characteristics of those minds. He knows a mind with greed, as it truly is, to be a mind with greed; and so on, in detail, until he knows a liberated mind, as it truly is, to be a liberated mind.

When one contemplates the characteristics of the mind in this way, all discernment of phenomena up to *vipaśyanā* constitutes the contemplation of the mind internally and externally, and is also called the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who unites his own mind with that of others into a single aggregate, observing and reflecting upon its many faults and afflictions; that is, he views this and that mind as a disease and as an abscess, and so on, as extensively explained, up to: "it is a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay."

When one reflects in this way upon the faults of the mind, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of the internal and external mind; it is also called the application of mindfulness to the mind.
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, one removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously explained.
