The Ninth Chapter on the Foundations of Mindfulness, Part Two: How does one dwell in the contemplation of phenomena with respect to these internal phenomena?
If one possesses right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
Regarding "internal phenomena," this refers to one's own aggregates of perception and formations that exist within the present continuum and have been attained without being lost.

Regarding the contemplation of phenomena in relation to internal phenomena: it refers to a bhikṣu who, with respect to the five hindrances as internal phenomena, observes and contemplates the various characteristics of internal phenomena. When there is the internal hindrance of sensual desire, he knows as it truly is: "In me there is the internal hindrance of sensual desire. When there is no internal hindrance of sensual desire, he knows as it truly is: "In me there is no internal hindrance of sensual desire. Furthermore, he knows as it truly is: how the unarisen internal hindrance of sensual desire arises; how the arisen internal hindrance of sensual desire is abandoned; and how, once abandoned, it does not arise again in the future.

When one reflects in this way upon these internal phenomena, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, is the contemplation of internal phenomena and is also called the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
When one accomplishes this contemplation, from its active manifestation and subsequent practice up to the stage of conduct through understanding, it is called "abiding.
That practitioner of contemplation who is able to arouse diligent effort and even further acts with urgency and swiftness in this regard is said to be "endowed with right exertion."
That practitioner of meditation who is able to initiate the discernment of phenomena and even bring it to completion and perfect fulfillment is said to be "endowed with correct knowledge.
That practitioner of meditation who possesses mindfulness, recollection, and even the faculty of mental clarity and retention is said to be "endowed with correct mindfulness."
Regarding all objects of desire, whatever constitutes greed, intense greed, and even that which belongs to the category of greed or arises from greed, is collectively termed "greed" (*rāga*).

Whatever mental distress, unequanimity, and sorrow arise from contact associated with feelings of dissatisfaction, and which is comprised within dejection and sorrow, is collectively termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*).

When that practitioner cultivates this contemplation, they are able to sever, fully comprehend, and even cause the disappearance and extinction of the two states—greed and sorrow—that arise regarding the world; therefore, it is said that they eliminate greed and sorrow for the world.

As it was said regarding the internal hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), so too it is for the internal hindrances of ill will (*vyāpāda*), sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha*), restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who observes and contemplates the characteristics of internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*) within the six internal fetters (*saṃyojana*). Regarding the presence of an internal eye-fetter, he knows as it truly is: "I have an internal eye-fetter. Regarding the absence of an internal eye-fetter, he knows as it truly is: "I do not have an internal eye-fetter. Moreover, he knows as it truly is: how this internal eye-fetter that has not yet arisen comes to arise; how that which has already arisen is abandoned; and how, once abandoned, it shall not arise again in the future.

When one reflects in this way upon these internal phenomena, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, is the contemplation of internal phenomena and is also called the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Abiding with right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, one removes worldly greed and sorrow, all as previously explained.
Just as it was said regarding internal fetters of the eye, so too should it be understood for the internal fetters of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who observes and contemplates the characteristics of internal phenomena regarding the seven factors of enlightenment within. When the factor of mindfulness of the internal is present, he knows as it truly is: "In me, the factor of mindfulness of the internal is present. When the factor of mindfulness of the internal is absent, he knows as it truly is: "In me, the factor of mindfulness of the internal is absent. Moreover, he knows as it truly is that the factor of mindfulness of the internal which has not yet arisen will arise; that once arisen, it will remain firm, be not forgotten, and through cultivation, fulfillment, increase, and expansion, he will realize it through direct knowledge.

When one reflects in this way upon these internal phenomena, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of internal phenomena and is also called the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, one removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously explained.
Just as it was said regarding the internal factor of enlightenment (dhamma-sambojjhaṅga), the same applies to the other six internal factors of enlightenment and so forth.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, regarding the internal aggregates of perception and mental formations as they have been taught, contemplates and reflects upon their many defects, thinking: "These phenomena are like a disease, like an abscess," and so on, up to: "they are subject to transformation and decay."

When one contemplates the defects of phenomena in this way, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of internal phenomena and is also called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Abiding with right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.
How does he abide in the contemplation of phenomena regarding those external phenomena?
If one possesses right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.

Regarding external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*), these refer to one's own aggregates of perception and formations (*saṃjñā-skandha* and *saṃskāra-skandha*) that are either currently present within one's continuum, not yet attained, or already lost, as well as the aggregates of perception and formations of other sentient beings.

Regarding the contemplation of phenomena in accordance with phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*) with respect to external phenomena: it refers to a bhikṣu who, regarding the five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*) as external phenomena, observes and contemplates their various characteristics. He knows as it truly is that when the external hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is present, "there is the external hindrance of sensual desire"; he knows as it truly is that when the external hindrance of sensual desire is absent, "there is no external hindrance of sensual desire. Furthermore, he knows as it truly is how the unarisen external hindrance of sensual desire arises, how the arisen one is abandoned, and how, once abandoned, it does not arise again in the future.

When one contemplates these external phenomena in this manner, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of external phenomena and is also called the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, one removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously explained.
As it was said regarding the hindrance of external sensual desire, so too it is for the other four external hindrances.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, regarding the six external fetters (*bāhya-saṃyojana*), observes and contemplates the various characteristics of external phenomena. He knows, as it truly is, that when an external fetter of the eye exists, "there is an external fetter of the eye"; he knows, as it truly is, that when an external fetter of the eye does not exist, "there is no external fetter of the eye. Moreover, he knows, as it truly is, that the unarisen external fetter of the eye arises, that the arisen one is abandoned, and that once abandoned, it will not arise again in the future.

When one contemplates those external phenomena in this way, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of external phenomena and is also called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, one removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously explained.
As it was said regarding the external fetter of eye, so it is for the remaining five external fetters.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, regarding the phenomena of the other seven factors of enlightenment, observes and contemplates the characteristics of external phenomena. When there is the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness directed toward external objects, he knows as it truly is: "There is the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness directed toward external objects. When there is no factor of enlightenment of mindfulness directed toward external objects, he knows as it truly is: "There is no factor of enlightenment of mindfulness directed toward external objects. Moreover, he knows as it truly is how the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness directed toward external objects that has not yet arisen comes to arise, and once arisen, remains firm and stable; this is explained at length up to the point of realizing it through wisdom.

When one contemplates those external phenomena in this way, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of external phenomena and is also called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right situational awareness, one removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously explained.
Just as it was taught regarding the external factor of the awakening factor of mindfulness, so too should it be understood for the other six external awakening factors and so forth.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, regarding the external aggregate of perception and the aggregate of formations as previously described, contemplates and reflects upon their many disadvantages, thinking: "Those phenomena are like a disease, like an abscess," and so on, up to: "they are phenomena subject to transformation and decay."

When one contemplates the defects of phenomena in this way, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, is the contemplation of external phenomena and is also called the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Abiding with right effort, right comprehension, and right mindfulness, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.
How does one dwell in the contemplation of dharmas regarding internal and external dharmas?
If one possesses right effort, right awareness, and right mindfulness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
Regarding "internal phenomena," this refers to one's own aggregate of perception and aggregate of formations that exist within the present continuum and have been attained without being lost.

External phenomena refer to one's own aggregates of perception and formations that are either currently present in the continuum but have not yet been attained or have already been lost, as well as the aggregates of perception and formations of other sentient beings.
The combination of these two types is called internal and external phenomena (*dharmas*).

Regarding the practitioner who contemplates phenomena according to the phenomena (*dhammānupassī*) within these internal and external phenomena: it refers to a bhikṣu who combines the previously mentioned aggregates of self and others and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) into a single mass, observing and reflecting upon the characteristics of the phenomena of self and others—namely, the aforementioned five hindrances, six fetters, seven factors of enlightenment, and so forth—and discerning their presence or absence, whether they have arisen or not yet arisen, and the characteristic of their cessation such that they do not arise again.

When one contemplates internal and external phenomena in this manner, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including *vipaśyanā*, is the contemplation of internal and external phenomena, and it is also called the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removes worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who combines the aggregates of self and others, as well as the aggregate of formations, into a single mass; he observes and contemplates them as having many faults and afflictions, thinking: "These and those phenomena are like a disease, like an abscess," and so on, as extensively explained, up to: "they are phenomena subject to transformation and decay."

When one contemplates the defects and disadvantages of phenomena in this way, the discernment of phenomena that arises, up to and including vipaśyanā, is the contemplation of internal and external phenomena, and it is also called the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Abiding in right effort, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension, he removed worldly greed and sorrow, as previously described.
Chapter Eleven: The Noble Truths. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"This is the Noble Truth of Suffering.
If one reflects correctly upon such a Dharma never heard before, it will certainly give rise to vision, knowledge, illumination, and awakening."

Regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering, if one reflects upon these previously unheard teachings in accordance with reality, it will certainly give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.

Regarding this noble truth of the cessation of suffering, if one reflects upon these previously unheard teachings in accordance with reality, it will certainly give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.

This is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; if one reflects properly upon such previously unheard teachings, it will certainly give rise to vision, knowledge, wisdom, and awakening.
Furthermore, monks!

This noble truth of suffering should be fully known through higher wisdom; if one reflects properly upon such previously unheard teachings, it will certainly give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.

"This noble truth of the origin of suffering should be permanently abandoned through higher wisdom; if one reflects properly upon these teachings unheard before, there will certainly arise in them vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening."

"This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized through direct knowledge; if one reflects properly upon these teachings unheard before, there will surely arise vision, knowledge, wisdom, and awakening."

"This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering in this realm should be cultivated with higher wisdom; if one reflects properly upon such previously unheard teachings, there will certainly arise vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening."
Furthermore, monks!

This noble truth of suffering has been fully known by me through higher wisdom; if one reflects properly upon such previously unheard teachings, it will certainly give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.

"This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been permanently abandoned by me through higher knowledge; if one reflects properly upon such previously unheard teachings, it will certainly give rise to vision, wisdom, clarity, and awakening."

"This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized by me through direct knowledge; if one reflects properly upon such previously unheard teachings as these, there will certainly arise vision, wisdom, clarity, and awakening."

"This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering has been cultivated by me through direct knowledge; if one reflects properly upon such previously unheard teachings, it will certainly give rise to vision, wisdom, clarity, and awakening."

"O bhikṣus, you should know that regarding these Four Noble Truths, as long as I had not yet performed the three turnings of the twelve aspects—meaning as long as the eye, knowledge, wisdom, and awakening had not arisen—I was unable to liberate myself from and transcend this world of gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas; because my mind still dwelt extensively in perversion and had not been eliminated, I could not yet truthfully declare of myself: 'I have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"

Regarding these Four Noble Truths, when I had already performed the three turnings and twelve aspects—having thereby generated the eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening—I was able to attain liberation and deliverance from this world of gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, because I had eliminated the mind that dwells extensively in perversion.
"I have also already been able to truthfully declare for myself that I have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

When this Dharma was spoken, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya and eighty thousand devaputras were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, and the pure Dharma-eye arose within them regarding all phenomena.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kauṇḍinya, saying:
"Have you understood the Dharma that has been taught?
Kauṇḍinya replied:
"I have now understood.
A second and a third time he spoke thus.
Because Kauṇḍinya was the first to understand the Dharma, the world collectively named him Ajñāta.
Upon hearing these words, the Earth-Spirit Yakṣa leaped for joy and cried out in a loud voice:

"The Buddha has now, at this Deer Park in the Place of the Sages' Discourse in Vārāṇasī, out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world and desiring to enable them to attain benefit and happiness, turned the Wheel of Dharma three times—a wheel endowed with twelve aspects of activity."
Among the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, celestial Māras, and Brahmās in the world, none are able to turn it according to the Dharma.
Because the Buddha has turned this unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, Kauṇḍinya and the others have already seen the Noble Truths.
From this day forth, the hosts of devas shall gradually increase, while the hosts of asuras shall gradually diminish.
Consequently, through this succession of events, all devas and humans shall obtain supreme benefit, welfare, and peace.
When the *khecarī* yakṣas heard this sound, they joyfully proclaimed it to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
They, in turn, raised their voices and passed the word on to one another, so that in a mere moment the sound reached the Brahma Heaven.

At that time, having heard this, the Great Brahmā King rejoiced, celebrating that the Buddha had turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to boundless sentient beings.
Since this discourse explains the matter of turning the wheel of Dharma, it is therefore titled the *Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma*.
At that time, the five bhikṣus and eighty thousand devaputras, having heard this sutra, rejoiced, believed, accepted, and practiced it.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering?

It refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; in brief, it is the suffering of all the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
What is the suffering of birth?
"Birth" refers to the various classes of sentient beings.

Within each respective assembly of sentient beings, it denotes birth, rebirth, entering, manifestation, the acquisition of the aggregates (*skandha*), the acquisition of the elements (*dhātu*), and the acquisition of the sense bases (*āyatana*); the arising of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) within the aggregates is collectively termed "birth."
For what reason is birth said to be suffering? When sentient beings are born, they experience and undergo various bodily sufferings;

they experience and undergo various mental sufferings; they experience and undergo various sufferings of both body and mind; they experience and undergo various bodily torments; they experience and undergo various mental torments; they experience and undergo various torments of both body and mind; they experience and undergo various bodily burnings; they experience and undergo various mental burnings; they experience and undergo various burnings of both body and mind. For these reasons, birth is said to be suffering.
Furthermore, at the time of birth, one experiences two kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
second, the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Therefore, it is called the suffering of birth.

What is the suffering of old age? Old age refers to the state of being aged: the hair falls out and turns white; the skin becomes slack and the face wrinkled; the body bends and the back stoops; breathing becomes increasingly labored; one walks leaning on a staff; the limbs become mottled and blackened; one declines and becomes dull-witted; the faculties ripen and deteriorate; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) become worn out and decayed; and one becomes decrepit, frail, and impaired. All of this is collectively termed "old age."
For what reason is aging said to be suffering?

When sentient beings grow old, they experience and undergo various forms of physical suffering, and so forth, up to experiencing and undergoing various forms of the burning of body and mind; therefore, aging is said to be suffering.
Furthermore, in old age one experiences three kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā);
second, the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
The third is the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkha); thus it is called the suffering of old age. What is the suffering of illness?

Illness refers to headaches, eye pain, ear pain, nose pain, tongue pain, facial pain, lip pain, tooth pain, palate pain, throat pain, heart pain; wind disorders, coughing disorders, respiratory disorders, belching disorders; leprosy, hemorrhoids, dysentery, smallpox; cold-fever disorders, heat-fever disorders, insanity, epilepsy; vomiting, ulcers and swellings, scabies, ringworm, moles, goiters; diarrhea, discharges and leakage, abdominal tumors, emaciation from consumption, and various other ailments arising from the body and mind—collectively these are termed "illness."
For what reason is illness said to be suffering?

Because when sentient beings are ill, they experience and undergo various physical sufferings, and so forth, up to experiencing and undergoing various instances of the burning of body and mind; for these reasons, illness is said to be suffering.
Furthermore, at the time of illness, one experiences two kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā);
second, the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā). Therefore, it is called the suffering of illness.
What is the suffering of death?

Death refers to the various classes of sentient beings as they shift, disintegrate, and vanish from their respective groups; it is their falling away and separation, the cessation of vitality, warmth, and consciousness, the non-functioning of the life-faculty, the destruction of the aggregates, and their premature demise or passing away—this is collectively termed "death."
For what reason is death said to be suffering?

Because at the time of death, sentient beings experience and undergo various forms of physical suffering, and so forth, up to experiencing and undergoing various forms of the burning of both body and mind; for these reasons, death is said to be suffering.
Furthermore, at the time of death, one undergoes three kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā);
second, the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
Third is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*); hence it is called the suffering of death.
What is the suffering of association with the disliked (*apriyasaṃprayogaduḥkha*)?

Association with the disliked refers to when sentient beings encounter those who are unlovely, unpleasant, disagreeable, and contrary to their will—being together with them, sharing a single location as companions, not being separated or distinct, not parting or dispersing, but gathering and uniting; this is collectively termed "association with the disliked."
For what reason is association with the disliked said to be suffering?

It is because when sentient beings encounter those they dislike, they experience and undergo various forms of physical suffering, and so forth, up to experiencing and undergoing various forms of the burning of both body and mind; for these reasons, it is called suffering.
Furthermore, when encountering those one hates, one experiences two kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā);
second, the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā). Therefore, it is called the suffering of encountering those one hates.
What is the suffering of separation from the beloved?

Separation from the beloved refers to sentient beings being separated from those who are dear, pleasant, delightful, and agreeable—to not being together with them, not being in the same place, not being companions, being distinct and scattered, not gathering, and not being in union; this is collectively termed "separation from the beloved."
For what reason is separation from the beloved said to be suffering?

It is because when sentient beings experience separation from those they love, they undergo and take upon themselves various physical sufferings, and so forth, up to undergoing and taking upon themselves various instances of the burning of both body and mind; for these reasons, it is called suffering.
Furthermore, at the time of separation from what is loved, one undergoes three kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā); second, the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
The third is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*), which is why it is called the suffering of separation from the beloved (*priyaviprayogaduḥkha*).
What is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks (*yad apīcchan paryeṣamāṇo na labhate*)?

"Not obtaining" refers to seeking after agreeable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and various requisites for sustaining the body; when these are not obtained, not acquired, not met, not encountered, not accomplished, and not brought together, this is collectively termed the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
For what reason is it said that not obtaining what one seeks is suffering?

It is because when sentient beings do not obtain what they seek, they experience and undergo various forms of physical suffering, and so forth, up to experiencing and undergoing various forms of the burning affliction of both body and mind; for these reasons, it is called suffering.
Furthermore, when one fails to obtain what is sought, two kinds of suffering are experienced:
first, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
second, the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Therefore, it is called the suffering of not obtaining what is sought (*apriya-saṃprayoga-duḥkha*).
What is the brief explanation of the suffering of all five aggregates of clinging?

The five aggregates of clinging refer to the aggregate of form-clinging and the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness-clinging; these collectively are termed the five aggregates of clinging.
For what reason are all five aggregates of clinging briefly described as suffering?
It is because the five aggregates of clinging are impermanent and fluctuating, weary and frail, and are by nature subject to disintegration.
Swift and unceasing, subject to decay and impermanence, and unreliable—these are phenomena characterized by transformation and disintegration.
They increase and decrease; they abide briefly before swiftly perishing; they exist having previously been non-existent, and having existed, they return to non-existence.
For this reason, it is briefly stated that all five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
As it is said, the nature of the aggregates of clinging is suffering because they are unstable and because they are contrary to the minds of the Noble Ones.

Regarding these various sufferings being called the Truth of Suffering: it means that what is called "impermanent" is truly impermanent, and what is called "suffering" is truly suffering. Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, such dharmas of suffering abide as phenomena within the realm of reality (dharmadhātu).

All Tathāgatas have spontaneously attained mastery and, through their perfect awakening, proclaim, establish, differentiate, and reveal it so that it is made manifest: namely, "this is impermanence," "this is suffering," "this is the nature of impermanence," "this is the nature of suffering"; it is true, it is real, it is the truth, it is suchness; it is not false, not deceptive, not inverted, and not otherwise. Therefore, it is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Regarding the term "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*): "Noble" refers to the Buddhas and their disciples; these are their truths, meaning that they know, see, understand, and perfectly awaken to them as truths.
For these reasons, it is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.

Furthermore, the Noble Truth of Suffering is a conventional designation, a conceptual construct, and a verbal expression termed "the Noble Truth of Suffering," because Buddhas and their disciples, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, have all collectively established such a name.
What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?

It refers to all craving, craving for renewed existence, craving accompanied by delight, and the specific delight and craving for this or that; such, in brief, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

If explained in detail, then the two cravings, the three cravings, and further the three, four, five, and six cravings; as well as all unwholesome dharmas, all wholesome dharmas associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), and all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*)—all these are called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.

For what reason are all forms of craving, craving for future existence, craving accompanied by delight, and the specific cravings for this or that, all termed the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering?

It is because these four types of craving are the root, the path, and the causal condition for suffering in the past, future, and present; as it is explained at length, even until after the dissolution of this body, the fruit of suffering arises with these as its cause. Therefore, they are called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.

For what reason are the two types of craving, the three types of craving, and furthermore the three, four, five, and six types of craving—as well as all unwholesome dharmas, all wholesome dharmas associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), and all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*)—all designated as the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering?

It means that all these phenomena are the fundamental cause, the path, and the condition for suffering in the past, future, and present; as explained at length, even until after the destruction of this body, the fruit of suffering arises with these as its cause.
As it has been said, craving and so forth are all causes of suffering and serve as its root, for they draw forth manifold sufferings.

Thus, when craving and so forth are called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), it means that what is named "craving" and so forth is in reality indeed craving and so forth; what is named "origination" is in reality indeed origination. Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, this dharma of origination abides as such within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). All Tathāgatas naturally penetrate this, and through their equal awakening, they proclaim, designate, establish, differentiate, and reveal it so that it is made manifest, saying: "This is craving and so forth; this is origination; this is the nature of craving and so forth; this is the nature of origination. It is true and real, the truth and suchness; it is not false, not deceptive, not inverted, and not otherwise. Therefore, it is called the Truth of Origination.

Regarding the term "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*): "Noble" refers to the Buddhas and their disciples; these are their truths, meaning that they know, see, understand, and perfectly awaken to these as truths.
For these reasons, it is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.

Furthermore, regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering: it is a conventional designation, a conceptual label, and a verbal expression termed "the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering," because Buddhas and their disciples, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, have all collectively established such a name.
What is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering?

It is the complete and permanent abandonment, relinquishing, vomiting out, exhaustion, fading away, cessation, pacification, and disappearance of that very craving, the craving for renewed existence, the craving accompanied by delight, and the delight in this or that; such, in brief, is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

If explained in detail, it refers to the two cravings, the three cravings, and furthermore the three, four, five, and six cravings; as well as all unwholesome dharmas, all contaminated wholesome dharmas, and all fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and entanglements—when these are abandoned without remainder, forever relinquished, vomited out, exhausted, detached from passion, ceased, stilled, and vanished, they are all called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

For what reason are craving, craving for renewed existence, craving accompanied by delight, and the specific cravings for this or that—when these are abandoned without remainder, relinquished, vomited out, exhausted, detached from passion, ceased, stilled, and vanished—all termed the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering?

That is to say, if these four types of craving have not been abandoned, not fully understood, not extinguished, and not vomited out, then the fruits of suffering in future existence will continue to arise;
if they have been abandoned, fully understood, extinguished, and vomited out, then the fruits of suffering in future existence will no longer arise.
Therefore, this permanent cessation and so forth is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

For what reason are these—namely, the two types of craving, the three types of craving, and furthermore the four, five, six, and all types of craving; as well as all unwholesome dharmas, all wholesome dharmas associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), and all fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*)—when they are abandoned without remainder, cast off, vomited out, exhausted, detached from passion, ceased, stilled, and vanished, all collectively termed the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering?

That is to say, if these phenomena have not been abandoned, have not been fully understood, have not been extinguished, and have not been vomited out, then the subsequent fruit of suffering will continue to arise;
if they have been abandoned, have been fully understood, have been extinguished, and have been vomited out, then the subsequent fruit of suffering will no longer arise.
Therefore, this permanent cessation and so forth is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

This very Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is also called a dwelling, an island, a refuge, a sanctuary, a destination, freedom from sorrow, freedom from illness, immortality, the absence of burning, the absence of feverish affliction, security, coolness, tranquility, a virtuous state, auspiciousness, bliss, immovability, and Nirvana.
As it is said that *nirvāṇa* is the true cessation of suffering, for it is the ultimate fruit of all ascetics (*śramaṇa*).

Thus, that which is called "cessation" and so forth refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): this is named *nirvāṇa* and is truly *nirvāṇa*; this is named "cessation" and is truly cessation. Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, such a dharma of cessation abides as the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). All Tathāgatas naturally penetrate it, fully awaken to it, proclaim it, establish it, analyze and reveal it so that it is made manifest, saying: "This is *nirvāṇa*, this is cessation, this is the nature of *nirvāṇa*, this is the nature of cessation. It is true and real; it is the truth and suchness; it is not false, not deceptive, not inverted, and not otherwise. Therefore, it is called the Truth of Cessation.
Regarding the term "Noble Truth" (*āryasatya*): "Noble" refers to the Buddhas and their disciples; this is their truth, meaning that they know, see, understand, and perfectly awaken to this as truth.
For these reasons, it is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

Furthermore, regarding the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering: it is a conventional designation, a mental construct, and a verbal expression termed "the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering," because Buddhas and their disciples, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, have all collectively established this name.
What is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?

It refers to that which is the path and the noble practice, which, regarding the past, future, and present, can bring about the permanent severance, the relinquishing, the vomiting out, the exhaustion, the detachment from passion, the cessation, the pacification, and the disappearance of suffering.
What, then, is this? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
What is right view?

It refers to a noble disciple who contemplates suffering as suffering, origination as origination, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; associated with untainted mental attention, it consists of all discernment, thorough discernment, and supreme discernment regarding phenomena; as well as comprehension, equal comprehension, and proximate comprehension; keenness, penetration, investigation, sagacity, the practice of awakening, clarity, wisdom, and insight (*vipaśyanā*). This is called right view.
What is right thought?

It refers to when a noble disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, up to contemplating the path as the path; it consists of all thought, thorough thought, and proximate thought associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*); seeking, thorough seeking, and proximate seeking; investigating, thorough investigation, and proximate investigation; that which causes the mind to engage with phenomena through coarse movement—this is called right thought.
What is right speech?

It refers to a noble disciple who, through the power of discernment associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), contemplates suffering as suffering up to the contemplation of the path as the path; thereby, setting aside the four types of verbal misconduct that lead to wrong livelihood, they attain—regarding other forms of verbal misconduct—an untainted abstention, superior abstention, proximate abstention, extreme abstention, the discipline of tranquility, non-action, non-creation, relinquishment, protection, a raft, a bridge, a dam, a wall, and a moat. This unmanifest vocal karma (*avijñapti-vāk-karman*) which does not transgress nor possess the nature of transgressing, and does not overstep nor possess the nature of overstepping those restraints, is called right speech.
What is right action?

It refers to a noble disciple who, by contemplating suffering as suffering up to contemplating the path as the path, through the power of discernment associated with untainted attention, abandons the three types of bodily misconduct that lead to wrong livelihood; the untainted abstention from remaining bodily misconduct, up to the unmanifest bodily karma, is called right action.
What is right livelihood?

It refers to a noble disciple who contemplates suffering as suffering, up to contemplating the path as the path; through the power of discernment associated with untainted mental attention, they attain the untainted abandonment of physical and verbal misconduct that constitutes wrong livelihood, up to the unmanifest karma of body and speech—this is called right livelihood.
What is right effort?

It refers to the noble disciple who, contemplating suffering as suffering and so forth up to contemplating the path as the path, possesses all that is diligence, vigor, fortitude, power, intensity, and fervor associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), which is difficult to restrain, exerts the mind, and does not cease; this is called right effort.
What is right mindfulness?

It refers to the noble disciple’s mindfulness, recollection, focused attention, and memory associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), which consists of contemplating suffering as suffering, up to contemplating the path as the path; it is non-forgetfulness, non-loss, non-omission, non-leakage, the nature of not losing the dharma-nature, and the mind’s quality of clear recollection. This is called right mindfulness.
What is right concentration?

It refers to the noble disciple’s mental abiding, thorough abiding, close abiding, and stable abiding—associated with untainted attention—which consists of contemplating suffering as suffering, up to contemplating the path as the path; which is undistracted, unconfused, collected, stilled, and unified in one-pointedness of mind. This is called right concentration.
The aforementioned Noble Eightfold Path and other untainted (anāsrava) formations are called the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

As it is said, the noble practices (*ārya-caryā*) are the true path that ultimately brings about the departure from suffering and leads to nirvāṇa; therefore, these noble practices are called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). This means that what is called "noble practice" is truly noble practice, and what is called "path" is truly a path. Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, this Dharma of the path remains established in the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). All Tathāgatas naturally penetrate it, fully awaken to it, proclaim it, designate it, establish it, analyze it, reveal it, and make it manifest, declaring: "This is noble practice; this is the path; this is the nature of noble practice; this is the nature of the path. Because it is real, authentic, true, and suchness; because it is not false, not deceptive, not inverted, and not different, it is called the Truth of the Path.
Regarding the term "Noble Truth" (*āryasatya*): "Noble" refers to the Buddhas and their disciples; this is their truth, meaning that they know, see, understand, and perfectly awaken to this as truth.
For these reasons, it is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

Furthermore, regarding the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering: "the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering" is a conventional designation, a conceptual construct, and a verbal expression established by all the Buddhas and their disciples—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—who collectively designate it by such a name.
Chapter Eleven: On Meditative Concentration (Dhyāna). Part One. At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"There are four paths to heaven that cause sentient beings who are not yet pure to become pure, and those who are already pure to become bright white.
What are these four?"

That is to say, there is a class of persons who, having detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied and sustained thought, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, dwell having attained the first dhyāna; this is called the first heavenly path.

Furthermore, there is another class who, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, attain internal clarity and mental unification, free from applied and sustained thought, and possessing the joy and bliss born of concentration; they dwell fully in the second dhyāna. This is called the second heavenly path.

Furthermore, there is another class who, with the fading away of joy, dwell in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body; that which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity and mindfulness," they enter and abide in the third dhyāna—this is called the third path to heaven.

Furthermore, there is another class who, having abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain, and with prior joy and sorrow extinguished, dwell in the fourth dhyāna—neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness; this is called the fourth heavenly path.
These four types all cause sentient beings who are not yet purified to become pure, and those who are already pure to become bright white.
Regarding "being free from desire, evil, and unwholesome states," what is meant by "desire"?
That is to say, greed is also called "desire" (*kāma*), the desire realm is also called "desire," and the objects of the five exquisite sensual pleasures are also called "desire.
In this context, the intended meaning is that the objects of the five exquisite sensual pleasures are what is termed "desire."

Why is this so? Because the five objects of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*) are extremely dear, extremely intoxicating, extremely desirable, extremely delightful, extremely covetable, extremely sought after, extremely bewildering, extremely binding, extremely longed for, and extremely fettering; herein they are called "desire" (*kāma*).
However, the five types of exquisite sensual pleasures are not the true essence of desire; the true essence of desire is the craving that takes them as its object.
As the Blessed One said:
"The various exquisite objects in the world are not true desire; true desire is the craving of human conceptualization."
"Exquisite objects remain as they are in the world; the wise have already eliminated desire within them.
The meaning of this verse is that desirable and exquisite forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles are not the true essence of desire.
The essence of desire refers to the conceptual attachment that arises conditioned by those objects.
Since the objects of desire remain as they were, the wise are said to be "detached from desire" with respect to them.
The Venerable Śāriputra once spoke this verse for the sake of others:
At that time, a certain heterodox practitioner of wrong livelihood was standing not far away; he challenged Śāriputra with a verse, saying:

"If the exquisite objects of the world are not true desire, And true desire is said to be the greed of human conceptualization, Then a bhikṣu should be called a person who experiences desire, Because he gives rise to evil conceptualizations and discursive thoughts."
Then Śāriputra replied to the non-Buddhist:
"To give rise to evil thoughts is truly what is called 'indulging in sensual desires.
It is not because all bhikṣus give rise to unwholesome conceptualizations regarding the sublime objects of the world that you should raise such an objection."
He rebuked that non-Buddhist with a verse, saying:
"If the exquisite objects of the world were true desire, And you say that desire is not the greed of human conceptualization,
Then your teacher should be called one who indulges in desire, For he constantly contemplates pleasing and exquisite forms."
At that time, the non-Buddhist was silent and unable to answer, for his teacher had been truly observing a lovely form.
From this it is known that desire is craving and not the object itself.
At that moment, there was a woman drawing water who, upon hearing the above verse, spoke a stanza:
“I wish to know your origin, O Desire; you are born from conceptual construction.
Since I no longer engage in conceptual construction, from whom will you arise?
At that time, there was another member of the Aṭṭhila clan who, having heard the above verse, also spoke in verse:
"The Sage sleeps in peace; encountering evil, he has no sorrow or affliction.
One whose mind delights in meditative concentration does not dally with sensual desires.
The meaning of this verse is that all lovely and wonderful objects are not true desire; rather, the conceptual craving that arises toward them is true desire.
Therefore, in this context, one should formulate four propositions.
First, there is a class of persons (*pudgala*) who, regarding the objects of sensual desire, are physically detached but not mentally so.
That is to say, for example, there is someone who has shaved off their hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and gone forth out of right faith.
Though his body has joined the ranks of the Dharma-fellows, his mind still yearns for the various sensual desires he once experienced, repeatedly giving rise to fierce and intense craving.
His body has left the household life, yet his mind has not; this is called being physically detached from desire but not mentally so.
2. There is a class of persons whose minds are detached from the objects of sensual desire, though not physically so.

That is to say, there is one who, although possessing a wife and children, enjoys excellent fields, houses, bedding, perfumes, garlands, necklaces, clothing, and food; who keeps various kinds of gold, silver, and precious gems; who employs servants, slaves, and laborers; and who occasionally initiates actions such as beating or scolding them.
Yet, he does not give rise to attachment toward sensual desires, nor does he repeatedly arouse intense craving.
Although his body remains at home, his mind has already departed; this is called the mind being detached from desire while the body is not.
Third, there is a class of individuals who are physically and mentally detached from all objects of sensual desire.
That is to say, there is one who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and gone forth out of right faith.

Having joined the ranks of the Dharma-fellows, his mind harbors no lingering attachment toward the objects of desire; he does not repeatedly give rise to craving directed toward them, and should such forgetfulness momentarily arise, he feels deep remorse and shame.
When one has renounced that body, the mind also renounces; this is called being detached from both body and mind regarding sensual desires.
Fourth, there is a class of persons who are neither detached from nor detached in body and mind regarding the objects of sensual desire.

That is to say, there is one who keeps a wife and raises children; enjoys excellent fields, houses, bedding, perfumes, garlands, necklaces, clothing, and food and drink; possesses various kinds of gold, silver, and precious jewels; employs slaves, servants, and laborers; initiates various acts such as beating and scolding; and furthermore, develops deep attachment and defilement toward sensual desires, repeatedly giving rise to intense craving and love.
When both body and mind do not go forth [into homelessness], this is called not being detached from desire in either body or mind.
What is detachment from desire?
It refers to the distancing from all desires, the thorough distancing, their emptiness, and their unattainability; therefore, it is called detachment from desire.
What are the evil and unwholesome dharmas?

They are the five hindrances, namely: the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.

What is the hindrance of sensual desire? It refers to all greed, equal greed, and attachment toward various sensual pleasures; it is the grasping, hoarding, guarding, and firm clinging [to them]; the fondness for them, the delusion and infatuation with them; the indulgence and pervasive indulgence in them; the internal bondage and longing for them; the immersion in them and the accumulation of suffering; that which belongs to the category of greed and arises from greed—this is collectively termed sensual desire.

In this way, sensual desire covers the mind, obscures the mind, obstructs the mind, entangles the mind, hides the mind, eclipses the mind, envelops the mind, and overpowers the mind; therefore, it is called a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
It is precisely because it is covetousness that it is called the "hindrance of covetousness" (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*).

What is the "hindrance of ill-will" (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*)? It refers to the desire to cause harm toward sentient beings; harboring within one's mind a latent resentment with the intent to cause disturbance and affliction; having been angry, being about to be angry, or currently being angry; delighting in malice, being extremely malicious, and having an extremely agitated and resentful mind; and desiring to cause harm toward all sentient beings through mutual opposition and contrariety—having already caused harm, being about to cause harm, or currently causing harm. This is collectively termed "ill-will."
In this way, ill-will covers the mind, shrouds the mind, and even envelops and obscures the mind; therefore, it is called an "obscuration" (*nīvaraṇa*).
Since the obscuration itself is ill-will, it is termed the "ill-will obscuration."
What is the hindrance of sloth and torpor?

It refers to heaviness of body, heaviness of mind, unserviceability of body, unserviceability of mind, sluggishness of body, sluggishness of mind, and mental dullness and confusion; these collectively are termed sloth.

All sleep and dreaming within the category of defiled mental states—which lack the capacity for sustained support and consist of a state of mental dullness and contraction—is collectively termed "sleep.
Thus, what has been described as torpor and sleep covers the mind, obscures the mind, and even envelops and shrouds the mind; therefore, they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).
Since it consists of precisely lethargy (*styāna*) and drowsiness (*middha*), it is called the hindrance of lethargy-and-drowsiness (*styānamiddhanīvaraṇa*).
What is the hindrance of restlessness-and-remorse (*auddhatyakaukṛtyanīvaraṇa*)?
It refers to the lack of tranquility in the mind, agitation, and the state of mental agitation; these collectively are termed "restlessness" (*auddhatya*).

All mental transformations, mental distress, and mental regret within the category of defiled states of mind—namely, "I have done wrong" (*kaukṛtya*) and the nature of doing wrong—are collectively termed "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*).
Likewise, what has been described as restlessness and remorse—that which obscures the mind, covers the mind, and even envelops or hinders the mind—is collectively termed a "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*).
Because it is precisely restlessness and remorse, it is called the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*).
What is the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*)?

It refers to the arising of doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; it is the state of being divided into two parts or two paths, hesitation, the arrow of doubt, lack of certainty, lack of finality, lack of decisive resolution, not having reached a single direction in the past, not being destined for a single direction in the future, and not currently tending toward a single direction—this is collectively termed doubt.
This nature of doubt covers the mind, obscures the mind, and even envelops and shrouds the mind; therefore, it is called a "hindrance" (nīvaraṇa).
Since the hindrance itself is doubt, it is termed the "hindrance of doubt" (vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa).
What is meant by "being free from evil and unwholesome states"?

It refers to the fact that regarding such evil and unwholesome states, one is distant from them, utterly distant from them, empty of them, and they are unapprehendable; therefore, it is called being free from evil and unwholesome states.
