The Remainder of Chapter Eleven, on Meditative Concentration (*Dhyāna*). Regarding "with vitarka and with vicāra": what is *vitarka*?

It refers to the mental seeking, thorough seeking, and close seeking of one who has abandoned sensual desires and unwholesome states; it is the mind’s manifestation, intense manifestation, and manifest presence; its investigation, conceptualization, reflection, and discrimination—collectively termed *vitarka*.
What is investigation (*vicāra*)?

It refers to the mental state of one who has abandoned sensual desires and unwholesome, evil states; it is the mind’s examining, thorough examining, close examining, following along, revolving with, flowing with, and being subject to [the object], which is collectively termed investigation.
What is the distinction between vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought)?
Vitarka is that which causes the mind to be coarse in nature; vicāra is that which causes the mind to be subtle in nature.
Furthermore, how are these two?
Just as when a bell is struck, a coarse sound issues forth momentarily and a subtle sound follows in succession;
the coarse sound is a metaphor for *vitarka* (initial inquiry), and the subtle sound is a metaphor for *vicāra* (sustained examination).
The same applies to the metaphors of the two sounds—coarse and subtle—used for shaking a bell, striking a bowl, blowing a conch, beating a drum, shooting an arrow, or the crashing of thunder.
Furthermore, it is like various birds flying through the sky; they must flap their wings and lift their bodies to move according to their will.

Flapping the wings is a metaphor for *vitarka* (applied thought), and lifting the body is a metaphor for *vicāra* (sustained thought); this is called the distinction between the two characteristics of *vitarka* and *vicāra*.
What is meant by "with vitarka and vicāra"?
It refers to the state where one who has abandoned sensual desires and unwholesome states possesses both vitarka and vicāra within the category of mental concomitants.
Regarding "joy and bliss born of seclusion," what is meant by "seclusion"?

That is to say, freedom from desire is also called "separation"; freedom from evil and unwholesome states is also called "separation"; renunciation is also called "separation"; the wholesome roots of the form realm are also called "separation"; and the first dhyāna is also called "separation."
In this context, the meaning intended is that the first *dhyāna* is called "separation" (*viveka*).
What is joy (*prīti*)?

It refers to the state of one who has become separated from sensual desires and unwholesome states; it is the mind’s gladness, extreme gladness, manifest gladness, the nature of gladness, and the category of gladness; it is what is agreeable and pleasing, the nature of joy and the category of joy; it is the union with bliss, non-separation, exultation and delight, the state of being capable, leaping up and the nature of leaping up, and the state of jubilation and the category of jubilation—all of these together are termed "joy."
What is pleasure?

It refers to that which is obtained by one who has abandoned sensual desires and unwholesome states, having severed heaviness of body and heaviness of mind, and unserviceability of body and unserviceability of mind; it is the pliancy of body and pliancy of mind, the flexibility of body and flexibility of mind, the serviceability of body and serviceability of mind, the state of being free from hindrances in body and mind, the tranquility of body and tranquility of mind, the absence of feverish distress in body and mind, and the adaptability of body and adaptability of mind—all of these are collectively termed "pleasure."
What is the joy and happiness born of seclusion?

It refers to the preceding joy and happiness that have seclusion as their cause, rely upon seclusion, and are established by means of seclusion; because they arise, co-arise, are produced, co-produced, enter into, and manifest through the power of seclusion, they are called "joy and happiness born of seclusion."
"Initial" (ādi) means that this dhyāna occupies the very first position in the sequence of enumeration;
furthermore, it stands at the forefront among the nine successive meditative attainments (anupūrva-samāpatti).

Regarding meditative absorption (*dhyāna*): it refers to the state within this concentration where vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and one-pointedness of mind—these five factors taken together—are called the first dhyāna.
As a verse says:
"If one practices meditative concentration while the mind follows the course of desire, or again follows the course of hatred,
the Buddhas do not praise such a person."
When the mind is entangled by the hindrance of lethargy and sleep, one practices meditative concentration without true understanding;
though the physical form appears tranquil, the Buddhas do not praise such a state.
When the mind is entangled by the hindrance of restlessness and regret, the sense faculties are not at peace.
Though they diligently practice meditative concentration, the Buddhas do not praise them.
Those who harbor doubt within their minds regarding the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths—
though they diligently practice meditative concentration— the Buddhas do not praise them.
Distant from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with applied and sustained thought in accordance with reality,
his body becomes supple and tranquil, experiencing the joy and bliss born of seclusion;
his body is like a bathed statue, every limb moistened and glistening.
Neither too forceful nor too weak, it cannot be swept away by the waters of craving;
with its five factors such as applied thought and sustained investigation, this is what the noble sages and seers have realized.
It is collectively named the first dhyāna, praised by all the Buddhas.
In this meditative concentration, all mental states, cognitions, and consciousnesses are called the mind concomitant with the first dhyāna.
All volitions, equal volitions, manifest volitions, past volitions, and future volitions that construct mental and vocal karma are called the mental action concomitant with the first dhyāna.
All mental resolves—those already resolved, those currently being resolved, and those yet to be resolved—are called the resolve coexistent with the first dhyāna.

Within this meditative concentration, whatever is feeling, perception, aspiration, attention, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom, these are termed the various factors coexistent with the first dhyāna.
These phenomena are also termed "the first dhyāna.
By what meaning is this name "dhyāna" established?

It is so called because it can pacify unwholesome and evil dharmas, as well as other defilements, the burning of future existence, the maturation of future suffering, and all outflowing (sāsrava) phenomena such as birth, aging, and death; therefore, it is named "dhyāna."

Furthermore, because one has already pacified various evil and unwholesome dharmas, as well as other defilements, the burning of future existence, the ripening of suffering, and the outflowing dharmas such as birth, aging, and death—thereby giving rise to, causing to arise, producing, causing to be produced, entering into, and manifesting this meditative absorption—it is therefore called *dhyāna* (meditative absorption).

Furthermore, because it has already stilled various evil and unwholesome dharmas, as well as other defilements, the burning of future existence, the ripening of future suffering, and the outflowing dharmas such as birth, old age, and death, and because it illuminates extensively with intense clarity through this meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is therefore called "meditative concentration."

"Endowment" means that based on these wholesome dharmas arising from renunciation and seclusion, one practices with diligence, without interval or interruption, until they reach fulfillment; therefore, it is called "endowment."

"Abiding" refers to the accomplishment of this dhyāna; because it involves its manifestation, its concomitants, its universal concomitance, its pervasive concomitance, its movement, and its analytical practice, it is called "abiding."
Regarding "the stilling of applied and sustained thought" (*vitarka-vicāra-śānti*): applied thought and sustained thought are as previously explained.
In the second dhyāna, these two are stilled, thoroughly stilled, closely stilled, empty, and non-existent; therefore, it is called "the stilling of applied and sustained thought."
Regarding "inner serenity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*): what is inner serenity?

It refers to the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). It is the various forms of faith, the nature of faith, the nature of manifest faith, compliance and approval, longing and the nature of longing, mental clarity, and mental purity; these taken together are termed inner serenity.
Regarding "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*): what is meant by one-pointedness of mind?

It refers to the state where, due to the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), the mind is neither distracted, nor scattered, nor flowing away, but dwells stably upon a single object; therefore, it is called one-pointedness of mind.

"Without applied thought and sustained thought" refers to the second dhyāna; because applied and sustained thought are neither obtainable nor active, and do not exist even as latent dispositions, it is called "without applied and sustained thought."
Regarding "the joy and happiness born of concentration," what is concentration?

It refers to the mind’s abiding, thorough abiding, close abiding, and stable abiding when vitarka and vicāra have subsided; its state of being undistracted and unconfused, its withdrawal and meditative absorption, and its one-pointedness of mind—this, in brief, is called concentration.
What is joy (*prīti*)?

It refers to the mind’s delight and intense delight of one for whom discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) have subsided; it is generally termed joy, encompassing everything from the detailed explanation up to the nature of gladness and rapturous joy.
What is pleasure?

It refers to the state of one whose discursive thought and investigation have become stilled, who has abandoned heaviness of body and heaviness of mind, and so forth, up to the pliancy of body and the pliancy of mind; this, in brief, is called pleasure.
What is the joy and happiness born of concentration?

It refers to the aforementioned joy and happiness that arise because they have concentration as their cause, rely upon concentration, are established by concentration, and—through the power of concentration—originate, co-originate, arise, co-arise, enter into, and manifest; therefore, this is called "joy and happiness born of concentration."
The second refers to the fact that this dhyāna occupies the second position within the sequential enumeration;
furthermore, it is so called because it stands as the second among the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*).

Regarding meditative absorption (*dhyāna*): within this concentration, there are internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). The totality of these four factors is called the second dhyāna.
As a verse says:
"When vitarka and vicāra are both stilled, like rain settling the dust,
the mind becomes inwardly pure and one-pointed, touching the sublime bliss of bodhi."
"Without applied thought or sustained thought, possessing joy, with internal purity and concentration—
this is called the second dhyāna, praised by all Buddhas.
Within this meditative absorption, the various mind, mentation, and consciousness are termed the "mind concomitant with the second dhyāna."
All volitions, inclinations, and so forth, up to the mental karma of intention, are called the mental karma associated with the second dhyāna.
All mental resolutions, those already resolved, and those yet to be resolved, are called the resolution associated with the second dhyāna.
In this meditative absorption, whatever sensations, perceptions, or even wisdom there may be, are called the factors co-arising with the second dhyāna.
These factors may likewise be designated as the second dhyāna itself.
The meaning of this dhyāna as the basis, its fulfillment, and its abiding are all as previously explained.
Regarding "being free from joy" (*vītarāga*): what is joy?
It refers to the mind's state of delight, extreme delight, up to gladness and rapturous joy; collectively, these are termed "joy."
The mind is joyful here, yet through detachment it is liberated; therefore, it is called "freed from joy.
Regarding "dwelling in equanimity with right mindfulness and clear comprehension," at that time, one dwells securely established in equanimity, right mindfulness, and clear comprehension.
What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
It refers to the state of mental evenness, the state of mental rectitude, and the state of dwelling in tranquility without mental agitation when joy has ceased; these together are termed equanimity.
What is right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*)?
It refers to all mindfulness and recollection when one is free from joy, up to and including the nature of mental clarity and retention; these taken together are termed right mindfulness.
What is right awareness (*samprajanya*)?

This refers to the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) that arises when one is free from joy, up to and including *vipaśyanā*; these are collectively termed "correct knowledge" (*saṃprajanya*).

Regarding the phrase "the body experiences bliss" (*kāyena sukhaṃ vedayate*): "body" here refers to the mental body (*manomaya-kāya*), because within this mental body there is the experience of bliss, whereby even the physical body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) attains composure. For this reason, it is said that "the body experiences bliss."

In this context, "pleasure" refers to the state when one is free from rapture (*prīti*); it is the cessation of bodily heaviness and mental heaviness, up to and including bodily pliancy and mental pliancy, which is collectively termed pleasure.
"This is the experience of pleasure, not the pleasure of pliancy (praśrabdhi).
'The Noble Ones say it should be abandoned'—the Noble Ones refer to the Buddhas and their disciples.

'Say' means to proclaim; they explain and reveal that those practicing meditative concentration should abandon this pleasure, rather than relishing it, and should abide solely in equanimity (upekṣā) with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension."
It is called "the third" because it occupies the third position within the sequential enumeration of these dhyānas;
furthermore, it is so called because it stands as the third among the nine successive meditative attainments (anupūrva-samāpatti).

Regarding the meditative absorption (dhyāna): it refers to equanimity, right mindfulness, right situational awareness, the experience of physical pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind within this concentration; these five factors taken together are called the third dhyāna.
As it is said in a verse:
"Free from joy, the supreme state, Equanimity, mindfulness, and the awareness of bliss in concentration—
This is called the third dhyāna, Praised by all the Buddhas."
In this meditative absorption, all mental states, consciousnesses, and cognitions are termed the mind concomitant with the third dhyāna.
All volitions, intentions, and even the mental and intentional karmas performed therein are termed the mental karma concomitant with the third dhyāna.
All mental resolves—those already resolved, those currently being resolved, and those yet to be resolved—are called the resolve concomitant with the third dhyāna.
Whatever sensation, perception, or even wisdom exists within this meditative absorption is called the various phenomena concomitant with the third dhyāna.
These dharmas are also designated as the third dhyāna.
The meaning of the basis for this designation of "dhyāna," as well as its fulfillment and maintenance, are also as previously explained.
Regarding the "abandonment of pleasure": what is pleasure?
It refers to the bodily pleasure and mental pleasure arising from contact conducive to pleasure; that which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity is collectively termed "pleasure."
Furthermore, when practicing the third dhyāna, the mental pleasure arising from contact conducive to pleasant feeling, which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity, is called "pleasure.
Regarding the phrase "the cessation of suffering": what is suffering?
That is to say, the bodily suffering arising from contact conducive to suffering, which is comprised within the category of unbalanced feeling (*vedanā*), is called "suffering.

When both this suffering and pleasure are simultaneously subject to full knowledge (*parijñā*), become detached and utterly detached, subdued and utterly subdued, and are eclipsed, eliminated, and extinguished, it is therefore said that "pleasure is abandoned and suffering is abandoned."
Regarding "first, the subsiding of joy and sorrow": what is joy?
It refers to the mental joy arising from a contact conducive to joy, which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity; this is called joy.
Furthermore, when cultivating the second dhyāna, the mental joy arising from contact conducive to the feeling of joy, which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity, is called joy (*prīti*).
What is grief (*daurmanasya*)?
That is to say, the mental sorrow arising from contact conducive to sorrow, which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity (*vedanā*), is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*).

This, together with the aforementioned joy (*prīti*), at that time both attains full knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇaparijñā*) up to its disappearance and cessation; therefore, it is said that "previously, joy and sorrow have vanished."
Furthermore, upon entering the first dhyāna, mental distress (*daurmanasya*) attains the full knowledge of abandonment;
upon entering the second dhyāna, physical suffering (*duḥkha*) attains the full knowledge of abandonment;
upon entering the third dhyāna, joy (*prīti*) attains the full knowledge of abandonment.

Upon entering the fourth dhyāna, whether it be pleasure or pain, or joy or grief, all are fully known and abandoned, utterly distanced and thoroughly subdued, becoming obscured and extinguished; therefore, it is said that "pleasure is abandoned and pain is abandoned."

Regarding "previously joy and sorrow having subsided, there is neither suffering nor pleasure": this indicates that within this state, the two sensations of suffering and pleasure are absent, and there exists only the third, which is neither suffering nor pleasure. Regarding "the sensation of equanimity is purified through mindfulness," what is meant by equanimity?

That is to say, at that time, the mind’s state of equanimity, the mind’s state of rectitude, and the mind’s state of dwelling in tranquility without agitation—these collectively are termed equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)?
This refers to all those moments of mindfulness and recollection at that time, explained in detail up to the mind’s capacity for clear retention; these are collectively termed "mindfulness.
At that time, whether it be equanimity or mindfulness, both attain purity; because pleasure, pain, joy, sorrow, and both vitarka and vicāra have all ceased, it is called "purity."
The fourth refers to this dhyāna being situated as the fourth in the sequential enumeration;
furthermore, it is because it occupies the fourth position among the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*).

Regarding meditative absorption (*dhyāna*): within this concentration, there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, equanimity and mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind; these four factors taken together are called the fourth meditative absorption.
As a verse says:
"When pleasure, pain, and so forth have already ceased, the mind dwells firm and unmoving;
having attained the pure divine eye, one is able to see all forms extensively."
"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, pure equanimity, mindfulness, and concentration—
this is called the fourth dhyāna, praised by all Buddhas.
Within this meditative absorption, all mental states, cognitions, and consciousnesses are termed "the mind co-existent with the fourth dhyāna."
All volitions, including those that are equivalent to volition, up to the mental karma of intention, are called the mental karma concomitant with the fourth dhyāna.
All mental resolve, past resolve, and future resolve, are called the resolve concomitant with the fourth dhyāna.
In this meditative absorption, whatever sensations, perceptions, or even wisdom there may be are called the various phenomena coexistent with the fourth dhyāna.
Such phenomena may also be designated as the fourth dhyāna itself.
The name of this dhyāna, its underlying meaning, its fulfillment, and its maintenance are all as previously explained.
Chapter Twelve: The Immeasurables (Apramāṇa). At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
“There are four immeasurables. What are the four?

This refers to a certain class of person who, by virtue of having well-cultivated a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—free from enmity and hostility, devoid of malice and harm, vast and immeasurable—dwells pervading one direction with a resolute conviction of its sufficiency;
and likewise toward the second, third, and fourth directions, above, below, and across, throughout the entire world. This is called the first [meditation].

Furthermore, there is another class [of practitioners] who, through the thorough cultivation of a mind accompanied by compassion—one that is free from enmity and hostility, devoid of malice and harm, vast and immeasurable—dwell having resolved upon and suffused one direction with this perception until it is complete.
They do likewise toward a second, a third, and a fourth direction, as well as above, below, and across, throughout the entire world; this is called the second [immeasurable].
Furthermore, there is another class [of practitioners] whose mind is accompanied by joy, free from enmity and hostility, remote from affliction and harm, vast and immeasurable;

because they have skillfully cultivated it, they dwell having attained the resolute conviction that this state pervades one direction, and likewise toward the second, third, and fourth directions, above, below, and across—in all worlds. This is called the third [attainment].

Furthermore, there is another class [of practitioners] who, through the thorough cultivation of a mind accompanied by equanimity—free from enmity, free from hostility, remote from malice and harm, vast and immeasurable—abide having attained the resolute conviction that it pervades one direction in its entirety;
and likewise for the second, third, and fourth directions, above, below, and across, throughout the entire world. This is called the fourth [immeasurable].
What is loving-kindness (*maitrī*)?
It refers to a certain class of persons who form this thought:
"May all sentient beings attain supreme happiness."

Based on that renunciation or seclusion, the various wholesome states of loving-kindness belonging to the meditative absorptions of the form realm, which are internally initiated through the power of discernment, are called "pity and the nature of pity" and "compassion and the nature of compassion"; collectively, they are termed "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*).

Furthermore, the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising in conjunction with them and the formations dissociated from mind, are also called "loving-kindness.

What is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the concentration of the mind of loving-kindness, and what preparatory application must be cultivated to enter the concentration of the mind of loving-kindness?
It refers to a certain class of persons who give rise to such a thought:
"May all sentient beings attain supreme happiness.
Although they have this thought, they lack resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the wish that all sentient beings attain such-and-such specific forms of supreme happiness.

Although that mind is virtuous, pure, and sublime, compliant with polishing and refinement, increasing its adornment, worthy of offerings, and possesses constant, diligent companions and provisions, it is not yet called the preparatory stage of the concentration of loving-kindness, nor is it called entry into the concentration of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, there is another class who utter these words:
"May all sentient beings attain supreme happiness.
Although they speak these words, they lack resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that all sentient beings may attain such-and-such supreme happiness.

Although those words are virtuous, pure, and sublime, even up to being a provision for the path, they are not yet called the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), nor are they called entering the concentration of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, there is another class who gives rise to such a thought and utters such words:
"May all sentient beings attain supreme happiness."
Although such a thought and such words exist, there is no resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that "may all sentient beings obtain such and such supreme happiness.

Although that thought and those words are indeed wholesome, pure, and sublime, and even constitute a provision (*sambhāra*), they are not yet called the preliminary application (*prayoga*) for the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), nor are they called entering the concentration of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, there is another class [of beings] who give rise to such a thought, utter such words, and possess such resolute conviction:
"May all sentient beings attain such and such supreme happiness."

Although that mind, speech, and resolute conviction are all virtuous, pure, and sublime—even constituting the provisions—they are not yet termed the preliminary application (*prayoga*) for the concentration of loving-kindness, nor are they termed "entering" the concentration of loving-kindness.
What is this matter like?
It is as when a certain class of people, oppressed by the suffering of cold, obtains warmth and experiences pleasure.
Grasping this mark of pleasure, they give rise to such a thought and utter these words:
"May all sentient beings obtain such and such supreme happiness.

Although that mental state, speech, and resolute conviction are all virtuous, pure, and sublime—even constituting the provisions—they are not yet called the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), nor are they called the entry into the meditative concentration of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, there is another class of beings who, oppressed by the suffering of heat, obtain coolness and experience pleasure.
Grasping this mark of pleasure, they give rise to such a thought and utter these words:
"May all sentient beings attain such and such supreme happiness."

Although that mental state, speech, and resolve are all wholesome, pure, and sublime—even constituting the provisions—they are not yet called the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), nor are they called the entry into the concentration of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, there is another class [of beings] who, oppressed by the suffering of hunger, experience pleasure upon obtaining food.
Grasping this mark of pleasure, they give rise to such a thought and utter these words:
"May all sentient beings obtain such and such supreme happiness."

Although that mind, speech, and resolve are all wholesome, pure, and sublime—even constituting the provisions—they are not yet termed the preparatory application for the concentration of loving-kindness, nor are they termed entering the concentration of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, there is another class of beings who, oppressed by the suffering of thirst, obtain the pleasure of drinking.
Grasping this mark of pleasure, they give rise to such a thought and utter these words:
"May all sentient beings obtain such and such supreme happiness."

Although that mind, speech, and resolute conviction are all virtuous, pure, and sublime—even constituting the provisions—they are not yet called the preliminary application (*prayoga*) for the concentration of loving-kindness, nor are they called the entry into the concentration of loving-kindness.

Furthermore, there is another class of beings whose bodies are defiled and their limbs are weary, who lack various necessities and are separated from their kinsmen; yet, upon encountering bathing facilities, massage, necessary provisions, and reunion with their kinsmen, they experience various forms of pleasure.
Taking up this mark of happiness, one gives rise to such a thought and utters such words:
"May all sentient beings obtain such and such supreme happiness.

Although that thought, speech, and resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) are all virtuous, pure, and sublime—even constituting the provisions (sambhāra)—they are not yet called the preparatory stage (prayoga) for the concentration of loving-kindness (maitrī-samādhi), nor are they called entering the concentration of loving-kindness.

Furthermore, there is another class of beings who, during the intense heat of midsummer, are tormented by the blazing rays of the sun; becoming deluded and faint from thirst and heat, their bodies and minds are consumed with distress. Upon encountering a cool pond, they cast themselves in to bathe and drink, thereby giving rise to pleasure.
Taking up this mark of pleasure, one gives rise to such a thought and utters such words:
"May all sentient beings obtain such and such supreme happiness.

Although that thought, speech, and resolute conviction are all virtuous, pure, and sublime—even constituting the provisions (*sambhāra*)—they are not yet called the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), nor are they called entering the concentration of loving-kindness.

Thus, regarding the objects of sensual pleasure experienced in the desire realm and the superior pleasures experienced in the three dhyānas, one grasps the signs of those pleasures and gives rise to thought and speech, saying:
"May all sentient beings attain such and such superior pleasures."

Although that mind, speech, and resolve are all virtuous, pure, and sublime—even serving as the provisions—they are not yet called the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), nor are they called the entry into the concentration of loving-kindness.
If there is one who has recently entered the third dhyāna in this life and, perceiving the mark of that bliss, gives rise to such a thought and utters these words:
"May all sentient beings attain such and such supreme bliss."

That mind, speech, and resolve are all supremely wholesome, pure, and sublime, conforming to and serving as the provisions for [the goal]; thus they may be called the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), and are also termed "entering the concentration of loving-kindness."
Furthermore, within this meditative concentration, all mental states—mind, intellect, and consciousness—are termed "mental states associated with loving-kindness.
All volitions, equal volitions, manifest volitions, past volitions, and future volitions that produce mental and vocal karma are termed "vocal and mental karma associated with loving-kindness."
All mental resolves—those already resolved, those currently resolving, and those yet to resolve—are termed "resolves concomitant with loving-kindness.

Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, whatever sensations, perceptions, aspirations, acts of attention, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and so forth there may be, are termed "all phenomena concomitant with loving-kindness."
These dharmas are also called the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), and they are also called entering the concentration of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of concentration of loving-kindness: first, the limited (*parītta*);
[and second, the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*)].
2. The Immeasurable.

What is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for the concentration of limited loving-kindness (*maitrī-cittasamādhi*), and what preparatory practice leads to entry into the concentration of limited loving-kindness?

It is as follows: there is a certain class of person who, toward those sentient beings who are lovely, pleasant, delightful, and agreeable—namely, parents, brothers, sisters, and other various relatives and friends—directs their mind toward these limited sentient beings so that it abides, abides closely, abides near, and remains settled, becoming disciplined, tranquil, and utterly serene, attaining one-pointed concentration (*ekāgratā-samādhi*), with the aspiration: "May all these sentient beings obtain supreme happiness."

At that time, if his mind is distracted and flows toward other objects, unable to focus on a single point or maintain mindfulness so that it dwells upon a single object, yet he still aspires for limited sentient beings to attain happiness.

At this stage, it is not yet called the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the concentration on limited loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), nor is it yet called entering the concentration on limited loving-kindness.

If, at that time, one restrains one's own mind so that it does not scatter or flow toward other objects, but is able to become single-pointed, abide in mindfulness upon a single focal object, and contemplate the signs of limited sentient beings while wishing that limited sentient beings obtain happiness—[this constitutes the preparatory stage].

Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort that is courageous, powerful, intense, blazing, difficult to restrain, and characterized by an unremittingly resolute mind; this is called the preparatory application for the concentration of limited loving-kindness, and it is also called entering the concentration of limited loving-kindness.

Once that path has arisen, through its cultivation and repeated practice, he causes the mind to abide, to abide evenly, to abide closely, and to abide securely; it becomes one-pointed, concentrated, non-dual, and non-retrogressive, while wishing that those limited sentient beings may obtain happiness.
This is called having entered the concentration of the limited state of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).
Furthermore, within this concentration, all mental activities—mind, intellect, and consciousness—are termed "mental states associated with limited loving-kindness.
All volitions, intentions, and even the mental karma of intending and performing are termed "mental karma associated with limited loving-kindness."
All mental states of resolve—those already resolved, those currently resolving, and those yet to resolve—are termed the resolve concomitant with limited loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, whatever there may be of feeling, perception, or even wisdom, these are termed the various phenomena concomitant with limited loving-kindness.

These dharmas are also called the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the concentration of limited loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), and they are also called entering the concentration of limited loving-kindness.

What is the preparatory application for the immeasurable concentration of loving-kindness? By practicing what preparatory application does one enter the immeasurable concentration of loving-kindness? It is said that by repeatedly cultivating the very same concentration of limited loving-kindness, one causes the mind to become compliant, disciplined, and tranquil.

Repeatedly training and refining it, one makes it upright, supple, and serviceable, so that it may serve as the basis for subsequent superior meditative concentration; thereafter, one gradually causes the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) to become all-pervasive, wishing for all immeasurable sentient beings in the eastern direction and elsewhere to attain happiness.

At that time, if his mind is distracted and wanders toward other objects, such that he cannot focus one-pointedly or maintain mindfulness to dwell upon a single object, yet he still aspires for immeasurable sentient beings to attain happiness.

This is not yet called the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the concentration of immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-samādhi*), nor is it yet called entering the concentration of immeasurable loving-kindness.

If, at that time, one restrains one's own mind so that it does not scatter or flow toward other objects, but is able to settle single-mindedly upon a single focal point while contemplating the signs of immeasurable sentient beings and wishing that immeasurable sentient beings may attain happiness.

Reflecting in this way, one rouses diligent effort and exerts the mind until it ceases not; this is called the preparatory practice for the concentration of immeasurable loving-kindness, and is also called entering the concentration of immeasurable loving-kindness.

Having given rise to this path, through its cultivation and repeated practice, he causes the mind to abide, to abide evenly, to abide closely, and to abide securely; it becomes one-pointed, concentrated, non-dual, and irreversible, while wishing that immeasurable sentient beings may attain happiness.
This is called having entered the concentration of immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).
Furthermore, within this concentration, all mind, intellect, and consciousness are termed "mind associated with immeasurable loving-kindness.
All volitions (*cetanā*), mental intentions, and even the mental karma of intention are termed "mental karma associated with immeasurable loving-kindness."
All mental states of resolve—those already resolved, those currently resolving, and those yet to resolve—are termed the resolve concomitant with immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, whatever constitutes feeling, perception, and so forth up to wisdom, are termed the various phenomena concomitant with immeasurable loving-kindness.
These dharmas are also called the preparatory application for the concentration of immeasurable loving-kindness, and they are also called entering the concentration of immeasurable loving-kindness.
What is compassion?
This refers to a certain class of persons who reflect thus:
"May all sentient beings be free from suffering.

Based on renunciation or seclusion, through the power of discernment, they internally give rise to various forms of wholesome compassion (*karuṇā*) pertaining to the meditative absorptions of the form realm—whether it be the nature of compassion, the nature of pitying sorrow, or the nature of poignant distress—all of which are collectively termed "compassion."

Furthermore, the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness associated with compassion, as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising in conjunction with them and the formations dissociated from mind, are also termed "compassion.
Furthermore, there are two types of meditative concentration of the compassionate mind:
first, the limited; [and second, the immeasurable].
2. Immeasurable.
What is the preparatory application for the concentration of limited compassion? What preparatory application must be cultivated to enter the concentration of limited compassion?

It refers to a certain class of persons who, toward various sentient beings who are lovely, pleasant, delightful, and agreeable—namely, parents, brothers, sisters, and other various relatives or friends—[direct their attention].

Regarding those beings who are thus limited, he establishes his mind—conjoined with limited compassion—in stability, thorough stability, close stability, and firm abiding; he brings it to mastery, tranquility, supreme tranquility, one-pointedness, and meditative concentration, wishing that all those beings may be free from suffering.

At that time, if his mind were distracted and wandering toward other objects, unable to focus on a single point or maintain mindfulness so as to abide upon a single object, yet he still aspires for limited sentient beings to be free from suffering.
At this stage, it is not yet called the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the concentration on limited compassion, nor has one entered the concentration on limited compassion.

However, if at that time one restrains one's own mind so that it does not scatter or flow toward other objects, but is able to settle it single-pointedly upon a single focal object, contemplating the characteristics of limited sentient beings and wishing that those limited sentient beings be free from suffering—[this constitutes the preparatory application].

Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the preparatory application for the concentration of limited compassion, and it is also called entering the concentration of limited compassion.

Having given rise to this path and having cultivated it repeatedly, he causes the mind to abide, to abide evenly, to abide closely, and to abide securely; it becomes one-pointed in concentration, non-dual, and non-regressive, as he wishes that those limited sentient beings be free from suffering.
This is called having entered the meditative concentration of limited compassion (*parītta-karuṇā-samādhi*).
Furthermore, within this concentration, all mind, thought, and consciousness are termed "mind associated with limited compassion.
All volitions (*cetanā*), mental engagements, and even the mental karma of intention are termed "mental karma associated with limited compassion."
All mental resolves—those already resolved, those currently being resolved, and those yet to be resolved—are called the resolve concomitant with limited compassion.
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, whatever sensations, perceptions, or even wisdoms there may be, are called the various phenomena concomitant with limited compassion.

These dharmas are also called the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the concentration of limited compassion (*parītta-karuṇā-samādhi*), and they are also called entering the concentration of limited compassion.

What is the preparatory application for the concentration of immeasurable compassion (*apramāṇa-karuṇā-samādhi*), and by practicing what preparatory application does one enter the concentration of immeasurable compassion?
This means that one repeatedly cultivates the meditative concentration on compassion that is initially narrow and limited, thereby making the mind compliant, subdued, and tranquil.

By training it again and again, one makes it upright, supple, and serviceable, establishing it as the basis for subsequent superior concentrations. Thereafter, one gradually causes the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) to become all-pervasive, wishing for all immeasurable sentient beings in the eastern direction and elsewhere to be free from suffering.

At that time, even if his mind were distracted and wandering toward other objects, unable to focus single-mindedly or maintain mindfulness so as to abide upon a single object, he would still aspire for immeasurable sentient beings to be free from suffering.

This is not yet called the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the concentration of immeasurable compassion (*apramāṇa-karuṇā-samādhi*), nor is it yet called entering the concentration of immeasurable compassion.

If, at that time, one restrains and gathers one's own mind so that it does not scatter or flow toward other objects, and is able to cause it to focus one-pointedly on a single object while dwelling in mindfulness, contemplating the forms of immeasurable sentient beings and wishing that immeasurable sentient beings be free from suffering.

Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the preparatory application for the concentration of immeasurable compassion, and it is also called entering the concentration of immeasurable compassion.

Having given rise to this path, through its cultivation and repeated practice, he causes the mind to abide, to abide evenly, to abide closely, and to abide securely; it becomes one-pointed, concentrated, non-dual, and non-retrogressive, with the aspiration that immeasurable sentient beings may be free from suffering.
This is called having entered the meditative concentration of immeasurable compassion (*apramāṇa-karuṇā-samādhi*).
Furthermore, within this concentration, all mental states—mind, thought, and consciousness—are termed "mental states associated with immeasurable compassion.
All volitions, intentions, and even the mental karma of intention and will are termed "mental karma associated with immeasurable compassion."
All mental resolves—those already resolved, those currently resolving, and those yet to resolve—are termed "resolves concomitant with immeasurable compassion.
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, whatever sensations, perceptions, and so forth, up to wisdom, are termed "dharmas concomitant with immeasurable compassion."
These dharmas are also called the preparatory practice for the concentration of immeasurable compassion, and they are also called entering the concentration of immeasurable compassion.
What is sympathetic joy?
This refers to a certain class of persons who reflect:
"It is truly a cause for deep consolation that sentient beings have obtained benefit.

Based on renunciation or seclusion, through the power of discernment, they give rise within themselves to a wholesome mind of the form realm characterized by joy, extreme joy, manifest joy, the nature of joy, the category of joy, agreeableness, pleasantness, the nature of gladness, the category of gladness, delight in union and aversion to separation, the nature of jubilation and exultation, the nature of leaping up and leaping about, and the nature of rapture and rejoicing; all these taken together are termed *prīti* (joy).

Furthermore, the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with joy, as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising in conjunction with them and the formations dissociated from mind, are also called "joy.
Furthermore, there are two types of concentration of a joyful mind:
first, the limited; [second, the immeasurable].
2. Immeasurable.
What is the preparatory application for the meditative concentration on limited sympathetic joy (*parītta-muditā-samādhi*), and what application must be cultivated to enter this concentration?

It refers to a certain class of persons who, toward those sentient beings who are lovely, pleasant, delightful, and agreeable—namely, parents, brothers, sisters, and other various relatives or friends—[direct their attention].

Regarding such beings of limited scope, he causes their minds to abide, remain steadfastly, dwell closely, and settle securely, accompanied by limited joy; he brings them to mastery, tranquility, supreme tranquility, one-pointedness, and meditative concentration, so that those beings may transcend [suffering] and attain happiness, being freed from pain.

At that time, if his mind were distracted and wandering toward other objects, unable to focus single-pointedly or maintain mindfulness so as to abide upon a single object, he would not be able to deliver sentient beings of limited capacity and grant them benefit.

At this stage, it is not yet called the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for the meditative absorption of limited joy (*parītta-prīti-samādhi*), nor has one entered the meditative absorption of limited joy.

If, at that time, one restrains one’s own mind so that it does not become distracted or wander toward other objects, but is able to settle it single-pointedly on a single focal object, contemplating the characteristics of limited sentient beings, rejoicing in the characteristics of limited sentient beings, and rejoicing that limited sentient beings have obtained benefit—[this constitutes the preparatory stage].

Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the preparatory practice for the meditative concentration of limited joy, and it is also called entering the meditative concentration of limited joy.

Having given rise to this path, through its cultivation and repeated practice, he causes the mind to abide, to abide evenly, to abide closely, and to abide securely; it becomes one-pointed, concentrated, non-dual, and non-regressive. He experiences joy and consolation that limited sentient beings have obtained benefit; up to this point, it is called having entered the meditative absorption of the narrow and small mind of joy.
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, all minds, mentations, and consciousnesses are termed "mind associated with limited joy.
All volitions, intentions, and even the mental and volitional karmas produced therein are termed "mental karma associated with limited joy."
All mental states of resolve—those already resolved, those currently resolving, and those yet to be resolved—are termed "resolve accompanied by limited joy.
Furthermore, within this meditative concentration, whatever constitutes feeling, perception, and so forth up to wisdom, are termed "dharmas accompanied by limited joy."
These dharmas are also called the preparatory application for the concentration of limited joy (*parītta-prāmodya-citta-samādhi*), and they are also called entering the concentration of limited joy.

What is the preparatory application for the immeasurable concentration of joy (*apramāṇa-prāmodya-citta-samādhi*), and by practicing what preparatory application does one enter the immeasurable concentration of joy?
This means that one repeatedly cultivates the meditative concentration of joy based on a limited scope, thereby making the mind compliant, subdued, and tranquil.

By repeatedly training and refining it, one makes the mind upright, supple, and serviceable, so that it may serve as the basis for subsequent superior concentrations. Thereafter, one gradually causes the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) to become all-pervasive, taking delight in the benefit obtained by immeasurable sentient beings in the eastern direction and so forth.

At that time, if his mind becomes distracted and wanders toward other objects, such that he cannot focus it on a single point or maintain mindfulness so that it abides upon a single object, he nonetheless rejoices in the immeasurable benefit obtained by sentient beings.

This is not yet called the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the concentration of immeasurable sympathetic joy (*muditā-cittasamādhi*), nor is it yet called entering the concentration of immeasurable sympathetic joy.

If, at that time, he restrains his own mind so that it does not become distracted or flow toward other objects, and is able to cause it to remain one-pointedly on a single object while contemplating the signs of immeasurable sentient beings and rejoicing that immeasurable sentient beings have obtained benefit—[this constitutes the preparatory stage].

Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the preparatory practice for the concentration of immeasurable sympathetic joy, and it is also called entering the concentration of immeasurable sympathetic joy.

Having given rise to this path and having cultivated it extensively through repeated practice, he causes the mind to abide, to abide evenly, to abide closely, and to abide securely; it becomes one-pointed, concentrated, non-dual, and non-regressive. He rejoices that immeasurable sentient beings have obtained benefit. Up to this point, it is called "having entered the meditative absorption of immeasurable sympathetic joy."
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, all minds, mentations, and consciousnesses are termed "minds associated with immeasurable joy.
All volitions, equal volitions, and even the mental karma of intention and action are termed "mental karma associated with immeasurable joy."
All mental states of resolve, those already resolved, and those yet to be resolved, are termed the resolve coexistent with immeasurable joy (*muditā*).
Furthermore, within this meditative concentration, whatever sensations, perceptions, or even wisdom there may be, are termed the various factors coexistent with immeasurable joy.
These dharmas are also called the preparatory practice for the concentration of immeasurable sympathetic joy, and they are also called entering the concentration of immeasurable sympathetic joy.
What is equanimity?
This refers to a certain class of persons who think:
"I should abide in equanimity toward sentient beings.

Based on renunciation or seclusion, through the power of discernment, they give rise internally to the state of mental evenness, mental rectitude, and the state of dwelling in tranquility without agitation within the wholesome mind of the form realm; this is collectively termed equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Furthermore, the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with equanimity, as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising in conjunction with them and the formations dissociated from mind, are also called equanimity.
What is the preparatory application for the concentration of the mind on equanimity, and what preparatory application must be cultivated to enter the concentration of the mind on equanimity?

This refers to a certain class of persons who, although they see sentient beings who are lovely, pleasant, delightful, and agreeable, do not give rise to the conceptual discrimination that "this is my mother," "this is my father," or even "this is my friend," but instead give rise solely to the resolute conviction that they are equal sentient beings.

It is like a person seeking nothing who enters a forest; although they see *sāla* trees, or *tāla* trees, or *kovidāra* trees, or *aśvakarṇa* trees, or *udumbara* trees, or *nyagrodha* trees and so forth, they do not give rise to the discrimination that "this is a *sāla* tree," "this is a *tāla* tree," or even "this is a *nyagrodha* tree," but instead gives rise only to the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) of the forest as a uniform whole.

One who practices the cultivation of equanimity does not give rise to conceptual discrimination toward sentient beings; it should be understood that this is likewise the case here. This is called the preparatory application for the meditative absorption of equanimity, and it is also called entering the meditative absorption of equanimity.
Furthermore, there are two types of the concentration of equanimity:
first, the limited;
second, the immeasurable.

What is the preparatory application for the meditative concentration on the limited mind of equanimity, and what application must be cultivated to enter this concentration? It refers to a certain class of persons who, toward those sentient beings who are lovely, pleasant, delightful, and agreeable—namely, parents, brothers, sisters, and other various relatives, friends, and so forth—[direct their attention].

Regarding such limited sentient beings, he causes them to abide, remain closely settled, dwell near, and become firmly established with a mind accompanied by limited equanimity; he brings them to discipline, tranquility, supreme tranquility, and one-pointed concentration, and thus abides in impartial equanimity toward those sentient beings.

At that time, if his mind becomes distracted and wanders toward other objects, such that he is unable to focus one-pointedly or maintain mindfulness so as to abide upon a single object, he dwells in equanimity toward those sentient beings.

This is not yet called the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the meditative absorption of the limited equanimity mind, nor is it yet called entering the meditative absorption of the limited equanimity mind.

If, at that time, he restrains his own mind so that it does not scatter or flow toward other objects, and is able to cause it to become one-pointed, abiding in mindfulness upon a single focal object, he contemplates the signs of limited sentient beings and dwells in impartial equanimity toward those beings.

Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the preparatory application for the meditative concentration of the limited equanimity mind, and it is also called entering the meditative concentration of the limited equanimity mind.

Having given rise to this path, through its cultivation and repeated practice, he causes the mind to abide, to abide evenly, to abide closely, and to abide securely; it becomes one-pointed, concentrated, non-dual, and non-regressive. Toward those sentient beings, he dwells in equanimity. Up to this point, it is called having entered the meditative absorption of the limited state of equanimity.
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, all minds, mentations, and consciousnesses are termed "mind associated with limited equanimity.
All volitions, intentions, and even the mental karma of intending and acting are termed "mental karma associated with limited equanimity."
All mental states of resolve—those already resolved, those currently resolving, and those yet to resolve—are called the resolve concomitant with limited equanimity.
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, whatever sensations, perceptions, or even wisdom there may be, are called the various phenomena concomitant with limited equanimity.
These dharmas are also called the preparatory application for the concentration of limited equanimity, and they are also called entering the concentration of limited equanimity.
What is the preparatory application for the concentration of immeasurable equanimity, and what application must be cultivated to enter the concentration of immeasurable equanimity?
This means that one repeatedly cultivates the meditative absorption of equanimity toward a limited scope, thereby making the mind compliant, subdued, and tranquil.

One further refines it again and again until it becomes upright, supple, and serviceable, serving as the basis for subsequent superior absorptions. Thereafter, one gradually causes the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) to pervade all sentient beings in the eastern direction and so forth, dwelling in impartial equanimity.

At that time, if his mind is distracted and wanders toward other objects, unable to focus on a single direction or maintain mindfulness so as to abide upon a single object, he dwells in equanimity toward those sentient beings.

This is not yet called the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the concentration of immeasurable equanimity (*apramāṇopekṣā-citta-samādhi*), nor is it yet called entering the concentration of immeasurable equanimity.

When, at that time, he restrains his own mind so that it does not scatter or flow toward other objects, but is able to settle one-pointedly with mindfulness fixed on a single focal point, and contemplates the signs of immeasurable sentient beings while abiding in impartial equanimity toward those beings.

Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the preparatory practice for the concentration of immeasurable equanimity, and it is also called entering the concentration of immeasurable equanimity.

Having given rise to this path, through its cultivation and repeated practice, he causes the mind to abide, to abide evenly, to abide closely, and to abide securely; it becomes one-pointed, concentrated, non-dual, and non-regressive. Toward those sentient beings, he dwells in equanimity. Up to this point, it is called having entered the meditative absorption of immeasurable equanimity.
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, all instances of mind, thought, and consciousness are termed "mind associated with immeasurable equanimity.
All volitions, intended volitions, and even the mental karma of intention are termed "mental karma associated with immeasurable equanimity."
All mental states of resolve—those already resolved, those currently resolving, and those yet to be resolved—are called the resolve concomitant with immeasurable equanimity.
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, whatever sensations, perceptions, or even wisdom there may be, are called the various dharmas concomitant with immeasurable equanimity.

Such dharmas are also termed the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for the concentration of immeasurable equanimity (*apramāṇopekṣā-samādhi*), and they are also termed entering the concentration of immeasurable equanimity.
*Abhidharma-dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*, Fascicle Seven.
