Chapter Thirteen: On the Formless Realm. At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
“There are four formless states. What are the four?

It refers to a bhikṣu who, transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space, fully possessing it; this is called the first [attainment].

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, transcending the sphere of infinite space in every respect, enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwells fully accomplished therein; this is called the second [attainment].

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness in every respect, enters the sphere of nothingness and dwells fully accomplished in the sphere of nothingness; this is called the third [liberation].
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, transcending all modes of the sphere of nothingness, enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called the fourth [dhyāna].
Regarding "transcending all perceptions of form," what are these perceptions of form?

This refers to the perception (saṃjñā), equal perception, manifest perception, the perception of having understood and grasped an image, and the perceptions of what has been perceived and what will be perceived associated with visual consciousness;

these are collectively termed "perception of form" (rūpa-saṃjñā). Some state that the perception, equal perception, up to the perception of what has been perceived and what will be perceived associated with the five consciousnesses, are collectively termed "perception of form."

In this context, the perception associated with visual consciousness—ranging from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and representative cognition (*saṃjñā-anuvyañjana*) up to past perceptions and future perceptions—is collectively termed "perception of form" (*rūpa-saṃjñā*).
Such perception of form is at that time transcended and thoroughly transcended; therefore, it is called the "extinction of all perceptions of form."
Regarding "perception of resistance" (*sappaṭighasaññā*): what is perception of resistance?

It refers to the perception, ideation, and so forth associated with the four consciousnesses beginning with the ear-consciousness, as well as past perceptions and future perceptions; these collectively are termed "perception of resistance."

Some say that the perception (saṃjñā), conceptualization (saṃjñā-anuvyañjana), and so forth, up to past and future perceptions associated with aversion, are collectively termed "perception of resistance" (pratigha-saṃjñā).

In the present context, however, the perception, conceptualization, and so forth, up to past and future perceptions associated with the four consciousnesses of the ear and the other [senses], are collectively termed "perception of resistance."

In this way, when the perception of sensory resistance is severed and fully understood, distanced and utterly distanced, subdued and utterly subdued, concealed and extinguished, it is therefore called the "cessation of the perception of sensory resistance."
Regarding "not contemplating various perceptions," what are these various perceptions?

They refer to all defiled perceptions of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles belonging to those who possess the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*); all unwholesome perceptions; all perceptions induced by improper reasoning (*ayoniśomanasikāra*); and all perceptions that obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*). These, taken together, are termed "various perceptions."

At that time, he no longer initiates, no longer recollects, no longer contemplates, no longer has contemplated, and no longer will contemplate those perceptions; therefore, it is called "not contemplating various perceptions."

Regarding "entering and abiding fully in the sphere of infinite space through the emptiness of infinite space": what is the preparatory application for the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, and what preparatory application is cultivated to enter that absorption?

This means that a beginner in this meditative concentration should first contemplate the fourth dhyāna as coarse, painful, and obstructive, and subsequently contemplate the sphere of infinite space as peaceful, sublime, and detached.

At that time, if his mind becomes distracted and wanders toward other objects, such that he cannot focus one-pointedly or maintain mindfulness to dwell upon a single object while cultivating the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, this is not yet called the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, nor is it called "entering" the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.

If, at that time, he restrains his own mind so that it does not become distracted or flow toward other objects, he is able to direct it one-pointedly, abide in mindfulness upon a single object, and cultivate the mental sign of the Sphere of Infinite Space through contemplation.

Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort—courageous, powerful, fierce, intense, and difficult to restrain—exerting the mind without ceasing. This is called the preparatory application for the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, and it is also called entering the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.

Having given rise to this path and having cultivated it extensively through repeated practice, he causes the mind to abide, to abide evenly, to abide closely, and to abide securely; it becomes one-pointed, concentrated, non-dual, and non-regressive. Up to this point, it is said that he has entered the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space.
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, all minds, mentations, and consciousnesses are termed "the mind concomitant with the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.
All volitions, equal volitions, and even the mental karma of intention and action are termed "the mental karma concomitant with the concentration of the sphere of infinite space."

All mental states of resolve—those already resolved, those currently resolving, and those yet to resolve—are termed the resolve concomitant with the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*).

Furthermore, within this concentration, whatever sensations, perceptions, or even wisdom there may be, are termed the various phenomena concomitant with the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.
These dharmas are also called the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.

Regarding "transcending all modes of the sphere of infinite space": it means that at that time, one transcends and thoroughly transcends the perception of the sphere of infinite space; therefore, it is called "transcending all modes of the sphere of infinite space."

Regarding "entering and abiding fully in the sphere of infinite consciousness": what is the preparatory application for the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness, and what preparatory application must be cultivated to enter the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness?

Regarding this concentration, a beginner should first contemplate the sphere of infinite space as coarse, painful, and obstructive; next, they should contemplate the sphere of infinite consciousness as peaceful, sublime, and detached. The rest is explained in detail as in the case of the sphere of infinite space.

"Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness" means that at that time, one transcends and thoroughly transcends the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness; therefore, it is called "transcending all aspects of the sphere of infinite consciousness."

Regarding "entering and dwelling fully in the sphere of nothingness": what is the preparatory application for the concentration of the sphere of nothingness, and what application must be cultivated to enter the concentration of the sphere of nothingness?

Regarding this meditative absorption, a beginner should first contemplate the sphere of infinite consciousness as coarse, painful, and obstructive; next, they should contemplate the sphere of nothingness as peaceful, sublime, and detached. The rest is explained in detail as in the case of the sphere of infinite space.

"Transcending all aspects of the sphere of nothingness" means that at that time, one transcends and thoroughly transcends the perception of the sphere of nothingness; therefore, it is called "transcending all aspects of the sphere of nothingness."

Regarding "entering and abiding fully in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception": what is the preparatory application for the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and what preparatory application must be cultivated to enter that absorption?

Regarding this meditative absorption, a beginner should first contemplate the sphere of nothingness as coarse, painful, and obstructive; next, they should contemplate the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as peaceful, sublime, and detached. The rest is explained in detail as in the case of the sphere of infinite space.
Chapter Fourteen: On the Cultivation of Concentration. At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"There are four meditative cultivations. What are the four?
That is to say, there is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and frequently cultivated, enables one to realize dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Furthermore, there is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and frequently cultivated, enables one to realize superior knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, there is the cultivation of concentration, which, through practice, cultivation, and frequent application, enables the realization of superior analytical wisdom.
Furthermore, there is the cultivation of concentration, which, through practice, cultivation, and frequent application, enables the realization of the permanent exhaustion of all taints (*āsrava*).
What is the cultivation of concentration such that, through its practice, cultivation, and frequent application, one is able to realize dwelling in happiness in the present life? It is this:

a bhikṣu, within his own body, moistens, thoroughly moistens, fills, thoroughly fills, gladdens, and thoroughly gladdens it with the joy and bliss born of seclusion. Because of this, there is not even the slightest part of his body that is not filled with the joy and bliss born of seclusion. This is called the cultivation of concentration such that, through its practice, cultivation, and frequent application, one is able to realize dwelling in happiness in the present life.
What is the cultivation of concentration such that, through its practice, cultivation, and frequent application, one is able to realize superior knowledge and vision?

It is when a bhikṣu thoroughly masters, thoroughly contemplates, thoroughly cultivates, and thoroughly penetrates the perception of light; whether by day or night there is no distinction, whether before or after there is no distinction, and whether below or above there is no distinction; with an open mind free from hindrances, he cultivates a mind accompanied by illumination and abandons a mind shrouded in darkness, practicing immeasurable concentration. This is called the cultivation of concentration such that, through its practice, cultivation, and frequent application, one is able to realize superior knowledge and vision.
What is the cultivation of concentration such that, through its practice, development, and frequent application, one is able to realize superior analytical wisdom?

It is when a bhikṣu thoroughly understands the arising of feeling, thoroughly understands the persistence of feeling, and thoroughly understands the cessation, exhaustion, and disappearance of feeling; he dwells with mindfulness established therein and not without mindfulness. Furthermore, he thoroughly understands perception and thoroughly understands discursive thought; he dwells with mindfulness established therein and not without mindfulness. This is called the cultivation of concentration such that, through its practice, development, and frequent application, one is able to realize superior analytical wisdom.
What is the cultivation of concentration such that, through its practice, its development, and its frequent application, one is able to realize the permanent exhaustion of all taints?

It is this: a bhikṣu dwells repeatedly contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging, thinking: "This is form; this is the origin of form; this is the cessation of form. These are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this is the origin of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this is the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This is called the cultivation of concentration such that, through its practice, its development, and its frequent application, one is able to realize the permanent exhaustion of all taints.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to summarize the preceding meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having severed sensual thoughts and distress, And being free from lethargy and regret,
One attains pure equanimity and mindfulness, With the investigation of phenomena as the precursor."
"First is the bliss of the present life; next is superior knowledge, vision, and wisdom;
then one destroys the outflows such as ignorance; finally, one realizes the fruit of liberation.

Regarding "in one's own person": this means that the body is called 'person,' the sense faculties are also called 'person,' the five material sense faculties are also called 'person,' and the aggregate formed by the four great elements is also called 'person.'
In this context, the intended meaning is that the term "body" (*kāya*) refers to an aggregate produced by the four great elements.

Regarding "joy and bliss born of seclusion": the joy and bliss belonging to the first *dhyāna* are comprised within the category of equanimous feeling; they consist of physical lightness and ease (*praśrabdhi*) and mental lightness and ease, and these are termed "joy and bliss."

Such joy and bliss arise from the departure from sensual desires and unwholesome states; they originate, co-originate, are produced, and manifest through that departure. Therefore, it is called "joy and bliss born of seclusion."

"Suffusing, thoroughly suffusing; filling, thoroughly filling; gladdening, thoroughly gladdening" refers to the arising, co-arising, birth, co-birth, accumulation, and manifestation of the joy and bliss born of seclusion within one's own body, which is a composite of the four primary elements.

To moisten and thoroughly moisten is one meaning; to fill and thoroughly fill is one meaning; to gladden and thoroughly gladden is one meaning—distinguished by the differences of lower, middle, and superior nourishment.
It is like a farmer who first irrigates his fields with a small amount of water; at that time, the fields become moistened and thoroughly moistened.
Next, he irrigates the fields with a moderate amount of water; at that time, the fields become filled and thoroughly filled.
Later, when one irrigates the furrows and mounds with abundant water, at that time the furrows and mounds become refreshed and thoroughly refreshed.

It is the same for the bhikṣu: initially, by means of the joy and bliss born of seclusion of an inferior degree, he nourishes the body composed of the great elements and their derivatives; at that time, his own person becomes moistened and thoroughly moistened.
Next, by means of the medium-grade joy and bliss born of seclusion, the aggregate body composed of the great elements is nourished; at that time, one's own body is filled and completely suffused.

Thereafter, by means of the superior-grade joy and bliss born of seclusion, the aggregate body composed of the great elements is further nourished; at that time, one's own body experiences a state of well-being and complete suffusion through the joy and bliss born of seclusion.

Within one's own body, there is not even the slightest part that is not filled; that is to say, from the feet to the crown of the head, the rapture and bliss born of seclusion perform the work of nourishment, such that nothing remains unfilled.
This is called the practitioner who cultivates concentration (*samādhi*). What is concentration?

It refers to the state in which one’s own body is moistened, thoroughly moistened, saturated, thoroughly saturated, filled, and thoroughly filled with the joy and bliss born of seclusion; it is the state in which the mind dwells, dwells evenly, dwells closely, and dwells securely, being undistracted, unconfused, collected, stilled, and unified in a single object—this totality is termed concentration.

What is cultivation? It refers to this meditative concentration: whether it be cultivation (*bhāvanā*) or practice (*abhyāsa*), performing the preparatory application (*prayoga*) constantly and continuously without abandoning it—this is collectively termed "cultivation.
To say that one practices, cultivates, or performs it extensively indicates that one has attained mastery over this concentration.

Regarding "that which enables the realization of abiding in happiness in the present life": this means that if one practices, cultivates, or frequently engages in this meditative concentration, one realizes an abiding in happiness within the present life—an abiding that is lovely, delightful, joyful, and agreeable; it is free from longing, free from yearning, and characterized by tranquility and peace. Therefore, it is called "abiding in happiness."
Because one attains accomplishment, approaches, and realizes this pleasant abiding therein, it is called "realization.
Furthermore, the one-pointedness of mind accompanied by the joy and bliss born of seclusion, which is subsumed under the first dhyāna, is termed "concentration" (samādhi).
If one cultivates or practices this very concentration, performing the preparatory application constantly and continuously without abandoning it, this is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
To practice, cultivate, or perform it extensively demonstrates mastery over it.
It enables the realization of dwelling in happiness in the present life; the meaning is as previously explained.

Regarding "skillfully grasping the perception of light" and so forth: what is the preparatory application for the concentration on light, and what application must be cultivated to enter the concentration on light?

This means that a beginner in this meditative concentration should first properly apprehend the sign of a pure lunar disc, or else properly apprehend the sign of a pure solar disc; or else properly apprehend the light of medicinal herbs, mani-jewels, celestial palaces, or the constellations; or else properly apprehend the light of lamps and candles; or else properly apprehend the light of the burning of cities, towns, rivers, and lands; or else properly apprehend the light of the burning of mountains, marshes, and wildernesses; or else properly apprehend the light of a fire burning ten loads, or twenty loads, or thirty loads, or forty loads, or fifty loads, or a hundred loads, or a thousand loads, or a hundred thousand loads, or immeasurable hundreds of loads, or immeasurable thousands of loads, or immeasurable hundreds of thousands of loads of firewood.
This fire’s radiance is blazing, most intensely blazing; it is brilliantly radiant, all-pervasively radiant.
Having grasped any one of these characteristics of light, one reflects upon it with precision, understands it, observes it, resolves upon it, dwells firmly in it, and discerns it.

At that time, if his mind becomes distracted and wanders toward other objects, such that he is unable to focus one-pointedly or maintain mindfulness so as to dwell upon a single object while contemplating the signs of light he has grasped, this does not yet constitute the preparatory application for the concentration of light, nor does it constitute entry into the concentration of light.

If, at that time, he restrains his own mind so that it does not become distracted or flow toward other objects, and is able to cause it to remain one-pointedly with mindfulness fixed on a single object, he contemplates these signs of light in this manner.

Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the preparatory practice for the concentration of light, and it is also called entering the concentration of light.

Having given rise to this path, through its cultivation and repeated practice, he causes the mind to abide, to abide evenly, to abide closely, and to abide securely; it becomes one-pointed, concentrated, non-dual, and non-retrogressive. He contemplates such signs of light, and up to this point, it is called "having entered the concentration of light," yet it is not yet called the "perception of the concentration of light."
What is called the "perception of the light-concentration" (*āloka-samādhi-saṃjñā*)?

It refers to relying upon the aforementioned light-concentration to contemplate the various signs of light as previously described; the perceptions, equal perceptions, comprehension, grasping of images, past perceptions, and future perceptions [thereof] are termed the perception of the light-concentration.
This meditative perception of light is called the "perception of light.
To be well-received by this perception of light means to receive it with reverence, to receive it with diligence, and to receive it with respect.
One is said to "properly grasp" by reflecting upon its cause, its gateway, its principle, its skillful means, and its mode of activity.
"Proper reflection" refers to repeatedly giving rise to the perception of light and repeatedly contemplating the perception of the signs of light.
"Thoroughly cultivated" means that one repeatedly practices, repeatedly cultivates, and repeatedly performs this perception; therefore, it is called "thoroughly cultivated.
"Thoroughly penetrating" means that one thoroughly understands, thoroughly comprehends, and thoroughly examines this perception; therefore, it is called "thoroughly penetrating."

Regarding the absence of distinction between day and night: this means that just as during the daytime one reflects with careful discernment, understands, observes, resolves, remains steadfastly established, and discriminates upon those aforementioned signs of light, so too is it during the nighttime.
Just as during the night one carefully contemplates, understands, observes, resolves upon, firmly abides in, and discerns the aforementioned signs of light, so too does one do so during the day.
Therefore, it is said that there is no distinction between day and night, and no distinction between before and after.

This means that just as when facing [the light], one thoroughly contemplates, understands, observes, resolves with conviction, firmly abides in, and discerns the aforementioned signs of light, so too is it when turning one's back to them.
As it was with his back turned, so it is when facing him.
Furthermore, just as at the earlier time he had carefully reflected upon, understood, observed, resolved upon, firmly established, and analyzed those various signs of light, so it is now as well.
As it is at this present time, so it was in former times;
therefore, it is said that there is no distinction between what precedes and what follows.

Regarding the absence of distinction between below and above: this means that just as one carefully contemplates, understands, examines, resolves upon, firmly abides in, and discerns the various signs of light in the direction below, one does exactly the same in the direction above.
As it is with the upper direction, so it is with the lower direction;
therefore, there is no distinction between below and above.
"Opening the mind" refers to generating a mind that is accompanied by luminosity, clear illumination, and purity.
"Free from hindrances" means being far removed from the mental hindrance of the entanglements of lethargy and drowsiness.
"Practicing with a mind that is clear and accompanied by illumination" means cultivating a mind that proceeds together with the light of luminosity and the clarity of discernment.

"Eliminating the mind of obscurity" means that within this mind, no signs of obscurity arise; rather, only signs of radiance arise, just as the light of a lamp or candle clearly illuminates and dispels darkness.
Regarding the cultivation of the immeasurable concentrations (*apramāṇa-samādhi*): this refers to cultivating the concentration on the sign of immeasurable light; this is called "cultivation.
As for "concentration" (*samādhi*): what is concentration?

That is to say, the mind’s abiding, its thorough abiding, up to its one-pointedness—arising from deliberation, comprehension, observation, resolute conviction, firm stability, and discernment directed precisely toward that very light—is collectively termed concentration (*samādhi*).

What is cultivation? It refers to this meditative concentration: whether it be cultivation (*bhāvanā*) or practice (*abhyāsa*), constant performance, regular performance, application of effort (*prayoga*), and non-abandonment—collectively these are termed "cultivation.
To say that one practices, cultivates, or performs it extensively indicates that one has attained mastery over this concentration.
Regarding that which enables one to realize superior knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*): what is meant by "superior knowledge and vision"?

It refers to the fact that when one practices, cultivates, or repeatedly performs this meditative concentration until reaching the stage of perfection, there arises at the site of the old eyes a pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) produced from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Based on this divine eye, a pure visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) arises; based on this visual consciousness, one is able to universally observe all forms (*rūpa*) in front, behind, to the left, to the right, above, and below.

Just as the pure divine eye, produced from the primary elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), arises from the vicinity of the original eye, so too does the pure visual consciousness arise; relying upon this visual consciousness, one experiences and examines various forms—this is what is called "superior knowledge and vision" (*jñānadarśana*) in this context.
Some maintain this view: because the mind is purified, one perceives through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), whereby the human fleshly eye is transformed into the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*);

this is called "superior wisdom-vision" (*jñānadarśana*). In the present context, it refers to the superior wisdom associated with the aforementioned purified visual consciousness; this is designated as both "wisdom" and "vision. Specifically, the superior wisdom associated with the divine-eye consciousness that experiences and examines various forms is what is meant here by "superior wisdom-vision."
If one practices, cultivates, or frequently applies oneself to this meditative concentration, one is able to realize superior knowledge and vision.
Because one attains, achieves, approaches, touches, and realizes superior knowledge and vision, it is called "realization."
Furthermore, one-pointedness of mind accompanied by the perception of light is called concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding this very concentration, if one cultivates it, practices it, constantly performs it, habitually applies the preparatory effort (*prayoga*), and does not abandon it, this is called cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Whether practiced, cultivated, or frequently performed, these manifest his mastery.
That he is able to realize superior knowledge and vision has the same meaning as previously explained.

"Skillfully knowing the arising of feeling, skillfully knowing the abiding of feeling, and skillfully knowing the cessation, exhaustion, and disappearance of feeling" refers to the thorough observation of the arising of feeling, the thorough observation of the abiding of feeling, and the thorough observation of the cessation, exhaustion, and disappearance of feeling therein.

"Abiding in mindfulness, not being without mindfulness" means: observing with mindfulness and clear comprehension when feeling arises; observing with mindfulness and clear comprehension when feeling persists; and observing with mindfulness and clear comprehension when feeling ceases, fades away, and disappears.

Regarding "skillfully contemplating and skillfully knowing thoughts and applied thought": this refers to carefully observing the arising of thoughts and applied thought, carefully observing the abiding of thoughts and applied thought, and carefully observing the cessation, exhaustion, and disappearance of thoughts and applied thought therein.

"Abiding in mindfulness, not being without mindfulness" means that when examining thoughts and discursive thinking as they arise, one possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension; when examining thoughts and discursive thinking as they abide, one possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension; and when examining thoughts and discursive thinking as they cease, vanish, and disappear, one possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension—this is called cultivation.
Regarding concentration: what is concentration?
It means that at that time, he forms this thought:

"I should correctly contemplate all phenomena so as to not give rise to unwholesome states and to give rise to wholesome states; not to give rise to indeterminate states and to give rise to determinate states; so that unwholesome states do not endure for long, wholesome states may endure for a long time, indeterminate states do not endure for long, and determinate states may endure for a long time."
At that time, he also observes the mind and observes mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).

When he observes the mind and mental factors, the state of mind that arises—ranging from stability (*sthiti*) and thorough stability (*susaṃsthiti*) up to one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*)—is collectively termed concentration (*samādhi*).
What is cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?

It refers to this meditative concentration: whether it be cultivated, practiced, performed constantly, or performed regularly through application (*prayoga*) without relinquishing it—this is collectively termed "cultivation.
As for "practicing," "cultivating," or "performing extensively," it means being able to attain mastery (*vaśitā*) over this concentration.

Regarding "able to cause the realization of superior analytical wisdom": this means that if one practices, cultivates, or frequently applies oneself to this meditative concentration, it can destroy all unwholesome wisdom, wisdom induced by improper reasoning, and all unwholesome wisdom that obstructs concentration; these are all abandoned and prevented from arising, while the opposing wisdom grows, becomes firm, and remains established.
For this reason it is said that one is able to realize superior analytical wisdom (*pravicaya-prajñā*).
Because one attains, achieves, approaches, and directly realizes this very wisdom, it is called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Furthermore, the one-pointedness of mind that accompanies feeling, perception, and discursive thought, when examined closely, is called concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding this very concentration, if one cultivates it, practices it, constantly performs it, habitually applies effort toward it, and does not abandon it, this is called cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Whether it be practiced (*śikṣita*), cultivated (*bhāvita*), or frequently performed (*bahulīkṛta*), these terms reveal its mastery.
It is able to cause one to realize superior analytical wisdom (*prajñā-vicaya*); the meaning is as previously explained.

Regarding "dwelling while repeatedly contemplating the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*)," this means knowing, in accordance with reality, the arising and transformation of form (*rūpa*), and knowing, in accordance with reality, the arising and transformation of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); this is called cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding concentration (*samādhi*): what is concentration?

It refers to dwelling in the repeated contemplation of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging; the mental abiding, even abiding, up to one-pointedness of mind that arises therein is collectively termed concentration.
What is cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?

It refers to this meditative concentration: whether it be practiced (*bhāvita*), cultivated (*vāsita*), performed constantly, or performed regularly through application (*prayoga*) without relinquishing it—this is collectively termed "cultivation.
To say that one "practices," "cultivates," or "performs it extensively" indicates that one has attained mastery (*vaśitā*) over this concentration.

Regarding "able to bring about the realization of the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*)," "outflows" refers to the three outflows: namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).

When one practices, cultivates, or frequently applies oneself to this meditative concentration, it can cause these three outflows to be exhausted, equally exhausted, universally exhausted, and ultimately exhausted; therefore, it is called the "permanent exhaustion of all outflows."
Because one attains accomplishment, approaches, and realizes the permanent exhaustion of these [defilements], it is called "realization.

Furthermore, the one-pointedness of mind included within the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) leading to arhatship, which is associated with pure equanimity and mindfulness and is subsumed under the fourth dhyāna, is termed "concentration" (*samādhi*).

Regarding this very meditative concentration, if one cultivates it, practices it, constantly performs it, habitually applies the preparatory effort (*prayoga*), and does not abandon it, this is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
If one practices it, cultivates it, or performs it extensively, this demonstrates mastery over it.
It enables one to realize the permanent exhaustion of all outflows; the meaning is as previously explained.
Chapter Fifteen: The Factors of Enlightenment (Bodhyanga-varga), Part One. At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a bhikṣu approached the place where the Buddha was staying. Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The World-Honored One has previously spoken of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga)."
"What is the meaning of this term 'factors of enlightenment'?
The Blessed One replied,
"This term 'factors of enlightenment' refers to the seven factors of enlightenment."
What are the seven?

They are the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of rapture, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity.
"In this way, the factors of enlightenment arise gradually, are attained gradually, and are cultivated to perfection.
Then that bhikṣu addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"In what manner do the factors of enlightenment arise gradually, are attained gradually, and are cultivated to perfection?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“If one dwells in the contemplation of the body regarding the body, abiding in right mindfulness and remaining free from delusion, at that time the awakening factor of mindfulness arises.”
He attains the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness and cultivates it to perfection.

By means of this mindfulness, he discriminates, thoroughly discriminates, extensively investigates, extensively examines, and scrutinizes phenomena with precise investigation; at that time, the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena arises.
He attains the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena and cultivates it to perfection.
Through that investigation of phenomena, he arouses diligent effort and his mind does not become inferior; at that time, the awakening factor of effort arises.
He attains the awakening factor of energy and cultivates it to perfection.
Through that energy, he gives rise to sublime joy and remains detached from the savoring of pleasure; at that time, the awakening factor of joy arises.
He attains the factor of enlightenment of joy and cultivates it to perfection.
Through this joy, his body and mind become pliant and tranquil, and he is freed from heaviness; at that time, the factor of enlightenment of pliancy arises.
He attains the awakening factor of tranquility and cultivates it to perfection.
Through that tranquility, he experiences happiness; because of that happiness, his mind becomes concentrated, and at that time, the awakening factor of concentration arises.
He attains the awakening factor of concentration and cultivates it to perfection.
Through mental concentration, he is able to extinguish sensual desire and grief, abiding in superior equanimity; at that time, the awakening factor of equanimity arises.
One attains the awakening factor of equanimity and cultivates it to perfection.
Regarding feelings, the mind, and phenomena, one dwells observing feelings, the mind, and phenomena; the detailed explanation is likewise.
In this way, these awakening factors arise gradually and are attained gradually, as one cultivates them to perfection.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness?
The Blessed One has said:
"If a noble disciple dwells contemplating the body in this internal body, possessing right effort, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, he removes worldly greed and sorrow."
Abiding in contemplation of the body with regard to that external body, if one possesses right effort, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
Abiding in contemplation of the body with regard to both internal and external bodies, if one possesses right effort, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
The detailed explanation for the three—feelings, mind, and phenomena—regarding both the internal and external is likewise the same.

When practicing these four foundations of mindfulness, all that is associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*)—namely, mindfulness, recollection, focused attention, and memory; its non-forgetfulness, non-loss, non-omission, and non-leakage; its non-deviation from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the mind’s quality of clear recollection—is collectively termed "mindfulness" (*smṛti*). It is also called the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, and right mindfulness. It is noble, supramundane, untainted, and free from grasping; it is the path that follows the path, accompanies the path, and proceeds with the path, capable of correctly exhausting suffering and bringing an end to suffering.

All those in training reflect upon and examine all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) just as they have been seen, bringing them to ultimate realization; they perceive the faults within conditioned phenomena with deep insight and perceive the merits of eternal nirvāṇa with deep insight.

If an Arhat, like the liberated mind, contemplates and examines until reaching the ultimate, all untainted mental applications (*manasikāra*) associated with mindfulness, recollection, and even the nature of the mind’s clear retention—this is called the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena? The Blessed One said:

It is when a noble disciple is able to know, as they truly are, wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; blameworthy and blameless phenomena; phenomena to be cultivated and not to be cultivated; inferior and sublime phenomena; dark and bright phenomena; phenomena that are opposed; and dependently arisen phenomena.
Regarding one who can know wholesome and unwholesome phenomena as they truly are: what are wholesome phenomena?

They are wholesome bodily and verbal actions, wholesome states of mind and mental factors, wholesome formations dissociated from the mind, and analytical cessation; these are called wholesome phenomena.
What are unwholesome phenomena?
They are unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, unwholesome mental states and their associated mental factors, and unwholesome formations dissociated from mind; these are called unwholesome phenomena.

Regarding such wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, he discriminates, thoroughly discriminates, universally investigates, universally examines, and scrutinizes them with correct wisdom as they truly are; this is called being able to know wholesome and unwholesome phenomena as they truly are.
Regarding one who can know, as they truly are, the dharmas that are blameworthy and those that are blameless: what are the blameworthy dharmas?
They are the three types of misconduct, the three unwholesome roots, and the ten unwholesome paths of action; these are called the blameworthy dharmas.
What are the blameless phenomena?
They are the three types of sublime conduct, the three roots of virtue, and the ten paths of wholesome action; these are called blameless phenomena.

When one uses correct wisdom as it truly is to discern, thoroughly discern, extensively investigate, extensively examine, and carefully scrutinize such blameworthy and blameless phenomena, this is called being able to know blameworthy and blameless phenomena as they truly are.
Regarding one who is able to know, as they truly are, the dharmas that should be cultivated and those that should not be cultivated: what are the dharmas that should be cultivated?

They are the three types of sublime conduct, the three roots of goodness, the ten paths of wholesome action, associating with virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, proper mental attention, practice in accordance with the Dharma, listening with reverence, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, and being diligent in cultivating all virtues without sleeping during the first or last watches of the night; these are called the dharmas that should be cultivated.

Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the four right practices, the four tracks of the Dharma, and serenity (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) are also called the dharmas to be cultivated.
What are the dharmas that should not be cultivated?

They are: the three types of unwholesome conduct, the three unwholesome roots, the ten unwholesome paths of action; associating with unwholesome persons, hearing what is not the true Dharma, improper mental attention, practicing what is contrary to the Dharma, listening without respect, questioning without respect, failing to guard the doors of the sense faculties, lack of moderation in eating, and constantly indulging in sleep during the first and last watches of the night rather than diligently cultivating the wholesome—these are called the dharmas that should not be cultivated.

Regarding these dharmas that should be cultivated and those that should not be cultivated, he discriminates, thoroughly discriminates, universally investigates, universally examines, and scrutinizes them with correct wisdom as they truly are; this is called being able to know, as it truly is, the dharmas that should be cultivated and those that should not be cultivated.

Regarding one who can know, as they truly are, the inferior and the sublime dharmas: what are the inferior dharmas? They are unwholesome dharmas and obscured-unspecified dharmas; these are called inferior dharmas.
What are the sublime and excellent dharmas?
They are all wholesome dharmas and those that are non-obscured and neutral; these are called the sublime and excellent dharmas.

When one discriminates, thoroughly discriminates, universally investigates, universally examines, and scrutinizes with precise examination such inferior and sublime dharmas by means of correct wisdom as it truly is, this is called being able to know inferior and sublime dharmas as they truly are.
Regarding one who is able to know black and white phenomena as they truly are:

what are black and white phenomena? Unwholesome phenomena are called black; wholesome phenomena are called white. Phenomena with fault are called black; phenomena without fault are called white. Phenomena that should not be cultivated are called black; phenomena that should be cultivated are called white. Inferior phenomena are called black; superior and sublime phenomena are called white. These are called black and white phenomena.

Regarding these black and white phenomena, he discriminates, thoroughly discriminates, universally investigates, universally examines, and scrutinizes them with correct wisdom as they truly are; this is called being able to know black and white phenomena as they truly are.
One who can know, as it truly is, the phenomena that are mutually antagonistic—what are these phenomena that are mutually antagonistic?

They are: greed and non-greed are mutually antagonistic; hatred and non-hatred are mutually antagonistic; delusion and non-delusion are mutually antagonistic. These are called the phenomena that are mutually antagonistic.

When one discriminates, thoroughly discriminates, extensively investigates, extensively examines, and scrutinizes with precise examination those phenomena that are mutually antagonistic by means of correct wisdom as it truly is, this is called knowing phenomena that are mutually antagonistic as they truly are.
Regarding those who can know phenomena produced by conditions as they truly are: what are phenomena produced by conditions?
They are the phenomena of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the phenomena that have arisen dependently; these together are termed "phenomena produced by conditions."

When one discriminates, thoroughly discriminates, universally investigates, universally examines, and scrutinizes such dependently arisen phenomena with correct wisdom as it truly is, this is called knowing dependently arisen phenomena as they truly are.

When he knows dharmas that are wholesome and unwholesome as they truly are—and so on, as extensively explained, up until the time of the dependently arisen dharmas—there is a state associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), which consists of the discernment, thorough discernment, and supreme discernment of dharmas; the understanding, equal understanding, and proximate understanding; the sagacity, penetration, investigation, and intelligence; the clarity of awakening, wisdom, and mental activity; and *vipaśyanā*. This is collectively termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*). It is also called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-sambodhyaṅga*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). It is noble, supramundane, untainted, without grasping, the path that follows the way, the path that accompanies the way, and it is capable of correctly exhausting suffering and bringing an end to suffering.

All those in training, regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they have seen them, contemplate and examine them until reaching their ultimate limit; they perceive the faults within all conditioned phenomena with great depth, and they perceive the merit of eternal *nirvāṇa* with great depth.

If an Arhat, like one whose mind is liberated, contemplates and examines until reaching the ultimate, then all that is associated with untainted attention—from the discernment of phenomena up to vipaśyanā—is called the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
What is the enlightenment factor of energy?
The Blessed One said:
When a noble disciple, for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, arouses desire, exerts effort, applies energy, upholds the mind, and sustains the mind.
In order that unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise, one arouses desire, exerts effort, applies energy, upholds the mind, and sustains the mind.
In order that unarisen wholesome states may arise, one arouses desire, exerts effort, applies energy, upholds the mind, and sustains the mind.

In order to cause wholesome states that have already arisen to remain firm, not be forgotten, to be cultivated to fulfillment, to increase, to expand, and to be realized through direct knowledge, one arouses desire, exerts effort, applies diligence, uplifts the mind, and sustains the mind.

When he cultivates these four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), all that is associated with untainted attention (*anāsravamanasikāra*)—the diligence, vigor, fortitude, intensity, fervor, and irresistible exertion of mind that is tireless—is collectively termed "vigor. It is also called the faculty of vigor, the power of vigor, the factor of enlightenment of vigor, and right effort. It is noble, supramundane, untainted, and without grasping; it is the path that follows the path, co-arises with the path, and proceeds along with the path, capable of correctly exhausting suffering and bringing an end to suffering.

All those in training, regarding all conditioned phenomena as they have been seen, contemplate and examine them until they reach the ultimate; within these conditioned phenomena, they deeply perceive their defects, and within eternal nirvāṇa, they deeply perceive its virtues.

If an Arhat, like one whose mind is liberated, contemplates and observes until reaching the ultimate, all the diligent vigor associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), up to and including the unremitting exertion of the will—this is called the factor of enlightenment of vigor (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*).
What is the factor of awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? The Blessed One said:
"Mahānāman, you should know this:

if a noble disciple recollects the Buddhas with such characteristics, thinking, 'This Blessed One is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons, a trainer of men, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Bhagavān.'"

When that noble disciple recollects the Buddha with such characteristics, greed does not entangle his mind, hatred does not entangle his mind, and delusion does not entangle his mind; toward the Tathāgata, his mind is upright.

Because the mind is upright, one attains the majestic power of meaning and the majestic power of the Dharma; one is able to arouse joy toward the Tathāgata. From joy, a joyful mind arises; from joy, the body becomes tranquil; from bodily tranquility, one experiences bliss; from bliss, the mind becomes concentrated; and from concentration of the mind, one abides in equanimity toward all sentient beings who are otherwise unequal, and abides in non-harm toward all sentient beings who might cause harm, thereby entering the stream of the Dharma.
By cultivating mindfulness of the Buddhas, one may even realize ultimate nirvana. Furthermore, Mahānāma,

if a noble disciple recollects the True Dharma with such characteristics— namely, that the Buddha’s True Dharma is well-expounded, directly visible, free from feverish affliction, timely, leading onward, inviting inspection, and to be personally realized by the wise.

When that noble disciple recollects the Dharma with such characteristics, greed does not ensnare his mind, hatred does not ensnare his mind, and delusion does not ensnare his mind. Toward the True Dharma, his mind becomes upright; because his mind is upright, he attains the majesty of meaning and the majesty of the Dharma. Because he can give rise to a sense of joyful exultation toward the True Dharma, a joyful mind arises. Due to joy, the body becomes tranquil; due to physical tranquility, he experiences happiness; due to happiness, the mind becomes concentrated; and due to mental concentration, he abides in equanimity toward all sentient beings who are otherwise unequal, and he dwells without malice toward those sentient beings who harbor harm. Thus, he enters the stream of the Dharma.
By cultivating mindfulness of the True Dharma, one is even able to realize ultimate nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Mahānāman,

if a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha with these characteristics— namely, that the disciples of the Buddha are endowed with excellent conduct, upright conduct, rational conduct, conduct in accordance with the Dharma, harmonious and respectful conduct, and conduct following the Dharma.

Furthermore, among the disciples of the Buddha, there are those entering the stream (srotāpattipratipannaka) and those who have attained the fruit of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna); those entering the stage of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka) and those who have attained the fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin); those entering the stage of non-returning (anāgāmipratipannaka) and those who have attained the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmin); and those entering the stage of arhatship (arhattvapratipannaka) and those who have attained the fruit of arhatship (arhat). Thus, in total, there are these four pairs and eight types of individuals (pudgala).

Such is the Saṅgha, complete in virtue, complete in concentration, complete in wisdom, complete in liberation, and complete in the knowledge and vision of liberation; they are worthy of invitation, worthy of veneration, and worthy of respect—the unsurpassed field of merit to whom the world should offer its offerings.

When that noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha with such characteristics, greed does not entangle his mind, hatred does not entangle his mind, and delusion does not entangle his mind. Toward the Saṅgha, his mind becomes upright; because his mind is upright, he attains the majesty of the goal and the majesty of the Dharma. Toward the Saṅgha, he is able to arouse gladness; from gladness, joy arises; because the mind is joyful, the body becomes tranquil; because the body is tranquil, he experiences happiness; because of happiness, the mind becomes concentrated; and because the mind is concentrated, he abides in equanimity toward all sentient beings who are unequal, and he abides without malice toward those sentient beings who cause harm, thereby attaining entry into the stream of the Dharma.
By practicing the recollection of the Saṅgha, one is even able to realize ultimate nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahānāma!

If a noble disciple recollects his own precepts with such characteristics as: "My pure precepts are unbroken, unperforated, unmixed, unsullied, worthy of offerings, unblemished, perfectly complete, well-undertaken, and praised by the wise, never being subject to reproach."

When that noble disciple recollects his own ethical discipline (*śīla*) with such characteristics, greed does not ensnare his mind, hatred does not ensnare his mind, and delusion does not ensnare his mind. Regarding his own ethical discipline, his mind becomes upright; because his mind is upright, he attains the majestic power of meaning (*artha-vaśitā*) and the majestic power of the Dharma (*dharma-vaśitā*). Toward his own ethical discipline, he is able to give rise to gladness (*prāmodya*); from gladness, joy (*prīti*) arises; because the mind is joyful, the body becomes tranquil (*praśrabdha*); because the body is tranquil, he experiences happiness (*sukha*); because of happiness, the mind becomes concentrated (*samāhita*); and because the mind is concentrated, he abides in equanimity toward all sentient beings who are unequally disposed, and he dwells without malice toward those sentient beings who harbor harm. Thus, he enters the stream of the Dharma (*dharma-srotas*).

By cultivating mindfulness of one's own ethical discipline (*śīla*), one may even realize ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, Mahānāman, if a noble disciple recollects his own generosity with such characteristics as these—thinking, "I have now attained a great benefit;

though dwelling among a multitude of beings ensnared by immeasurable stains of stinginess, my mind remains far removed from all such stains and I am able to practice giving"—then even while living at home, he is able to remain unattached to all wealth and treasures, extending his hand in charity, performing great sacrifices, making offerings to the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), being fully endowed with liberality, and delighting in the equal distribution of goods.

When that noble disciple recollects his own giving with such characteristics, greed does not ensnare his mind, hatred does not ensnare his mind, and delusion does not ensnare his mind. Regarding his own giving, his mind is upright; because his mind is upright, he attains the power of meaning and the power of the Dharma. He is able to arouse joy regarding his own giving; from joy, rapture arises; because the mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; because the body is tranquil, he experiences happiness; because of happiness, the mind becomes concentrated; and because the mind is concentrated, he dwells in equanimity toward all sentient beings who are unequally disposed, and dwells without malice toward those sentient beings who cause harm. Thus, he enters the stream of the Dharma.
By means of recollecting the practice of one's own giving, one is even able to realize ultimate nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahānāman!

If a noble disciple recollects the devas by way of these characteristics, namely: the Cāturmahārājika devas, the Trāyastriṃśa devas, the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas.

Thus, these devas, by virtue of having accomplished faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom, pass away from this place and are reborn in that celestial realm to experience various pleasures.
"I too possess faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom; I, too, shall be reborn there and experience happiness together with the assembly of devas.

When that noble disciple recollects the devas with such characteristics, greed does not ensnare his mind, hatred does not ensnare his mind, and delusion does not ensnare his mind. Toward the devas, his mind becomes upright. Because his mind is upright, he attains the power of meaning and the power of the Dharma. Regarding the devas, he is able to arouse joy; because of joy, rapture arises; because the mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; because the body is tranquil, he experiences bliss; because of bliss, the mind becomes concentrated; and because the mind is concentrated, he dwells in equanimity toward all sentient beings who are unequal, and dwells without malice toward those sentient beings who cause harm. Thus, he enters the stream of the Dharma.
Because he cultivates the recollections (*anusmṛti*) regarding the devas, he is even able to realize ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

When he cultivates these six recollections, all that is associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*)—the mind’s gladness, extreme gladness, manifest gladness, the nature of gladness, the category of gladness; its agreeableness, its delightfulness, the nature of joy, the category of joy; its union with bliss, its non-separation, its exultation, its state of being uplifted, its state of being elated, its state of being joyful and delighted—is collectively termed "joy" (*prīti*). It is also called the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prītisambodhyaṅga*). It is noble, supramundane, untainted, without grasping, the path that follows the way, the path that proceeds together with the way, which is capable of correctly exhausting suffering and abiding at the limit of suffering.

All those in training, regarding all conditioned phenomena as they have been seen, contemplate and examine them until they reach the ultimate; within these conditioned phenomena, they deeply perceive their defects and, regarding eternal nirvana, they deeply perceive its virtues.

If an Arhat, like one whose mind is liberated, contemplates and examines until reaching the ultimate, whatever state of mind associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*) is characterized by gladness, extreme gladness, up to joy and rapture—this is called the factor of awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
