The Remainder of Chapter Fifteen: The Factors of Enlightenment (Bodhyaṅga). What is the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (praśrabdhi-bodhyaṅga)?
As the Blessed One said:

Ānanda, you should know that when one enters the first dhyāna, speech ceases; with this as a condition, other phenomena also cease. This is called the first characteristic conducive to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

When entering the second dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are stilled; with this as a condition, other dharmas are likewise stilled. This is called the second characteristic conducive to pliancy (praśrabdhi).

When entering the third dhyāna, all forms of joy (prīti) come to rest; with this as the condition, other factors also come to rest. This is called the third characteristic conducive to pliancy (praśrabdhi).
When entering the fourth dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation cease; conditioned by this, other phenomena also cease. This is called the fourth characteristic conducive to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

When entering the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling are stilled; with this as a condition, other dharmas are also stilled. This is called the fifth characteristic conducive to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

Ānanda, you should know that there is furthermore a sixth kind of sublime pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), which is superior, most superior, supreme, and unsurpassed; such pliancy is the highest and most exquisite, and no other pliancy can surpass it.
What, moreover, is this?

It refers to the mind’s liberation through detachment from greed, and its liberation through detachment from hatred and delusion; this is called the sixth characteristic conducive to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

Contemplating this sign, all those factors associated with untainted attention—namely, physical pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*), mental pliancy (*citta-praśrabdhi*), the nature of pliancy, and the category of pliancy—are collectively termed "pliancy. It is also called the "factor of enlightenment of pliancy" (*praśrabdhi-sambodhyaṅga*). It is noble, supramundane, untainted, without grasping, a path that follows the way, accompanied by the path, and proceeding in accordance with the path; it is capable of rightly exhausting suffering and bringing about the final limit of suffering.

All those in training, regarding all conditioned phenomena as they have been seen, contemplate and investigate them until reaching the ultimate; within these conditioned phenomena, they deeply perceive their defects and, regarding eternal nirvāṇa, they deeply perceive its merits.

If an Arhat, like one whose mind is liberated, contemplates and examines [the mind] until it reaches its ultimate state, then all untainted mental applications (manasikāra) associated with bodily pliancy (kāya-praśrabdhi), mental pliancy (citta-praśrabdhi), the nature of pliancy, and the category of pliancy—this is called the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga).
What is the factor of enlightenment of concentration?
The Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that I declare that by relying on the first dhyāna one can exhaust all outflows; likewise, I declare that by relying on the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness, one can exhaust all outflows."
“Bhikṣus, you should know on what basis I make such a statement: that by means of the first dhyāna one can exhaust all outflows.

That is to say, there is a bhikṣu who, by means of such characteristics of these formations, becomes detached from desires and unwholesome states; possessing vitarka and vicāra, he dwells having fully attained the first dhyāna, which is born of detachment and characterized by joy and bliss.”

He does not contemplate the characteristics or marks of these conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), but contemplates only that which has been attained and toward which he is directed—namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—thinking: "These phenomena are like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow piercing and afflicting; they are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
Having developed a deep sense of weary detachment toward these phenomena, fearing them and restraining them, he then withdraws his mind and places it within the realm of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
He contemplates this realm as tranquil and sublime; abandoning all dependencies, with craving exhausted and defilements departed, there is the eternal cessation of *nirvāṇa*.

Just as a skilled archer or his disciple first practices shooting at nearby targets such as clay balls or straw figures, and later becomes able to shoot at distant, solid objects and even cause them to be destroyed.

The bhikṣu is likewise: first, by means of such characteristics of these formations, he becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he fully attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

He does not contemplate the characteristics or marks of these conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), but contemplates only that which has been attained and that toward which he is proceeding—namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—considering these phenomena to be like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow piercing and afflicting, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

Having developed a deep sense of weary detachment toward these phenomena, fearing them and restraining from them, he subsequently withdraws his mind and places it within the realm of ambrosia (*amṛta*). He contemplates this realm as tranquil and sublime; abandoning all dependencies, craving is exhausted, defilements are left behind, and there is eternal cessation in *nirvāṇa*.

Because he knows thus and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), and his mind is also liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhavāsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyāsrava*).
Having attained liberation, he is able to know and see for himself that he has attained liberation:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
It is based on this that I make such a statement: by relying on the first dhyāna, one can exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).

Just as it is said that by relying on the first dhyāna one can exhaust all outflows, so too it is said that by relying on the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one can exhaust all outflows.
The same applies accordingly; that is to say, regarding the second dhyāna, one should speak as follows:

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, by means of such characteristics of these formations, having stilled vitarka and vicāra, with internal clarity and mental one-pointedness, free from vitarka and vicāra, and possessing the joy and bliss born of concentration, dwells fully endowed with the second dhyāna.
He does not contemplate the characteristics and marks of these conditioned phenomena, and so forth, as explained at length.

Up to the sphere of nothingness, it should be stated thus: furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, by means of such characteristics and marks of conditioned phenomena, transcends in every respect the sphere of infinite consciousness and enters the sphere of nothingness, abiding fully therein.

He does not contemplate the characteristics and marks of these various formations (*saṃskāra*), but contemplates only the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that he has attained and toward which he has proceeded, and so forth, as explained at length.

Bhikṣus, you should know that even the attainment of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samāpatti*) can accomplish such tasks as these; furthermore, there are the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
I say that regarding those bhikṣus who cultivate meditative concentration, they should repeatedly enter and emerge from it.

When they thus cultivate the seven bases of meditative concentration, all the mind’s abiding, thorough abiding, up to one-pointedness of mind associated with untainted attention, is collectively termed "concentration. It is also called the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and right concentration. This is noble, supramundane, untainted, and free from grasping; it is the path that follows the way, the path that proceeds together with the way, which can correctly exhaust suffering and bring about the end of suffering.

All those in training, regarding all conditioned phenomena as they have been seen, contemplate and examine them until reaching their ultimate limit; within these conditioned phenomena, they deeply perceive their faults and disadvantages, and within eternal nirvana, they deeply perceive its merits.

If an Arhat, like one whose mind is liberated, reflects and examines until reaching the ultimate, all states of mental abiding, thorough abiding, up to one-pointedness of mind associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), are called the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to a bhikṣu who contemplates the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*), the realm of detachment (*virāgadhātu*), and the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*); by means of this, he gives rise to evenness of mind (*cittasamatā*), rectitude of mind (*cittapraśathatā*), and a state of peaceful abiding free from mental agitation (*avyupaśāntavihāratā*).
He reflects thus:
"I should now abandon greed, hatred, and delusion regarding those phenomena that accord with greed, hatred, and delusion.
From this, he gives rise to equanimity of mind, rectitude of mind, and a state of abiding in tranquility free from agitation. He further reflects:
"I should now not mentally grasp at the phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion.
From this, he gives rise to equanimity of mind, rectitude of mind, and a state of dwelling in tranquility free from mental agitation.

When he carefully contemplates the mental equanimity, mental rectitude, and the state of peaceful abiding without agitation that correspond to the untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*) associated with all six factors conducive to equanimity, this is collectively termed "equanimity" (*upekṣā*). It is also called the "limb of awakening of equanimity" (*upekṣā-sambodhyaṅga*). It is noble, supramundane, untainted, and without grasping; it is the path that follows the way, accompanies the way, and proceeds with the way, capable of correctly exhausting suffering and bringing an end to suffering.

All those in training, regarding the conditioned phenomena as they have been seen, contemplate and examine them until reaching their ultimate limit; within these conditioned phenomena, they perceive deeply their defects and, regarding eternal nirvāṇa, they perceive deeply its virtues.

If an Arhat, like one whose mind is liberated, contemplates and examines until reaching the ultimate, the state of equanimity of mind, the state of rectitude of mind, and the state of dwelling in tranquility free from agitation associated with untainted mental attention—this is called the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Chapter Sixteen: Miscellaneous Matters. Chapter Sixteen on Miscellaneous Matters. At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"If you are able to permanently sever one dharma, I guarantee that you will certainly attain the state of non-returning (anāgāmin).
This one dharma is craving (rāga); if it is permanently severed, I can guarantee that such a person will certainly attain the state of non-returning."
Likewise, there are hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, envy,
stinginess, deceit, guile, lack of shame, lack of dread, pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride,
the pride of "I," overweening pride, inferiority pride, false pride, arrogance, negligence, haughtiness, and outbursts of fury.
Deceit, hypocrisy, guile, hinting, belittling, seeking profit through profit, evil desire, great desire,
manifest desire, lack of contentment, lack of respect, uttering evil speech, delighting in evil friends, intolerance,
indulgence and pervasive indulgence, stained greed, unrighteous greed, and clinging greed.
...evil greed, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of existence (*bhavadr̥ṣṭi*),
the view of non-existence (*vibhavadr̥ṣṭi*), sensual desire, ill will, lethargy, torpor, restlessness, remorse, doubt,
mental dullness, lack of joy, yawning and stretching, irregularity of diet, mental sluggishness, and various perceptions.
Lack of attention, heaviness and rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*), contentiousness, gluttony, lack of gentleness, lack of flexibility,
lack of conformity to one's peers, thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill-will,
thoughts of harm, thoughts of kin, thoughts of country, thoughts of immortality, thoughts of contempt, thoughts of false lineage, sorrow, and lamentation.
"Suffering, sorrow, and vexation— if one were to permanently sever this single dharma, I could guarantee that he would certainly attain the state of a non-returner.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to summarize the preceding meaning, spoke these verses:
“Sentient beings bound by craving repeatedly go to the various evil realms;
the wise are able to correctly sever it and do not return to this world.
In this same way, there are individual verses for hatred, delusion, and even agitation; they should be understood as being analogous to the verse on craving.
What is greed?

It refers to all forms of greed and pervasive greed regarding objects of desire; it includes grasping and hoarding, guarding and protecting, firm attachment, longing and delight, delusion and bewilderment, indulgence and total indulgence, internal bondage, yearning, immersion in suffering and its origin, and that which belongs to the category of greed or arises from greed—all these together are termed greed.

What is hatred (*dveṣa*)? It refers to the desire to cause harm toward sentient beings; harboring an internal resentment with the intent to disturb and afflict them; having hated, about to hate, or currently hating; delighting in misfortune and extreme misfortune; being intensely enraged in mind; and desiring to cause harm to all sentient beings through mutual opposition and hostility—having caused harm, about to cause harm, or currently causing harm. All of these taken together are termed hatred.
What is delusion (*moha*)?
It refers to ignorance regarding the past, ignorance regarding the future, and ignorance regarding both the past and the future;
ignorance regarding the internal, ignorance regarding the external, and ignorance regarding both the internal and the external; and ignorance regarding karma and its maturation (*vipāka*).
Ignorance regarding the ripening of karma; ignorance regarding wholesome actions performed, unwholesome actions performed, and both wholesome and unwholesome actions performed;
ignorance regarding causes and ignorance regarding the phenomena produced by causes;
ignorance regarding the Buddha, ignorance regarding the Dharma, and ignorance regarding the Saṅgha; ignorance regarding suffering and ignorance regarding its origin.
Ignorance regarding knowledge; ignorance regarding cessation; ignorance regarding the path;
ignorance regarding wholesome phenomena and unwholesome phenomena; ignorance regarding blameworthy phenomena and blameless phenomena;
ignorance regarding phenomena to be cultivated and phenomena not to be cultivated; ignorance regarding inferior phenomena and sublime phenomena.
He lacks knowledge regarding dark phenomena, lacks knowledge regarding bright phenomena, lacks knowledge regarding opposing phenomena,
lacks knowledge regarding dependently arisen phenomena, and lacks knowledge of the six bases of contact as they truly are.

Thus, lack of knowledge and lack of vision; that which is not clear realization (*abhisamaya*); darkness and delusion; the blindness and obscurity of ignorance (*avidyā*); being enveloped within a net; being stubborn, foolish, and turbid; the arising of blindness through hindrances and coverings; the arising of sightlessness, the arising of lack of wisdom, the arising of inferior intelligence; that which obstructs the wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*) and prevents *nirvāṇa*; the outflow (*āsrava*) of ignorance, the flood (*ogha*) of ignorance, the yoke (*yoga*) of ignorance; the poisonous root of ignorance, the poisonous stem of ignorance, the poisonous branch of ignorance, the poisonous leaf of ignorance, the poisonous flower of ignorance, and the poisonous fruit of ignorance; delusion, further delusion, extreme delusion; delight, further delight, extreme delight; and whatever belongs to the category of delusion or is born from delusion—all these together are termed "delusion" (*moha*).
What is anger? It is said that there are two kinds of anger:
first, anger associated with attachment; [second, anger associated with aversion].
2. Anger directed toward those who are not loved.
Anger directed toward those who are loved refers to the anger that arises toward one's father, mother, brothers, sisters, wives, concubines, sons, daughters, or any other relative or friend.
With anger, he says:
"Why do you not give me this thing, but instead give me such a thing?
Why do you not do this for me, but instead do such a thing for me?"

From this, there arises anger, pervasive anger, extreme anger, past anger, future anger, and present anger; heat, intense heat, smoke, intense smoke, flame, intense flame; ferocity, coarseness, and wickedness; the arousal of the mind, the manifestation of an evil countenance, and the utterance of evil words—this is called anger belonging to craving.
Regarding those who belong to the category of resentment toward what is unpleasant:

this refers to a certain class of persons who think to themselves, "He now intends to do me harm, intends to bring me disadvantage, intends to cause me lack of well-being, intends to cause me lack of nourishment, and intends to cause me lack of security."
Yet they have done me harm, will do me harm, and are currently doing me harm.
While there are those who wish me harm, even unto ill-being, I instead wish them well-being, I wish them benefit, I wish them happiness, I wish them nourishment, and I wish them security.
Furthermore, regarding those [beings], there are those who have acted for my benefit, will act for my benefit, or are currently acting for my benefit;
yet, while desiring to bring me benefit even unto peace and security, they instead desire to bring me harm even unto lack of peace and security.
From this, there arises various forms of anger, from minor irritation up to the manifestation of a foul countenance and the utterance of harsh words; this is called anger belonging to the unlovely.
This [anger] belonging to the lovely and the unlovely is collectively termed "anger" (*krodha*).
What is resentment?
It refers to a certain class of persons who think:
"Since he has intended to do me harm as described extensively above, I shall do the same to him."

This capacity to incite anger arises from hatred; it consists of harboring resentment, various grudges, pervasive grudging, and extreme hostility. It is difficult to turn back in its activity, it is entangled by karma, it establishes firm karmic formations, and it gives rise to enmity and resentment. This nature of the mind characterized by resentment is collectively termed *upanāha* (enmity).
What is concealment?

It refers to a certain class of persons who have violated their precepts, violated their views, violated their pure livelihood, and violated their rules of conduct; they are unable to bring their original undertaking of the precepts to completion, unable to maintain them purely, and unable to fulfill them perfectly.
Having already become aware that he had committed an offense long ago, he reflects thus:

"If I were to proclaim, reveal, designate, or establish the various matters of my offenses to others, there would be ill repute and bad fame; I would be censured and loathed, or subjected to disparagement or formal accusation, and consequently would not receive the respect and offerings of others."
"I would rather fall into the three evil destinies because of this than ever confess the transgressions I have committed.

Since he fears ill repute and bad reputation, even to the point of fearing the loss of respect and offerings, he then gives rise toward his own offenses to various forms of concealment—concealing, fully concealing, and pervasive concealing; hiding, fully hiding, and pervasive hiding; protecting, fully protecting, and pervasive protecting; and storing, fully storing, and pervasive storing—whether already concealed, yet to be concealed, or currently being concealed; all of these together are termed "concealment" (*mrakṣa*).
What is *khila* (obstinacy)?
It refers to a certain class of persons who, within the Saṃgha or similar assemblies, engage in strife and litigation on account of what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
Although the bhikṣus and others, for the sake of reconciliation and pacification, offer them exhortations and instructions, they stubbornly refuse to accept them.

This nature of refusing counsel, this nature of refusing instruction, extreme obstinacy, extreme grasping, perverse grasping, non-righteous grasping, the difficulty of being exhorted to relinquish, clumsy response, lion-like stubbornness, the stinging nature of the mind, and the headstrong nature of the mind—these collectively are termed *khila* (obstinacy).
What is envy (*īrṣyā*)?

It refers to a certain class of persons who, seeing others obtain honor, offerings, respect, praise, and the five desirable sense objects—namely, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites—think to themselves:
"Since they have already obtained such things as honor, while I have not."

From this arise various forms of grief and extreme grief, suffering and extreme suffering, envy and extreme envy, and jealousy and extreme jealousy; these collectively are termed "jealousy" (*īrṣyā*).
What is "miserliness" (*mātsarya*)?
That is to say, there are two kinds of stinginess:
first, stinginess regarding material wealth;
second, stinginess regarding the Dharma.

Stinginess regarding wealth refers to obstructing and preventing others from obtaining any of one's own desirable five sensory objects—clothing, food, drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites—so that they may not receive them.

Regarding one's own beloved possessions and requisites, not giving, not giving universally, not giving extensively, not relinquishing, not relinquishing universally, not relinquishing extensively, and having a nature of mental stinginess—this is called stinginess regarding wealth (*āmiṣamātsarya*).

Regarding stinginess with the Dharma (*dharmamātsarya*): it refers to obstructing and preventing others from obtaining any of the *sūtras*, *vinaya*, or *abhidharma*; or the personal instructions and admonitions of one's preceptors (*upādhyāya*) or instructors (*ācārya*); or the secret essential teachings transmitted through successive lineages. To withhold these so that others may not obtain them constitutes stinginess with the Dharma.

Regarding all such dharmas as these that one possesses, not bestowing them upon others nor explaining them to them—neither giving, nor giving universally, nor giving in accordance with universal giving; neither relinquishing, nor relinquishing universally, nor relinquishing in accordance with universal relinquishing; but rather having a nature of mental stinginess—this is called *dharmamātsarya* (stinginess regarding the Dharma).
This stinginess regarding material wealth and the Dharma is collectively termed "miserliness" (*mātsarya*).
What is "deception" (*śāṭhya*)?
It refers to using false measures, false bushels, or false scales toward others, or employing deceptive speech and boasting to entice them, causing others to believe it is real.
Deceit (*māyā*), along with its various forms—deceiving, deceiving everywhere, deceiving thoroughly, and deceiving to the utmost—is collectively termed "deceit.
What is guile (*śāṭhya*)?

It refers to the nature of the mind to conceal, the nature of the mind to be crooked, the nature of the mind to be turbid, the nature of the mind to be stagnant, the nature of the mind to be unmanifest, the nature of the mind to be non-straightforward, and the nature of the mind to be unresponsive; these together are collectively termed "guile."
What is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)?

It refers to being without shame, having nothing for which to feel shame, and lacking distinct shame; being without bashfulness, having nothing for which to feel bashful, and lacking distinct bashfulness; being without reverence and lacking the nature of reverence; being without self-mastery and lacking the nature of self-mastery; and the absence of fear toward those who possess mastery. This is collectively termed lack of shame.
What is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)?

It refers to being without shame, having nothing for which to feel shame, and no distinct sense of shame; it is being without disgrace, having nothing for which to feel disgrace, and no distinct sense of disgrace; it is not being afraid of or terrified by various transgressions, nor perceiving them as fearful. This is collectively termed lack of shame.
What is pride (*māna*)?

It refers to regarding oneself as superior when one is inferior, or regarding oneself as equal when one is equal; arising from this, there is the act of being proud, having been proud, or will be proud, as well as the loftiness of mind, the reliance [on such views], and the self-appropriation of the mind—all of these are collectively termed pride.
What is overweening pride (*adhimāna*)?

It refers to regarding oneself as superior to those who are equal, or regarding oneself as equal to those who are superior; arising from this, it includes all forms of pride up to the mind’s self-exaltation, which is collectively termed overweening pride.
What is *mānātimāna* (conceit beyond conceit)?

It refers to regarding oneself as superior when one is actually inferior; arising from this, it includes all forms of pride up to the mind’s self-exaltation, which is collectively termed *mānātimāna*.
What is *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am")?

That is to say, regarding the five aggregates of clinging and so forth, to perceive them as "I" or "mine," and from that to give rise to conceit up to the mind's self-appropriation—this is collectively termed "the conceit of 'I'."
What is overweening pride (*adhimāna*)?

It refers to claiming to have attained what has not been attained, claiming to have acquired what has not been acquired, claiming to have touched what has not been touched, and claiming to have realized what has not been realized; arising from these, it ranges from conceit up to the mind’s self-appropriation, which is collectively termed overweening pride.
What is the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*)?

It refers to regarding oneself as slightly inferior when one is actually much superior; from this arising of conceit up to the mind’s self-appropriation, it is collectively termed the pride of inferiority.
What is the pride of error (*mithyāmāna*)?
To claim to possess virtues when one lacks them, and from this to give rise to conceit up to the mind’s self-aggrandizement—this is collectively termed *mithyāmāna* (false pride).
What is *mada* (intoxication/arrogance)?
It refers to a certain class of persons who reflect as follows:
"Whether it be my lineage, family, physical strength, craftsmanship, wealth, status, or my morality, concentration, and wisdom—any one of these is preeminent."

From this arises conceit, extreme conceit, intoxication, extreme intoxication, stupor, extreme stupor, arrogance of mind, self-importance of mind, arising and further arising, being born and further being born, heightening and further heightening, exaltation and further exaltation, and the state of mental pervasiveness; all these collectively are termed *mada*.
What is negligence?

It refers to failing to cultivate or practice, failing to act with constancy or regularity, and abandoning application toward the abandonment of unwholesome dharmas and the accumulation of wholesome dharmas; this is collectively termed negligence.

What is arrogance? It refers to a certain class of persons who fail to make offerings to those worthy of offerings; fail to show respect to those worthy of respect; fail to honor those worthy of honor; fail to praise those worthy of praise; fail to inquire after the welfare of those worthy of such inquiry; fail to prostrate to those worthy of prostration; fail to rise to receive those worthy of being received; fail to invite others to sit when they are worthy of being invited to sit; and fail to yield the path to those worthy of yielding the path.

Arising from this, there is a lack of physical humility, a lack of equal humility, and a lack of extreme humility; it includes physical arrogance, mental arrogance, and the nature of self-conceitedness—collectively termed pride (*māna*).
What is resentment?

It refers to a nature of physical aggression, a nature of mental aggression; a nature of physical agitation and anger, a nature of mental agitation and anger; physical resentment, mental resentment; having already resented, or being about to resent—collectively, these are termed "resentment."
What is hypocrisy?

It refers to those who are excessively greedy and, for the sake of offerings, for the sake of requisites, for the sake of respect, or for the sake of fame, perform such acts as plucking out their hair and singeing their beards, lying on ashes or exposing their bodies, walking slowly with downcast eyes, raising their voices to display an air of authority, or manifesting their own skills and ascetic practices; these are collectively termed hypocrisy.
What is deceit?
It refers to one who is excessively greedy, who, for the sake of obtaining the aforementioned offerings and so forth, goes to another's house and speaks as follows:
"You have now well obtained this human body; those who recite and uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma..."
Delighting in preaching the essentials of the Dharma; being well-versed in the biographies of the patriarchs; composing commentaries and treatises; delighting in forest hermitages (āraṇya);
delighting in possessing only the three robes; delighting in constant circumambulation and prostration; delighting in rag-robes (pāṃśukūla); delighting in practicing alms-gathering (piṇḍapāta);
delighting in eating from a single bowl; delighting in accepting food only once; delighting in eating while seated once; and delighting in dwelling at the foot of a tree.
Dwelling in the open air, delighting in staying among burial mounds, delighting in sitting rather than lying down, delighting in sitting wherever one finds a seat,
attaining the contemplation of impurity, attaining mindfulness of breathing, attaining the four dhyānas, attaining the four immeasurables,
attaining the four formless attainments, attaining the four noble fruits, attaining the six supernormal knowledges, and attaining the eight liberations— these...
The noble sages who enter your home all receive from you offerings, respect, honor, and praise, and are made their refuge.
My conduct and virtue have not diminished compared to those predecessors; now that I have come to your home, I truly hope to be treated as one of them.
This is called deceit.
Furthermore, there is another form of deceit: one who is full of greed, in order to obtain the aforementioned offerings and so forth, goes to another's house and speaks these words:
"You should regard me as a parent; I, too, shall regard you as a child."
From this day forward, we shall be kinsmen; our joys and sorrows, our honors and disgraces, shall all be shared in common.
Previously, people in the world have generally addressed me as a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas; from now on, they shall all address me as "the śramaṇa of your family."
"All the requisites for my sustenance that I require—such as clothing, medicine, and other items—you have provided them all.
If you were unable to do so, I would surely go elsewhere to other faithful households; would this not bring you disgrace?"
Such various forms of speech involving unreal expedients are collectively termed "deceit.
What is "hinting" (*nimitta*)?
It refers to one who is excessively greedy, who, for the sake of obtaining the aforementioned offerings and so forth, goes to another's house and speaks as follows:
"Virtuous man, virtuous woman!

These robes, this bowl, these bedding and seating requisites, and these upper and lower garments—if I were to obtain them, they would be of great necessity for my sustenance; I shall always cherish and protect them as treasures to bring you merit."
"Except for you who can relinquish it, who else would grant it as a gift?
To obtain profit by employing such expedients is collectively termed "hinting" (*nimitta*).
What is "inciting" (*saṃsarga*)?
This refers to one who is full of greed; in order to obtain such offerings as mentioned before, he goes to another's house and speaks these words:

"Your parents and others were endowed with pure faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom; by virtue of this wholesome karma, they have already been reborn among humans or devas, or have attained liberation."

Yet you lack faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom; since you possess no wholesome karma, when your life eventually comes to an end, you will certainly be reborn in the evil realms—what will you do about that?
Thus, those who praise or disparage in order to seek gain are collectively termed "inciters" (*kṣepaka*).
What is meant by "seeking gain through gain"?

It refers to a certain class of people who first obtain robes, bowls, or other requisites for sustaining their bodies and lives from one household, and then carry them to another household to display them, saying:
"That certain family has given me this item;
moreover, that donor has constantly provided me with robes, bowls, and other necessities for a long time.
If your family can give as that donor does, then it too shall be a place where I rely upon."
Regarding "obtaining subsequent benefit by means of prior expedient means," this is collectively termed "seeking profit through profit.
What is "evil desire"?

It refers to a certain class of persons who, in reality, do not recite or uphold the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and so forth, up to those who have not actually realized the eight liberations; yet they desire to cause others to know that they truly are those who recite and uphold the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and thereby obtain offerings, respect, honor, and praise, acting as a refuge for others.
Furthermore, although one lacks in reality the wholesome dharmas born of renunciation and seclusion, one proclaims, reveals, and displays to others that one has attained them.
Such categories as these are collectively termed "evil desire."
What is great desire?

It refers to one who is excessively greedy; for the sake of obtaining vast wealth, profit, and so forth, they give rise to desire—having desired, currently desiring, or about to desire—which is collectively termed "great desire."
How is desire manifested?

It refers to a certain class of persons who truly recite and uphold the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and have extensively practiced up to the attainment of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) and the fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), yet they lack reputation and are unknown to others.
Desiring that others recognize these virtues so as to thereby obtain offerings, honor, respect, and praise, and to serve as their refuge;
furthermore, although one truly possesses the wholesome qualities born of renunciation and seclusion, one proclaims, reveals, and displays them to others to manifest one's own realization.
These and similar categories are collectively termed "manifest desire.
What is meant by "lack of contentment"?

It refers to a certain class of persons who, having already obtained objects of form, fragrance, flavor, tangibility, and other requisites, do not give rise to contentment; instead, they continue to hope for, long for, delight in, and seek them further. This is collectively termed "lack of contentment."
What is disrespect?

It refers to a certain class of persons to whom their preceptors or those like preceptors, teachers or those like teachers, and other respected, trustworthy friends with whom they associate, have spoken according to the Dharma, saying:

"From this day forward, do not corrupt your physical actions, do not corrupt your verbal actions, do not corrupt your mental actions; do not go to improper places, do not associate with evil friends, and do not perform deeds that lead to the three miserable realms."

Thus instructed, this teaching is in accordance with the Dharma and timely; it conforms to the path being cultivated, polishing it, increasing its adornment, making it suitable for constant application, and serving as a supportive provision.

Yet those sentient beings do not feel delight or joy, nor do they feel affection or pleasure; they act in opposition to the words of their teachers and others, taking them to the left rather than the right, and disparaging or repudiating them—all such behaviors as these are termed "lack of respect."
What is the arising of harsh speech?

It refers to a certain person to whom their preceptor or one like a preceptor, their instructor or one like an instructor, or any other respected and trustworthy friend with whom they associate, speaks according to the Dharma, saying:

"From this day forward, do not corrupt your physical actions; do not corrupt your verbal actions; do not corrupt your mental actions; do not engage in improper conduct; do not associate with evil friends; and do not perform deeds that lead to the three miserable realms."

Thus instructed—teachings that accord with the Dharma and are timely—they serve as a means of refinement for the path being cultivated, as an increase in its adornment, as a constant and diligent application, and as the supportive provisions for its companionship.
Yet those sentient beings do not rejoice, do not delight, do not love, and do not find pleasure in the words of their teacher;
they act in opposition and take to the left,
rather than taking to the right.
To disparage and repudiate [the Dharma],
and to give rise to violent and abusive speech toward one's teachers and others— such acts as these are called "giving rise to evil speech.
What is meant by "delighting in evil friends"?
This refers to a certain class of people who delight in associating with evil friends.

As for "evil friends," these refer to sheep-butchers, poultry-butchers, pig-butchers, bird-catchers, fishers, hunters, robbers, executioners, prison wardens, those who bind dragons, dog-cookers, and those who set snares and traps; these are called evil friends.

Furthermore, there is another class who violate the precepts (*śīla*), practice unwholesome dharmas, and harbor internal corruption while appearing outwardly steadfast. They are like filthy snails, possessing the spiral sound of a conch yet the behavior of a dog; though not truly śramaṇas, they call themselves śramaṇas, and though not truly practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), they call themselves practitioners of the holy life. These, too, are called evil friends.
To associate with, serve, follow, and take pleasure in such evil friends as these is called "delighting in evil friends.
What is "intolerance"?

It refers to a certain class of persons who are unable to endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, wind, rain, mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, and other unpleasant tactile sensations, as well as other painful matters.

Furthermore, there is another class of persons who, when confronted by the violent and wickedness of others, are unable to endure the sharp, fierce, and harsh impulses that arise within themselves, nor can they bear the agonizing physical sensations of life-threatening pain or the cruel and foul speech [of others].
This and what preceded it are collectively termed "intolerance.
What is meant by "attachment" (*gardha*) and "pervasive attachment"?
It refers to the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of weak-grade greed, hatred, and delusion; these are called "attachment."
That which is of medium degree in this context is called pervasive attachment (*pari-yoga*).
Furthermore, the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of greed, hatred, and delusion that are of medium degree are called attachment;
those that are of superior degree are called pervasive attachment.
What is defiled greed?
It refers to the various forms of greed, equal greed, and even the arising of greed and its categories regarding all sensual desires; this is collectively termed defiled greed.
What is unrighteous greed?

That is to say, when one gives rise to lust, excessive lust, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, or passionate craving toward one's mother, daughter, sister, or any other relative, it is called unrighteous lust.
What is attachment to greed?

It is the arising of greed and further greed toward one’s own wealth and possessions, as well as those things one has taken up; it is the act of hoarding, guarding, firmly clinging to, and being stained by affection for them—this is called attachment to greed.
What is malicious greed?
It refers to the arising of greed and further greed toward the wealth and possessions of others; to hoarding, guarding, and firmly clinging with passionate attachment—this is called malicious greed.
Furthermore, there is malicious greed, which schemes for the lives of others and covets their skins, horns, and so forth, drinking their blood and eating their flesh.
These two types together are collectively termed "malicious greed."
What is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?

It refers to the arising of the notion of "I" and "mine" with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*); the acceptance, delight, wisdom, contemplation, and vision that arise from this is called the view of a self-identity.
What is the view of existence (*bhavadrṣṭi*)?

It refers to the arising of the notion of permanence and constancy regarding the self and the world; from this, one gives rise to acceptance, pleasure, wisdom, and contemplative vision—this is called the view of existence.
What is the view of non-existence (*vibhava-dṛṣṭi*)?

It refers to the arising of the notion that the self and the world are neither eternal nor permanent; from this, there arises acceptance, pleasure, wisdom, observation, and vision, which is called the view of non-existence.
What is sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*)?
It refers to the arising of longing, delight, seeking, pursuit, and yearning toward various objects of desire; this is called sensual desire.
Some explain it thus: the various forms of greed, equal greed, and even the categories of greed that arise toward various objects of desire are collectively termed sensual desire.
What is ill-will (*vyāpāda*)?
It refers to the desire to cause harm toward sentient beings, harboring internal resentment and even manifesting as a source of affliction; this is collectively termed ill-will.
What is torpor (*styāna*)?
It refers to heaviness of the body, heaviness of the mind, and even drowsiness and mental confusion; these collectively are termed torpor.
What is sleep (*middha*)?

That which refers to various states of drowsiness and dreaming, characterized by an inability to maintain [mental clarity] and a state of mental dullness and contraction, is collectively termed *middha* (sleep).
What is *auddhatya* (restlessness)?
It refers to the lack of tranquility in the mind; it is agitation, extreme agitation, and the state of mental agitation, which is collectively termed *auddhatya*.
What is remorse (*kaukṛtya*)?
It refers to mental transformation, mental distress, and mental regret; the state of "I have done wrong" and the nature of having done wrong—these collectively are termed remorse.
What is doubt (*vicikitsā*)?

This refers to the arising of doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; being divided into two parts or two paths, and even failing to manifest a single direction—this is collectively termed "doubt."
What is torpor (*styāna*)?

It refers to heaviness of body, heaviness of mind, unserviceability of body, unserviceability of mind, torpidity of body, torpidity of mind; that which has been torpid, that which will be torpid, and that which is currently torpid—collectively these are termed torpor.
What is "lack of delight"?

It refers to a certain class of person who, having received instruction and exhortation from a preceptor or one like a preceptor, a teacher or one like a teacher, or any other respected and trustworthy companion with whom they associate, nevertheless applies their mindfulness to dwellings and bedding; thus, their mind is not joyful, does not find affection or delight, but is despondent and sorrowful—this is collectively termed "lack of delight."
What is yawning and stretching?
The lowering and raising of the body, and the contraction and extension of the hands and feet, is called yawning (*vijṛmbhikā*).
The opening and closing of the nose and face, and the distorting and gaping of the lips and mouth, is called stretching (*vijṛmbha*).
What is the nature of immoderate eating?
It refers to the arising of painful sensations due to fasting, or eating in excess, or eating what is unsuitable; these are collectively termed the nature of immoderate eating.
What is the nature of mental dullness and inferiority?
It refers to the mind being clouded, weak, and cramped; this is collectively termed the nature of mental dullness and inferiority.
What are various perceptions?

This refers to all defiled perceptions of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch, as well as unwholesome perceptions, perceptions induced by improper reasoning, and perceptions that obstruct meditative concentration, belonging to those who are bound by the hindrances; these are collectively termed "various perceptions."
What is non-attention?

It refers to not inducing, not recollecting, not reflecting upon, not having reflected upon, not about to reflect upon, and the lack of mental alertness regarding the wholesome dharmas arising from renunciation and seclusion; this is collectively termed non-attention.
What is *dauṣṭhulya*?

It refers to the heaviness of the body, the heaviness of the mind, the unserviceability of the body, the unserviceability of the mind, the rigidity of the body, the rigidity of the mind, the lack of flexibility of the body, and the lack of flexibility of the mind; these collectively are termed *dauṣṭhulya*.
What is meant by "obstructive behavior" (*pratikuṣṭa*)?

It refers to a certain class of people who, at the time of receiving food, demand cooked food when raw is given, demand raw food when cooked is given, demand coarse food when fine is given, or demand fine food when coarse is given; they give unequally and unrighteously; they give or do not give based on whether they know or do not know [the recipient]; and in this process, they repeatedly utter contradictory speech—this is called obstructive behavior.

Furthermore, there is another class of persons: if their preceptor or one like a preceptor, their instructor or one like an instructor, or any other respected and trustworthy friend with whom they associate, should say to them:
"Venerable one!..."
"You should perform such and such tasks in this sequential order.
He then thought to himself:
"What are these various tasks that require me to act in such a sequence?"
In this regard, to repeatedly utter contradictory speech is called "obstinate defiance" (*pragādha*).

Furthermore, there is another class [of persons]: whether they come themselves to apologize, or are instructed by others to apologize; whether they initiate a request themselves, or are prompted by others to make a request—in these instances, to repeatedly utter contradictory speech is called "obstinate defiance."
Thus, when one repeatedly utters contradictory speech while engaged in tasks such as mending clothes or conducting business, it is collectively termed *pratighāta* (obstruction/impertinence).
What is *tṛṣṇā* (gluttony/covetousness)?
This refers to a certain class of people who, when dividing wealth and profit, abandon one thing and take another, their desires being insatiable and unstable; this is called "greed" (*tāu*).

Furthermore, at times before and after eating, when going to a place for food and drink, they taste this and sip that, their preferences being inconsistent and undetermined; this is called "gluttony" (*tiē*).
This, together with what preceded it, is collectively termed "gluttony" (*tāo-tuō*).
What is meant by "lack of pliancy"?

It refers to a mind that is rigid, a mind that is harsh, a mind that is stubborn, a mind that is not clear and pure, a mind that is not smooth, a mind that is not supple, and a mind that lacks adaptability; these are collectively termed "lack of pliancy."
What is meant by "unpliable nature"?

It refers to a body that is rigid, a body that is harsh and stiff, a body that is obstinate, a body that is not clear and pure, a body that is not smooth, a body that is not supple, and a body that lacks functional capacity; these collectively are termed "unpliable nature."
What is meant by "not conforming to one's peers"?

It refers to a certain class of persons who do not properly conform to their preceptors or those similar to preceptors, their instructors or those similar to instructors, and any other respected, trustworthy companions with whom they associate; this is called not conforming to one's peers.
What is the thought of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*)?

It refers to all mental investigations, thorough investigations, proximate investigations, mental manifestations, intense manifestations, manifest appearances, deliberations, constructions, reflections, and discriminations associated with sensual craving; these collectively are termed the thought of sensual desire.
What is the thought of ill-will (*vyāpāda-vitarka*)?
It refers to all mental seeking, thorough seeking, up to contemplation and discrimination associated with hatred; these collectively are termed the thought of ill-will.
What is the thought of cruelty (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*)?

That is to say, all mental states associated with harmfulness—ranging from initial inquiry (*paryeṣaṇā*) and thorough inquiry (*viparyeṣaṇā*) up to reflection (*vitarka*) and discrimination (*vicāra*)—are collectively termed "harmful inquiry" (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*).
What is "inquiry regarding kinsmen" (*jñāti-vitarka*)?

It refers to the desire for one's kinsmen to be at ease and happy, to obtain superior companions, to be free from affliction and harm, to achieve all qualities that prevent affliction and harm, to be cherished by kings and ministers, to be respected and admired by the people of the country, and for the five grains to ripen in abundance with timely rains.
Based on these factors, the arising of thought, seeking, thorough seeking, and so forth, up to reflection and discrimination, is collectively termed the "thought of relatives.
What is the "thought of country"?
This refers to the desire for the well-being and happiness of one’s beloved country and its people, extending in detail even to the wish for timely rains.

Based on these factors, the arising of thought, seeking, thorough seeking, and so forth, up to reflection and discrimination, is collectively termed "investigation of the country" (*janapada-vitarka*).
What is the pursuit of immortality?
It refers to a certain class of persons who think as follows:

"I have not yet practiced the sublime meditative concentrations taught in the Buddha’s teachings; first, I should memorize and uphold the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, proclaim the essential points of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, study the various biographies, and compose commentaries and treatises. Dwelling in an araṇya, wearing only the three robes—and so forth, as extensively described, even sitting wherever one happens to find a seat—once these tasks are completed, I shall then practice concentration."
Furthermore, there is another class who thinks:

"I have not yet practiced the sublime concentrations taught in the Buddha’s teachings; first, I should travel through mountains, rivers, lands, gardens, groves, ponds, caves, and cemeteries, circumambulate caityas, and visit various monasteries. Only after having done these things will I practice concentration."
Furthermore, there is another class who thinks:

"I have not yet practiced the sublime concentrations taught in the Buddha’s teaching; I shall wait until seven years, six years, five years, four years, three years, two years, or one year has passed, or until seven months, down to one month, or seven days, down to one day, or until this day or this night has passed, and only after this time has elapsed will I practice concentration."

Reflecting in this way, one fails to realize that one’s own life is precarious and fragile; the arising of the thought to seek, the pervasive seeking, and even the subsequent reflection and discrimination, are collectively termed the "thought of immortality."
What is the search for contempt?
It refers to a certain class of persons who think to themselves:
"My lineage, family, physical strength, craftsmanship, occupation, wealth, status, or any one of the qualities such as ethical discipline, concentration, or wisdom is superior."
Relying on this, one gives rise to contempt for others.
Due to such factors, the arising of thought, thorough seeking, and so forth, up to reflection and discrimination, is collectively termed the "search for contempt."
What is the vitarka of falsely assuming kinship?

It refers to a certain class of people who, regarding those who are not their kin, falsely claim them to be kin, desiring to bring them peace and happiness, to secure them superior companions, to ensure they are free from harm, to enable them to accomplish all dharmas free from affliction, to be cherished by kings and ministers, to be admired by the people of the land, to have the five grains ripen in abundance, and for rain to fall at the proper time.
On account of these things, the arising of thought, seeking, thorough seeking, and even reflection and discrimination is collectively termed *vitarka* (investigation).
What is *daurmanasya* (sorrow)?

It refers to a certain class of persons who, due to the death of parents, brothers, sisters, teachers, or friends; or due to the total extinction of their kinsmen; or due to the complete loss of wealth and status, give rise within themselves to sharp, fierce, and harsh mental afflictions that seize the life-force—painful and agonizing sensations.

At that time, his mind becomes feverish, equally feverish, internally heated, and thoroughly inflamed; he gives rise to grief—past, present, and future—and the arrow of grief within the heart; all these together are termed "grief."
What is lamentation?
It refers to a certain class of persons who, due to the death of parents, brothers, sisters, teachers, friends, or others, give rise to physical [agitation] and even painful sensations.
At that time, his mind was burning, even to the point of a sorrowful arrow piercing his heart.
For this reason, he uttered this lamentation:
"Alas, alas! How bitter, how bitter!"
"My father! My mother!"—and so on, as extensively described, down to "my wealth" and "my status"—how is it that all at once, suddenly, this has come to pass?
All the words of lamentation and grievance therein, as well as the various vocal actions [thereof], are collectively termed "sighing" (*tāna*).
What is suffering (*duḥkha*)?
It refers to the unequal sensations associated with the five consciousnesses; collectively, these are termed suffering.
What is grief (*daurmanasya*)?
That which is called "sorrow" (daurmanasya) refers to the unbalanced feeling associated with the mental consciousness; this is collectively termed sorrow.
What is "distress" (upāyāsa)?
It refers to the mind’s being distressed, having been distressed, about to be distressed, the nature of distress, and the category of distress; these are collectively termed distress.
From greed, hatred, and delusion up to agitation and distress, all are termed "miscellaneous matters.
Regarding these miscellaneous matters, if one is permanently severed, one will certainly attain the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Since the remaining [defilements] may be severed along with it when one is severed, the Buddha guarantees that such a person will certainly attain the state of Non-returner.
