Chapter Seventeen: On the Faculties (Indriya-varga). At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Jātiśroṇa who approached the Buddha, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a few questions of the Venerable Gautama."
"I only pray that you will grant me permission.
Then the World-Honored One addressed that brahmin:
"Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it for you."
The brahmin asked:
"How many kinds of faculties (indriya) are there?
The World-Honored One replied:
“There are twenty-two. What are the twenty-two? They are:

the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, the faculty of equanimity, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of ‘I shall come to know the unknown,’ the faculty of ‘knowing,’ and the faculty of ‘one who has known.’”
"These twenty-two encompass all faculties.
When that brahmin heard what the Buddha had said, he rejoiced with leaping joy and departed with respectful salutation.
What is the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)?
It refers to the eye that has seen, is seeing, or will see forms, as well as its "homogeneous part" (*sabhāga*); this is called the eye-faculty.

Furthermore, it is that which, with the predominance of the eye, gives rise to visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), and which has discerned, is discerning, or will discern forms, as well as its homogeneous part; this is called the eye-faculty.
Furthermore, that which is the eye’s obstruction toward forms—past, present, or future—and its corresponding homogeneous part (sabhāga), is called the eye faculty.
Furthermore, that which is the eye’s engagement with forms—past, present, or future—and its corresponding homogeneous part is called the eye faculty.

In this way, all eyes whatsoever—past, future, and present—are called the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*); they are also called that which is known, that which is cognized, that which is thoroughly penetrated, that which is fully understood, that which is to be abandoned, that which is resolved, that which is seen, that which is attained, that which is awakened to, that which is manifest awakening, that which is comprehended, that which is equally comprehended, that which is observed, that which is equally observed, that which is scrutinized, that which is discerned, that which is contacted, that which is equally contacted, that which is realized, and that which is equally realized.
What, furthermore, is this?

It refers to translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) derived from the four great elements, whether belonging to hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, humans, or those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), as well as that produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*). All the names, synonyms, designations, conceptualizations, and conventional expressions applied to it—such as "eye," "eye-base" (*cakṣur-āyatana*), "eye-element" (*cakṣur-dhātu*), "eye-faculty" (*cakṣur-indriya*), "vision," "path," "guide," "white," "pure," "treasury," "gate," "field," "entity," "stream," "pond," "ocean," "sore," "opening of a sore," and "this shore"—are [the eye].
Thus, the eye faculty is included within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
What is the ear faculty?
It refers to that which hears, has heard, or will hear sounds, as well as its corresponding homogeneous part (*tatsabhāga*); this is called the ear faculty.

Furthermore, that which is dominated by the ear and gives rise to auditory consciousness, having already, currently, or about to cognize sounds, as well as its homogeneous counterpart (sabhāga), is called the ear-faculty.

Furthermore, that which is dominated by the ear and is obstructed by sounds, having already, currently, or about to be so obstructed, as well as its homogeneous counterpart, is called the ear-faculty.
Furthermore, that which has functioned, is currently functioning, or will function with respect to sounds, as well as its homogeneous counterpart (sabhāga), is called the ear-faculty (śrotrendriya).
Likewise, all ears—whether past, future, or present—are called the ear-faculty; they are also termed "the knowable" (jñeya) up to "that which is to be fully realized" (sākṣātkartavya).

What, then, is this? It refers to translucent matter derived from the four great elements—whether pertaining to the hells up to those produced through cultivation—which is designated by various names, diverse terms, designations, concepts, and verbal expressions, such as "ear," "ear-base," "ear-element," "ear-faculty," "hearing," "the path," and so forth, up to "this shore."
In this way, the ear faculty is included within the internal bases.
What is the nose faculty?
It refers to that which, regarding odors, has smelled, is smelling, or will smell, as well as its homogeneous counterpart; this is called the nose faculty.

That which, with the nose-faculty as its predominant condition, gives rise to nose-consciousness, and which has already, is currently, or will be cognizing odors, as well as its homogeneous counterpart (sabhāga), is called the nose-faculty.
Furthermore, that which, with respect to odors, has already, is currently, or will be obstructed [by them], as well as its homogeneous counterpart, is called the nose-faculty.
Furthermore, that which is the nose’s past, present, and future engagement with odors, as well as its homogeneous state (*sabhāga*), is called the nose faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*).
Likewise, all noses belonging to the past, future, and present are termed the nose faculty; they are also termed "the known" (*jñeya*) up to "that which is to be fully realized" (*sākṣātkartavya*).
What, furthermore, is this?

It refers to the translucent matter derived from the four great elements, whether belonging to the hells or even up to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is not produced by cultivation. All its designations, synonyms, metaphors, concepts, conceptualizations, and verbal expressions—namely, what is called "nose," "nose-base" (*ghrāṇāyatana*), "nose-element" (*ghrāṇadhātu*), "nose-faculty" (*ghrāṇendriya*), "smelling," "the path," and so forth, up to "this shore"—are [mere conventions].
Thus, the nose faculty is included within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
What is the tongue faculty?
It refers to the tongue in relation to tastes—whether already tasted, being tasted, or yet to be tasted—as well as its homogeneous counterpart (*sabhāga*); this is called the tongue faculty.

Furthermore, that which arises with the tongue as its dominant condition, the tongue-consciousness, which has already, is currently, or will be cognizing tastes, and its corresponding part (tat-sabhāga)—this is called the tongue-faculty (jihvendriya).
Moreover, that which is the tongue’s resistance to tastes, having already, is currently, or will be so, and its corresponding part—this is called the tongue-faculty.

Furthermore, that which the tongue has engaged with, is currently engaging with, or will engage with regarding tastes, as well as its homogeneous counterpart (sabhāga), is called the tongue-faculty (jihvendriya).
Thus, all tongues—whether past, future, or present—are termed the tongue-faculty, and are also termed "the knowable" (jñeya) up to "that which is to be fully realized" (sākṣātkartavya).
What, furthermore, is this?

It refers to translucent matter derived from the four great elements, pertaining to beings from those in the hells up to those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). It is not produced by cultivation. All its designations, synonyms, metaphors, concepts, notions, and verbal expressions—namely, what is called "tongue," "the tongue-base" (*jihvāyatana*), "the tongue-element" (*jihvādhātu*), "the tongue-faculty" (*jihvendriya*), "tasting," "the path," and so on, up to "this shore"—are [merely such conventions].
Such is the tongue faculty; it is included within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
What is the body faculty?
It refers to that which, with respect to tangibles, has been felt, is being felt, or will be felt, as well as its corresponding homogeneous part (*sabhāga*); this is called the body faculty.

Furthermore, that which arises with the body as its dominant condition and discerns, has discerned, or will discern tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*), as well as their counterparts (*tatsabhāga*), is called the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Moreover, that which obstructs, has obstructed, or will obstruct tangible objects, as well as its counterpart, is called the body faculty.

Furthermore, that which has already functioned, is currently functioning, or will function with respect to tangibles, as well as its homogeneous counterpart (sabhāga), is called the body-faculty (kāyendriya).
Thus, all bodies—whether past, future, or present—are termed the body-faculty, and are also termed the "knowable" (jñeya) up to the "fully realized" (sākṣātkṛta).
What, furthermore, is this?

It refers to translucent matter derived from the four great elements, pertaining to those from the hells up to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is not produced by cultivation. All that is designated by names, synonyms, designations, concepts, conceptualizations, and verbal expressions—namely, the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), the sphere of name-bodies, the element of name-bodies, the faculty of name-bodies, the awakening to names, the path of names, and so forth, up to "this shore"—is what is meant.
Thus, the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) is included among the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
What is the female faculty (*strīndriya*)?
It refers to the female state, the female nature, the female sphere of influence, and the female function.
Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to the flow of the physical body’s sinews and vessels located below the navel-wheel and above the knee-wheel.
If one engages in sexual union with a male at this location, giving rise to the experience of an equal feeling of pleasure, this is called the female faculty (*strīndriya*).
What is the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*)?
It refers to the male body, the male nature, the male sphere of influence, and the male function.
Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to the flow of the physical body’s sinews and vessels from below the navel wheel to above the knee wheel.
If one engages in sexual union with a woman at this location, giving rise to an experience of equal pleasure, it is called the male organ (*puruṣendriya*).
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?

It refers to that which, among various sentient beings within their respective groups of beings, does not shift, does not change, is not destroyed, does not perish, is not lost, and does not decline; it is the abiding of life, its continued existence, its protection and thorough protection, its turning and thorough turning; this is life, this is the life-faculty—this is called the life-faculty.
What is the faculty of mind (*manendriya*)?

It refers to the mind with respect to mental objects (*dharma*)—whether already known, currently being known, or yet to be known—and its corresponding homogeneous states; this is called the faculty of mind.

Furthermore, it is that which, through the predominance of the mind, gives rise to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and which, with respect to mental objects, has already discerned, is currently discerning, or will discern them, along with their corresponding homogeneous states; this is called the faculty of mind.

Furthermore, that which is the past, present, or future obstruction of the mind with respect to mental objects (*dharma*), as well as its homogeneous counterpart (*sabhāga*), is called the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*).
Furthermore, that which is the past, present, or future activity of the mind with respect to mental objects, as well as its homogeneous counterpart, is called the mind-faculty.
All such mental faculties (manas) belonging to the past, future, and present are called the faculty of mind (mana-indriya), and are also termed "the knowable" up to "that which is fully realized.
Furthermore, what is this?

It refers to mind, mentation, and consciousness; or hell, up to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); or that which is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*). All its designations, synonyms, appellations, concepts, conceptualizations, and verbal expressions—namely, it is called "mind," "mind-base" (*manāyatana*), "mind-element" (*manodhātu*), "mind-faculty" (*manendriya*), "cognition," "the path," and so forth, up to "this shore."
Thus, the faculty of mind (*manas*) is included within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
What is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?
It refers to physical and mental pleasure produced by contact conducive to pleasure, which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣāvedanā*); this is called the faculty of pleasure.

Furthermore, in the cultivation of the third dhyāna, the mental pleasure produced by a contact conducive to pleasure, which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), is called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
What is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*)?
That which is bodily pain produced by contact conducive to suffering, comprised within the category of unbalanced feeling (*vedanā*), is called the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
What is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)?
That which is mental joy produced by contact conducive to joy, comprised within the category of balanced feeling, is called the faculty of joy.

Furthermore, when one cultivates the first and second dhyānas, the mental joy produced by contact conducive to joy—which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity—is called the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
What is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)?
That which is mental distress produced by contact conducive to distress, comprised within the category of unbalanced feeling (*vedanā*), is called the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
What is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
That which is bodily or mental equanimity produced by contact conducive to equanimity, comprised within the category of neither balanced nor unbalanced feeling, is called the faculty of equanimity.

Furthermore, the equanimity of mind produced by contact that is neither painful nor pleasant—which arises during the cultivation of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*)—and which is comprised within feeling that is neither even nor uneven, is called the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
What is the faculty of faith?

It refers to the various forms of faith, the nature of faith, and the nature of manifest faith that arise based on the wholesome dharmas born of renunciation and seclusion; it is compliance and approval, longing and the nature of longing, and the clarity and purity of the mind. This is called the faculty of faith.

Furthermore, the faith of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the faith of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and all faith that is neither of training nor beyond training are collectively termed the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
What is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*)?

It refers to the diligent effort, vigor, fortitude, intensity, and fervor that arise based on the wholesome dharmas produced by renunciation and seclusion; it is an unrestrainable, ardent application of the mind that does not cease—this is termed the faculty of diligence.

Furthermore, the diligence of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the diligence of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and all diligence that is neither of training nor beyond training are collectively termed the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
What is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?

It refers to the various forms of mindfulness, recollection, focused attention, and remembrance that arise based on the wholesome dharmas produced by renunciation and seclusion; it is the state of not forgetting, not losing, not omitting, and not leaking [the object], the non-forgetting of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the mind’s quality of clear recollection—this is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).

Furthermore, the learning of mindfulness (*śaikṣasmṛti*), the non-learning of mindfulness (*aśaikṣasmṛti*), and all wholesome mindfulness that is neither pertaining to learning nor non-learning are collectively termed the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
What is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)?

It refers to the mental abiding, thorough abiding, close abiding, and stable abiding; its non-distraction and non-disorder; its gathering and right concentration; and the one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) arising from the wholesome dharmas produced by renunciation and seclusion—this is termed the faculty of concentration.

Furthermore, the concentration of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the concentration of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and all wholesome concentrations that are neither of training nor beyond training are called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
What is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)?

It refers to the discernment, thorough discernment, and supreme discernment of phenomena; the understanding, equal understanding, and proximate understanding arising from the wholesome dharmas born of renunciation and seclusion; the sagacity, penetration, investigation, intelligence, clarity, and wise practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*)—this is called the faculty of wisdom.

Furthermore, the wisdom of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and all wholesome wisdom that is neither of training nor beyond training are collectively called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvyājñendriya*)?

This refers to those who have already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*): their wisdom of training (*śaikṣa-prajñā*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), and their practice of following faith or following the Dharma; for the sake of realizing the four noble truths which they have not yet realized, these faculties are activated. This is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
What is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*)?

It refers to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) and the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) belonging to those who have already seen the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*), as well as those who possess the liberation through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and those who have realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*). Having already realized the four noble truths through direct comprehension (*abhisamaya*), these faculties function for the sake of abandoning the remaining afflictions; this is called the faculty of one who has already known.
What is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*)?

It refers to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) belonging to the wisdom of an Arhat who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) and those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). Having already realized and currently realizing the four noble truths, these faculties function for the sake of attaining dwelling in happiness in the present life; this is called the faculty of one who has already known.
Chapter 18: On the Bases (Āyatana-varga). At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Jātiśroṇa who approached the place where the Buddha was, joined his palms in reverence, and greeted the World-Honored One with various words of affectionate inquiry.
The Buddha also spoke with words of affection to comfort him.
Having exchanged greetings, he withdrew to sit at one side, bowed with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a few questions of the Venerable Gautama; I only pray that you will grant me leave to speak briefly."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed that brahmin:
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you.
The brahmin asked:
“What is meant by ‘all phenomena’?
The Blessed One replied,
“All phenomena refers to the twelve sense bases.”

What are the twelve? They are the sense base of the eye, the sense base of forms; the sense base of the ear, the sense base of sounds; the sense base of the nose, the sense base of odors; the sense base of the tongue, the sense base of tastes; the sense base of the body, the sense base of tangibles; the sense base of the mind, and the sense base of mental phenomena. These are called the twelve.

If someone were to say, "This is not all; there is another distinct phenomenon that constitutes 'all,'" they would merely have words without any factual basis, and if questioned further, they would be unable to explain themselves.
Later, as he reflected deeply, he became bewildered and distressed, for all dharmas are not within his domain.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin rejoiced with great elation and departed with respectful devotion.
What is the sense-base of the eye?
It should be defined by its characteristics as the visual faculty.
What is the sense-base of form?
That is to say, visible forms which have been seen, are being seen, or will be seen by the eye, as well as their counterparts (*sabhāga*), are called the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*).

Furthermore, visible forms which, with the eye as their predominant condition, have given rise to visual consciousness, have been cognized, are being cognized, or will be cognized, as well as their counterparts, are called the sense-base of form.
Furthermore, visible form that has obstructed, does obstruct, or will obstruct the eye, as well as its homogeneous counterpart, is called the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
Furthermore, visible form that has been the object of, is being the object of, or will be the object of the eye, as well as its homogeneous counterpart, is called the sense-base of visible form.
In this way, all forms belonging to the past, future, and present are called the "form base" (*rūpāyatana*), and are also called "the knowable," up to "that which is to be fully realized.
Furthermore, what is this?

It refers to that which is derived from the four great elements: blue, yellow, red, white; clouds, smoke, dust, and mist; long, short, square, round, high, low, regular, and irregular; shadow, light, brightness, and darkness; the distinct colors of space; mixed colors such as crimson, purple, azure, green, black, and brown; and all other things seen by the eye-faculty and cognized by the eye-consciousness, including all names, synonyms, designations, conceptualizations, and conventional expressions.
That is to say: name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the realm of name-and-form, the sphere of name-and-form, and the further shore of name-and-form.
Thus, the sphere of form is included within the external spheres.
What is the sphere of the ear?
That is to say, just as with the ear faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), its characteristics should be explained.
What is the sphere of sound (*śabda-āyatana*)?
It refers to sounds that have been heard, are being heard, or will be heard by the ear, as well as those that are of the same class (*sabhāga*); this is called the sphere of sound.

Furthermore, sound that arises with the ear as its dominant condition, and which has already, is currently, or will be cognized by the auditory consciousness, along with its "homogeneous part" (sabhāga), is called the sense-base of sound.
Furthermore, sound that has already, is currently, or will be obstructed by the ear, along with its "homogeneous part," is called the sense-base of sound.
Furthermore, sound that has already been perceived by the ear, is currently being perceived, or is its homogeneous counterpart (*sabhāga*), is called the sound-base (*śabda-āyatana*).
Likewise, all sounds—whether past, future, or present—are called the sound-base, and are also termed the "knowable" (*jñeya*) up to the "fully realized" (*sākṣātkartavya*).

What, furthermore, is this? It refers to sounds produced by the four great elements: the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and footsteps; the sounds of conchs and bells; the sounds of large and small drums; the sounds of singing, chanting, praise, and the Brahma-voice; as well as the sounds of the mutual contact of the four great elements; and all vocal sounds of speech throughout the day and night, as well as everything else heard by the ear-faculty and cognized by the ear-consciousness—including all names, various terms, designations, conceptualizations, and conventional expressions—which are called "sound," the "element of sound," the "base of sound," and the "sphere of sound."
Thus, the sphere of sound is included among the external spheres.
What is the sphere of the nose?
It refers to the faculty of the nose; its characteristics should be explained accordingly.
What is the sense-base of odor (*gandhāyatana*)?
It refers to that which is an odor and has been, is being, or will be smelled by the nose, as well as its corresponding homogeneous state (*sabhāga*); this is called the sense-base of odor.

Furthermore, it refers to that which is an odor and, with the nose as its predominant condition, has been, is being, or will be cognized by the olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*), as well as its corresponding homogeneous state; this is called the sense-base of odor.
Furthermore, that which has been, is being, or will be obstructed by the nose, as well as its homogeneous counterpart, is called the sense-base of odor (*gandhāyatana*).
Furthermore, that which has been, is being, or will be experienced by the nose, as well as its homogeneous counterpart, is called the sense-base of odor.
Thus, all odors belonging to the past, future, and present are called the odor-base (*gandhāyatana*), and they are also called the "knowable" up to the "fully realized.
Furthermore, what are these?

It refers to that which is derived from the four great elements: the fragrance of roots, the fragrance of stalks, the fragrance of branches, the fragrance of leaves, the fragrance of flowers, and the fragrance of fruits; fragrances that are pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral; and all else whatsoever that is smelled by the olfactory faculty and cognized by olfactory consciousness—namely, whatever designations, synonyms, metaphors, concepts, notions, and verbal expressions there may be, such as "fragrance," "the fragrance element," "the fragrance base," or "the other shore."
Such a place of fragrance is included within the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
What is the base of the tongue?
It refers to the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*); its characteristics should be explained accordingly.
What is the sense-field of taste (*rasāyatana*)?
It refers to that which is tasted by the tongue—whether past, present, or future—and its corresponding homogeneous part; this is called the sense-field of taste.

Furthermore, it refers to that which, with the tongue as its dominant condition, gives rise to gustatory consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*), and is cognized—whether past, present, or future—and its corresponding homogeneous part; this is called the sense-field of taste.
Furthermore, that which is tasted by the tongue—whether past, present, or future—and its corresponding homogeneous state (sabhāga) is called the sense base of taste (rasāyatana).
Furthermore, that which serves as the object for the tongue—whether past, present, or future—and its corresponding homogeneous state is called the sense base of taste.
In this way, all tastes of the past, future, and present are called the sense-base of taste (*rasāyatana*), and they are also called the "knowable" up to the "fully realized.
Furthermore, what are these?

This refers to that which is derived from the four great elements: the taste of roots, the taste of stalks, the taste of branches, the taste of leaves, the taste of flowers, the taste of fruits; the taste of food, the taste of drink, and the tastes of various liquors; bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland tastes; pleasant and unpleasant tastes, and tastes conducive to equanimity; and all else whatsoever that is tasted by the tongue-faculty and cognized by tongue-consciousness—all the names, synonyms, designations, conceptualizations, and verbal expressions for these are called "taste," "the element of taste," "the sphere of taste," and "the other shore of taste."
Such is the sense-base of taste; it is included among external phenomena.
What is the sense-base of the body?
It should be explained according to the characteristics of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
What is the sense base of tangibles?
It refers to that which has been, is being, or will be experienced by the body as tangible, as well as its homogeneous counterparts; this is called the sense base of tangibles.

Furthermore, it refers to that which, with the body as its predominant condition, gives rise to body-consciousness and is cognized—having been, being, or yet to be—as such, as well as its homogeneous counterparts; this is called the sense base of tangibles.
Furthermore, that which has touched, is touching, or will touch the body, as well as its homogeneous counterpart, is called the sense-field of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
Furthermore, that which has been traversed, is being traversed, or will be traversed by the body, as well as its homogeneous counterpart, is called the sense-field of tangibles.
In this way, all contacts—whether past, future, or present—are called the "sphere of contact" (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), and are also called "the knowable," up to "that which is to be fully realized.
Furthermore, what is this?

This refers to the four great elements and the qualities derived from the four great elements—namely, smoothness, roughness, lightness, heaviness, cold, heat, hunger, and thirst—as well as all other things perceived by the body-faculty and cognized by body-consciousness; all those designations, synonyms, expressions, concepts, notions, and verbal conventions such as "contact," "the element of contact," "the sphere of contact," and "the further shore."
Such is the sphere of tangibles; it is included among external [bases].
What is the sphere of the mind?
It should be explained according to the nature of the faculty of mind.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana)?
It refers to that which the mind has known, knows, or will know; this is called the sphere of mental objects.

Furthermore, it refers to that which consciousness, arising with the mental objects as its predominant condition, has discerned, discerns, or will discern; this is called the sphere of mental objects.
Furthermore, those phenomena that have been, are being, or will be apprehended by the mind are called the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Furthermore, those phenomena that have been, are being, or will be cognized by the mind are called the sphere of mental objects.
Thus, all phenomena of the past, future, and present are named the sphere of mental objects; they are also termed the "knowable," and so forth, up to the "fully realized."

What, then, are these? They are: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, desire, resolve, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, applied thought, sustained thought, heedlessness, non-heedlessness, and the roots of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
The faculties; all fetters, bonds, latent dispositions, secondary afflictions, and obsessions; all forms of knowledge, vision, and clear realization;
the attainment of the meditative absorption of non-perception, the meditative absorption of cessation, and the state of non-perception; the life-faculty; the maintenance of the homogeneous class;
the acquisition of things; the basis of acquisition; birth, aging, duration, and impermanence; the sets of names, phrases, and syllables; and space.
Space, cessation through deliberation, cessation not through deliberation, and all else that is known by the faculty of mind and cognized by the mental consciousness—
all those designations, synonyms, metaphors, concepts, notions, and verbal expressions such as "dharma," "dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu),
"dharma-base" (dharmāyatana), and "the further shore"— are called dharma.
Such a sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is included within the external spheres (*bāhyāyatana*).
Chapter Nineteen: The Aggregates (*skandhavarga*). At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"There are five aggregates. What are the five?
They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness; these are called the five aggregates.
What is the aggregate of form?
Whatever is form, all of it consists of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements; this is called the aggregate of form.
What is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*)?
It refers to all feelings—whether general feeling, specific feeling, or the nature of feeling—which are subsumed under feeling; this is called the aggregate of feeling.
Furthermore, there are two types of feeling designated as the aggregate of feeling: namely, bodily feeling (*kāyikī-vedanā*) and mental feeling (*caitasikī-vedanā*).
What is bodily feeling?
It refers to all feelings associated with the five groups of consciousness, up to and including those subsumed under feeling; this is called bodily feeling.
What is mental feeling?
That which refers to all feelings associated with the mental consciousness, up to and including those subsumed under feeling, is called mental feeling.

Furthermore, there are two types of feeling designated as the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*): namely, feeling accompanied by relish (*sāsvāda-vedanā*) and feeling devoid of relish (*nirāsvāda-vedanā*).
What is feeling with relish (*sāsvāda-vedanā*)?
It refers to all feelings associated with tainted attention (*sāsrava-manasikāra*), up to and including those comprised within feeling; this is called feeling with relish.
What is feeling without relish (*nirāsvāda-vedanā*)?

This refers to all feelings associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), up to and including those subsumed under feeling; these are called "flavorless" feelings (*arasa-vedanā*).

Some say that feelings associated with mental attention in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are called "flavored" feelings (*sāsvāda-vedanā*), while feelings associated with mental attention in the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*) are called "flavorless" feelings.

In this context, feeling associated with tainted attention (*sāsrava-manasikāra*) is called "tasting feeling" (*sāsvāda-vedanā*), while feeling associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*) is called "untasted feeling" (*nirāsvāda-vedanā*).

Just as there are tasting and untasted feelings, so it is with feeling that falls [into saṃsāra] and feeling that does not fall; feeling based on attachment and feeling based on renunciation; feeling conducive to fetters and feeling not conducive to fetters; feeling conducive to grasping and feeling not conducive to grasping; feeling conducive to entanglements and feeling not conducive to entanglements; and worldly feeling and supramundane feeling are likewise.
Furthermore, there are three types of feeling, which are called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*): namely, pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is pleasant feeling?

It refers to bodily pleasure and mental pleasure produced by contact conducive to pleasure; being comprised within the category of feeling that is experienced with equanimity, this is called pleasant feeling.

Furthermore, when one cultivates the first, second, and third dhyānas, the mental pleasure arising from contact conducive to pleasant feeling—comprised within the category of feeling as equanimity—is called pleasant feeling.
What is the feeling of suffering?
It refers to the bodily and mental suffering produced by contact conducive to suffering; it is an unbalanced feeling included within the category of feeling. This is called the feeling of suffering.
What is the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant?

That is to say, the bodily equanimity and mental equanimity produced by contact conducive to neither-pain-nor-pleasure, which is a feeling comprised within feeling that is neither even nor uneven—this is called the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

Furthermore, when one cultivates the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the fourth dhyāna, and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), there arises a mental equanimity born of contact that is neither painful nor pleasant; this is an experience comprised within feeling that is neither even nor uneven. This is called the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant.

Furthermore, there are four types of feeling, which are called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*): namely, feeling pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), feeling pertaining to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), feeling pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and unconditioned feeling (*apratisaṃyukta-vedanā*).
What is feeling pertaining to the desire realm?
That is to say, all feelings associated with mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the desire realm, up to and including those comprised within feeling, are called "feelings of the desire realm.
What are feelings of the form realm?
That is to say, all feelings associated with mental attention of the form realm, up to and including those comprised within feeling, are called "feelings of the form realm."
What is feeling pertaining to the formless realm?
It refers to all feelings associated with mental attention of the formless realm, up to and including those comprised within feeling; this is called feeling pertaining to the formless realm.
What is non-bound feeling (*aniyata-vedanā*)?
It refers to all feelings associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*), up to and including those subsumed under feeling; this is called non-bound feeling.
Furthermore, there are five feelings that are taught as the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*): pleasant feeling, painful feeling, joyful feeling, sorrowful feeling, and equanimous feeling.
These five types of feeling are explained in detail as in the *Indriya-varga*.

Furthermore, there are six types of feeling designated as the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), namely: feeling born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
What is feeling born of eye-contact?
It refers to the arising of visual consciousness with the eye and visible forms as conditions; from the conjunction of these three arises contact, and with contact as condition, feeling arises.

In this context, with the eye as the dominant condition, visible forms as the object, eye-contact as the cause, and eye-contact as the originator, it belongs to the category of eye-contact, is produced by eye-contact, and is associated with attention produced by eye-contact.
Regarding the various feelings, up to those comprised within feeling, that are cognized by visual consciousness with respect to forms: these are called feelings produced by eye-contact.
The same applies, in detail, to feelings produced by ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.
This is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
As with the aggregate of feeling, so it is with the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); they should be explained in detail accordingly.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?
That is to say, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is of two kinds:
first, formations associated with the mind (citta-saṃprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha);
second, formations dissociated from the mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha).
What is the aggregate of formations associated with the mind (*citta-saṃprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*)?
It refers to volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and attention (*manasikāra*), and so forth, up to all forms of knowledge (*jñāna*), vision (*darśana*), and clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Furthermore, there are other such factors associated with the mind; these are called the aggregate of formations associated with the mind.
What is the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*)?
It refers to acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and so forth, up to the collection of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*).
Furthermore, all other such dharmas that are not associated with the mind are called the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind.

Thus, the aggregate of formations associated with the mind (*citta-saṃprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*) and the aggregate of formations dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*) are collectively termed the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Chapter Twenty: The Many Elements (*Bahudhātuka-varga*), Part One. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Ānanda was dwelling alone in a quiet room and reflected thus:
"Those who give rise to fear and those who give rise to calamities and afflictions are all fools, not wise ones."

Having reflected thus, he emerged from his private chamber later in the day and went to where the Blessed One was. Prostrating at the Blessed One’s feet, he withdrew to stand to one side and related in detail to the Blessed One the matter upon which he had been reflecting.
The Buddha’s seal may be stated thus: “It is so, it is so.
Those who give rise to fear and those who give rise to calamities, afflictions, and disturbances are all fools, not wise ones.”
Just as placing fire within a house of dry reeds, grass, or within a multi-storied pavilion or tower results in its being consumed by flames, so too it is with the fool:
due to a lack of wisdom, they give rise to various fears, calamities, and afflictions.
Ānanda, you should know that fear, calamity, and affliction—whether past, future, or present—all arise from the foolish, not from the wise, because the wise do not give rise to them.
Ānanda, you should know this: fools have fear, while the wise have no fear;
fools have afflictions, while the wise have no afflictions;
fools have disturbances, while the wise have no disturbances.

Therefore, Ānanda, you should know the dharmas of the foolish and the wise; having known them, you should distance yourself from all the dharmas of the foolish and correctly practice the dharmas of the wise.
Ānanda said, "To what extent are they designated as 'fools'?
The Buddha said:

"If there are those who are unskilled in the elements (dhātu), the sense bases (āyatana), the aggregates (skandha), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), and the principles of what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna-dharma), they are reckoned among the foolish.
Ānanda asked: "To what extent are they designated as being among the wise?"
The Buddha said:

"If there are those who have attained skillfulness regarding the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), the aggregates (skandha), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), and the principles of what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna-dharma), they are counted among the wise."
Ānanda asked: "In what way is a wise person skilled in the elements (dhātu)?
The Buddha said:
“The wise one knows and sees the eighteen elements as they truly are; this is skillfulness regarding the elements. That is to say, he knows and sees them as they truly are:

the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.”

Furthermore, one possesses skill regarding the elements through knowing and seeing the six elements as they truly are; that is, one knows and sees the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element as they truly are.

Furthermore, one possesses skill regarding the elements by knowing and seeing the six elements as they truly are; that is, by knowing and seeing the element of desire, the element of ill will, the element of harmfulness, the element of non-desire, the element of non-ill will, and the element of non-harmfulness as they truly are.

Furthermore, one possesses skill in the elements by knowing and seeing the six elements as they truly are; that is, one knows and sees the element of pleasure, the element of pain, the element of joy, the element of grief, the element of equanimity, and the element of ignorance as they truly are.

Furthermore, one possesses skill regarding the elements by knowing and seeing the four elements as they truly are; that is, one knows and sees the element of sensation, the element of perception, the element of formations, and the element of consciousness as they truly are.

Furthermore, one possesses skill regarding the elements through knowing and seeing the three realms as they truly are; that is, knowing and seeing the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as they truly are.

Furthermore, one possesses skill regarding the elements through knowing and seeing the three realms as they truly are; that is, knowing and seeing the realm of form, the formless realm, and the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*) as they truly are.

Furthermore, one possesses skill in the elements by knowing and seeing the three realms as they truly are; that is, one knows and sees the past realm, the future realm, and the present realm as they truly are.

Furthermore, one possesses skill in the elements through knowing and seeing the three realms as they truly are; that is, one knows and sees the inferior realm, the middling realm, and the superior realm as they truly are.

Furthermore, one possesses skill in the elements through knowing and seeing the three realms as they truly are; that is, one knows and sees the wholesome realm, the unwholesome realm, and the indeterminate realm as they truly are.

Furthermore, one possesses skill regarding the elements by knowing and seeing the three realms as they truly are; that is, one knows and sees the realm of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the realm of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the realm of those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*) as they truly are.

Furthermore, one possesses skill in the elements by knowing and seeing two elements as they truly are: namely, knowing and seeing the contaminated element (*sāsrava-dhātu*) and the uncontaminated element (*anāsrava-dhātu*) as they truly are.

Furthermore, one possesses skill in the elements by knowing and seeing two elements as they truly are: namely, knowing and seeing the conditioned element (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*) and the unconditioned element (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) as they truly are.
"This is called the wise person’s skillfulness regarding the elements (dhātu). Ānanda asked:
'What is the wise person’s skillfulness regarding the bases (āyatana)?"’"

The Buddha said: "The wise person possesses skill regarding the bases (*āyatana*) by knowing and seeing them as they truly are. That is to say, they know and see the base of the eye and the base of forms; the base of the ear and the base of sounds; the base of the nose and the base of odors; the base of the tongue and the base of flavors; the base of the body and the base of tangibles; and the base of the mind and the base of mental phenomena. This is called the wise person’s skill regarding the bases."
Ānanda asked: "In what way is a wise person skilled in the aggregates?
The Buddha said:

“The wise one possesses skill regarding the aggregates by knowing and seeing the five aggregates as they truly are; that is, by knowing and seeing the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness as they truly are—this is called the wise one’s skill regarding the aggregates.”
Ānanda asked, "In what way is a wise person skillful regarding dependent origination?
The Buddha said:

“The wise one who knows and sees the twelve factors of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) in their direct and reverse order as they truly are is skilled in dependent origination. That is to say, he knows and sees as it truly is: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. Namely: conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*) are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness (*vijñāna*); conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); conditioned by the six sense bases is contact (*sparśa*); conditioned by contact is feeling (*vedanā*); conditioned by feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); conditioned by craving is clinging (*upādāna*); conditioned by clinging is existence (*bhava*); conditioned by existence is birth (*jāti*); conditioned by birth arise aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.”

Furthermore, one knows as it truly is: "With this not being, that is not; from the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. In this way, this entire mass of suffering comes to cease.
"This is called the wise person’s skillfulness regarding dependent origination. Ānanda asked,
"In what way is the wise person skillful regarding what is possible and what is impossible?"
The Buddha said:

"The wise person possesses skill in discerning what is possible and what is impossible by knowing and seeing possibility and impossibility as they truly are. That is to say, they know as it truly is that there is no possibility and no occasion for unwholesome conduct of body, speech, or mind to result in a ripening that is desirable, lovely, delightful, or agreeable."
It is impossible and there is no occasion for unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind to result in an agreeable, pleasant, delightful, or desirable maturation.
It is impossible and there is no occasion for wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind to result in an disagreeable, unpleasant, undelightful, or undesirable maturation.
It is possible and reasonable that virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind may result in a desirable, pleasant, delightful, and agreeable maturation.

It is impossible and unreasonable that, having engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, one could—by reason of that cause—upon the breakup of the body after death, be reborn in the higher realms.

It is impossible and out of the question that one who has practiced misconduct of body, speech, and mind could, on account of that cause and condition, at the breaking up of the body after death, fall into the miserable destinies.

It is impossible and out of the question that one who has practiced excellence of body, speech, and mind could, on account of that cause and condition, at the breaking up of the body after death, fall into the miserable destinies.

It is possible and reasonable that, having practiced excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind, one will—by reason of this cause and condition—be reborn in the various happy realms after the dissolution of the body at the end of life.
This is skill in what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, he knows and sees as it truly is that there is no possibility and no occasion for two wheel-turning monarchs to arise simultaneously in a single world-system, neither before nor after the other;
whereas there is indeed the possibility and the occasion for one wheel-turning monarch to arise in a single world-system, neither before nor after another.
It is impossible and there is no occasion for two Tathāgatas to appear simultaneously in a single world-system, neither before nor after the other;
it is possible and there is occasion for one Tathāgata to appear in a single world-system, neither before nor after another.
He possesses skill in the possible and the impossible.

Furthermore, he knows and sees, as it truly is, that there is no possibility and no occasion for a woman to become a wheel-turning monarch, Śakra, Māra, or Brahmā, nor to realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

There is the possibility and the opportunity for a man to become a wheel-turning monarch, Śakra, Māra, or Brahmā, or to realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He possesses skill in discerning what is possible and what is impossible.

Furthermore, he knows and sees, as it truly is, that there is no possibility and no occasion for one who possesses the noble vision to intentionally harm his mother, harm his father, harm an arhat, cause a schism in the Saṃgha, or with an evil mind draw blood from the body of a Buddha.
It is possible and there is scope for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) to commit the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
It is impossible and there is no scope for one who possesses the noble vision (*āryadṛṣṭi*) to intentionally take the life of a living being.
It is possible and there is scope for ordinary worldlings to intentionally take the life of a living being.
It is impossible and there is no occasion for one who possesses the noble vision to intentionally transgress the precepts;
however, it is possible and there is occasion for an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) to intentionally transgress the precepts.

It is impossible and out of the question for one who possesses the noble vision to abandon superior training rules and resort to inferior ones; or to seek teachers among non-Buddhists, or to seek fields of merit among non-Buddhists, or to gaze upon the faces of non-Buddhist śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, or to regard various divinations and auspicious rites as pure, or to undergo an eighth existence.
There is possibility and scope for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) to experience such things;
this is skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, knowing and seeing as it truly is that there is no possibility or scope for the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*)—which defile the mind, weaken the power of wisdom, obstruct the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*), and oppose nirvāṇa—to remain unsevered, his mind dwells well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).

It is possible and appropriate that, having abandoned the five hindrances which defile the mind, weaken the power of wisdom, obstruct the factors of enlightenment, and oppose nirvana, the mind may dwell securely in the four foundations of mindfulness.

It is impossible and there is no occasion for one who has not abandoned the five hindrances—and so forth, as extensively described, up to being contrary to nirvāṇa—to cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment while the mind is not well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness.

It is possible and appropriate that one who has abandoned the five hindrances—and so forth, as extensively described, up to those factors contrary to nirvāṇa—having well-established the mind within the four foundations of mindfulness, is able to cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.

It is impossible and there is no occasion for one who has not abandoned the five hindrances—and so on, as extensively explained, up to one who is contrary to nirvāṇa—to cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment while the mind is not well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, and thereby realize the unsurpassed enlightenment of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

It is possible and appropriate that one who has abandoned the five hindrances—expounded at length up to those factors that oppose nirvāṇa—and whose mind is well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, can cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment and thereby realize the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or unsurpassed bodhi.
"This is called the skillfulness of the wise regarding what is possible and what is impossible. Ānanda said,
"What is the name of this Dharma-gate?"
"How should it be received and upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This Dharma-gate is named 'The Four Turnings,' and is also named 'The Great Mirror of the Dharma,' and is also named 'The Drum of Ambrosia,' and is also named 'The Many Realms. It should be upheld in this way."
Then Ānanda joyfully and respectfully accepted [the instruction].
What is the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*)?
It is as described for the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
What is the form element (*rūpadhātu*)?
It is as described for the form base (*rūpāyatana*).
What is the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?

That is to say, the eye-consciousness that arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms—in this regard, the eye serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati*) and visible form as the objective condition (*ālambana*)—that which cognizes, differentiates, and individually distinguishes the various visible forms cognized by the eye is called the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
The remaining five elements of the three realms should also be explained in detail accordingly.
What is the earth element?
The earth element is of two kinds: [the internal and the external].
First, internal;
second, external.
What is the internal earth element?
This refers to whatever within this body is individual, solid, and of a solid nature, which is grasped and appropriated.
What, then, is this? It refers to hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and so forth, up to excrement and filth.
Furthermore, whatever else within the body is individual, solid, of a solid nature, possessed of grasping, and possessed of appropriation—this is called the internal earth element.
What is the external earth element?
It refers to that which is outside this body, included among external things, solid, of a solid nature, without grasping, and without appropriation.

What, then, are these? They are the great earth and mountains, various stones and rubble; oysters, clams, and snails; copper, iron, tin, and lead; mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, jade, gold, silver, stone treasuries, and vajra-treasures; crystal, red pearls, and right-spiraling conchs; sand, soil, grasses, trees, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.

Furthermore, there is earth that rests upon the water-circle; moreover, whatever else exists outside this body that is solid in nature, of a solid kind, non-appropriated, and non-sensate—this is called the external earth element.
That which is internal and external is collectively termed the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
What is the water element (*ab-dhātu*)?
It is said that the water element is of two kinds:
First, the internal;
second, the external.
What is the internal water element?
This refers to whatever distinct moisture and moist categories exist within this body, which are clung to and appropriated. What, then, are these?
They are tears, sweat, and so forth, up to urine.
Furthermore, whatever else within the body is individual, moist, and of a moist nature, possessing grasping and sensation, is called the internal water element (*ab-dhātu*).
What is the external water element?
It refers to all that is external to this body, comprised of the external, which is moist and of a moist nature, lacking grasping and sensation.

What, then, are these? They are the sap and dew of roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; wine, milk, curd, ghee, oil, honey, and molasses; ponds, pools, and lakes; the Gaṅgā River, the Yamunā River, the Sarayū River, the Aciravatī River, the Mahī River; and the eastern, western, southern, and northern oceans—the waters of the four great oceans.

Furthermore, there is water that rests upon the wind-circle, as well as other moist substances and moist categories existing outside of this, which are without grasping and without sensation; these are called the external water element.
That which is internal and external is collectively termed the water element (*ābdhātu*).
What is the fire element (*tejodhātu*)?
It is said that the fire element is of two kinds:
I. Internal; II. External.
What is the internal fire element?
This refers to whatever individual nature of heat and categories of heat exist within this body, which are possessed of grasping and sensation. What, then, is this?

It refers to all the heat, intense heat, and pervasive heat within this body by means of which what is eaten, chewed, and drunk is properly digested; yet if this [heat] becomes excessive, it causes the body to burn with feverish heat.

Furthermore, whatever else within the body is individually characterized as the nature of heat or the category of heat, which is possessed of grasping and possessed of sensation, this is called the internal fire element (*tejodhātu*).
What is the external fire element?
It refers to all that is outside this body, comprised of the external, which is the nature of heat or the category of heat, and is without grasping and without sensation.

What, then, is this? It refers to the warmth of earth, fire, the sun, medicinal herbs, jewels, palaces, constellations, clusters of fire, and the flames of lamps; the fires that burn villages, cities, rivers, and wildernesses; the fires that consume ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, or even immeasurable loads of firewood and grass, blazing and fiercely radiant; or the warmth found in mountains, marshes, rivers, ponds, caves, houses, halls, pavilions, and in the roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of plants and trees.
Furthermore, there is that which is of a hot nature or of the category of heat, being non-appropriated and non-sensed; this is called the external fire element (*tejodhātu*).
The aforementioned internal and this external together are collectively termed the fire element.
What is the wind element (*vāyudhātu*)?
That is to say, the wind element is of two kinds:
first, internal;
second, external.
What is the internal wind element?
It refers to whatever within this body is of a distinct nature of motion or belongs to the category of motion, which is appropriated and clung to.
Furthermore, what is it?

That is to say, within this body there are winds that move upward, winds that move downward, or winds that move horizontally; winds of the flanks, winds of the back, winds of the chest, winds of the abdomen, winds of the heart, and winds of the navel; the *utpala* wind, the *kubjaka* wind, the sword wind, the blade wind, and the needle wind; the constricting wind, the enveloping wind, the pulling wind, the pressing wind, the forceful wind, the wind that follows the limbs and joints, and the winds of inhalation and exhalation.
Furthermore, whatever else within the body is of a distinct nature of motion, belonging to the class of motion, possessing appropriation and sensation—this is called the internal wind element.
What is the external wind element?
It refers to all that is outside this body, comprised of the external, which is of a nature of motion, belonging to the class of motion, and is without appropriation or sensation.

What, then, are these? They are: east winds, west winds, south winds, and north winds; winds with dust and winds without dust; whirlwinds, tempests, and vāyu-vātās (veḷuvana-winds); small winds, great winds, and immeasurable winds; wind-circles and winds that move through space.
Furthermore, there is that which is of a mobile nature and belongs to the category of the mobile, being without grasping and without sensation; this is called the external wind element (*vāyudhātu*).
The aforementioned internal and this external together are collectively termed the wind element.
What is the space element (*ākāśadhātu*)?
That is to say, the space element is of two kinds:
first, internal;
second, external.
What is the internal space element?
It refers to whatever is individual, empty, and of the nature of emptiness within this body, which is grasped and appropriated.
Furthermore, what is it?

This refers to the cavities within this body, such as those following the skin, flesh, blood, marrow, and bones; the sockets of the eyes, the orifices of the ears and nose, the mouth, the throat, the heart, the abdomen, the intestines, and the stomach—by means of these, it stores what is drunk and eaten and causes them to be discharged below.
Furthermore, whatever else constitutes the distinct internal emptiness and empty-like nature within the body is called the internal space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
What is the external space element?
It refers to all that is external to this body, comprised of the external, which is empty and empty-like, ungrasped, and unappropriated.
What, then, is this? It refers to the external, open, and unobstructed matter (*avakāśa-rūpa*), which is called the external space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*).
This internal [space] and this external [space] together are collectively termed the space element.
What is the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*)?
It refers to the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) and the contaminated mental consciousness (*sāsravamano-vijñāna*); this is called the element of consciousness.
