The remainder of the twentieth chapter, "On the Many Realms" (*Bahudhātuka-varga*): What is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
It refers to the arising of various forms of greed, intense greed, and even the categories of greed toward objects of desire; this, in general, is termed the desire realm.

Furthermore, sensual desire, as well as the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with sensual desire, together with the bodily and vocal actions arising therefrom and the formations dissociated from them, are collectively termed the "desire realm" (kāmadhātu).
What is the element of ill will (*vyāpādadhātu*)?
It refers to the desire to cause harm toward sentient beings, up to and including manifesting as an actual affliction; this is collectively termed the element of ill will.

Furthermore, hatred and the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with hatred, together with the bodily and vocal actions arising therefrom and the formations dissociated from mind—all these are collectively termed the element of ill will.
What is the element of cruelty (*vihiṃsā-dhātu*)?

It refers to striking sentient beings with any one of various instruments of suffering, such as the hand, clods of earth, knives, or staffs; all forms of injuring, harming, and cruelty arising from malice that can produce painful states—this is collectively termed the element of cruelty.

Furthermore, all harms, as well as the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with harm, together with the bodily and vocal actions they give rise to and the formations dissociated from them, are collectively termed the element of harm (*vihimsā-dhātu*).
What is the absence of desire for the realm of desire?

It refers to contemplating the defects of the realm of desire and thus resolving with faith and upholding that this realm of desire consists of unwholesome dharmas; that it is despised by the Buddhas and their disciples, as well as by noble and virtuous persons; that it can cause harm to oneself, harm to others, and harm to both; that it can destroy wisdom, obstruct those of similar nature, and hinder nirvāṇa; and that upholding these dharmas does not give rise to supernormal knowledge, does not lead toward enlightenment, and does not result in the realization of nirvāṇa.
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the realm of non-desire (*vītarāga-dhātu*).

Furthermore, in order to abandon the realm of desire, one contemplates the merits of the realm of non-desire. One thus resolves upon, accepts, and upholds this realm of non-desire as a wholesome dharma, as something sublime and excellent—one that is praised and commended by the Buddhas, their disciples, and noble virtuous persons; it does not harm oneself, nor harm others, nor harm both; it increases wisdom, does not obstruct those of similar kind, and does not hinder *nirvāṇa*. By upholding this dharma, one can give rise to supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), lead toward enlightenment (*bodhi*), and realize *nirvāṇa*.
Reflecting in this way, one exerts diligent effort and applies oneself with unremitting energy; this is called the realm of non-desire (*an-iccha-dhātu*).

Furthermore, one reflects upon the realm of desire (*kāma-dhātu*) as being like a disease, like an abscess, like a piercing arrow that causes affliction and harm; it is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, subject to fluctuation; it is wearying, debilitated, and grave; it is a phenomenon subject to ruin and destruction; it is swift and never ceasing, decaying and non-eternal, unreliable, and a phenomenon subject to transformation and disintegration.
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort; this is called the realm of non-desire.
Furthermore, in order to abandon the realm of desire, one reflects that its cessation is cessation and is detachment, and reflects that its path is the path and is deliverance.
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the realm of non-desire (*an-iccha-dhātu*).

Furthermore, it refers to reflecting upon the concentration of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta-samādhi*) and the Path associated with that concentration of equanimity, as well as the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the realm of non-desire (*anabhijjhādhātu*).

Furthermore, non-desire together with the associated feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, as well as the bodily and vocal actions it initiates and the formations dissociated from them, are collectively termed the realm of non-desire.
What is the element of non-ill will?

It refers to contemplating the faults and perils within the element of ill will, such that one understands: "This element of ill will is an unwholesome dharma... and so forth, up to: it does not lead to the realization of Nirvāṇa."
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the element of non-ill will (*avyāpāda-dhātu*).

Furthermore, in order to abandon the element of ill will, one contemplates the merits of the element of non-ill will, thinking: "This element of non-ill will is a wholesome dharma, and so forth, up to its ability to realize *nirvāṇa*."
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the realm of non-ill will (*avyāpādadhātu*).
Furthermore, one reflects upon the realm of ill will as being like a disease, like an abscess, and so forth, even unto a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay.
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort; this is called the element of non-ill will.
Furthermore, in order to abandon the element of ill will, one reflects that its cessation is cessation and detachment, and reflects that its path is the path and the escape.
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing;
this is called the element of non-ill will (*avyāpādadhātu*).
Furthermore, it is when one reflects upon the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrīsamādhi*) and the path associated with that concentration of loving-kindness.
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing;
this is called the element of non-ill will (*avyāpādadhātu*).

Furthermore, non-ill will together with the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with it, along with the bodily and vocal actions that arise in conjunction with them and the formations dissociated from mind—all these are collectively termed the element of non-ill will.
What is the realm of non-harm?
It refers to contemplating the faults of the realm of harm, such that this realm of harm is an unwholesome dharma and so forth, up to not realizing nirvāṇa.
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the element of non-harming (*avihiṃsā-dhātu*).

Furthermore, in order to abandon the element of harming, one contemplates the merits of the element of non-harming, thinking: "In this way, the element of non-harming is a wholesome dharma, and so forth, until it can lead to the realization of nirvāṇa."
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the element of non-harming.
Furthermore, one reflects on the element of harming as being like a disease, like an abscess, and so forth, up to being a phenomenon subject to disintegration.
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort; this is called the element of non-harming.
Furthermore, in order to abandon the element of harming, one reflects that its cessation is cessation and is detachment, and reflects that its path is the path and is deliverance.
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the element of harmlessness (*avyāpādadhātu*).
Furthermore, it is when one reflects upon the concentration of compassion (*karuṇāsamādhi*) and the path associated with that concentration of compassion.
Reflecting in this way, one arouses diligent effort and exerts the mind without ceasing; this is called the element of non-harming (*avihiṃsā-dhātu*).

Furthermore, non-harming itself, along with the associated feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, together with the bodily and vocal actions that arise in accordance with them, and the dissociated formations—these collectively are named the element of non-harming.
What is the element of pleasure (*sukha-dhātu*)?

It refers to the bodily pleasure and mental pleasure arising from contact conducive to pleasure, which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*); this is called the element of pleasure.

Furthermore, it refers to the mental pleasure arising from contact conducive to pleasant feeling during the cultivation of the third dhyāna, which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity; this is called the element of pleasure.
What is the element of suffering?
It refers to bodily suffering arising from contact conducive to suffering, which is comprised within the feeling of unequilibrium; this is called the element of suffering.
What is the element of joy?
That which is mental joy arising from contact conducive to joy, comprised within the feeling of equanimity—this is called the element of joy (*sukha-dhātu*).
Furthermore, when one cultivates the first and second dhyānas, the mental joy arising from contact conducive to joy, comprised within the feeling of equanimity—this is called the element of joy.
What is the element of grief (*daurmanasya-dhātu*)?
It refers to the mental grief arising from contact conducive to grief, which is comprised within the category of unbalanced feeling (*vedanā*); this is called the element of grief.
What is the element of equanimity (*upekṣā-dhātu*)?

That is to say, the bodily equanimity and mental equanimity arising from contact conducive to equanimity—which is a feeling included within the category of feeling that is neither even nor uneven—is called the element of equanimity (*upekṣā-dhātu*).

Furthermore, the mental equanimity arising from contact conducive to neither-pain-nor-pleasure when one cultivates the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the formless attainments—which is a feeling included within the category of feeling that is neither even nor uneven—is called the element of equanimity.
What is the element of ignorance?
It refers to the lack of knowledge regarding the three realms; this is called the element of ignorance.
What is the element of sensation?
This refers to the six groups of feeling, namely: feeling born of eye-contact, up to feeling born of mind-contact.
This is called the element of feeling (*vedanā-dhātu*).
What is the element of perception (*saṃjñā-dhātu*)?
The six groups of perception (*saṃjñā-kāya*)—namely, perception born of eye-contact up to perception born of mind-contact—are called the element of perception (*saṃjñā-dhātu*).
What is the element of formations (*saṃskāra-dhātu*)?
The six groups of volition (*cetanā-kāya*)—namely, volition born of eye-contact up to volition born of mind-contact—are called the element of formations.
What is the element of consciousness?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness, namely, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; this is called the element of consciousness.
What is the desire realm? It refers to those phenomena in which desire and greed increase and proliferate; this is called the desire realm.
Furthermore, the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates bound to the desire realm are called the desire realm.
Furthermore, from the Avīci Hell below up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven above, all form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness contained therein are called the desire realm.
What is the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?
It refers to those phenomena in which desire for form increases; this is called the realm of form.
Furthermore, the fourteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*) associated with the realm of form are called the realm of form.

Furthermore, from the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude below up to the Heaven of Ultimate Form above, all that exists therein—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—is called the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
What is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
It refers to those phenomena in which attachment to the formless increases; this is called the formless realm.
Furthermore, that which is bound to the formless realm consists of the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates; this is called the formless realm.

Furthermore, just as in the desire and form realms, locations are established with fixed boundaries so that they do not overlap or become confused— a situation that does not exist in the formless realm—
nevertheless, the distinctions of superiority and inferiority arising from meditative concentration establish the hierarchy of higher and lower levels.

From the sphere of infinite space below up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception above, all that exists therein—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—is called the formless realm.
What is the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
It refers to the desire realm and the form realm collectively termed the form realm.
What is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
The four formless [attainments] are called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
What is the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*)?
It refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*); these are called the realm of cessation.
Furthermore, all phenomena possessing form are collectively termed the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

With the exception of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), all remaining formless phenomena are termed the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): these are called the element of cessation (*nirodha-dhātu*).
What is the past element?
It refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the past; these are called the past element.
What is the future realm?
It refers to the five aggregates of the future; this is called the future realm.
What is the present realm?
That is to say, the five aggregates of the present are called the "present realm" (*pratyutpanna-dhātu*).
What is the "inferior realm"?
That is to say, unwholesome (*akuśala*) and obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena are called the "inferior realm."
What is the intermediate realm?
It refers to tainted wholesome phenomena and non-obscured neutral phenomena; these are called the intermediate realm.
What is the sublime realm?
That which refers to untainted wholesome phenomena is called the sublime realm (*praṇīta-dhātu*).
What is the wholesome realm?

It refers to wholesome bodily and vocal actions, mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta*), dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); these are called the wholesome realm.
What is the unwholesome element (*akuśala-dhātu*)?

It refers to unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*); these are called the unwholesome element.
What is the indeterminate element (*avyākṛta-dhātu*)?

That is to say, indeterminate matter, the mind and mental factors, the formations dissociated from the mind, as well as space and non-analytical cessation—these are called the indeterminate realm (*avyākṛta-dhātu*).
What is the realm of training (*śaikṣa-dhātu*)?
That which refers to the five aggregates of one in training is called the realm of training (*śaikṣadhātu*).
What is the realm of no-more-training (*aśaikṣadhātu*)?
That which refers to the five aggregates of one beyond training is called the realm of no-more-training.
What is the realm that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

It refers to the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), as well as space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); these are called the realm that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is the contaminated realm (*sāsravadhātu*)? It refers to the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); this is called the contaminated realm.
What is the uncontaminated realm (*anāsravadhātu*)?

It refers to the five uncontaminated aggregates, as well as space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); this is called the uncontaminated realm.
What is the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*)?
It refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); this is called the conditioned realm.
What is the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*)?
That is to say, space and the two types of cessation are called the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*).
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
There are sixty-two realms; the eighteen realms are the first.
Three, six, one, four kinds; six, three, two, two kinds.
Chapter Twenty-one: Dependent Origination (Nidāna), Part One. At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:

“I shall now proclaim for you the dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) and the dependently arisen phenomena (pratītyasamutpanna-dharma). You should listen attentively and apply your minds with great care.”

What is dependent origination? It means: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. In this way, there is the accumulation of this entire great mass of suffering.

"O Bhikṣus, you should know that birth is the condition for old age and death. Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, this dependent origination remains established in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu). All Tathāgatas naturally penetrate it, fully awaken to it, proclaim it, designate it, establish it, analyze it, and reveal it so that it is made manifest, saying: 'Birth is the condition for old age and death. It should be understood that this applies likewise, up to: 'Ignorance is the condition for volitional formations.'"

Whatever herein constitutes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the fixedness of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the principle of phenomena (dharmasthititā), and the course of phenomena (dharmanetrī)—which is true, real, authentic, and suchness; which is neither false nor deceptive, neither inverted nor divergent—this is called dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
What is called "dharmas arisen through conditions"?

They are ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death; these are called dharmas arisen through conditions.

"Monks, you should know that old age and death are impermanent, conditioned, produced, and dependently arisen; they are subject to the nature of exhaustion, the nature of disappearance, the nature of detachment, and the nature of cessation."
Birth, existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, volitional formations, and ignorance are likewise.

Bhikṣus, you should know that my many-heard noble disciples, regarding this dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena, are able to see them as they truly are with right wisdom, knowing them well, understanding them well, reflecting upon them well, and penetrating them well; thus they do not give rise to delusion or confusion concerning the past, asking: "Did I exist in the past, or did I not exist?"
"What was I in the past?
How was I in the past?"—one does not give rise to delusion and confusion regarding the future limit, such as thinking: "Will I exist or not exist in future lives?"
"What shall I become? How shall I become?
Nor does he give rise to delusion based on the internal, wondering, "What is this self?"
What is this "I"? To whom does this "I" belong?
Who will this "I" become?
"From where have these sentient beings come?
Having passed away from this place, where will they go?

Because he knows and sees thus, regarding all the various worldly views—namely, those associated with theories of a self (*ātman*), theories of sentient beings (*sattva*), theories of a life-principle (*jīva*), and theories of auspiciousness and misfortune—which are embellished and guarded, grasped as "mine," and which involve suffering, obstruction, calamity, and feverish distress.
At that time, he attains the thorough knowledge of abandonment; like cutting the root of a tree or the crown of a *tāla* tree, it has no further power and shall never arise again. Why is this so?

It refers to my well-heard noble disciple who, regarding this dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena, is able to see them as they truly are with right wisdom, knowing them well, understanding them well, reflecting upon them well, and penetrating them thoroughly.
At that time, the bhikṣus received this with joy and reverence.

Within this context, although the essence of "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and "dependently arisen phenomena" (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*) is one, their meanings differ. That is to say: there are things that are dependent origination but not dependently arisen phenomena; there are things that are dependently arisen phenomena but not dependent origination; there are things that are both dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena; and there are things that are neither dependent origination nor dependently arisen phenomena.
There may be that which is a dependent origination but not a dependently arisen phenomenon; there is none such.

There may be that which is a dependently arisen phenomenon but not a dependent origination; these are ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age and death.

There are those that are both dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena; namely, birth is certain to produce aging-and-death. Thus, the limb of birth is certain to act as a condition, possessing the nature of dependent origination and the nature of being dependently arisen.

In this same way, one should understand that existence (*bhava*), grasping (*upādāna*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), feeling (*vedanā*), contact (*sparśa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) are likewise.
Regarding "neither dependent origination nor dependently originated phenomena," this refers to the exclusion of the aforementioned characteristics.

Furthermore, regarding "birth as the condition for aging and death," this means that although these links of existence arise and perish differently at each moment, the principle of dependent origination remains eternally determinate.
If past birth were not a condition for aging and death, then future birth would likewise not be a condition for aging and death.
If future birth were not a condition for aging and death, then past birth would likewise not be a condition for aging and death.
If birth in a past life were not a condition for aging and death, then birth in the present life would also not be a condition for aging and death.
If birth in the present life were not a condition for aging and death, then birth in a past life would also not be a condition for aging and death.
If future birth were not a condition for aging and death, then present birth would likewise not be a condition for aging and death.
If present birth were not a condition for aging and death, then future birth would likewise not be a condition for aging and death.

If birth occurring when a Buddha has appeared in the world were not a condition for old age and death, then birth occurring when a Buddha has not appeared in the world should likewise not be a condition for old age and death.

If birth occurring when a Buddha has not appeared in the world were not a condition for old age, then birth occurring when a Buddha has appeared in the world should likewise not be a condition for old age.
If the principle of dependent origination were subject to inversion, it would result in a bifurcation because it would lack definiteness;
it would also be subject to subversion because its logic would be confused.
If that were so, one could not establish dependent origination, and the Buddha should not have taught that birth conditions aging and death.

However, the principle that birth conditions aging and death, as taught by the Buddha, is definitive; whether Buddhas appear or do not appear in the past, future, or present worlds, it has never changed. The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally thus: it neither hides nor perishes, it neither tilts nor moves, and its principle is profoundly serene.
The sages of the past and the sages of the future have all traversed this same path; it is true, real, authentic, and suchness; it is not false, not empty, not inverted, and not different.

Therefore, the Buddha taught that birth is conditioned by aging and death, and likewise, existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, volitional formations, and ignorance are conditions for volitional formations.
Furthermore, regarding "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations," what is ignorance?
It refers to lack of knowledge regarding the past, lack of knowledge regarding the future, and lack of knowledge regarding both the past and the future;

lack of knowledge regarding the internal, lack of knowledge regarding the external, and lack of knowledge regarding both the internal and the external; and lack of knowledge regarding karma and its maturation.
Ignorance regarding the ripening of karma; ignorance regarding wholesome actions, ignorance regarding unwholesome actions, and ignorance regarding both wholesome and unwholesome actions;
ignorance regarding causes, ignorance regarding the phenomena produced by causes; ignorance regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
ignorance regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; and ignorance regarding wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.
Ignorance; ignorance regarding dharmas that are blameworthy and those that are blameless; ignorance regarding dharmas that should be cultivated and those that should not be cultivated;
ignorance regarding inferior and superior dharmas; ignorance regarding black and white dharmas;
ignorance regarding dharmas that have adversaries; ignorance regarding dependent origination; and ignorance regarding the six bases of contact as they truly are.

Thus, this lack of knowledge and lack of vision, which is not a clear realization (*abhisamaya*), but rather darkness, delusion, the blindness of ignorance (*avidyā*), being shrouded within a net, stubbornness, turbidity, the arising of obscuration, the arising of ignorance, the arising of lack of wisdom, the arising of inferior intelligence; that which obstructs wholesome qualities and prevents *nirvāṇa*; the outflow of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the poisonous root of ignorance, the poisonous stem of ignorance, the poisonous branch of ignorance, the poisonous leaf of ignorance, the poisonous flower of ignorance, and the poisonous fruit of ignorance; delusion, extreme delusion, and the height of delusion; delight, extreme delight, and the height of delight; that which belongs to the category of delusion and arises from delusion—this, in total, is called ignorance.
What is "ignorance as the condition for volitional formations"?
As the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that because ignorance is the cause and ignorance is the condition, greed, hatred, and delusion arise."
This nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is called "formations conditioned by ignorance.
Furthermore, as the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that because ignorance is the precursor and ignorance is the banner, immeasurable kinds of evil and unwholesome dharmas arise, namely: lack of shame, lack of dread, and so forth."

Due to a lack of shame and a lack of dread, various wrong views arise; due to wrong views, wrong intention arises; due to wrong intention, wrong speech arises; due to wrong speech, wrong action arises; due to wrong action, wrong livelihood arises; due to wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises; due to wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises; and due to wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises.

These—namely, wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration—are called "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance."
Furthermore, as the Blessed One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that the arising of immeasurable kinds of evil and unwholesome dharmas all have ignorance as their root, ignorance as their origin; they belong to the category of ignorance and arise from ignorance."

Those who have fallen into the realm of ignorance do not know, as they truly are, wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; blameworthy and blameless phenomena; phenomena to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated; inferior and sublime phenomena; dark and bright phenomena; phenomena that are opposed; and all phenomena that arise through conditions.

Because one does not know these phenomena as they truly are, there arise wrong view, wrong intention, and so forth, up to wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration; this is called "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations."
Furthermore, in the *Kumbhopama-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke thus:
"With ignorance as a condition, one performs meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations (*saṃskāra*).
What are meritorious formations?"
This refers to contaminated wholesome bodily and vocal actions, mind and mental factors, and non-associated formations.

Such conditioned phenomena are able, throughout the long night, to bring about desirable, pleasant, delightful, and agreeable results of maturation; these results are called merit (*puṇya*) and also called the fruit of merit (*puṇyaphala*).
Because it is the matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) of such meritorious karma, it is called "meritorious action" (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).
What is non-meritorious action?
It refers to all unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, as well as the mind, mental factors (*citta-caitta*), and formations dissociated from the mind (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).

Such formations, throughout the long night, are able to bring about ripened fruits that are undesirable, unpleasant, unenjoyable, and disagreeable; these fruits are called non-merit, and are also termed the fruit of non-merit.
Because this is not the ripened fruit of meritorious karma, it is called non-meritorious conduct (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*).
What is immovable conduct (*āniñjyābhisaṃskāra*)?
It refers to the four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamādhi*).
All contaminated wholesome states are called immovable formations (*āniñjya-saṃskāra*).
How does one, with ignorance as a condition, create non-meritorious formations?
It refers to a certain class of persons who, because their minds are bound by the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion, commit the three kinds of unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
These three types of unwholesome conduct are called non-meritorious formations (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, one falls into hell; there, one again performs non-meritorious formations and so forth. This is what is meant by "with ignorance as a condition, non-meritorious formations are produced."
As it has been taught regarding the hells, so should it be understood for the animal realm and the realm of hungry ghosts.
How does ignorance serve as a condition for the formation of meritorious volitional formations?
It is said that there is a certain class of beings who fixate their minds upon and long for the pleasures of the human realm, and they form this thought:
“May I be born into the human realm with its common lot, and experience happiness together with all other human beings.
Driven by this aspiration, one performs the sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind that brings about rebirth in the human realm.
These three types of sublime conduct are called meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

By reason of this cause and condition, when the body breaks up at the end of life, one is reborn in the human realm and experiences happiness together with other human beings; there, one further performs various meritorious formations and so forth. This is called "with ignorance as a condition, one performs meritorious formations."

There are those who do not fix their minds on seeking human happiness, but rather, because their minds are obscured and moved by ignorance, they perform the three kinds of sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind.
These three kinds of sublime conduct are called meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is reborn in the human realm; there, one further performs various meritorious formations and so forth. This is called "with ignorance as a condition, meritorious formations are produced."

As it has been explained regarding the human realm, so too should one understand it for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmanarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Furthermore, there is another class who fix their minds on the desire for rebirth among the Brahmakāyika devas, thinking:
"May I be born into the homogeneous class of the Brahmakāyika devas."

Thereupon, seeking this goal, he diligently applied himself to practice; free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained investigation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he dwelt having attained the first dhyāna.
Within this meditative concentration, the various forms of bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and purity of livelihood are called meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is reborn among the fellowship of the Brahmakāyika devas; there, one further performs various meritorious formations and so forth. This is called "meritorious formations conditioned by ignorance."

There are those who do not fix their minds on the desire for rebirth there, but solely because their minds are obscured and agitated by ignorance, they diligently cultivate the preparatory application (*prayoga*); free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and possessing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, they dwell fully established in the first dhyāna.
Within this meditative concentration, the various forms of bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and purity of livelihood are called meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn among the class of beings of the Brahmakāyika devas; there, one further creates various meritorious formations and so forth. This is what is meant by "with ignorance as a condition, meritorious formations are produced."

As it was said regarding the Brahmakāyika gods, so it should be explained in detail for the Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, and Bṛhatphala gods, according to what is appropriate for each.
Furthermore, there is another class who fix their minds upon the Heaven of Non-conception and long for it, thinking:
"May I be born among the beings of the Heaven of Non-conception."

"Therefore, seeking this goal, he diligently applies himself to the practice, contemplating that all perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are coarse, painful, and obstructive, while contemplating that the absence of perception (*asaṃjñā*) is peaceful, sublime, and liberating.
Through this contemplation, he is able to extinguish all perceptions and abide in the state of non-perception."
When those various perceptions have ceased and one dwells in the state of non-perception, it is called the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
At the time of entering this attainment, the restraint of body, the restraint of speech, and the purity of livelihood are termed meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one is reborn among the gods of the realm of non-perception (asaṃjñisattva-deva). Therein, one is also able to perform minor meritorious actions; this is called "meritorious formations conditioned by ignorance."

There are those who do not fix their minds on the desire for rebirth there, but solely because their minds are obscured and agitated by ignorance, they diligently practice preparatory application (*prayoga*), contemplating that all perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are coarse, painful, and obstructive, and contemplating that the absence of perception (*asaṃjñika*) is peaceful, sublime, and a state of liberation.
Through this reflection, one is able to extinguish all perceptions and abide in non-perception (*asaṃjñā*).
When those perceptions have been extinguished and one dwells in non-perception, it is called the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
At the time of entering this attainment, the restraint of body, the restraint of speech, and the purity of livelihood are termed "meritorious formations" (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one is born into the homogeneous class of the Heaven of Non-conception; there too, one is able to perform a small amount of meritorious action. This is called "meritorious formations conditioned by ignorance."
How is it that with ignorance as a condition one performs immovable karma?
It refers to a certain class of beings who fix their minds upon and long for rebirth among the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space, thinking to themselves:
"May I be born into the common lot of the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space."

"Therefore, seeking this goal, he diligently applies himself to the practice; transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and no longer attending to perceptions of diversity, he enters and dwells, having fully attained the sphere of infinite space."

Within this meditative concentration, all volitions (*cetanā*), equal volitions, present volitions, past volitions, future volitions, the nature of volition, the category of volition, and the mental and vocal karma created by the mind are called immovable formations (*āneñjya-saṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one is reborn among the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana). There, one further creates immovable karma (āneñjya-saṃskāra); this is called "conditioned by ignorance, one creates immovable karma."

There are those who do not fix their minds on the desire for rebirth there, but through the agitation of a mind obscured by ignorance, they diligently cultivate the preparatory application; transcending all perceptions of form and extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, they no longer attend to perceptions of diversity and enter the sphere of infinite space, abiding fully perfected in the sphere of infinite space.

Within this meditative absorption, all volitions (*cetanā*), equal volitions, manifest volitions, past volitions, future volitions, the nature of volition, the category of volition, and the mental karma that constructs the mind—these are called "unshakable formations" (*āneñjya-saṃskāra*).

By reason of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is reborn among the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space; there, one further creates immovable karma. This is called "conditioned by ignorance, one creates immovable karma."
As it has been explained regarding the sphere of infinite space, so too should one understand the spheres of infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Thus, because these formations have ignorance as their condition, ignorance as their support, and ignorance as their foundation, they arise, co-arise, are produced, co-produced, accumulate, and manifest; therefore, they are called "formations conditioned by ignorance."
What is consciousness conditioned by formations?

It refers to a certain class of beings who, due to volition arising together with greed, hatred, and delusion as a condition, give rise to various forms of consciousness arising together with greed, hatred, and delusion; this is called consciousness conditioned by formations.

Furthermore, there is another class [of beings] for whom, conditioned by volition (cetanā) arising together with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, there arise various consciousnesses (vijñāna) arising together with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; this is called "conditioned by formations, consciousness arises" (saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam).

Furthermore, with the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises. In this context, the eye is an internal conditioned formation (*saṃskāra*), and forms are the external condition that gives rise to eye-consciousness; this is called "conditioned by formations is consciousness" (*saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam*).

...up to the point where the mind and mental objects serve as conditions for the arising of mind-consciousness: herein, the mind is the internal conditioned formation, and mental objects are the external condition for the arising of mind-consciousness; this is called "formations as the condition for consciousness."
Furthermore, in the *Kumbhopama-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke thus:
"Having performed meritorious, non-meritorious, or immovable karmic formations, there arises a consciousness that follows after the meritorious, non-meritorious, or immovable [formations]."
What is the consciousness that follows the performance of non-meritorious action?
It refers to a certain class of persons who, because their minds are bound by the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion, perform the three types of unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
These three types of unwholesome conduct are called non-meritorious formations (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, when the body breaks up at the end of life, one falls into hell; there, consciousness arises, which is called "having created non-meritorious formations, there is subsequently non-meritorious consciousness."
As it has been explained regarding the hells, one should know that the same applies to the animal realm and the realm of hungry ghosts.
What is the consciousness accompanied by merit for one who has performed meritorious actions?
It refers to a certain class of beings who fix their minds upon and long for the pleasures of the human realm, and they form this thought:
"May I be born into the human realm with a similar lot, and experience happiness together with all other human beings.
Driven by this aspiration, one performs sublime deeds of body, speech, and mind that are capable of producing rebirth in the human realm.
These three types of sublime conduct are called meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, when the body breaks up at the end of life, one is reborn in the human realm; there, consciousness arises. This is called having a meritorious consciousness that follows upon the performance of meritorious formations.

There are those who do not fix their minds on seeking human happiness, yet, solely due to the agitation of the mind obscured by ignorance, they perform the three kinds of sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind.
These three types of sublime conduct are called meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one is reborn in the human realm; there, consciousness arises. This is called "having performed meritorious formations, there is subsequently meritorious consciousness."
As it has been explained regarding the human realm, one should know that the same applies to the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven.
Furthermore, there is a class of beings who fix their minds on the Brahmakāyika heaven with longing, and they form this thought:
"May I be reborn among the members of the Brahmakāyika host."

Therefore, seeking this goal, he diligently applied himself to practice; free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained investigation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he dwelt having fully attained the first dhyāna.
Within this meditative concentration, the restraint of body, the restraint of speech, and purity of livelihood are called meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is reborn among the fellowship of the Brahmakāyika devas; the consciousness that arises therein is called "having performed meritorious formations, there is consciousness accompanied by merit."

There are those who do not fix their minds on the desire for rebirth there, but who, solely due to the agitation of a mind shrouded by ignorance, diligently cultivate preparatory application—from the abandonment of sensual desires, unwholesome states, and evil dharmas, up to the purification of livelihood—this is called meritorious action (puṇyābhisaṃskāra).

By reason of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is reborn among the fellowship of the Brahmakāyika devas; there, consciousness arises—this is called "having performed meritorious formations, there is subsequently meritorious consciousness."
As it has been stated regarding the Brahmakāyika devas, so too should it be understood for the Brahmapurohita devas up to the Asaṃjñisattva devas.
What is the formation of immovable karma, and how does there subsequently arise immovable consciousness?
This refers to a certain class of persons who fix their minds on the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space with longing, thinking:
"May I be reborn among the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space, within their common lot."

Thereupon, seeking with joyful aspiration and diligently applying effort, he transcends all perceptions of form, extinguishes perceptions of sensory resistance, and no longer attends to perceptions of diversity; he enters the sphere of infinite space and dwells fully established therein.

Within this meditative absorption, all volitions (*cetanā*), equal volitions, manifest volitions, past volitions, future volitions, the nature of volition, the category of volition, and the mental karma of intention—these are called immovable formations (*āneñjya-saṃskāra*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn among the devas of the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana). Therein, consciousness arises; this is called having performed non-fluctuating karma (āniñjya-karma) and subsequently possessing non-fluctuating consciousness.

There are those who do not fix their minds on the desire for rebirth there, but who, solely due to a mind obscured and stirred by ignorance, diligently cultivate preparatory application (*prayoga*)—transcending all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) and even performing mental volitional actions (*manasaḥ saṃskārāḥ*)—which is called "unshakable action" (*āneñjya-karma*).

By reason of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is reborn among the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space; there, consciousness arises. This is called having performed immovable karma and subsequently possessing immovable consciousness.
As it has been said regarding the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space, so it should be understood for all others up to the gods of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.

Thus, because these various consciousnesses have formations as their condition, formations as their support, and formations as their basis, they arise, co-arise, are produced, co-produced, assemble, and manifest; therefore, it is called "consciousness conditioned by formations."
What is "consciousness conditions name-and-form"?

It refers to a certain class of beings for whom consciousness arising together with greed, hatred, and delusion serves as a condition; consequently, they give rise to bodily and vocal actions arising together with greed, hatred, and delusion, which are termed "form.
Furthermore, the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced by those very actions are termed "name. This is what is meant by "consciousness conditions name-and-form."

Furthermore, there is another class [of beings] for whom, conditioned by consciousness arising together with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, there arise bodily and vocal actions arising together with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; these are called "form.
The feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness produced from those are called "name. This is what is meant by "consciousness conditions name-and-form."
Furthermore, in the *Nandika-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke thus:
"If Nandika’s beloved friends and relatives undergo change, decay, and separation, he will give rise to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress."
Because this consciousness co-arising with sorrow serves as a condition, bodily and vocal actions co-arising with sorrow arise; these are called "form" (rūpa).

Furthermore, the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness produced by that [consciousness] are called "name" (nāma). This is what is meant by "conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form [arise]."
Furthermore, in the *Upāli-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke thus: "Upāli!
Because consciousness is a nutriment, future existence arises."
What is this consciousness? It is the final mind of the *gandharva*.

When the mind, mentation, and consciousness have increased and become firmly established, and have not been severed, fully understood, extinguished, or cast out, this consciousness immediately unites with the *kalala* body within the mother’s womb.
The integration of the kalala’s own substance is called "form" (rūpa);

the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced from that are called "name" (nāma). This is what is meant by "consciousness conditions name-and-form" (vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam).
Furthermore, in the *Sāṭyagopālaka-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke as follows:
"The three factors must come together for entry into the womb. What are these three? They are:

the father and mother come together and both give rise to a defiled mind; the mother is at that time in her fertile period; and a gandharva is present before them. When these three factors come together, there is entry into the womb."

In this context, the final mind, intellect, and consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the *gandharva* increase, become firm, and persist; they have not been severed, fully understood, extinguished, or cast out.
Immediately following this consciousness, it enters the mother’s womb. That which is thus entrusted to the womb is called "form" (*rūpa*);

the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) that arise from it are called "name" (*nāma*). This is what is meant by "consciousness conditions name-and-form" (*vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam*).
Furthermore, in the Mahānidāna-sūtra, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Does name-and-form have a condition?
The Buddha replied:
“There is a condition; this condition is consciousness.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If consciousness were not to enter the mother’s womb, would name-and-form be able to become the kalala?”
Ānanda said: “No, World-Honored One.”
“If consciousness were not to enter the mother’s womb, would name-and-form be able to arise in this realm? “No,
World-Honored One.”
“If consciousness were already severed and destroyed at the initial moment, would name-and-form be able to grow later on? “No,
World-Honored One.”
“If consciousness were entirely non-existent, could one designate it as ‘name-and-form’? “No,
World-Honored One.”
"Therefore, Ānanda! All name-and-form (nāmarūpa) have consciousness as their condition; this is called 'consciousness conditions name-and-form.

Because such name-and-form has consciousness as its condition, consciousness as its support, and consciousness as its foundation, they arise, co-arise, are produced, co-produced, accumulate, and manifest; therefore, it is called 'consciousness conditions name-and-form.'"
What is meant by "name-and-form conditions consciousness"?
It refers to the arising of eye-consciousness with the eye and forms as conditions.
Herein, the eye and forms are called "form" (rūpa).
The feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that arise from those [formative factors] are called "name" (nāma).

Within this context, attention and other such factors that are able to assist in the arising of visual consciousness are called "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form" (nāmarūpapratyaya-vijñāna).

Up to and including the case where mind and mental phenomena serve as conditions to give rise to mental consciousness: herein, whatever forms are cognized by those various mental consciousnesses are called "form" (rūpa);
and the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness produced therein are called "name" (nāma).
In this context, attention (*manasikāra*) and other factors that assist in the arising of mental consciousness are called "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form" (*nāmarūpapratyayaṃ vijñānam*).
Furthermore, in the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke as follows: "Upāli!..."
Because consciousness serves as nutriment, future existence arises.
What is this consciousness?
It is called the *gandharva*.
To speak at length, this continues until its integration with the kalala-body.
This integration with the kalala-body is called "form" (rūpa);
the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced from it are called "name" (nāma).

At that time, consciousness arising simultaneously with name-and-form (nāmarūpa) produced by improper attention (ayoniśomanasikāra), taking that as a condition, arises; this is called "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form.
Furthermore, in the *Sāti-sutta*, the Buddha said:
"The conjunction of three factors results in entry into the mother's womb," and so on at length, up to: "this consciousness enters the mother's womb immediately thereafter."
That which is entrusted to the womb is called "form" (rūpa);
the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced therein are called "name" (nāma).
At that time, name-and-form arising together with improper attention serves as the condition for consciousness arising together [with it]; this is called "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form."

Furthermore, there is another class of beings who, because their minds are bound by the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion, commit the three kinds of unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind.
Among these, the unwholesome conduct of body and speech is called "form" (rūpa);
the unwholesome conduct of mind is called "name" (nāma).

Due to these unwholesome actions, with name-and-form as condition, at the breaking up of the body after death, one falls into hell; there, consciousness arises—this is called "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form."
As it has been explained regarding the hells, one should know that the same applies to the animal realm and the realm of hungry ghosts.

Furthermore, there is a class of beings who fix their minds upon and long for the pleasures of the human realm; because of this longing, they perform wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind that are capable of producing rebirth in the human realm.
In this context, the excellent conduct of body and speech is called "form" (rūpa), and the excellent conduct of mind is called "name" (nāma).

With these excellent conducts—namely name and form—as conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is born into the human realm; there, consciousness arises. This is what is meant by "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form."

There are those who do not fix their minds on seeking human happiness, yet due solely to the agitation of the mind obscured by ignorance, they perform the three kinds of sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind.
Among these, the sublime conduct of body and speech is called "form" (rūpa);
the sublime conduct of mind is called "name" (nāman).

Due to this sublime conduct, with name-and-form as condition, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is born in the human realm; there, consciousness arises—this is called "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form."
As it has been explained regarding the human realm, so should it be understood for the gods from the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations.

Furthermore, there is another class of beings who fix their minds on the Heaven of the Brahma Assembly with longing; through this longing, they diligently practice the preparatory application, becoming detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, and thus fully abide in the first dhyāna.
Within this meditative concentration, the restraint of body, the restraint of speech, and purity of livelihood are called "form" (rūpa);
the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced therein are called "name" (nāma).

With this as a condition, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is reborn among the fellowship of the Brahmakāyika devas; there, consciousness arises—this is called "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form."

As it has been said regarding the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, and so forth up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it should be understood that the same applies accordingly to each case.
Furthermore, in the Mahānidāna Sūtra, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Do all consciousnesses have an object?"
The Buddha said:
"There is a condition; it is called name-and-form.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If name-and-form did not exist, would the various consciousnesses arise?
Ānanda replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
If there were no name-and-form as a basis, would the consciousness that undergoes birth, old age, and death in a future life arise? “No, it would not.”
“World-Honored One!
If name-and-form were entirely non-existent, could consciousnesses be established? “No.”
“World-Honored One!
[The Buddha replied: “Therefore, Ānanda!
All consciousnesses take name-and-form as their condition; this is called ‘name-and-form conditions consciousness.’”

Thus, because these various consciousnesses have name-and-form as their condition, name-and-form as their support, and name-and-form as their foundation, they arise, co-arise, are produced, co-produced, accumulate, and manifest; therefore, it is said that "consciousness has name-and-form as its condition."
What is meant by "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases"?
It refers to a certain class of beings who, oppressed by cold, long for warmth; because they obtain good warmth, there arise within their bodies the primary elements associated with warmth.
In this context, "warmth" and the primary elements co-arising with warmth are called "form" (*rūpa*);
the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced by those are called "name" (*nāma*).
Through this name-and-form, the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind all attain growth; this is called "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise."
One who is oppressed by heat and seeks coolness should be understood to be in the same situation.
Furthermore, there is another class of beings who, oppressed by hunger, seek food; because they obtain good food, the primary elements (mahābhūta) associated with eating arise within their bodies.
In this context, food and the primary elements co-arising with food are called "form" (*rūpa*);
the sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced by them are called "name" (*nāma*).
Because the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) grow by means of this name-and-form, it is said that "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise."
Furthermore, there is another class [of beings] who, oppressed by thirst, long for a drink; because they obtain a good drink, the great elements associated with drinking arise within their bodies.
In this context, both the drink and the great elements associated with it are called "form" (rūpa);
the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness produced thereby are called "name" (nāma).
From this, the six sense faculties grow within name-and-form; this is called "name-and-form as the condition for the six sense bases.

Furthermore, there is another class of beings who, oppressed by fatigue, seek rest, massage, or sleep; because their wishes are fulfilled, the primary elements associated with those [faculties] arise within the body.
In this context, things such as massage and the primary elements associated with them are called "form" (rūpa);
the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced by those are called "name" (nāma).
Due to this, the six sense bases arise with name-and-form as their predominant condition; this is called "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases.

Furthermore, there is another class of beings who, during the height of summer, being oppressed by heat and thirst, enter a cool pond and drink and bathe to their heart's content, whereby the primary elements (mahābhūta) associated with those [actions] arise within their bodies.
In this context, the clear, cool water and its corresponding primary elements (mahābhūta) are called "form" (rūpa);
the sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced by them are called "name" (nāma).
From this, the six sense bases develop through name-and-form; this is called "name-and-form as condition for the six sense bases.
Furthermore, in the *Upaniṣad-sūtra* (the *Kālāmasūtra*), the Buddha spoke thus: "Kālāma!"
Because consciousness serves as nutriment, future existence arises.
What is this consciousness?
It is the gandharva.
To speak at length, this continues until its integration with the physical substance of the kalala.
This integration with the physical substance of the kalala is called "form" (rūpa);
the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced from it are called "name" (nāma).

At that time, with name-and-form arising together with improper mental attention as condition, the six sense bases emerge within the mother's womb; this is called "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise."
Furthermore, in the *Sāṭyagāthā-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke as follows:
"The convergence of three factors leads to entry into the mother's womb," and so on at length, until: "this consciousness enters the mother's womb immediately thereafter."
That which is entrusted to the womb is called "form" (rūpa);
the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that arise from it are called "name" (nāma).

At that time, with name-and-form arising together with improper attention as a condition, the six sense bases emerge within the mother's womb; this is called "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases."

Furthermore, there is another class of beings who, because their minds are bound by the entanglements of greed, hatred, and delusion, commit three kinds of unwholesome conduct through body, speech, and mind.
Among these, unwholesome conduct of body and speech is called "form" (rūpa);
unwholesome conduct of mind is called "name" (nāman).

Conditioned by this unwholesome conduct consisting of name-and-form, at the breaking up of the body after death, one falls into hell where the six sense bases arise; this is called "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases."
As it has been said regarding the hells, so should it be understood for the animal realm and the realm of hungry ghosts.

Furthermore, there is a class of beings who fix their minds upon and long for the pleasures of the human realm; because of this longing, they perform wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind that can induce rebirth in the human realm.
In this context, the sublime conduct of body and speech is called "form" (rūpa), and the sublime conduct of mind is called "name" (nāma).

With these sublime conducts—namely name and form—as conditions, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one is born into the human realm and the six sense bases arise; this is called "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases."
As it was said regarding the human realm, so too should it be understood for the gods from the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations.

Furthermore, there is another class who fix their minds on the Brahma-pāriṣadya heaven with longing; through this longing, they diligently practice the preparatory application and, having become free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, dwell fully established in the first dhyāna.
Within this meditative concentration, the restraint of body, the restraint of speech, and purity of livelihood are called "form" (rūpa);
the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced therein are called "name" (nāma).

With this as a condition, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is born into the common lot of the Brahmakāyika devas, where the six sense faculties arise; this is called "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases."

As it has been said regarding the Brahmakāyika devas, so it should be understood for the Brahmapurohita devas up to the devas of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, according to what is appropriate.
This is called "name-and-form as the condition for the six sense bases."

Thus, because these six sense bases arise with name-and-form as their condition, with name-and-form as their support, and with name-and-form as their foundation—arising together, arising in succession, being produced, and appearing through accumulation—they are said to be "the six sense bases conditioned by name-and-form."

Volume Eleven. The Abhidharma Dharmaskandha-pāda Śāstra,
composed by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Volume Twelve.
