The Remainder of Chapter Twenty-one, "Dependent Origination" (Pratītyasamutpāda): What is meant by "conditioned by name-and-form is contact"?
It refers to the arising of visual consciousness conditioned by the eye and visible forms; through the conjunction of these three, contact arises.
In this context, the eye and forms are called "form" (rūpa);
the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced by them are called "name" (nāma).
Thus, with name-and-form as condition, eye-contact arises; this is what is meant by "contact conditioned by name-and-form."
Up to the point where, with the mind and mental objects as conditions, mind-consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact arises.
Within this, whatever form is cognized by the various mind-consciousnesses is called "form" (rūpa);
the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness produced therefrom are called "name" (nāma).
In this way, with name-and-form as condition, mental contact arises; this is called "with name-and-form as condition, there is contact.
Furthermore, in the *Sāleyyaka Sutta*, the Buddha spoke thus: "Sāleyyaka!..."
Because consciousness serves as nutriment, future birth arises.
What is this consciousness?
It is the gandharva.
To speak extensively, this continues until its integration with the physical substance of the *kalala*.
This integration with the physical substance of the *kalala* is called "form" (*rūpa*);
the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness produced therefrom are called "name" (*nāma*).

At that time, with name-and-form arising together with improper mental attention as a condition, various contacts are produced within the mother’s womb; this is called "contact conditioned by name-and-form.
Furthermore, in the *Sāti-sutta*, the Buddha spoke thus:
"The convergence of three factors results in entry into the mother’s womb," and so on at length, until: "this consciousness enters the mother’s womb immediately thereafter."
That which is entrusted to the womb is called "form" (rūpa);
the sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that arise from it are called "name" (nāma).

At that time, with name-and-form arising together with improper attention as a condition, the various contacts are produced within the mother’s womb; this is called "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases."
Furthermore, there is another class of beings who, because their minds are bound by the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion, commit the three types of unwholesome conduct of body,
speech, and mind. Among these, the unwholesome conduct of body and speech is called "form" (rūpa),
while the unwholesome conduct of mind is called "name" (nāma).

Due to these unwholesome actions, with name-and-form as condition, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one falls into hell where various contacts arise; this is called "contact conditioned by name-and-form.
As it is said regarding hell, so should it be understood for the animal realm and the realm of hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, there is another class of persons who fix their minds upon and long for the pleasures of the human realm;
because of this longing, they perform excellent deeds of body, speech, and mind that lead to rebirth in the human realm.
In this context, the sublime conduct of body and speech is called "form" (rūpa), and the sublime conduct of mind is called "name" (nāma).

With these sublime conducts—namely name and form—as conditions, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one is born in the human realm where various contacts arise; this is called "contact conditioned by name-and-form."
As it was said regarding the human realm, one should know that it is the same for the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven.

Furthermore, there is another class who fix their minds on the Brahmakāyika heaven with longing; through this longing, they diligently practice the preparatory application and, having abandoned sensual desires and unwholesome states, dwell fully established in the first dhyāna.
Within this meditative concentration, the restraint of body, the restraint of speech, and purity of livelihood are called "form" (rūpa);
the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness arising from those are called "name" (nāma).

With this as a condition, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one is reborn among the fellowship of the Brahmakāyika devas, where various contacts arise; this is called "contact conditioned by name-and-form.
As it has been stated regarding the Brahmakāyika devas, so it should be understood accordingly for the Brahmapurohita devas up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana devas.
Furthermore, in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Do all contacts have a condition?
The Buddha replied:
“There is a condition; this is called name-and-form (nāmarūpa).

To speak at length, up until: ‘If one relies upon this characteristic (nimitta) to designate the group of names (nāmakāya), if this characteristic were non-existent, could contact associated with designation (adhivacanasaṃsparśa) be designated?’”
“No, World-Honored One!
If one were to designate a physical body based on this characteristic.”
"If this characteristic were unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), could it be established that there is contact with resistance (sapratigha-sparśa)? "No,
World-Honored One."
“If name-and-form and the body were entirely non-existent, could there be the designation of various contacts? “No,
World-Honored One.”
"Therefore, Ānanda! All contacts have name-and-form as their condition; this is called 'contact conditioned by name-and-form.

Because these various contacts have name-and-form as their condition, name-and-form as their support, and name-and-form as their foundation, they arise, co-arise, are produced, co-produced, assemble, and appear; therefore, it is called 'contact conditioned by name-and-form.'"
What is contact conditioned by the six sense bases?

It refers to the arising of eye-consciousness conditioned by the eye and visible forms; through the conjunction of these three, contact arises. This continues up to the arising of mind-consciousness conditioned by the mind and mental phenomena; through the conjunction of these three, contact arises. This is called contact conditioned by the six sense bases.
Furthermore, with the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; through the conjunction of these three, contact arises.
In this process, the eye serves as the internal condition and visible forms serve as the external condition for the arising of visual contact.

...up to the point where, with the mind and mental objects as conditions, mind-consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact arises. In this context, the mind serves as the internal condition and mental objects serve as the external condition for the arising of mental contact.
This is called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases.
Furthermore, with the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact arises.

In this context, eye-contact has the eye, visible forms, and visual consciousness as its conditions. This continues up to: with the mind and mental phenomena as conditions, mental consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact arises.
In this context, mental contact has the mind, mental objects, and the mental consciousness as its conditions; this is called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases.
Furthermore, with the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; through the conjunction of these three, contact arises.
In this context, the eye, forms, and visual consciousness are not themselves contact; rather, contact arises through the conjunction of these three.
This continues up to the mental faculty and mental objects, which serve as conditions for the arising of mental consciousness; through the conjunction of these three, contact arises.
In this context, the mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness are not themselves contact; rather, contact arises through the conjunction of these three.
This is called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases.

Because these various contacts arise with the six sense bases as their condition, the six sense bases as their support, and the six sense bases as their foundation—arising, co-arising, being produced, co-produced, gathering, and appearing—they are therefore called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases."
What is feeling conditioned by contact?
It means that with the eye and forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact arises, and with contact as condition, feeling arises.

This continues up to: with the mind and mental phenomena as conditions, mental consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact arises, and with contact as condition, feeling arises.

This is called "feeling conditioned by contact. Furthermore, with the eye and forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; through the coming together of these three, contact arises—be it conducive to pleasant feeling, conducive to painful feeling, or conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. With contact conducive to pleasant feeling as condition, pleasant feeling arises; with contact conducive to painful feeling as condition, painful feeling arises; and with contact conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as condition, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.

Up to and including the case where the mind and mental phenomena serve as conditions for the arising of mental consciousness: through the conjunction of these three, contact arises—whether it be conducive to pleasant feeling, conducive to painful feeling, or conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. With contact conducive to pleasant feeling as a condition, pleasant feeling arises; with contact conducive to painful feeling as a condition, painful feeling arises; with contact conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as a condition, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. This is called "conditioned by contact, feeling arises."
Furthermore, as stated in the sūtra, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the householder Ghoṣila, saying:

"The eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element each have distinct intrinsic natures. With two of those conducive to pleasant feeling as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; through the conjunction of these three, contact arises, which is called 'contact conducive to pleasant feeling. With this contact conducive to pleasant feeling as a condition, pleasant feeling arises."

Conditioned by two factors that are conducive to painful feeling, eye-consciousness arises; through the conjunction of these three, contact arises, which is called "contact conducive to painful feeling. Conditioned by this contact conducive to painful feeling, painful feeling arises.

Conditioned by two factors that are conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, eye-consciousness arises; through the conjunction of these three, contact arises, which is called "contact conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Conditioned by this contact conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
The same detailed explanation applies to the remaining five [bases] within the three realms; this is called "feeling conditioned by contact.
Furthermore, in the *Mahānidāna Sūtra*, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Do all feelings have a condition?"
The Buddha said:
“There is a condition; this condition is contact (*sparśa*).
To speak at length: if there were no eye-contact, would there arise, conditioned by eye-contact, internal feelings of pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain?”
"No, World-Honored One! ...
Furthermore, if there were no mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), could there arise, conditioned by that mental contact, internal feelings of pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure?"
"No, World-Honored One.
If there were no contact at all, could any feelings be established?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Therefore, Ānanda!"
"There is no feeling whatsoever that does not have contact as its condition; this is called 'feeling conditioned by contact.

Thus, because these various feelings have contact as their condition, contact as their support, and contact as their foundation, they arise and co-arise, are produced and co-produced, and emerge through accumulation; therefore, they are called "feelings conditioned by contact."
What is craving conditioned by feeling?

It means that with the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; and with feeling as condition, craving arises.

...up to the point where, with the mind and mental objects as conditions, mind-consciousness arises; from the coming together of these three, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; and with feeling as condition, craving arises.
This is called "feeling as condition for craving.
Furthermore, because the tasting of feeling through the eye serves as a condition, one repeatedly dwells in conformity with the eye.
Due to this conformity, one repeatedly gives rise to lust, intense lust, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate craving toward the eye.
Furthermore, because feeling conditioned by mental objects serves as a condition, one repeatedly dwells in conformity with the mind.
Due to this conformity, one repeatedly gives rise to greed, intense greed, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate craving toward the mind.
This is called "craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, in the *Upādānaskandha-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke thus:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that I have thoroughly investigated the gratification in form (*rūpa-rasa*)."
Regarding those who have already experienced attachment to form or are currently experiencing attachment to it, I have clearly seen and clearly known this through right wisdom:
because they take the sensation of attachment to form as a condition, they repeatedly dwell in conformity with that form.
Because of such conformity, one repeatedly gives rise to desire, intense desire, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate craving for form;
and so on, up to my thorough investigation of the gratification in consciousness.
Regarding those who have already experienced the gratification of consciousness, or who are now experiencing its gratification, I have clearly seen and clearly known this through right wisdom:
because they take the gratification of consciousness as a condition for feeling, they repeatedly dwell in conformity with consciousness.

Because it conforms [to craving], one repeatedly gives rise to desire, intense desire, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate defilement toward consciousness; this is called "craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, in the *Upādānaskandha-sūtra*, the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that if there were no gratification whatsoever in form, sentient beings would not give rise to passion for form."
Because there is not a total absence of gratification within forms, sentient beings give rise to defilement toward them.
Taking that gratification in forms as a condition for feeling, they repeatedly dwell in accordance with those forms.
Because they conform [to it], beings repeatedly give rise to desire, intense desire, grasping, hoarding, protection, firm attachment, and passionate defilement toward form.
Furthermore, if there were no flavor whatsoever within consciousness, sentient beings would not become defiled by consciousness.
Because there is not a total absence of gratification within the various consciousnesses, sentient beings give rise to defilement toward them.
Taking the experience of the gratification of consciousness as a condition, they repeatedly dwell in conformity with consciousness.
Because of compliance with it, there arises greed and further greed; one clings to it, guards it, and is firmly attached with craving and defilement—this is called "craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, in the *Ṣaḍāyatana-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke thus:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that I have already thoroughly investigated the gratification of the eye."
Regarding those who have already experienced attachment toward the eye, or who are currently experiencing it, I clearly see and clearly know this with right wisdom:
because they take the feeling of attachment toward the eye as a condition, they repeatedly dwell in conformity with the eye.
Due to such conformity, one repeatedly gives rise to desire, intense desire, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate craving toward the eye;
even unto the point where one has thoroughly investigated and reflected upon the meaning of "self."
Regarding those who have already experienced attachment toward the mind or are currently experiencing attachment toward it, I have clearly seen and clearly known this through right wisdom:
because they take the experience of mental attachment as a condition, they repeatedly dwell in conformity with the mind.

Because it conforms [to craving], one repeatedly gives rise within the mind to greed, further greed, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate defilement; this is called "craving conditioned by sensation.
Furthermore, in the *Ṣaḍāyatana-sūtra*, the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that if there were no flavor at all in the eye, sentient beings would not give rise to passion for the eye."
Because there is not a total absence of flavor within the various eyes, sentient beings give rise to defilement toward the eye.
Taking the experience of that flavor as a condition, they repeatedly dwell in conformity with the eye.
Because they conform to it, one repeatedly gives rise to desire, intense desire, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate craving toward the eye.
This applies even to the mind: if there were no gratification within the mind, sentient beings would not give rise to passion for it.
Because there is not a total absence of gratification within the mental objects, sentient beings experience gratification in the mind.
Taking that feeling of gratification as a condition, they repeatedly dwell in conformity with the mind.

Because of this conformity, one repeatedly gives rise to desire, intense desire, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate craving toward the mind; this is called "craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, in the *Ṣaḍāyatana-sūtra*, the Blessed One further said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that I have already thoroughly investigated the gratification in form (*rūpa-rasa*)."
Regarding those who have already experienced attachment to form, or are now experiencing attachment to it, I have clearly seen and clearly known this with right wisdom:
because they take the experience of the gratification of form as a condition, they repeatedly dwell in conformity with that form.
Because of such conformity, one repeatedly gives rise to desire, intense desire, grasping, hoarding, protection, firm attachment, and passionate craving toward form;
even unto the point that I have thoroughly investigated the flavor of phenomena.
Regarding those who have already experienced the gratification of phenomena, or who are now experiencing it, I have clearly seen and clearly known this through right wisdom.
Because they take the experience of the gratification of phenomena as a condition, they repeatedly dwell in conformity with those phenomena.

Because it conforms [to craving], one repeatedly gives rise to desire, intense desire, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate defilement toward phenomena; this is called "craving conditioned by sensation.
Furthermore, in the *Ṣaḍāyatana-sūtra*, the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that if there were no gratification whatsoever in forms, sentient beings would not give rise to passion for forms."
Because there is not a total absence of gratification within forms, sentient beings give rise to attachment toward them.
Taking that gratification in forms as a condition for feeling, they repeatedly dwell in accordance with those forms.
Because they conform to it, beings repeatedly give rise to desire and intense desire for form, grasping at it, guarding it, clinging to it firmly, and becoming stained by craving.
Even if there were no flavor whatsoever in all phenomena, sentient beings would not give rise to defilement toward those phenomena.
Because there is not a total absence of flavor within all phenomena, sentient beings give rise to attachment toward them.
Taking that experience of the flavor of phenomena as a condition, they repeatedly abide in accordance with those phenomena.

Because it conforms [to craving], one repeatedly gives rise to desire, intense desire, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate defilement toward phenomena; this is called "craving conditioned by sensation.
Furthermore, the Buddha said to Mahānāman the Licchavi:

"Mahānāman, you should know that if form were exclusively suffering and not pleasure, if it were not accompanied by pleasure and not enveloped or clung to by pleasant and joyful feelings, then no sentient being would, for the sake of seeking pleasure, give rise to desire, give rise to defilement, or be bound by afflictions regarding forms."
"O Great Name!

Because form is not exclusively suffering—it is also pleasure, accompanied by pleasure, and entangled with the feelings of pleasure and joy—sentient beings, seeking pleasure, give rise to greed and defilement toward all forms, becoming bound by the fetters of affliction."
Because he takes the experience of the gratification of form as a condition, he repeatedly dwells in conformity with form.
Due to this conformity, he repeatedly gives rise to lust, intense lust, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate craving for form.

Furthermore, if consciousness were exclusively suffering and not pleasure—neither accompanied by pleasure nor bound by the experience of joy and pleasure—then no sentient being would, for the sake of seeking pleasure, give rise to greed, defilement, or the fetters of affliction toward various forms.
"Great Name!

Since consciousness is not exclusively suffering—it is also pleasure, accompanied by pleasure, and enveloped and clung to by pleasant and joyful sensations—therefore, sentient beings, in their quest for pleasure, give rise to craving and defilement toward all forms of consciousness, becoming bound by afflictions."
Because he takes the experience of the flavor of consciousness as a condition, he repeatedly dwells in conformity with consciousness.

Due to this conformity, he repeatedly gives rise to desire, intense desire, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate craving toward consciousness; this is called "craving conditioned by feeling."
Furthermore, in the *Pūrṇamāsa-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke thus:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that because form serves as a condition, pleasure arises and joy is born; this is called the gratification of form (*rūpa-āsvāda*)."
Because he takes the gratification in form as a condition for feeling, he repeatedly dwells in conformity with form.
Due to this conformity, he repeatedly gives rise to desire, intense desire, grasping, hoarding, guarding, firm attachment, and passionate craving toward form.
Up to and including the fact that, with consciousness as a condition, pleasure arises and joy is born—this is called the gratification of consciousness.
Through this gratification of consciousness, and with feeling as a condition, they repeatedly dwell in conformity with consciousness.
Because of compliance, there arises craving and further craving; one grasps, guards, clings firmly, and becomes stained by passion—this is called "craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda: "With craving as condition, there is seeking; with seeking as condition, there is acquisition;

with acquisition as condition, there is accumulation; with accumulation as condition, there is attachment; with attachment as condition, there is greed; with greed as condition, there is stinginess; with stinginess as condition, there is appropriation; with appropriation as condition, there is guarding. Because of guarding, one takes up weapons and staves, engages in fighting, litigation, and contention, and through deceit, fraud, and falsehood, gives rise to immeasurable kinds of evil and unwholesome dharmas."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Wielding weapons, engaging in strife, litigation, and competition, as well as practicing flattery, deceit, and falsehood—these give rise to immeasurable kinds of evil and unwholesome dharmas; all are caused by guarding and protecting."
"With guarding as a condition, such a thing exists.
If there were no guarding, would this thing exist?
Ānanda replied:
“No, World-Honored One. “Therefore,

the taking up of weapons such as swords and staves arises with protection as its preliminary condition (*nidāna*), protection as its cause (*hetu*), protection as its origin (*samudaya*), and protection as its condition (*pratyaya*).”
Such guarding arises because of embracing;
with embracing as a condition, there is guarding.
If embracing were absent, would there be guarding?
"No, World-Honored One. "Therefore,
guarding [the senses] arises with grasping as its preliminary condition, grasping as its cause, grasping as its origin, and grasping as its condition."
To speak at length, all such forms of seeking arise from craving; because craving serves as a condition, there is seeking.
If this craving were absent, would there still be seeking?
"No, World-Honored One! Therefore,
all forms of seeking have craving as their starting point, craving as their cause, craving as their origin, and craving as their condition for their arising."
Ānanda, you should know that craving is of two kinds:
first, craving for sensory pleasure;
second, craving for existence.
These two kinds of craving exist in dependence upon feeling (*vedanā*).
If feeling were absent, these two kinds of craving would also not exist; this is called "craving conditioned by feeling.

Thus, because all these cravings have feeling as their condition, feeling as their support, and feeling as their foundation, they arise and co-arise, are produced and co-produced, and manifest through accumulation; therefore, it is said that "craving is conditioned by feeling."
What is grasping conditioned by craving?
That which first arises is called craving;
when craving reaches a state of intensification, it is further termed grasping.
How is this so? It is as follows:
suppose there is someone who, focusing their mind on various objects of desire, gives rise to the entanglement of sensual craving.
From that entanglement, they further give rise to other entanglements; these become increasingly superior, more intense, and more fully developed.
The fetters that arise first are called craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
those that arise subsequently are termed grasping (*upādāna*). This is what is meant by "craving is the condition for grasping.

Furthermore, suppose there is someone who, with respect to various objects of form or formless objects, binds the mind in observation and gives rise to the fetter of craving for form or the fetter of craving for the formless.
From this entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), further entanglements arise; they become increasingly predominant, increasingly intense, and increasingly complete.
The entanglement that arose previously is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*);
the entanglement that arises subsequently is termed "clinging" (*upādāna*). This is what is meant by "with craving as condition, clinging arises."
Furthermore, in the *Khāṇu-khaṇḍa Sūtra*, the Buddha spoke thus:

"I shall proclaim for you, the assembly of bhikṣus, the essential Dharma for the discernment of the aggregates, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path."

When this essential Dharma for the discernment of the aggregates is thus proclaimed, there are certain individuals possessed of delusion who do not abide in intense faith, affection, and reverence toward what I have taught; they will be slow to realize the unsurpassed exhaustion of the outflows.

Furthermore, there is another class of individuals who possess wisdom; they are able to abide in intense faith, affection, and reverence toward what I have taught, and they swiftly realize the unsurpassed exhaustion of the outflows.

Furthermore, there is another class [of persons] who, regarding the phenomena of the aggregate of form taught by me, observe "I" therein. As for this act of observation, what serves as its condition, what serves as its origin, what is its nature, and from what does it arise?

This means that feeling born of contact associated with ignorance serves as the condition for craving; the formations produced thereby have that [feeling] as their condition, take it as their origin, are of its same nature, and arise from it.
This craving that is capable of arising—what serves as its condition, what serves as its origin, what is its category, and from what does it arise?

It is said: regarding all feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance, this craving that arises from them has feeling as its condition, has feeling as its origin, belongs to the category of feeling, and arises from feeling.
This feeling that is produced—of what is it the condition, by what is it accumulated, of what nature is it, and from what does it arise?
It is from contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*).
This feeling that has arisen has contact as its condition, contact as its origin, belongs to the category of contact, and is born from contact.
What is the condition for this contact that gives rise to it? What is its origin? To what does it belong? From what is it born?
This refers to the six sense bases.
The contact produced from these has the six sense bases as its condition, the six sense bases as its origin, belongs to the category of the six sense bases, and arises from the six sense bases.
Thus, these six sense bases are impermanent, conditioned, produced, and arisen from a multitude of causes.
Likewise, contact, feeling, craving, and the formations that lead to rebirth are also impermanent, conditioned, produced, and arisen from a multitude of causes.
For those who thus contemplate form as the self, this is the manifestation of the fetter of the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
From that fetter, further fetters arise, becoming increasingly dominant, increasingly intense, and increasingly complete.
The fetters that arise first are called craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
the fetters that arise subsequently are termed grasping (*upādāna*). This is what is meant by "craving is the condition for grasping.
There are those who do not contemplate the self in relation to form and so forth, yet still contemplate the self; there are various forms of existence (*bhava*) that are not equal.
Contemplating the self, there are those who, while correctly contemplating that "form is mine," do not correctly contemplate that "I am in form";

there are those who, while not correctly contemplating that "I am in form," correctly contemplate that "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are mine"; and there are those who do not correctly contemplate [feeling].
There is one who regards perception, formations, and consciousness as self and accordingly contemplates, "I have feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness";

there is one who does not accordingly contemplate that he has feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, but accordingly contemplates that perception, formations, and consciousness are "mine";

and there is one who does not accordingly contemplate that perception, formations, and consciousness are "mine," but accordingly contemplates, "I am in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness."
Within consciousness, there is one who does not observe with equanimity, giving rise to doubt regarding "I am in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness";
there is one who does not give rise to doubt but gives rise to the view of existence or the view of non-existence;
and there is one who does not give rise to the view of existence or non-existence yet does not abandon the conceit "I am."
Therefore, based on the equal and successive contemplation of "I" and "mine," the conceit of "I am" arises.
With respect to this conduct of conceit, what serves as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), what serves as its origin (*samudaya*), what is its nature (*jāti*), and from what does it arise?
That is to say, with the various feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance as a condition, craving arises.
These formations that are thus produced have that [craving] as their condition, take that as their origin, belong to its category, and arise from it.
To speak at length, up to these six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), they are impermanent, conditioned, produced through volitional effort, and arisen from a multitude of causes and conditions.

Likewise, contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) are also impermanent, conditioned, produced through volitional effort, and arisen from a multitude of causes and conditions.
Such is this conceit, which is a conceit-entanglement arising from the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
From that entanglement, further entanglements arise, becoming increasingly dominant, increasingly intense, and increasingly complete.
The fetters that arise first are called craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
those that arise subsequently are termed grasping (*upādāna*). This is what is meant by "craving conditions grasping.
Furthermore, there are those who hold the view that the world is eternal, or impermanent, or both eternal and impermanent, or neither eternal nor impermanent.
They cling to the world as being finite, or infinite, or both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite.
They cling to the vital principle (*jīva*) as being identical to the body, or they cling to the vital principle as being distinct from the body.
To grasp that the Tathāgata exists after death, or does not exist, or both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist—
all these are fetters arising from the currently manifest view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
From that entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), further entanglements arise; they become increasingly dominant, increasingly intense, and increasingly perfected.
The entanglement that arose previously is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*);
the entanglement that arises subsequently is termed "clinging" (*upādāna*). This is what is meant by "with craving as condition, clinging arises."
Furthermore, there are those who hold that the Blessed One is not a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, and so forth, up to not being a Teacher of Gods and Humans;
and who hold that the Buddha’s True Dharma is not well-expounded, not visible here and now, and so forth, up to not being personally realized by the wise within.
They hold that the disciples of the Buddha do not possess complete sublime conduct, up to and including not practicing in accordance with the Dharma;
or they hold that there is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path;
or they hold that there is no impermanence in all conditioned phenomena, no selflessness in all dharmas, and no tranquility in nirvāṇa.
All these are fetters currently arising from false views.
From these fetters, further fetters arise; they become increasingly predominant, increasingly intense, and increasingly complete.
The fetters that arise first are called craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
those that arise subsequently are termed grasping (*upādāna*). This is what is meant by "craving conditions grasping.
Furthermore, there are those who cling to the view that the world is eternal, asserting that this alone is real while all else is delusion and error.
Or that it is impermanent, up to the view that after the Tathāgata’s death he neither exists nor does not exist— these are all truly delusions and errors,
and are the fetters currently arising from the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
From those fetters (*paryavasthāna*), he further gives rise to other fetters; they become increasingly superior, increasingly intense, and increasingly complete.
The fetters previously arisen are called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*);
the fetters subsequently arisen are termed "clinging" (*upādāna*). This is what is meant by "with craving as condition, clinging arises."

Furthermore, there are those who give rise to adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), or give rise to adherence to ascetic vows (*vrataparāmarśa*), or give rise to adherence to both rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), thinking: "These rules, these vows, or these rules and vows, can purify, can liberate, can lead to deliverance, and can transcend suffering and pleasure to reach the state beyond suffering and pleasure."
All these are the fetters currently arising from the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
From these fetters, further fetters arise; they become increasingly dominant, increasingly intense, and increasingly complete.
The fetters that arise first are called craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
those that arise subsequently are termed grasping (*upādāna*). This is what is meant by "craving conditions grasping.
Furthermore, one may harbor doubt regarding the Blessed One, wondering: "Is he a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, or is he not?"
"Is he the Teacher of gods and humans, or is he not?
Regarding the Buddha’s true Dharma, they give rise to doubt: is it well-expounded and directly perceivable, or is it not well-expounded and directly perceivable?"
Is this something realized internally by the wise, or is it something realized internally by those who are not wise?
Regarding the disciples of the Buddha, one gives rise to doubt: do they possess perfect conduct, or do they not possess perfect conduct?
Is this one who practices in accordance with the Dharma, or one who does not practice in accordance with the Dharma?
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, they give rise to doubt: "Is this suffering, or is it not suffering?"
...up to the point of wondering whether this is the path or not the path;

they give rise to doubt regarding the three seals of the Dharma, wondering whether all conditioned phenomena are impermanent or whether it is not the case that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
Is it that all phenomena are without self, or is it that not all phenomena are without self?
Is it that nirvana is quiescent, or is it that nirvana is not quiescent?
These are all the fetters arising from present doubt.
From these fetters (*paryavasthāna*), he further gives rise to other fetters; they become increasingly predominant, increasingly intense, and increasingly complete.
The fetters previously arisen are called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*);
the fetters subsequently arisen are termed "grasping" (*upādāna*). This is what is meant by "with craving as condition, grasping arises."
Furthermore, all four types of clinging have craving as their condition, have craving as their origin, belong to the category of craving, and arise from craving.
What are these four types of clinging?
1. Grasping at sensual desires;
2. Grasping at views;
3. Grasping at rules and observances.
4. Clinging to the doctrine of self (ātmavādopādāna).
What is clinging to sensual desire (kāma-upādāna)?

It refers to those fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and obsessions associated with the realm of desire, excluding the various views; this is called clinging to sensual desire.
What is the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)?
It refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and the grasping of views itself.
These four views are called the grasping of views.
What is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?

It refers to a certain class of persons who cling to rules, cling to observances, and cling to both rules and observances, regarding them as capable of purification, capable of liberation, capable of transcendence, and capable of surpassing suffering and pleasure to reach the state beyond suffering and pleasure; this is called the clinging to rules and observances.
What is the clinging to the doctrine of self (ātmavādopādāna)?

It refers to the fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and entanglements associated with the realms of form and formlessness, excluding the various views; this is called the clinging to the doctrine of self.
Furthermore, in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Are the various types of clinging (*upādāna*) conditioned by existence (*bhava*)?
The Buddha replied:
“There is a condition; this condition is craving.
To speak at length, up until: if there were no craving whatsoever, could the various forms of grasping be conceived? “No, sir.”
“World-Honored One!
Therefore, Ānanda, all forms of grasping have craving as their condition; this is called ‘craving conditions grasping.’”

Thus, because these various types of grasping have craving as their condition, craving as their support, and craving as their foundation, they arise and co-arise, are born and co-born, and gather and appear; therefore, it is said that "grasping has craving as its condition."

What is existence conditioned by grasping? It means that with grasping as a condition, there is the designation of "existence" (bhava) in many ways. That is to say, the Buddha sometimes speaks of the five aggregates of the three realms as existence; sometimes he speaks of the karma capable of producing future existence as existence; and sometimes he speaks of the five aggregates of the birth-state as existence. How is it that the five aggregates of the three realms are called existence?
As it is said regarding the three realms of existence— namely, the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)—
why is karma that brings about future existence called "existence" (*bhava*)?
As the Blessed One told Ānanda:
If karma can induce existence in a future life,
why is it said that the five aggregates constituting birth are called "existence" (*bhava*)?
As the Blessed One told Potaliputra:
Because consciousness serves as nutriment, future existence arises.
Furthermore, in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Do all conditioned phenomena have a condition?"
The Buddha said:
"There is a condition; this condition is called clinging (*upādāna*).
To speak at length, even unto this: if there were no clinging whatsoever, could the various realms of existence (*bhava*) be conceptually established?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Therefore, Ānanda!"
"All forms of existence (bhava) have grasping (upādāna) as their condition; this is called 'existence conditioned by grasping'.

Thus, because all these forms of existence arise with grasping as their condition, with grasping as their support, and with grasping as their foundation, they emerge, arise, are produced, are generated, accumulate, and appear; therefore, it is called "existence conditioned by grasping."
What is birth conditioned by existence?
It refers to a certain class of beings who, because their minds are bound by the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion, perform the three types of unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind.
These three unwholesome conducts are called "existence as karma" (karmabhava).
Due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one falls into hell.

There, among those various births, one is born, enters, and appears; there is the acquisition of aggregates, the acquisition of elements, and the acquisition of bases; the arising of the aggregates, life, and the life-faculty is called "birth."
Because this birth arises conditioned by existence (*bhava*), it is called "birth conditioned by existence.
As it is said regarding the hells, one should know that the same applies to the animal realm and the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Furthermore, there is another class [of beings] who fix their minds upon the pleasures of the human realm and long for them, thinking:
"May I be born into the human realm with a similar lot, and experience happiness together with all other people.
Out of this aspiration, one performs wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind that are capable of inducing birth in the human realm.
These three types of sublime conduct are called karmic existence (*karmabhava*).

By reason of this cause and condition, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is born into the common lot of the human realm; the arising therein of birth, rebirth, and so forth, up to the emergence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), is called birth (*jāti*).
Because this birth arises conditioned by existence (*bhava*), it is called "birth conditioned by existence" (*bhavapratyayā jātiḥ*).
As it is said regarding the human realm, one should know that the same applies to the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven.
Furthermore, there is another class who fix their minds on the desire realm of the Brahmakāyika devas, thinking:
"May I be reborn among the members of the Brahmakāyika host."

Thus, through this aspiration, he diligently applies himself to the practice; free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he dwells having fully attained the first dhyāna.
In this meditative absorption, the restraint of body, the restraint of speech, and the purity of livelihood are called "karmic existence" (*karmabhava*).

By reason of these causes and conditions, upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one is born into the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) of the Brahmakāyika devas; the arising therein of birth, rebirth, and so forth, up to the emergence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), is called "birth" (*jāti*).
Because this birth arises conditioned by existence, it is called "birth conditioned by existence.
As it is said regarding the Brahmakāyika devas, one should know that the same applies to the Brahmapurohita devas and up to the Bṛhatphala devas.
Furthermore, there is another class who fix their minds on the realm of non-perception and long for it, thinking:
"May I be born among the beings of the same category in the heaven of non-perception."

"Therefore, seeking this goal, one diligently applies effort and cultivation, contemplating that all perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are coarse, painful, and obstructive, while contemplating that non-perception (*asaṃjñā*) is peaceful, sublime, and liberating.
Through this contemplation, one is able to extinguish all perceptions and abide in non-perception."
When those various perceptions have ceased and one dwells in the state of non-perception, it is called the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
At the time of entering this attainment, the restraint of body, the restraint of speech, and the purity of livelihood are termed "karmic existence" (*karmabhava*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is reborn within the homogeneous class of the Heaven of Non-conception; the arising therein of all such births, including the emergence of the life-faculty, is called "birth."
Because this birth arises conditioned by existence, it is called "birth conditioned by existence.
Furthermore, there is another class who fixates their minds on the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space with longing, thinking:
"May I be born among the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space within their common lot."

Thus, through this aspiration, he diligently applies himself to the practice, transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and no longer attending to perceptions of diversity; he enters and dwells, fully possessing the sphere of infinite space, [thinking] "space is infinite."

Within this meditative absorption, all volitions (*cetanā*), equal volitions, present volitions, past volitions, future volitions, the nature of volition, the category of volition, and the mental and volitional karma produced by the mind—these are called "karmic existence" (*karmabhava*).

Due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is reborn within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the Sphere of Infinite Space; there, the arising of birth, and so forth, up to the arising of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), is called "birth" (*jāti*).
Because this birth arises conditioned by existence, it is called "birth conditioned by existence.
As it is said regarding the sphere of infinite space, one should know that the same applies up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Do all births have a condition?
The Buddha said:
“There is a condition; this condition is called existence (*bhava*).

To speak at length, even if there were no karmic existence (*karmabhava*), would those various sentient beings—fish, birds, snakes, scorpions, *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, *bhūtas*, *gandharvas*, gods, humans, and so forth; those with no feet, two feet, or many feet; those of diverse classes—be born, reborn, and so on, within their respective groups? Would they attain existence?”
"No, World-Honored One! If there were absolutely nothing at all,
could one conceptually designate the existence of various births?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Therefore, Ānanda!"
"All births take existence as their condition; this is called 'birth conditioned by existence' (*bhavapratyayā jātiḥ*).

Thus, because these various births have existence as their condition, existence as their support, and existence as their foundation, they arise, co-arise, are produced, are fully produced, are gathered, and appear; therefore, it is called "birth conditioned by existence."

What is birth as the condition for aging and death? It refers to the various beings, within their respective groups of beings, undergoing birth, being born, entering, and appearing; the acquisition of aggregates, the acquisition of elements, and the acquisition of bases; and the arising of the life-faculty of the aggregates—this is called birth.

The falling out of hair and its whitening, the slackening of skin and the wrinkling of the face, the curvature of the body and the stooping of the back, the increasing urgency of labored breathing, walking while leaning on a staff, the dark spots appearing on the limbs, the decline and dullness of the faculties, their maturation and deterioration, and the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are thus decayed, ruined, broken down, and weakened—this is called old age.

When any sentient being, within any such assembly of sentient beings, undergoes transition and dissolution, suffers decline and separation, and experiences the cessation of vitality, warmth, and consciousness; when the life-faculty ceases to function, the aggregates are destroyed, and one passes away, dies, and perishes—that is called death.
In this way, old age and death arise conditioned by birth; this is called "birth as the condition for old age and death.
Furthermore, in the *Mahānidāna Sūtra*, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Does old age and death have a condition?"
The Buddha said:
"There is a condition; this condition is called birth.

To speak at length, up to: if there were no birth, would the old age and death of those various sentient beings within their respective groups—the fish, birds, snakes, scorpions, nāgas, yakṣas, bhūtas, gandharvas, and other celestial beings, as well as those with no feet, two feet, or many feet—be possible?"
"No, World-Honored One! If there were no birth at all,
could aging and death be established as existing?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Therefore, Ānanda!"
Old age and death both take birth as their condition; this is called "birth as the condition for old age and death.

Thus, because old age and death have birth as their condition, birth as their support, and birth as their foundation, they arise, co-arise, are produced, are co-produced, accumulate, and manifest; therefore, it is called "birth as the condition for old age and death."
How do sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress arise?

It is said that there is a certain class of people who, due to the death of their parents, brothers, sisters, teachers, or friends; or due to the total extinction of their kinsmen; or due to the complete loss of wealth and status, give rise within themselves to intense, fierce, and harsh sensations that cut to the heart, snatch away life, and are painful and agonizing.

At that time, his mind becomes feverish, equally feverish, inwardly feverish, and thoroughly feverish; he gives rise to sorrow, has already sorrowed, and will continue to sorrow; this arrow of sorrow within the heart is called *daurmanasya* (sorrow).

Furthermore, there is another class of persons who, due to the death of parents, siblings, sisters, teachers, or friends, give rise within themselves to a fierce, harsh, and piercing mental state that seizes their life-force, resulting in agonizing and painful sensations.

At that time, his mind becomes feverish, equally feverish, inwardly feverish, and thoroughly feverish; he gives rise to sorrow—past sorrow, present sorrow, and future sorrow—and the arrow of sorrow pierces his heart.
For this reason, he utters a lamentation: "Alas! Alas!"
"My father! My mother!"—and so on, extensively, up to "my wealth! my status!"—how is it that all at once I have suddenly come to this?
All such words of lamentation and complaint, as well as various verbal actions, are termed "lamenting" (*parideva*).
Unequal feeling associated with the five consciousnesses is called suffering (*duḥkha*).
Unequal feeling associated with the mental consciousness is called grief (*daurmanasya*).

All mental disturbances—those that have been disturbed, those currently being disturbed, those that will be disturbed, the nature of disturbance, and the category of disturbance—are called affliction (*upāyāsa*).
At the stage of old age and death, there arise these various forms of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.
How is it that such a mass of pure great suffering thus accumulates?
It means that within this stage of old age and death, one accumulates a category of great calamities, great misfortunes, great afflictions, and a multitude of aggregates of suffering.
Furthermore, with the aggregate of suffering that is ignorance as condition, the aggregate of suffering that is volitional formations arises.
With the aggregate of suffering that is volitional formations as condition, the aggregate of suffering that is consciousness arises.
With the aggregate of suffering that is consciousness as condition, the aggregate of suffering that is name-and-form arises.
With the aggregate of suffering that is name-and-form as condition, the aggregate of suffering that is the six sense bases arises.
With the aggregate of suffering that is the six sense bases as condition, the aggregate of suffering that is contact arises.
With the aggregate of suffering that is contact as condition, the aggregate of suffering that is feeling arises.
Conditioned by the aggregate of suffering, the aggregate of craving arises.
Conditioned by the aggregate of craving, the aggregate of clinging arises.
Conditioned by the aggregate of clinging, the aggregate of existence arises.
With the mass of suffering as condition, the mass of suffering that is birth arises.
With the mass of suffering that is birth as condition, the mass of suffering that is aging-and-death arises.

Due to aging-and-death, various masses of suffering—namely, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—arise; therefore, it is said in summary: "In this way, there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering."

Postscript to the *Dharmaskandhapāda-śāstra*, Fascicle Twelve, composed by the Śramaṇa Jingmai. The *Dharmaskandhapāda-śāstra* is truly the inception of the Abhidharma and the great source of the Sarvāstivāda school.
This was composed by Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the foremost among those who have entered the chamber of the Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment.

Mirroring the wondrous wisdom of the six supernatural powers and illuminating the brilliance of the three types of omniscience, he struck the golden drum throughout the great trichiliocosm and blew the jade conch across ten billion worlds. He gathered the rare treasures from the ocean of the *piṭakas* and assembled the exquisite jewels from the mountain of the teachings. Desiring that the celestial mirror be ever suspended and the banner of the Dharma eternally planted, so that the various heterodoxies might cease their thorny growth and all disciples might enjoy the delight of playful sport, he wrote this treatise.

Thus, more than one hundred years after the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, the distinctions of the five divisions (*pañca-nikāya*) were successively revealed, and the differences between the eighteen schools (*aṣṭādaśa-nikāya*) were elucidated. Although each school possessed the noble value of a "linked city" (*liánchéng*) and was praised as a rare treasure that "illuminates a carriage" (*zhào chéng*), it is only the Sarvāstivāda school that stands preeminent and far surpasses all others—like Mount Sumeru rising from the vast ocean, or like the bright moon crowning the multitude of stars—is it not because its foundation is broad and its basis eternal?

As for those such as the eight sections of the *Khandakas*, which spread their excellence upon the field of the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna*, and the five hundred Arhats, who gained renown in the garden of the *Vibhaṅga*—all of them drew from these droplets of water and shared in fragments of this jade; thus they were able to ride upon the various schools with lofty strides and set foot upon the celestial highway.
Thus we know that one who ascends Mount Kunlun will surely regard all other mountains as mere mounds;
one who roams the vast ocean will likewise regard all other streams as mere puddles.
This is indeed the case!

How much more so when one analyzes doubts by following correct principles and dispels delusions by manifesting the true doctrine; there is nothing that does not reflect these constant human relations and mirror this Great Canon. Thus, it was made possible for the venerable Vasiṣṭha to humble our many worthies, such that those who sit at the head of the profound school find themselves surpassed in their grand aspirations.
The title "Abhidharma" distinguishes it as exceptional by contrasting it with the other two Piṭakas.
"Sarvāstivāda" designates its distinctiveness in relation to the seventeen [other schools].
The *Dharmaskandha-pāda* (The Section on the Aggregates of Dharma) reveals the preeminent title of this treatise.

It is called "dharma" because it maintains its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and serves as a model (*vidhi*), thus conforming to the meaning of "dharma. Because dharmas are accumulated and gathered together, they are termed "skandhas" (aggregates).
The core doctrine of this treatise consists of the three groups of seven categories of phenomena, all of which rely upon the Abhidharma; therefore, they are designated as its "feet.

The Tripitaka Master Xuanzang completed the translation by imperial decree at the Hongfa Garden of the Great Ci'en Monastery on the fourteenth day of the ninth month in the fourth year of the Xianqing era of the Great Tang.
